a.w: Migraine with aura also rules out the combined pill.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud checked Rasha's BMI before choosing her contraception.
a.x: Her BMI was off topic when choosing a pill for contraception.
a.w: A high BMI raises clot risk.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud asked Rasha about the blood clot her mother once had.
a.x: Her mother's clot was off topic for her own choice of pill.
a.w: A clot in a close relative raises her own risk.

t: Wilson disease missed in a young man
s:
Mr. Adel, 19, came with a shaky hand and trouble writing. His liver tests were raised for a year. His mood had changed and he had dropped out of university. His brother died of liver failure at 16.

Dr. Mervat examined him and found a tremor in both hands and slurred speech. She asked about drugs and alcohol, and he took none.

She checked his hepatitis tests, which were negative, and arranged a liver ultrasound.

His parents are cousins. He had been a top student but his grades had fallen, and he had become irritable at home. His mother said he dropped cups and his writing had become messy. His blood count showed mild anemia, and his urine had protein in it.

She said the tremor was "anxiety" and prescribed propranolol. She did not check caeruloplasmin or look at his eyes for copper rings.
h: She said the tremor was "anxiety" and prescribed propranolol

a.o: Dr. Mervat called Mr. Adel's tremor anxiety without testing for Wilson.
a.x: He needed caeruloplasmin, urine copper and an eye check.
a.w: A young man with liver disease, tremor, mood change and a brother who died of liver failure points to Wilson disease.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked Mr. Adel about his use of drugs and alcohol.
a.x: Asking about drugs and alcohol was unnecessary for his tremor.
a.w: Drugs and alcohol can cause tremor and liver disease.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mr. Adel's hepatitis tests given his abnormal liver tests.
a.x: Hepatitis tests were off topic for a young man with a tremor.
a.w: Viral hepatitis is a common cause of raised liver tests.

a.o: Dr. Mervat noted that Mr. Adel's parents were first cousins.
a.x: Asking whether his parents were related was rude to ask.
a.w: Recessive conditions like Wilson disease are more common when parents are related.

s:
Ziad, 13, came to clinic with his mother. His father had bowel cancer at 36 and was found to have familial adenomatous polyposis, a gene change that causes hundreds of polyps in the bowel. Ziad has no symptoms and plays football for his school.

Dr. Tamer explained the condition carefully, using a drawing of the bowel, and checked that Ziad understood. He asked Ziad whether he wanted to be tested, and Ziad said yes after talking with his mother.

The blood test showed Ziad carries the same APC gene change. Dr. Tamer told them about the genetics nurse and gave them a support group number. Ziad's mother asked about his younger sister, aged 9, and he offered testing for her when the family was ready.

Ziad asked whether he would get cancer like his father. Dr. Tamer said the risk was high but could be managed with regular checks.

He booked Ziad's first colonoscopy for when he turns 50, "like the national screening program".
h: He booked Ziad's first colonoscopy for when he turns 50

a.o: Dr. Tamer left Ziad's first bowel camera check until he turned fifty.
a.x: Ziad needed a colonoscopy every year or two from age 12 to 14.
a.w: In FAP, polyps start in the teens and cancer is almost certain by 40 without surgery.

a.o: Dr. Tamer offered Ziad a genetic test at 13, the age checks would begin.
a.x: Children should never have genetic tests until they are adults.
a.w: FAP testing is offered in childhood because checks start in the early teens.

a.o: Dr. Tamer asked Ziad himself whether he wanted to have the genetic test.
a.x: Only his mother needed to agree to the test on Ziad's behalf.
a.w: Involving the child in the decision is good practice.

a.o: Dr. Tamer offered testing for Ziad's sister when the family was ready.
a.x: His sister was not at any risk of the same bowel condition.
a.w: Each child of a parent with FAP has a 1 in 2 chance.

s:
Hana, 4, has many coffee-colored patches on her skin and freckles in her armpits. Her father has neurofibromatosis type 1, with soft lumps on his skin. Hana was diagnosed with NF1 last year and is otherwise well. She is learning her letters at nursery.

Dr. Nada measured her head, height and blood pressure, which were normal, and plotted them on her growth chart. She examined her spine for any curve, and it was straight.

She asked about Hana's learning and behavior, as children with NF1 can have learning problems, and asked the nursery for a report.

Her father asked whether she would get lumps like his. Dr. Nada said they usually appear in the teenage years and are mostly harmless.

She booked a review in two years and said Hana did not need eye checks "because she can see well".
h: said Hana did not need eye checks "because she can see well"

a.o: Dr. Nada skipped the yearly eye checks for Hana with neurofibromatosis.
a.x: Hana needed a yearly eye doctor exam until at least age 8 too.
a.w: Children with NF1 can grow a tumor on the optic nerve, which often shows no signs until vision is damaged.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked Hana's blood pressure as part of her yearly review.
a.x: Blood pressure is not checked in children as small as Hana.
a.w: NF1 can cause high blood pressure from narrowed kidney arteries.

a.o: Dr. Nada examined Hana's spine for any curve as part of the review.
a.x: Her back and spine were off topic for a child with skin marks.
a.w: Scoliosis is common in NF1.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked the nursery for a report on how Hana was learning.
a.x: Reports from the nursery about learning are not a doctor's job.
a.w: Learning difficulties are common in NF1 and help comes early.

t: High INR with warfarin carried on
s:
Mr. Fikry, 74, takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. His routine INR came back at 8.4; his target is 2 to 3. He had started a course of clarithromycin for a chest infection five days ago. He had no bleeding, no black stools and no blood in his urine.

Dr. Ghada phoned him to ask about bruising and nosebleeds, and he had none. She asked whether he had fallen recently or hit his head, and he had not.

She stopped the clarithromycin, as his chest was better, and noted to avoid it with warfarin in future. She told him to watch for bleeding and gave him the number of the anticoagulation clinic.

He asked whether he should stop his evening walk because of the bruising risk. She said walking was good for him and he should carry on, taking care on uneven ground.

She told him to carry on with his usual warfarin dose and to recheck his INR in two weeks.
h: She told him to carry on with his usual warfarin dose and to recheck his INR in two weeks

a.o: Dr. Ghada left Mr. Fikry on the same warfarin dose with an INR of 8.4.
a.x: He needed warfarin held, oral vitamin K and a recheck soon.
a.w: An INR above 8 carries a high bleeding risk, even without bleeding. Oral vitamin K brings it down safely.

a.o: Dr. Ghada stopped the clarithromycin Mr. Fikry had been given for his chest.
a.x: The antibiotic course should have been finished as prescribed.
a.w: Clarithromycin raises the INR, and his chest had already improved.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mr. Fikry about any falls or knocks to his head.
a.x: Falls and knocks to his head were off topic for a high INR.
a.w: A head injury with a high INR could cause a hidden brain bleed.

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mr. Fikry to keep up his gentle evening walks.
a.x: He should have stayed at home until his INR had settled down.
a.w: Staying active is good, and he had no bleeding.

t: Warfarin bleed treated with vitamin K alone
s:
Mrs. Nawal, 79, takes warfarin for a metal heart valve. She fell at home and came in drowsy, with a headache and vomiting. Her CT scan showed a bleed inside the skull. Her INR was 3.8 and her blood pressure 172/96.

Dr. Hamed stopped her warfarin and gave 10 mg of IV vitamin K. He called the neurosurgeons, who agreed to see her, and asked for her to be nursed with her head raised.

He brought her blood pressure down carefully with an IV drip, aiming for a top number of about 140. He checked her blood sugar and her platelets, which were normal.

Her son was worried about her metal valve and asked whether stopping the warfarin was safe. Dr. Hamed explained that the bleed was the bigger danger for now.

He said the vitamin K would "bring the INR down by morning", and did not give any other clotting treatment.
h: He said the vitamin K would "bring the INR down by morning", and did not give any other clotting treatment

a.o: Dr. Hamed relied on vitamin K alone for Mrs. Nawal's brain bleed.
a.x: She also needed prothrombin complex concentrate given fast.
a.w: IV vitamin K takes hours to work. In a brain bleed, every minute of bleeding matters.

a.o: Dr. Hamed stopped warfarin for now despite Mrs. Nawal's metal heart valve.
a.x: A metal valve means warfarin must never be stopped at all.
a.w: In a life-threatening bleed, the bleed comes first; the valve risk over a few days is lower.

a.o: Dr. Hamed brought down Mrs. Nawal's very high blood pressure with a drip.
a.x: Lowering her blood pressure would starve the brain of blood.
a.w: Careful lowering helps stop the bleed growing.

a.o: Dr. Hamed checked Mrs. Nawal's platelet count along with her clotting.
a.x: Her platelet count was off topic for a bleed on warfarin.
a.w: Low platelets would add to the bleeding.

s:
Omar, 19, has sickle cell disease. He came in with severe pain in his back and legs, which started after a cold swim. He rated it 9 out of 10. His temperature was 37.6°C and his oxygen 97% on air. His chest was clear.

Dr. Dina saw him within 20 minutes. She checked his blood count, which showed his usual hemoglobin of 8.4, and his reticulocytes, which were high. She asked how much pain relief he usually needed in a crisis.

She started IV fluids, kept him warm and asked the nurses to check his pain, breathing and oxygen every half hour. She gave him a breathing exerciser to use every hour.

He asked to be treated quickly because he knew this pain. She believed him and did not make him wait for blood results.

For the pain she gave him pethidine 100 mg by injection every three hours, writing "he asked for something strong".
h: For the pain she gave him pethidine 100 mg by injection every three hours

a.o: Dr. Dina used pethidine to control the pain of Omar's sickle crisis.
a.x: Omar needed morphine, often by a pump he controls himself.
a.w: Pethidine builds up a toxic product that can cause fits, and is avoided in sickle cell pain.

a.o: Dr. Dina gave Omar a breathing exerciser to use every hour while awake.
a.x: A breathing exerciser was unnecessary with a clear chest.
a.w: Deep breathing helps prevent acute chest syndrome in a crisis.

a.o: Dr. Dina gave Omar pain relief before his blood results came back.
a.x: She should have waited for the results before any pain relief.
a.w: Pain relief in a crisis should come within 30 minutes.

a.o: Dr. Dina kept Omar warm with blankets during his stay in the department.
a.x: Keeping him warm only makes the sickling of his cells worse.
a.w: Cold triggers crises; keeping warm helps.

t: Acute chest syndrome missed in sickle cell
s:
Laila, 16, has sickle cell disease and was admitted two days ago with pain in her ribs and back. Today she had a new cough, a temperature of 38.4°C and fast breathing. Her oxygen had fallen from 98% to 91% on air. She had crackles at the right base.

Dr. Fouad checked her blood count, which showed her hemoglobin had dropped from 8 to 6.6. He sent blood cultures and asked for her to be weighed and her fluids charted.

He increased her pain relief, as her rib pain was making it hard to breathe deeply, and asked the physiotherapist to help with breathing exercises.

Her mother was worried and asked whether her daughter had a chest infection. He said it was likely, and that it was common.

He started oral amoxicillin, gave her oxygen by mask, and did not order a chest X-ray or call the hematology team, writing "probable mild chest infection".
h: did not order a chest X-ray or call the hematology team

a.o: Dr. Fouad treated Laila's new chest signs as a mild chest infection.
a.x: Laila needed an X-ray, IV antibiotics and urgent hematology.
a.w: Fever, low oxygen and a new chest finding in sickle cell disease mean acute chest syndrome, the most common cause of death.

a.o: Dr. Fouad increased Laila's pain relief so she could breathe in deeply.
a.x: Strong painkillers slow her breathing and should have been cut.
a.w: Rib pain stops deep breathing, so good pain relief helps the lungs.

a.o: Dr. Fouad asked the nurses to chart all of the fluids Laila took in.
a.x: Fluid charts were not needed for a girl who was able to drink.
a.w: Too much or too little fluid can worsen sickle cell chest problems.

a.o: Dr. Fouad sent blood cultures from Laila before starting antibiotics.
a.x: Blood cultures were pointless for a girl with a sickle crisis.
a.w: Infection is a common trigger.

t: B12 deficiency treated with folic acid
s:
Mrs. Samia, 66, came in with tiredness and tingling in both feet for three months. She had become a little unsteady when walking in the dark. Her blood count showed large red cells and a hemoglobin of 9.8. Her B12 was very low and her folate low.

Dr. Ihab asked about her diet, which was normal, and about stomach operations, which she had never had. He sent a test for antibodies to intrinsic factor, which came back positive.

He explained that she had pernicious anemia, where the body cannot absorb B12 from food. She asked whether she needed to stop eating meat, and he said no.

He checked her thyroid, which was normal, as the two conditions often go together.

He started folic acid tablets and planned to start B12 injections "once her folate is back up".
h: He started folic acid tablets and planned to start B12 injections "once her folate is back up"

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave Mrs. Samia folic acid before her B12 had been replaced.
a.x: She needed B12 injections at once, then folic acid after that.
a.w: Folic acid alone can make the B12 nerve damage worse and lead to permanent damage to the spinal cord.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mrs. Samia's thyroid as she was tired and had low B12.
a.x: Her thyroid was off topic for a woman with a low B12 level.
a.w: Autoimmune thyroid disease often comes with pernicious anemia.

a.o: Dr. Ihab tested Mrs. Samia for intrinsic factor antibodies.
a.x: That antibody test was unnecessary for a woman with low B12.
a.w: It confirms pernicious anemia and means lifelong injections.

a.o: Dr. Ihab told Mrs. Samia she could keep eating meat as part of her diet.
a.x: She should eat only vegetables while her B12 is being replaced.
a.w: Her problem is absorbing B12, not her diet.

s:
Mr. Raouf, 71, was in hospital after a hip operation. His hemoglobin was 6.9, and he felt dizzy and short of breath. Dr. Hala decided he needed one unit of blood, explained why, and he agreed.

She checked that his group and save sample was valid and prescribed one unit to run over three hours. She checked his kidney function and noted he had a weak heart, so she added a small dose of furosemide.

She asked the nurses to check his temperature, pulse and blood pressure before the blood, after 15 minutes and at the end.

The ward was very busy. The blood arrived while Mr. Raouf was asleep in a bay with another patient of the same surname.

To avoid waking him, Dr. Hala hung the unit after checking the bag against the notes at the desk, without checking his wristband at the bedside.
h: without checking his wristband at the bedside

a.o: Dr. Hala hung blood without checking Mr. Raouf's wristband at the bed.
a.x: The bag needed checking against his wristband at the bedside.
a.w: Most wrong-blood errors happen at the bedside. With two patients of the same surname, the risk was even higher.

a.o: Dr. Hala gave Mr. Raouf a dose of furosemide along with the unit of blood.
a.x: Giving a diuretic with blood is dangerous for a man of his age.
a.w: In a weak heart, a diuretic can help prevent fluid overload.

a.o: Dr. Hala ran each unit of blood for Mr. Raouf over three hours.
a.x: Each unit of blood should be given in about thirty minutes.
a.w: A slower rate is safer for a weak heart.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked the nurses to check Mr. Raouf's observations at 15 minutes.
a.x: Checks at the very end of the transfusion would have been enough.
a.w: Serious reactions often start in the first 15 minutes.

t: Transfusion reaction treated by slowing the blood
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 58, was having a unit of blood for anemia after chemotherapy. Twenty minutes in, she said her back hurt and felt hot and anxious. Her temperature was 39°C, her pulse 124 and her blood pressure had fallen from 128/76 to 88/50. Her urine in the catheter bag looked dark.

Dr. Ayman came at once. He checked her airway and breathing, which were fine, and listened to her chest, which was clear.

He gave paracetamol for the fever and started IV fluids. He asked the nurse to keep a close watch and to call him if she got worse.

Her husband was frightened and asked if she was allergic to the blood. Dr. Ayman said reactions do happen and that she was in good hands.

He slowed the transfusion to half the rate and let the unit finish, saying "she really needs the blood".
h: He slowed the transfusion to half the rate and let the unit finish

a.o: Dr. Ayman let Mrs. Nadia's blood keep running during a serious reaction.
a.x: The blood should have stopped at once, with her identity checked.
a.w: Fever, back pain, low blood pressure and dark urine suggest an acute hemolytic reaction, often from the wrong blood. Every extra drop makes it worse.

a.o: Dr. Ayman started IV fluids for Mrs. Nadia when her blood pressure fell.
a.x: IV fluids were not needed for a reaction to a blood transfusion.
a.w: Fluids support blood pressure and protect the kidneys.

a.o: Dr. Ayman listened to Mrs. Nadia's chest while she was having the reaction.
a.x: Her chest was off topic for a reaction to a blood transfusion.
a.w: Fluid overload and lung injury can also follow a transfusion.

a.o: Dr. Ayman came to the ward to see Mrs. Nadia as soon as he was called.
a.x: A phone call to the nurse would have been enough at that point.
a.w: A sick patient with a reaction needs a doctor at the bedside.

s:
Mr. Medhat, 52, had chemotherapy for lymphoma eight days ago. He came in with a temperature of 38.6°C and shivering. His pulse was 112 and his blood pressure 104/66. He had no cough, and his urine was clear. He has a central line in his chest.

Dr. Rasha took blood cultures from his line and from his arm, and sent his blood count and kidney tests. She started IV fluids and asked the nurses to keep him in a side room.

She checked his line site, which looked clean, and asked about mouth ulcers and diarrhea, which he did not have.

His wife said the chemotherapy nurses had told them to come straight in with any fever. She was glad they had.

She decided to wait for his blood count before starting antibiotics, writing "may not be neutropenic". The count came back two hours later.
h: She decided to wait for his blood count before starting antibiotics

a.o: Dr. Rasha held back Mr. Medhat's antibiotics until his count came back.
a.x: He needed IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour.
a.w: A fever after chemotherapy is treated as neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise. Delays raise the risk of death.

a.o: Dr. Rasha took blood cultures from both Mr. Medhat's line and his arm.
a.x: One blood culture from either place would have been enough.
a.w: Comparing both helps tell if the line is infected.

a.o: Dr. Rasha kept Mr. Medhat in a side room away from other patients.
a.x: A side room was unnecessary for a man with a high temperature.
a.w: Protecting a patient who may have low white cells is good practice.

a.o: Dr. Rasha asked Mr. Medhat about any mouth ulcers or diarrhea since chemo.
a.x: Mouth ulcers and diarrhea were off topic for a man with a fever.
a.w: They are common sources of infection after chemotherapy.

t: Bleeding on dabigatran given vitamin K
s:
Mr. Labib, 78, takes dabigatran for atrial fibrillation. He fell and hit his head an hour ago. His CT scan shows a bleed on the brain. His last dose was four hours ago. His kidney function is moderately reduced.

Dr. Karim checked his GCS, which was 14, and called the brain surgeons. He kept his blood pressure below 160.

He checked his blood count and clotting tests, and stopped his dabigatran.

Mr. Labib's daughter said he had been confused this morning before the fall. The hospital pharmacy keeps the reversal drug, idarucizumab, in the ER.

The brain surgeons said they might need to operate within the hour if the bleed grew. Mr. Labib was becoming more drowsy, and his GCS dropped to 13 while they talked.

Dr. Karim gave him IV vitamin K to reverse the blood thinner and waited.
h: Dr. Karim gave him IV vitamin K to reverse the blood thinner and waited

a.o: Dr. Karim used vitamin K to reverse Mr. Labib's dabigatran in a bleed.
a.x: Mr. Labib needed idarucizumab right away to reverse the drug.
a.w: Vitamin K reverses warfarin only. Dabigatran has its own antidote, and a brain bleed needs it fast.

a.o: Dr. Karim brought down Mr. Labib's high blood pressure during the bleed.
a.x: His blood pressure did not matter while the bleed was going on.
a.w: High blood pressure can make the bleed grow.

a.o: Dr. Karim called the brain surgeons about Mr. Labib's bleed on the scan.
a.x: Calling the brain surgeons was too early before reversing it.
a.w: Surgeons may need to drain the bleed.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Mr. Labib's clotting tests as soon as he arrived.
a.x: His clotting tests were off topic for a bleed on dabigatran.
a.w: Tests help guide reversal.

t: Warfarin for a clot in pregnancy
s:
Mrs. Heba, 31, is 10 weeks pregnant. She came in with a swollen, painful left leg for three days. An ultrasound showed a clot in the vein behind her knee. She had no chest pain or breathlessness, and her oxygen was normal.

Dr. Sherine checked her blood count, kidney and liver tests, and her weight to work out the dose. She asked about any family history of clots, which there was none.

She explained that clots are more common in pregnancy and gave her compression advice and a leaflet. She asked the obstetric team to see her the next day.

Mrs. Heba asked whether the treatment would hurt the baby. Dr. Sherine said she would choose the safest one.

She started warfarin, aiming for an INR of 2 to 3, and booked her into the anticoagulation clinic.
h: She started warfarin, aiming for an INR of 2 to 3

a.o: Dr. Sherine started warfarin for Mrs. Heba's clot in early pregnancy.
a.x: She needed heparin injections through pregnancy and after.
a.w: Warfarin crosses the placenta and can cause birth defects, especially between 6 and 12 weeks, and bleeding in the baby.

a.o: Dr. Sherine weighed Mrs. Heba before working out her dose of treatment.
a.x: Her weight was off topic when choosing her clot treatment.
a.w: Heparin doses are worked out by weight.

a.o: Dr. Sherine asked Mrs. Heba about any blood clots in her family.
a.x: Family history of clots doesn't matter for her own treatment.
a.w: A family history can point to an inherited clotting problem.

a.o: Dr. Sherine asked the obstetric team to see Mrs. Heba about her care.
a.x: Obstetricians were not needed for a clot in early pregnancy.
a.w: The pregnancy and delivery need to be planned around her treatment.

t: ITP treated before a blood film
s:
Yara, 6, came in with bruises on her legs and tiny red spots on her chest that appeared over two days. She had a cold two weeks ago. She was otherwise well, with no bone pain, fever or tiredness. Her liver, spleen and glands were not enlarged.

Her platelets were 12, but her hemoglobin and white cells were normal. Dr. Rana asked about nosebleeds and blood in the urine, which she had not had.

She explained that the most likely cause was ITP, where the body attacks its own platelets after a virus, and that most children get better by themselves.

She told Yara's parents to avoid contact sports and ibuprofen for now, and gave them a card with the ward's number.

To bring the platelets up quickly, she started prednisolone that evening before a blood film was looked at.
h: she started prednisolone that evening before a blood film was looked at

a.o: Dr. Rana started steroids for Yara before her blood film was looked at.
a.x: Yara's blood film should have been checked by a specialist.
a.w: Steroids can hide leukemia, which can look like ITP, and delay the right diagnosis.

a.o: Dr. Rana told Yara's parents to avoid giving her any ibuprofen for now.
a.x: Ibuprofen is perfectly fine for children with a low platelet count.
a.w: NSAIDs affect platelets and raise bleeding risk.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked Yara's spleen and the glands in her neck and armpits.
a.x: Examining her spleen and glands was unnecessary for bruises.
a.w: Big glands or spleen point to leukemia, not ITP.

a.o: Dr. Rana told Yara's parents that most children get better by themselves.
a.x: ITP in children always needs treatment to make it go away.
a.w: Most childhood ITP settles within months.

s:
Mrs. Asmaa, 36, came in with confusion, a headache and purple spots on her legs. Her platelets were 14 and her hemoglobin 8.1, with broken red cells on the blood film. Her LDH was very high and her creatinine was mildly raised. She had a low fever.

Dr. Ahmed recognized the signs of TTP. He sent an ADAMTS13 test and called the hematologist, who agreed to start plasma exchange within hours.

He asked for a CT head because of her confusion, which was normal. He started steroids.

Her husband asked whether it was leukemia. Dr. Ahmed explained it was a different blood condition that could be treated.

While waiting for the line for plasma exchange, he gave her two units of platelets "to make the line safer".
h: he gave her two units of platelets "to make the line safer"

a.o: Dr. Ahmed gave a platelet transfusion to Mrs. Asmaa, who has TTP.
a.x: Platelets should be avoided unless the bleeding is deadly.
a.w: In TTP, platelets feed the clots that block small vessels in the brain and heart.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed started steroids for Mrs. Asmaa alongside her other treatment.
a.x: Steroids don't help TTP and should not have been started.
a.w: Steroids are part of standard treatment.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed asked for a CT scan of Mrs. Asmaa's head given her confusion.
a.x: The head scan was unnecessary for a woman with low platelets.
a.w: Confusion can mean a bleed or stroke.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed called the hematologist about Mrs. Asmaa as soon as he could.
a.x: The hematologist could have seen her the next morning instead.
a.w: TTP is an emergency, and plasma exchange is urgent.

t: Hemophilia boy sent home after a head bump
s:
Adam, 8, has severe hemophilia A. He hit his head on a door frame at home two hours ago. He cried but did not pass out. He now had a small bump on his forehead and was playing with his tablet. He had no vomiting or headache.

Dr. Hamed examined him and found no other injuries. His neurological examination was normal, and he was alert and chatty.

He asked his mother about his usual factor VIII and when he last had it; it was three days ago. She had his treatment card with her.

He explained the signs of a brain bleed to his mother: vomiting, headache, drowsiness or a fit.

He sent Adam home with a head injury leaflet, without giving any factor VIII or arranging a scan, because "he looks well".
h: He sent Adam home with a head injury leaflet, without giving any factor VIII or arranging a scan

a.o: Dr. Hamed sent Adam home after a head injury without giving factor VIII.
a.x: Adam needed factor VIII at once, then a CT of his head.
a.w: In severe hemophilia, even a small bump can cause a brain bleed that shows up hours later.

a.o: Dr. Hamed explained the warning signs of a brain bleed to Adam's mother.
a.x: Explaining the warning signs was too frightening for the mother.
a.w: Parents need to know warning signs.

a.o: Dr. Hamed asked when Adam had last had a dose of his factor VIII.
a.x: The timing of his last dose was off topic after a bump to the head.
a.w: The time since the last dose shows his level of protection.

a.o: Dr. Hamed looked at Adam's hemophilia treatment card in the department.
a.x: The treatment card was unnecessary for a simple bump to the head.
a.w: The card gives his dose and plan.

s:
Mr. Samy, 58, came in with headaches, itching after hot showers and a red face. His hemoglobin was 196 and his hematocrit 0.58. He has a JAK2 gene change. He does not smoke and his oxygen is normal.

Dr. Nermine examined him and found a big spleen. She asked about clots and he had none. She checked his blood pressure, which was 152/90, and started treatment for it.

She started low-dose aspirin and told him to drink plenty of water. She advised him to stay active and to report any chest pain or leg swelling.

His wife asked if it was cancer. Dr. Nermine explained it was a slow blood condition that could be managed.

She did not arrange venesection, writing "aspirin will thin the blood".
h: She did not arrange venesection, writing "aspirin will thin the blood"

a.o: Dr. Nermine relied on aspirin alone for Mr. Samy's polycythemia vera.
a.x: Mr. Samy needed regular venesection to bring his hematocrit down.
a.w: A high hematocrit raises the risk of stroke and heart attack. Aspirin does not lower the red cell count.

a.o: Dr. Nermine treated Mr. Samy's high blood pressure as part of his care.
a.x: Blood pressure is off topic for a man with too many red cells.
a.w: High blood pressure adds to clot risk.

a.o: Dr. Nermine asked Mr. Samy about any past blood clots or strokes.
a.x: Past clots were off topic for a man with too many red cells.
a.w: Polycythemia causes clots.

a.o: Dr. Nermine told Mr. Samy to drink plenty of water through the day.
a.x: Drinking more water makes his thick blood even worse.
a.w: Dehydration thickens the blood more.

s:
Mr. Karim, 28, had his spleen removed after a car crash two days ago. He was recovering well, eating and walking. His blood count showed high platelets, which can happen after the spleen is taken out.

Dr. Abeer checked his wound and his pain, and stopped his drip. She asked the physiotherapist to help him walk more.

She gave him blood-thinning injections while he was in hospital. She talked to him about returning to work and avoiding heavy lifting for six weeks.

He asked whether he would miss his spleen. She said he could live a normal life without it.

She sent him home without vaccines or antibiotics, telling him "the spleen isn't vital".
h: She sent him home without vaccines or antibiotics

a.o: Dr. Abeer sent Mr. Karim home after splenectomy without vaccines.
a.x: He needed vaccines, daily antibiotics and an alert card.
a.w: Without a spleen, infections can be overwhelming and fatal within hours.

a.o: Dr. Abeer gave Mr. Karim blood-thinning injections after his operation.
a.x: Blood-thinning injections were dangerous after his surgery.
a.w: They prevent clots, especially with high platelets.

a.o: Dr. Abeer advised Mr. Karim against heavy lifting while his wound healed.
a.x: Heavy lifting was fine for him straight after the operation.
a.w: Heavy lifting can strain a healing wound.

a.o: Dr. Abeer told Mr. Karim that he could live a normal life without a spleen.
a.x: Saying that was only false comfort after losing his spleen.
a.w: People live normal lives without a spleen with proper protection.

s:
Mrs. Rana, 26, came for a check before planning a pregnancy. Her hemoglobin was 112, with very small red cells. Her ferritin was normal. She was not tired and had no heavy periods. Her family is from Cyprus.

Dr. Mahmoud asked about her diet and periods. He checked her folate and started folic acid for the planned pregnancy.

He asked about her husband's health and family. She said they are not related.

She asked whether she could have another test to know more. He said the blood count was enough.

She works as a nursery teacher and eats meat most days. She had been told at school that she was 'a bit anemic' and had taken iron on and off since then without any change in her blood count. Her husband's family is also from the Mediterranean.

He told her she had iron deficiency and started iron tablets for three months, without ordering a hemoglobin electrophoresis.
h: He told her she had iron deficiency and started iron tablets for three months

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud gave iron to Mrs. Rana, whose ferritin was normal.
a.x: She needed tests for thalassemia trait, and her husband too.
a.w: Small red cells with normal iron points to thalassemia trait. Iron won't help and can build up; if both partners carry it, the baby could have thalassemia major.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud started Mrs. Rana on folic acid as she plans a pregnancy.
a.x: Folic acid was unnecessary for a woman with small red cells.
a.w: Folic acid before pregnancy prevents spine defects.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud asked Mrs. Rana about her husband and his family's health.
a.x: Her husband was off topic for her own small red blood cells.
a.w: Both partners matter for inherited blood disorders.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud asked Mrs. Rana how heavy her periods were each month.
a.x: Her periods were off topic for a woman with small red cells.
a.w: Heavy periods are a common cause of low iron.

s:
Mr. Ali, 23, was diagnosed with Burkitt lymphoma, a fast-growing cancer. He has a large mass in his belly. His white count was 42, his uric acid high and his potassium at the top of normal. His kidney function was slightly raised.

Dr. Rehab explained the treatment and checked his heart and lungs. She asked for a heart tracing, which was normal, and a line for chemotherapy.

She asked about fertility and offered sperm banking before treatment, and he agreed.

He asked if the chemotherapy would make him lose his hair. She said yes, but it would grow back.

She started chemotherapy that evening with normal fluids, without extra IV fluids, allopurinol or rasburicase.
h: She started chemotherapy that evening with normal fluids, without extra IV fluids, allopurinol or rasburicase

a.o: Dr. Rehab started Mr. Ali's chemotherapy without preventing tumor lysis.
a.x: He needed fast IV fluids and rasburicase before chemotherapy.
a.w: A fast-growing tumor that breaks down quickly floods the blood with potassium, phosphate and uric acid, which can cause kidney failure and heart arrest.

a.o: Dr. Rehab offered Mr. Ali sperm banking before his chemotherapy began.
a.x: Sperm banking was off topic before treating his blood cancer.
a.w: Chemotherapy can cause infertility.

a.o: Dr. Rehab asked for a heart tracing for Mr. Ali before his chemotherapy.
a.x: A heart tracing was unnecessary for a young man before chemo.
a.w: A tracing shows the effect of high potassium.

a.o: Dr. Rehab told Mr. Ali that his hair would grow back after treatment.
a.x: Saying that was only false comfort for a young man on chemo.
a.w: Hair loss from chemotherapy is usually temporary.

t: Massive bleed given only red cells
s:
Mr. Sabri, 34, was brought in after a motorbike crash. He had a broken pelvis and was bleeding heavily. His blood pressure was 78/40 and his pulse 140. The team activated the major hemorrhage protocol.

Dr. Inas gave tranexamic acid within an hour of the injury, and the team put a pelvic binder on. She kept him warm with blankets and a warming device for the fluids.

She called the surgeons and the radiologists, who prepared to stop the bleeding.

Mr. Sabri's brother arrived and asked if he would live. She said the team was doing everything possible.

Over an hour she gave him eight units of red cells and no plasma, platelets or cryoprecipitate, saying "the red cells are what he needs".
h: Over an hour she gave him eight units of red cells and no plasma, platelets or cryoprecipitate

a.o: Dr. Inas gave Mr. Sabri only packed red cells during his massive bleed.
a.x: He needed plasma and platelets alongside the red cells.
a.w: Red cells alone dilute the clotting factors and cause more bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Inas gave Mr. Sabri tranexamic acid early in his massive bleed.
a.x: Tranexamic acid causes clots and should have been avoided here.
a.w: Tranexamic acid within three hours reduces death in bleeding trauma.

a.o: Dr. Inas kept Mr. Sabri warm with blankets and warmed fluids and blood.
a.x: Warming him up was unnecessary while the blood was being given.
a.w: Cold makes clotting worse.

a.o: Dr. Inas put a pelvic binder around Mr. Sabri's hips after his crash.
a.x: The pelvic binder was unnecessary for a man bleeding this way.
a.w: A binder reduces bleeding from a broken pelvis.

s:
Mr. Amr, 56, had a metal aortic valve put in last year. He takes warfarin, but he finds the INR checks tiring and his INR swings a lot. He came to ask about changing.

Dr. Hala checked his kidney function, which was normal, and his weight. She asked about bleeding, and he had none.

She looked at his INR record, which showed many low and high values. She asked about his diet and alcohol, which were steady.

He asked whether he could use a home INR machine instead. She said that was possible but she had a better plan.

She stopped his warfarin and switched him to apixaban 5 mg twice a day, saying "no more blood tests".
h: She stopped his warfarin and switched him to apixaban 5 mg twice a day

a.o: Dr. Hala switched Mr. Amr from warfarin to apixaban with a metal valve.
a.x: Mr. Amr should have stayed on warfarin, with INR support.
a.w: Newer blood thinners do not prevent clots on metal valves and can lead to valve clots and strokes.

a.o: Dr. Hala looked over Mr. Amr's INR record from the past few months.
a.x: His old INR record was off topic when changing his treatment.
a.w: The record shows how stable his treatment is.

a.o: Dr. Hala checked Mr. Amr's kidney function before changing his tablets.
a.x: His kidney function was off topic when changing his tablets.
a.w: Kidney function guides blood thinner choice.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked Mr. Amr about his diet and any recent changes in it.
a.x: His diet doesn't affect warfarin or his INR in any real way.
a.w: Changes in vitamin K in food change the INR.

t: Myeloma back pain with weak legs
s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 68, has multiple myeloma. She came in with back pain for two weeks that was worse at night. Today her legs felt weak and she had trouble passing urine. Her calcium was high.

Dr. Fady examined her and found weakness in both legs and reduced feeling below her belly button. Her back was tender in the middle.

He gave her IV fluids for the high calcium and pain relief. He asked for a bladder scan, which showed she was holding urine, and put in a catheter.

Her daughter asked whether the myeloma had spread. He said it was possible.

He booked an MRI of her spine for the next week and did not give any steroids.
h: He booked an MRI of her spine for the next week and did not give any steroids

a.o: Dr. Fady delayed the MRI and steroids for Mrs. Fawzia's weak legs.
a.x: She needed dexamethasone at once and a spine MRI within a day.
a.w: Back pain with weak legs and trouble passing urine in cancer means spinal cord compression. Delay can cause permanent paralysis.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Mrs. Fawzia IV fluids to bring her high calcium down.
a.x: IV fluids were not needed for a woman with a high calcium level.
a.w: Fluids are the first treatment for high calcium.

a.o: Dr. Fady put in a urinary catheter when Mrs. Fawzia could not pass urine.
a.x: The urinary catheter was unnecessary for a woman with back pain.
a.w: She was holding urine.

a.o: Dr. Fady examined Mrs. Fawzia's legs for power, feeling and reflexes.
a.x: Examining her legs was unnecessary for a woman with back pain.
a.w: Weak legs and reduced feeling show where the cord is pressed.

t: Low iron in an older man given tablets only
s:
Mr. Sami, 72, has been tired and breathless on walking for two months. He takes aspirin for his heart. He has no stomach pain and has not seen any blood in his stool.

Dr. Ihab checked his blood count, which showed a hemoglobin of 98 with small red cells. His ferritin was low. His B12 and folate were normal.

He asked about his diet, which was varied and included meat, and checked for celiac disease, which was negative.

Mr. Sami said his bowels had become looser over the last few months. He had lost a little weight but thought it was from walking more.

His father had bowel cancer in his seventies. Mr. Sami asked whether he could just eat more red meat instead of taking tablets. He had never had a bowel screening test.

Dr. Ihab started iron tablets and planned to recheck his blood count in three months, without referring him for a camera test.
h: started iron tablets and planned to recheck his blood count in three months, without referring him for a camera test

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave Mr. Sami iron tablets without looking for the cause.
a.x: Mr. Sami needed urgent camera tests of his stomach and bowel.
a.w: Iron deficiency in an older man means blood loss from the gut until proven otherwise, often bowel cancer.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Sami's blood for celiac disease as a cause of low iron.
a.x: Celiac disease was off topic for an older man with low iron.
a.w: Celiac disease can cause low iron.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mr. Sami about his diet and how much meat he usually eats.
a.x: Asking about his diet was unnecessary for a man with low iron.
a.w: A poor diet can cause low iron.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Sami's B12 and folate levels along with his iron.
a.x: His B12 and folate were off topic for a man with low iron.
a.w: Mixed deficiencies are common.

t: DVT treatment stopped after two weeks
s:
Mr. Hesham, 45, had a clot in his calf vein after a long flight. He was started on rivaroxaban three weeks ago. He has no other illness and his leg swelling has gone.

Dr. Ihab checked his kidney function, which was normal. He asked about bleeding, which he had not had, and about leg pain, which was better.

He advised him to walk regularly and wear compression stockings if they helped with comfort.

Mr. Hesham said he had another long flight in a month. He asked if he should take an aspirin.

He works as a sales manager and flies often for work. He had no injury, surgery or illness before the flight. His father had a clot in his fifties. He was taking the tablets every day and said he found them easy to remember.

He told him to stop the rivaroxaban, as "the leg is better now".
h: He told him to stop the rivaroxaban, as "the leg is better now"

a.o: Dr. Ihab stopped Mr. Hesham's rivaroxaban after just three weeks.
a.x: Mr. Hesham should have continued it for at least 3 months.
a.w: Stopping blood thinners early after a clot raises the risk of another clot.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Hesham's kidney function before choosing his dose.
a.x: His kidney function was off topic for a clot in the leg.
a.w: Rivaroxaban is cleared by the kidneys.

a.o: Dr. Ihab advised Mr. Hesham to keep walking as normal with his clot.
a.x: Walking makes the clot move up to his lungs and should stop.
a.w: Walking helps recovery after a clot.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mr. Hesham about any bleeding since starting his tablets.
a.x: Bleeding was off topic for a man taking tablets for a clot.
a.w: Bleeding is the main side effect of blood thinners.

t: B12 injections stopped when levels normal
s:
Mrs. Nabila, 72, has pernicious anemia and has had B12 injections every three months for two years. She came for a check. Her blood count and B12 level are now normal and she feels well.

Dr. Ghada checked her thyroid, which was normal, and her feet for feeling, which were fine.

She asked about her mood and memory, which were good. She talked to her about her diet.

Mrs. Nabila said she hated the injections. She asked if she could take tablets instead.

She lives with her husband and walks to the market every morning. Before her diagnosis she had felt pins and needles in her feet and was very tired. She also takes levothyroxine for an underactive thyroid. She said the practice nurse was always kind but the injection left a bruise.

Dr. Ghada stopped the injections, saying "your level is normal now, so you're cured".
h: Dr. Ghada stopped the injections, saying "your level is normal now, so you're cured"

a.o: Dr. Ghada stopped Mrs. Nabila's B12 injections once levels were normal.
a.x: She needed B12 injections every three months for life.
a.w: Pernicious anemia never goes away. The level is normal only because of the injections.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mrs. Nabila's feet for numbness and loss of feeling.
a.x: Her feet were off topic for a woman having B12 injections.
a.w: B12 deficiency can damage nerves in the feet.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mrs. Nabila's thyroid as part of her yearly review.
a.x: Her thyroid was off topic for a woman having B12 injections.
a.w: Thyroid disease often comes with pernicious anemia.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mrs. Nabila about any problems with her memory lately.
a.x: Her memory was off topic for a woman having B12 injections.
a.w: B12 deficiency can affect memory.

t: Sickle cell child taken off penicillin
s:
Malik, 3, has sickle cell disease and takes penicillin twice a day. His mother brought him for his yearly review. He had been well, with no crises this year and no hospital stays. He is growing well and loves his tricycle.

Dr. Rana checked his spleen, which she could not feel, and his blood count, which showed his usual hemoglobin of 8.2. She arranged his yearly brain artery scan (a transcranial Doppler), which was normal.

She checked that his vaccines were up to date, including the extra pneumococcal one, and advised his mother to give him plenty to drink and keep him warm in winter.

His mother said he hated the taste of the penicillin, spat it out and cried every time. His grandmother thought he no longer needed it because he was so well.

Dr. Rana agreed to stop the penicillin, writing "well, vaccinated, no infections", and booked a review in a year.
h: Dr. Rana agreed to stop the penicillin

a.o: Dr. Rana stopped Malik's daily penicillin when he reached the age of 3.
a.x: Malik needed penicillin until at least 5, and often for life.
a.w: Children with sickle cell disease have a spleen that does not work, so infections like pneumococcus can kill within hours. Vaccines alone are not enough.

a.o: Dr. Rana arranged a yearly scan of the arteries in Malik's brain.
a.x: The brain scan was unnecessary for a boy with no symptoms.
a.w: A yearly Doppler finds children at high risk of stroke before it happens.

a.o: Dr. Rana told Malik's mother to keep him warm and well wrapped in winter.
a.x: Keeping him warm doesn't matter for a child with sickle cell.
a.w: Cold can trigger a sickle crisis.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked that Malik had had the extra pneumococcal vaccine.
a.x: The normal childhood vaccines are enough for a boy like Malik.
a.w: Children with sickle cell need extra protection against pneumococcus.

s:
Youssef, 12, has beta thalassemia major. He has had a blood transfusion every four weeks since he was a baby. His hemoglobin before each transfusion is kept around 95. His ferritin has risen to 3,200 over the last year.

Dr. Nermine checked his growth, which was a little slow, and his puberty, which had not started. She asked the hormone team to see him and checked his thyroid and sugar.

She asked for a heart scan and a special MRI to measure iron in his heart and liver, and checked his hepatitis and HIV tests, which were negative.

His father said Youssef used to take a chelation medicine but stopped it a year ago because it upset his stomach. Youssef said he did not want any more tablets.

Dr. Nermine agreed to leave the chelation for now "so he can enjoy being a child", and continued his monthly transfusions.
h: Dr. Nermine agreed to leave the chelation for now

a.o: Dr. Nermine left Youssef with no iron chelation between transfusions.
a.x: He needed chelation restarted, in a form he could manage.
a.w: Every transfusion adds iron. A ferritin of 3,200 means iron is building up in his heart, liver and glands, which can cause heart failure and early death.

a.o: Dr. Nermine asked for a heart MRI to look for iron in Youssef's heart.
a.x: His heart was off topic for a boy who has regular transfusions.
a.w: Iron in the heart is the main cause of death in thalassemia.

a.o: Dr. Nermine checked how Youssef's puberty was coming along for his age.
a.x: His puberty was off topic for a boy who has regular transfusions.
a.w: Iron overload damages the glands and delays puberty.

a.o: Dr. Nermine kept Youssef's hemoglobin around 95 before each transfusion.
a.x: His hemoglobin should be allowed to fall lower between them.
a.w: Keeping the hemoglobin above 90 to 100 lets children grow and stops the bone marrow overgrowing.

t: Meningococcal rash sent to hospital without antibiotics
s:
Nour, 17, came to the GP with her mother. She had a fever, a headache and pain in her legs since the morning. Her hands and feet were cold. She now had a few purple spots on her legs that did not fade when pressed with a glass.

Dr. Ghada checked her pulse, which was 128, and her blood pressure, 96/58. Her neck was a little stiff. She asked about allergies, and Nour had none.

She called an ambulance at once and phoned the hospital to warn them. She put Nour on oxygen and asked her mother to stay with her.

The practice had benzylpenicillin in its emergency bag, but the nurse said she had never seen it used. Nour's younger brother was at home, and her mother asked if he was at risk.

Dr. Ghada decided not to give antibiotics, so the hospital could "take blood cultures first", and waited with Nour for the ambulance, which arrived 35 minutes later.
h: decided not to give antibiotics, so the hospital could "take blood cultures first"

a.o: Dr. Ghada held back antibiotics from Nour with a meningococcal rash.
a.x: Nour needed benzylpenicillin given before the ambulance came.
a.w: Meningococcal sepsis can kill within hours. Giving antibiotics early saves lives, and blood cultures should never delay them.

a.o: Dr. Ghada called an ambulance for Nour as soon as she saw the rash.
a.x: Nour could have been driven to hospital by her mother instead.
a.w: A sick, septic teenager needs an emergency ambulance.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Nour's mother about any allergies to antibiotics.
a.x: Allergies don't matter at all in an emergency like this one.
a.w: Checking allergies is quick and avoids harm.

a.o: Dr. Ghada thought about the risk to Nour's brother who lives with her.
a.x: Family members who live with her are not at any risk from it.
a.w: Close contacts need preventive antibiotics.

t: Meningitis antibiotics delayed for a scan
s:
Mr. Waleed, 24, came in with a severe headache, fever of 39.2°C and neck stiffness for a day. He was alert and talking normally. His pupils were equal, with no weakness or fits. He had no rash and his blood pressure was normal.

Dr. Hossam took blood cultures straight away and sent bloods. He gave IV fluids and pain relief.

He planned a lumbar puncture, and asked the nurses to dim the lights because Mr. Waleed was sensitive to light.

Mr. Waleed's roommate said they shared a flat with three other students. The CT scanner was busy and had a two-hour wait.

Dr. Hossam decided to wait for a CT scan and lumbar puncture before giving antibiotics, writing "don't want to spoil the LP".
h: Dr. Hossam decided to wait for a CT scan and lumbar puncture before giving antibiotics

a.o: Dr. Hossam waited for a scan and LP before Mr. Waleed's antibiotics.
a.x: He needed IV ceftriaxone at once after cultures, and LP later.
a.w: Every hour of delay in bacterial meningitis raises the risk of death and brain damage. Blood cultures and PCR can still find the germ.

a.o: Dr. Hossam took blood cultures from Mr. Waleed before any antibiotics.
a.x: Taking blood cultures first only wastes precious time here.
a.w: Cultures take minutes and help find the germ.

a.o: Dr. Hossam dimmed the lights in the room for Mr. Waleed's headache.
a.x: Dimming the lights was unnecessary for a man with meningitis.
a.w: Light sensitivity is common in meningitis.

a.o: Dr. Hossam asked about the flatmates who share Mr. Waleed's home.
a.x: His flatmates were off topic for his own illness and treatment.
a.w: Close contacts may need preventive antibiotics.

t: Malaria in a traveler called flu
s:
Mr. Sherif, 38, came in with fever, chills, headache and aches all over for three days. He had come back from a business trip to Nigeria two weeks ago. He did not take malaria tablets because he "forgot". He had no cough or rash.

Dr. Nada found a temperature of 38.9°C and a pulse of 110. His blood count showed low platelets. His liver tests were mildly raised.

She gave him paracetamol and fluids, and asked if he had been bitten by mosquitoes, which he had. She asked about other travelers, and his colleague was also unwell.

He asked whether he could go back to work the next day because he had a big meeting. She said he needed rest.

She diagnosed flu and sent him home with paracetamol, without a malaria test.
h: She diagnosed flu and sent him home with paracetamol, without a malaria test

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Mr. Sherif home as flu without doing any malaria test.
a.x: He needed urgent malaria films, repeated if the first was clear.
a.w: Any fever after travel to a malaria area is malaria until proven otherwise. Falciparum malaria can kill within days.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked Mr. Sherif about any mosquito bites during his trip.
a.x: Mosquito bites were off topic for a man with a fever and aches.
a.w: Bites support the risk of malaria.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked about the colleague who travelled with Mr. Sherif.
a.x: His colleague was off topic for Mr. Sherif's own fever and aches.
a.w: A sick fellow traveler points to a shared infection.

a.o: Dr. Nada noticed Mr. Sherif's low platelets on his blood count.
a.x: His platelet count was off topic for a man with a flu-like illness.
a.w: Low platelets are common in malaria.

s:
Mrs. Amira, 30, came back from Uganda a week ago. She was admitted with fever, confusion and yellow eyes. Her blood film showed falciparum malaria with 8% of red cells infected. Her creatinine was raised and her sugar low.

Dr. Fouad gave her IV glucose for the low sugar and fluids carefully. He asked for her to be checked every hour.

He asked the intensive care team to see her and called the infectious diseases team for advice.

Her husband asked whether she would recover. He also asked if he should be tested, since he had been with her on the trip.

Dr. Fouad started oral chloroquine tablets, saying "she can swallow", and planned to repeat the blood film the next day.
h: Dr. Fouad started oral chloroquine tablets, saying "she can swallow"

a.o: Dr. Fouad treated Mrs. Amira's severe malaria with chloroquine tablets.
a.x: Mrs. Amira needed IV artesunate at once for severe malaria.
a.w: Confusion, jaundice, kidney injury and over 2% infected cells mean severe malaria. It needs IV treatment, and falciparum is often resistant to chloroquine.

a.o: Dr. Fouad gave Mrs. Amira IV glucose when her blood sugar was found low.
a.x: IV glucose was unnecessary for a woman with severe malaria.
a.w: Low sugar is common and dangerous in severe malaria.

a.o: Dr. Fouad called the intensive care team to come and see Mrs. Amira.
a.x: Intensive care was not needed for a woman with malaria.
a.w: Severe malaria can worsen quickly.

a.o: Dr. Fouad thought about testing Mrs. Amira's husband, who had travelled too.
a.x: Malaria is not her husband's concern, as he has no symptoms.
a.w: Her husband shared the same risk on the trip.

s:
Miss Hana, 24, was diagnosed with lung TB. She had a cough for two months and lost weight. Her sputum showed TB, sensitive to all drugs. She takes the combined pill for contraception. She is not pregnant.

Dr. Rasha started the four standard TB drugs: rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, with vitamin B6. She checked her liver tests and her eyesight first.

She arranged contact tracing for her family and flatmates, and advised her to stay home from work for two weeks.

Miss Hana asked if her urine would change color. Dr. Rasha said it would turn orange.

She did not warn Miss Hana that rifampicin makes the pill not work, and did not suggest other contraception.
h: She did not warn Miss Hana that rifampicin makes the pill not work

a.o: Dr. Rasha didn't warn Miss Hana that rifampicin stops the pill working.
a.x: She needed a coil or injection for contraception on TB drugs.
a.w: Rifampicin speeds up the breakdown of hormones, so the combined pill can fail and she could get pregnant.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Miss Hana's eyesight before her TB treatment began.
a.x: Her eyesight was off topic before starting TB treatment.
a.w: Ethambutol can damage the eyes.

a.o: Dr. Rasha gave Miss Hana vitamin B6 alongside her TB treatment.
a.x: Vitamin B6 was unnecessary for a young woman on TB treatment.
a.w: Isoniazid can cause nerve damage, which B6 prevents.

a.o: Dr. Rasha told Miss Hana that her urine and tears might turn orange.
a.x: Telling her about orange urine was frightening and unneeded.
a.w: Rifampicin turns body fluids orange; warning prevents worry.

t: Needlestick nurse made to wait for PEP
s:
Nurse Mona, 29, pricked her finger with a used needle while taking blood from a man with known HIV who was not on treatment. She came straight to the emergency department two hours later.

Dr. Hamed washed the wound with soap and water and let it bleed. He asked about her vaccines; she had had hepatitis B vaccines and was immune.

He asked for blood tests from her and, with consent, from the patient. He reported the injury to occupational health.

Nurse Mona was very upset and asked whether she could still breastfeed her baby.

He told her to wait for the patient's viral load result in three days before deciding on HIV medicines.
h: He told her to wait for the patient's viral load result in three days before deciding on HIV medicines

a.o: Dr. Hamed made Nurse Mona wait three days to start her HIV PEP.
a.x: Nurse Mona needed HIV PEP at once, ideally within hours.
a.w: PEP works best within 72 hours, and its effect falls with every hour. A source with untreated HIV is high risk.

a.o: Dr. Hamed let Nurse Mona's wound bleed freely and washed it under the tap.
a.x: Squeezing the wound hard is what helps after a needlestick.
a.w: Washing and gentle bleeding is the first step; squeezing is not advised.

a.o: Dr. Hamed checked Nurse Mona's hepatitis B immunity after the needlestick.
a.x: Her hepatitis B immunity was off topic after a needlestick.
a.w: Needlesticks can spread hepatitis B.

a.o: Dr. Hamed reported Nurse Mona's needlestick injury to occupational health.
a.x: Reporting a single needlestick injury was not needed at all.
a.w: Needlesticks must be reported.

s:
Salma, 18, has had a very sore throat, fever and tiredness for a week. She is studying for exams. She has no allergies.

Dr. Ihab found large, white-coated tonsils and swollen glands at the back of her neck and in her armpits. He felt her belly and found the spleen just below the ribs.

He sent a blood test for glandular fever, and her blood film showed unusual white cells. He advised her to drink plenty and rest.

Salma said she could barely swallow and asked for antibiotics, as her exams were in a week. Her boyfriend had a similar illness last month.

Dr. Ihab prescribed amoxicillin "to be safe" while waiting for the result.
h: prescribed amoxicillin "to be safe" while waiting for the result

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave amoxicillin for Salma's likely glandular fever.
a.x: Salma needed pain relief, fluids and rest, not antibiotics.
a.w: Amoxicillin in glandular fever causes an itchy rash in most people and doesn't help a virus.

a.o: Dr. Ihab felt Salma's tummy to check whether her spleen was enlarged.
a.x: Her spleen was off topic for a young woman with a sore throat.
a.w: Glandular fever can swell the spleen.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked the glands at the back of Salma's neck for swelling.
a.x: Checking her neck glands was unnecessary for a sore throat.
a.w: Back-of-neck glands point to glandular fever.

a.o: Dr. Ihab sent a blood test for glandular fever before she went home.
a.x: The glandular fever blood test was pointless for her sore throat.
a.w: It confirms the diagnosis.

s:
Mrs. Samia, 46, came in with a cough, fever and green phlegm for five days. Her chest had crackles on the right side and her oxygen was 96%. Her notes, flagged in red, said she had anaphylaxis to penicillin ten years ago, with a swollen throat and a night in hospital.

Dr. Ihab checked her pulse, breathing rate and blood pressure, which were normal, and worked out a CRB-65 score of 0. He asked about smoking; she had stopped five years ago.

He explained that she could be treated at home, advised rest and fluids, and told her to come back if she became breathless or confused. He planned a chest X-ray in six weeks to make sure the shadow had cleared.

She is a school secretary and was due to fly to her sister's wedding in a week. She asked for "the strongest antibiotic" so she would be well enough to travel.

He prescribed co-amoxiclav, saying "it isn't penicillin, it's a different antibiotic".
h: He prescribed co-amoxiclav, saying "it isn't penicillin, it's a different antibiotic"

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave Mrs. Samia co-amoxiclav after her penicillin anaphylaxis.
a.x: She needed a non-penicillin antibiotic, such as doxycycline.
a.w: Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin, which is a penicillin, so it can cause another anaphylaxis.

a.o: Dr. Ihab treated Mrs. Samia's mild pneumonia at home with tablets.
a.x: Every case of pneumonia needs a hospital bed and IV treatment.
a.w: A CRB-65 of 0 means low risk and home treatment is safe.

a.o: Dr. Ihab planned a repeat chest X-ray for Mrs. Samia in six weeks' time.
a.x: A repeat chest X-ray in six weeks was a waste of her time.
a.w: A follow-up X-ray checks that the shadow was not hiding something else.

a.o: Dr. Ihab told Mrs. Samia to come back at once if she became breathless.
a.x: Safety advice was not needed for a case as mild as hers.
a.w: Patients need to know the signs of getting worse.

t: Urine infection in a man treated for three days
s:
Mr. Hany, 45, came in with burning on passing urine and going often for two days. He had no fever, no back pain and no discharge. His urine dipstick was positive for nitrites and white cells. He has no other illnesses and has never had a urine infection.

Dr. Abeer checked his temperature, which was normal, and felt his belly, which was soft and not tender over the kidneys.

She sent his urine to the lab for culture, and asked about new partners and discharge, which he did not have. She asked about his prostate symptoms, such as a weak stream, and he had none.

He works as a taxi driver and said he often holds his urine for hours on long shifts and drinks little. He asked whether he could still go to the gym, and she said yes if he felt well.

She prescribed nitrofurantoin for three days, "the same as for women".
h: She prescribed nitrofurantoin for three days, "the same as for women"

a.o: Dr. Abeer gave Mr. Hany only three days of antibiotics.
a.x: Mr. Hany needed seven days of antibiotics, with a culture.
a.w: Urine infections in men are counted as complicated and can involve the prostate. Three days is only for women.

a.o: Dr. Abeer sent Mr. Hany's urine to the lab for culture before treatment.
a.x: The dipstick result was enough without any urine culture.
a.w: Urine infections in men need a culture to guide treatment.

a.o: Dr. Abeer asked Mr. Hany about any new sexual partners recently.
a.x: Asking about his sexual partners was rude and off topic.
a.w: A sexual infection can look like a urine infection.

a.o: Dr. Abeer let Mr. Hany keep going to the gym while he felt well enough.
a.x: He should have rested at home until his infection was cured.
a.w: Exercise is fine if he feels well and has no fever.

s:
Mrs. Hanem, 84, lives in a care home. She was admitted with confusion for two days. She had no fever, no burning and no new pain. Her urine dipstick showed white cells and nitrites. Her sodium was 126.

Dr. Mai checked her drug chart and found she had started a new water tablet a week ago. She stopped it.

She checked her chest and found it clear. She asked her daughter how she usually was, and she was normally chatty.

Her daughter said her mother had not been eating or drinking well since the new tablet.

Dr. Mai diagnosed a urine infection from the dipstick and started antibiotics, writing "UTI causing confusion".
h: Dr. Mai diagnosed a urine infection from the dipstick and started antibiotics

a.o: Dr. Mai blamed a dipstick urine infection for Mrs. Hanem's confusion.
a.x: Her low sodium from the water tablet was the real cause here.
a.w: Dipsticks are often positive in older women without infection. Her confusion came from low sodium.

a.o: Dr. Mai stopped the water tablet that Mrs. Hanem had just been started on.
a.x: The water tablet should have carried on at the same dose.
a.w: Water tablets can cause low sodium.

a.o: Dr. Mai asked Mrs. Hanem's family what she was like on a usual day.
a.x: Asking about her usual self was unnecessary for her confusion.
a.w: Knowing her usual state helps judge confusion.

a.o: Dr. Mai listened to Mrs. Hanem's chest as part of looking for a cause.
a.x: Her chest was off topic for an older woman who is confused.
a.w: A chest infection can cause confusion.

t: Shingles on the nose tip not referred
s:
Mr. Atef, 72, came in with a painful blistering rash on the right side of his forehead for two days. He also had blisters on the tip of his nose. His right eye was red and watery and felt gritty.

Dr. Ghada diagnosed shingles. She checked his vision, which was a little blurred in the right eye.

She started aciclovir tablets and gave him pain relief. She told him to keep the blisters clean and covered.

He asked whether his grandchildren could catch it. She said they could catch chickenpox from the blisters.

She told him to come back in a week, and did not refer him to an eye doctor.
h: She told him to come back in a week, and did not refer him to an eye doctor

a.o: Dr. Ghada didn't refer Mr. Atef to an eye doctor for his shingles.
a.x: Mr. Atef needed to see an eye doctor that very same day.
a.w: Blisters on the nose tip mean the eye nerve is involved, which can damage sight.

a.o: Dr. Ghada started Mr. Atef on aciclovir tablets for his shingles rash.
a.x: Antivirals are useless for shingles and should not be given.
a.w: Antivirals within three days shorten shingles.

a.o: Dr. Ghada warned Mr. Atef to keep away from his young grandchildren.
a.x: Shingles cannot spread to anyone, so the warning was wrong.
a.w: Blisters can spread chickenpox to people who haven't had it.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mr. Atef's vision in both eyes during the visit.
a.x: His vision was off topic for a shingles rash on his forehead.
a.w: Blurred vision suggests eye involvement.

t: Chickenpox contact in a pregnant woman
s:
Mrs. Heba, 28, is 16 weeks pregnant with her first baby. Her nephew had chickenpox, and she spent an afternoon playing with him three days ago before the spots appeared. She has never had chickenpox herself, as far as she knows. She feels well and has no rash.

Dr. Soha sent a blood test for chickenpox immunity the same day, which came back negative. She checked her blood pressure and listened to the baby's heartbeat, which was normal.

She told her to avoid other people with chickenpox and to stay away from the antenatal clinic waiting room until 21 days after contact, in case she became infectious.

Mrs. Heba works as a nursery teacher and was very worried. She asked whether the baby was at risk and whether she should stay off work.

Dr. Soha told her to come back only if she got a rash, and did not offer any preventive treatment.
h: told her to come back only if she got a rash, and did not offer any preventive treatment

a.o: Dr. Soha offered Mrs. Heba nothing after her contact with chickenpox.
a.x: She needed aciclovir from day 7 after contact, or immunoglobulin.
a.w: Chickenpox in pregnancy can cause severe pneumonia in the mother, and before 20 weeks it can harm the baby.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked Mrs. Heba's chickenpox immunity with a blood test first.
a.x: A blood test for immunity was a waste of time for Mrs. Heba.
a.w: Many adults are immune without knowing, and then need no treatment.

a.o: Dr. Soha kept Mrs. Heba out of the antenatal waiting room for now.
a.x: Keeping her out was wrong, as she was not infectious to anyone.
a.w: She could become infectious from day 8 to 21 and spread it to other pregnant women.

a.o: Dr. Soha told Mrs. Heba to avoid any other cases of chickenpox for now.
a.x: One more contact with chickenpox makes no difference to her.
a.w: Avoiding further exposure is sensible.

s:
Mr. Sami, 40, injects drugs. He was admitted with fever for two weeks, night sweats and weight loss. He had a new heart murmur and small dark lines under his nails. He was alert, with a blood pressure of 124/78 and a pulse of 98. His chest was clear.

Dr. Nadia asked for an urgent heart scan and checked his HIV and hepatitis tests. She checked his urine, which showed blood.

She asked the addiction team to see him and offered him a substitute medicine so he would not go into withdrawal on the ward.

He was anxious and wanted to leave for a few hours to see his mother. Dr. Nadia talked with him calmly and he agreed to stay.

She started IV antibiotics at once, before taking any blood cultures, writing "start treatment early".
h: She started IV antibiotics at once, before taking any blood cultures

a.o: Dr. Nadia started Mr. Sami's antibiotics before taking blood cultures.
a.x: Stable, he needed three sets of cultures before antibiotics.
a.w: In stable endocarditis, finding the germ guides weeks of treatment. Antibiotics first can make the cultures negative.

a.o: Dr. Nadia asked for an urgent heart scan for Mr. Sami on the ward.
a.x: The heart scan could wait until his antibiotics were finished.
a.w: A heart scan shows growths on the valves.

a.o: Dr. Nadia gave Mr. Sami a substitute medicine to manage his withdrawal.
a.x: A substitute medicine only rewards his drug use on the ward.
a.w: Treating withdrawal helps him stay for treatment.

a.o: Dr. Nadia talked Mr. Sami into staying on the ward for his treatment.
a.x: She should have let him go home when he first asked to leave.
a.w: Leaving mid-treatment risks death from endocarditis.

s:
Mr. Kareem, 70, was admitted with a kidney infection and sepsis. He was started on IV gentamicin once a day with a second antibiotic. His creatinine was 160, higher than his usual 110. He weighs 68 kg.

Dr. Hala worked out the gentamicin dose by his weight and his kidney function. She asked for his urine output to be measured every hour and gave IV fluids.

She asked about ringing in his ears and dizziness, which he did not have, and noted his hearing was good.

He is a retired engineer and wanted to know exactly how long each drug would last. His wife asked if he would need long-term antibiotics; Dr. Hala said the course would switch to tablets once he was better.

She did not ask for any gentamicin blood levels, writing "dose checked by weight".
h: She did not ask for any gentamicin blood levels, writing "dose checked by weight"

a.o: Dr. Hala gave Mr. Kareem gentamicin without checking his blood levels.
a.x: He needed gentamicin levels checked, with the dose changed.
a.w: Gentamicin can damage the kidneys and inner ear. Levels must be checked, especially with weak kidneys.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked the nurses to measure Mr. Kareem's urine every single hour.
a.x: Measuring his urine every hour was far too much fuss for him.
a.w: Urine output shows how his kidneys cope with sepsis.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked Mr. Kareem about any ringing in his ears or dizziness.
a.x: His ears were off topic in a man with a kidney infection.
a.w: Gentamicin can damage hearing and balance.

a.o: Dr. Hala worked out Mr. Kareem's gentamicin dose from his body weight.
a.x: A fixed dose of gentamicin is better for every patient.
a.w: Dosing by weight is safer.

t: Measles child sent to the waiting room
s:
Ahmed, 3, came in with fever, a cough, runny nose and red eyes for four days. Today he had a red, blotchy rash starting behind his ears and on his face. He had not had his MMR vaccine because his parents were worried about side effects.

Dr. Rana looked inside his mouth and saw tiny white spots on the inside of his cheeks. His chest was clear and he was drinking.

She advised fluids and paracetamol and told his mother to watch for fast breathing, drowsiness or fewer wet nappies.

His mother said his 7-month-old sister was at home. She asked whether it was too late for the MMR vaccine for Ahmed, and Dr. Rana said they could talk about it once he was well.

While she wrote a letter, she asked them to wait in the busy waiting room, next to other children and a pregnant woman.
h: she asked them to wait in the busy waiting room, next to other children and a pregnant woman

a.o: Dr. Rana sent Ahmed, with likely measles, out to the busy waiting room.
a.x: Ahmed needed a separate room, with public health told too.
a.w: Measles spreads through the air and is dangerous to babies, pregnant women and people with weak immunity.

a.o: Dr. Rana looked inside Ahmed's mouth for spots on the inside of his cheeks.
a.x: Ahmed's mouth was off topic for a child with a rash and fever.
a.w: White spots inside the cheeks are a sign of measles.

a.o: Dr. Rana raised the MMR vaccine with Ahmed's mother during the visit.
a.x: Talking about vaccines at a time like this was too pushy.
a.w: A good moment to talk about vaccines protects him and his sister later.

a.o: Dr. Rana thought about the risk to Ahmed's baby sister at home.
a.x: His baby sister was not at any risk of catching measles.
a.w: Babies under one are at high risk of measles complications.

s:
Mr. Samir, 34, was bitten on his hand by a stray dog while jogging in a country where rabies is common. The dog ran away and could not be found. The bite broke the skin and bled.

Dr. Inas washed the wound for 15 minutes with soap and running water, and cleaned it with antiseptic. She checked his tetanus status, which was up to date.

She left the hand wound open rather than stitching it, gave him co-amoxiclav to prevent infection and checked that he could move all his fingers.

He is a teacher and was worried about missing work. He asked whether the dog might have been sick, because it had been foaming at the mouth.

She told him rabies was rare and did not give a rabies vaccine.
h: She told him rabies was rare and did not give a rabies vaccine

a.o: Dr. Inas gave Mr. Samir no rabies treatment after a stray dog bite.
a.x: He needed rabies vaccines and immunoglobulin into the wound.
a.w: Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start. A stray dog bite where rabies is common needs treatment at once.

a.o: Dr. Inas washed Mr. Samir's bite wound with soap and water for 15 minutes.
a.x: A quick rinse under the tap is enough for a bite like this.
a.w: Long washing lowers the risk of rabies.

a.o: Dr. Inas left Mr. Samir's hand wound open instead of stitching it closed.
a.x: All dog bites should be stitched closed in the department.
a.w: Hand bites are often left open to lower the risk of infection.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked that Mr. Samir could move all of his fingers fully.
a.x: Checking his finger movement was unnecessary for a dog bite.
a.w: Bites can damage tendons.

s:
Mr. Fathi, 60, a farmer, cut his shin deeply on a rusty plough this morning. The wound was full of soil and manure. He could not remember ever having a tetanus injection, and his records showed none.

Dr. Nada gave him local anesthetic and washed the wound well with lots of saline. She removed dirt and dead tissue, then closed it loosely with a few stitches.

Because the wound was dirty, she gave him co-amoxiclav for a week. She checked his sugar, which was normal, and his foot pulses, which were strong.

He asked when the stitches could come out, and she said in about ten days. His son asked whether he could keep working, and she said he could do light jobs if he kept it clean.

She sent him home with a dressing and advice, without any tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin.
h: She sent him home with a dressing and advice, without any tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Mr. Fathi home with a dirty wound and no tetanus cover.
a.x: He needed a tetanus vaccine and tetanus immunoglobulin.
a.w: A soil-dirty wound in someone with no record of vaccines is high risk for tetanus, which can be deadly.

a.o: Dr. Nada removed the dead tissue from Mr. Fathi's wound before dressing it.
a.x: Removing dead tissue only makes the wound bigger than before.
a.w: Removing dead tissue lowers infection risk.

a.o: Dr. Nada gave Mr. Fathi a course of antibiotics for his dirty wound.
a.x: Antibiotics were unnecessary for a wound like Mr. Fathi's.
a.w: Dirty wounds can get infected.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked the pulses in Mr. Fathi's foot as part of her exam.
a.x: The pulses in his foot were off topic for a dirty wound.
a.w: Good blood supply helps a shin wound heal.

t: Syphilis in pregnancy treated with doxycycline
s:
Mrs. Reem, 25, is 14 weeks pregnant with her first baby. Her routine booking blood test showed syphilis. She had no sores or rash. She is not allergic to penicillin and has had it before for a sore throat.

Dr. Soha explained the result kindly and in private, and said it could be treated. She asked about her husband and offered him a test and treatment.

She checked her HIV and hepatitis B tests, which were negative, and planned to repeat the syphilis blood test after treatment to check it had worked.

Mrs. Reem was very upset and asked whether her baby would be harmed. She also said she was scared of needles and asked if there was a tablet instead.

Because of the fear of needles, Dr. Soha prescribed doxycycline tablets for two weeks.
h: Dr. Soha prescribed doxycycline tablets for two weeks

a.o: Dr. Soha gave Mrs. Reem doxycycline for her syphilis in pregnancy.
a.x: She needed a benzathine penicillin injection, with support.
a.w: Doxycycline harms the baby's bones and teeth, and does not treat the baby. Penicillin treats both mother and baby.

a.o: Dr. Soha offered Mrs. Reem's husband a test for syphilis as well.
a.x: Her husband was off topic for her own treatment in pregnancy.
a.w: Partners need testing and treatment, or she can be reinfected.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked the result of Mrs. Reem's HIV test from her booking visit.
a.x: HIV tests were unnecessary for a woman being treated for this.
a.w: Syphilis and HIV often go together.

a.o: Dr. Soha planned a repeat blood test for Mrs. Reem after treatment.
a.x: One treatment always works, so repeat tests are not needed.
a.w: A repeat test shows the treatment worked.

s:
Mr. Tarek, 22, came in with a yellow discharge from his penis and burning on passing urine for three days. His swab showed gonorrhea. He had two partners in the last month and did not always use condoms.

Dr. Ihab gave him a ceftriaxone injection the same day. He also tested him for HIV, syphilis and chlamydia, and offered a hepatitis B vaccine.

He advised him to avoid sex for a week after treatment and to use condoms in future. He booked a test of cure in two weeks.

Mr. Tarek is a university student and was embarrassed. He asked whether his partners needed to know, and said he did not want to tell them himself.
