Dr. Fady checked his blood gas, which showed low oxygen. He checked his inhalers and his technique, which was good.

He offered pulmonary rehab and stop-smoking help, which Mr. Hamdy said he would think about.

Mr. Hamdy lives with his wife, who also smokes. He said he would never give up cigarettes.

Their flat is on the fourth floor with no lift. Their grandchildren visit every weekend and play in the living room.

Dr. Fady arranged home oxygen for 16 hours a day, without discussing the fire risk.
h: Dr. Fady arranged home oxygen for 16 hours a day, without discussing the fire risk

a.o: Dr. Fady gave home oxygen to Mr. Hamdy, who still smokes.
a.x: Home oxygen was unsafe while he still smokes.
a.w: Smoking near oxygen causes burns, house fires and deaths.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Hamdy's blood gas before deciding on oxygen.
a.x: His blood gas was unnecessary before deciding on home oxygen.
a.w: The gas shows if oxygen is needed.

a.o: Dr. Fady offered Mr. Hamdy a place on a pulmonary rehab course.
a.x: Pulmonary rehab is useless for a man with COPD like Mr. Hamdy.
a.w: Rehab improves breathlessness.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Hamdy's inhaler technique during the visit.
a.x: His inhaler technique was off topic for a man needing oxygen.
a.w: Poor technique wastes medicine.

s:
Mr. Raouf, 55, has smoked 20 a day since he was 18. He came in with a cough most mornings and breathlessness on stairs for a year. He gets two or three chest infections every winter. He has no weight loss.

Dr. Ihab listened to his chest and heard a mild wheeze. His oxygen was 96%. A chest X-ray showed slightly overinflated lungs but no other changes.

He advised him strongly to stop smoking and offered a stop-smoking course and nicotine patches, which Mr. Raouf accepted.

Mr. Raouf works as a taxi driver and said he did not have time for more tests. His brother has asthma and uses inhalers.

Dr. Ihab diagnosed COPD from the history and X-ray and started inhalers, without spirometry.
h: Dr. Ihab diagnosed COPD from the history and X-ray and started inhalers, without spirometry

a.o: Dr. Ihab diagnosed COPD in Mr. Raouf without doing any spirometry.
a.x: He needed spirometry to confirm COPD and to rule out asthma.
a.w: COPD can only be confirmed with spirometry. Asthma, heart failure and other illnesses can look the same and need different treatment.

a.o: Dr. Ihab offered Mr. Raouf nicotine patches to help him stop smoking.
a.x: Nicotine patches are just as harmful as smoking cigarettes.
a.w: Patches double the chance of quitting.

a.o: Dr. Ihab did a chest X-ray on Mr. Raouf as part of the work-up.
a.x: The chest X-ray was unnecessary for a man with a smoker's cough.
a.w: An X-ray looks for cancer and other causes.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mr. Raouf about any weight loss in recent months.
a.x: Weight loss was off topic for a man with a smoker's cough.
a.w: Weight loss in a smoker is a warning sign.

t: Baby with coughing fits and pauses sent home
s:
Baby Mariam, 6 weeks old, has had a cough for ten days that comes in fits. During the fits she goes red, then blue, and sometimes stops breathing for a few seconds. Between fits she seems well. She was born at term.

Dr. Dina watched a coughing fit, which ended with a gasp and vomiting. Her oxygen dropped to 85% during the fit and came back to 98% after. Her chest was clear between fits.

She asked about vaccines, and Mariam was too young for her first ones. Her mother had not had the whooping cough vaccine in pregnancy.

Mariam's 8-year-old brother has had a bad cough for a month. Her mother asked whether it was just a cold.

Dr. Dina sent her home with advice to come back if the fits got worse.
h: Dr. Dina sent her home with advice to come back if the fits got worse

a.o: Dr. Dina sent Baby Mariam home with whooping cough and breath pauses.
a.x: She needed admission for monitoring and a macrolide.
a.w: Whooping cough in babies under 2 months can cause apneas and death. Blue spells and pauses need hospital care.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked whether Baby Mariam's mother had the vaccine in pregnancy.
a.x: The mother's vaccine in pregnancy was off topic for the baby.
a.w: The pregnancy vaccine protects newborns.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked about the long cough that Baby Mariam's brother has.
a.x: Her brother's cough was off topic for the baby's own illness.
a.w: Older children often spread whooping cough.

a.o: Dr. Dina watched one of Baby Mariam's coughing fits in the room.
a.x: Watching a coughing fit was unnecessary for a baby like her.
a.w: Seeing a fit helps make the diagnosis.

t: Shipyard worker's chest pain called muscular
s:
Mr. Kamel, 70, worked fitting pipes in a shipyard for 30 years. For three months he has had a dull ache on the right side of his chest and breathlessness. He has lost 6 kg. He stopped smoking 20 years ago.

Dr. Mervat found reduced breath sounds and dullness at the right base. A chest X-ray showed fluid around the right lung and thickening of the lining.

She checked his blood tests, which were normal apart from a mild anemia.

Mr. Kamel said many of his old colleagues had died of "lung problems". His wife worried about him.

Dr. Mervat said the ache was muscular from age, prescribed painkillers and did not drain the fluid or arrange a CT.
h: Dr. Mervat said the ache was muscular from age, prescribed painkillers and did not drain the fluid or arrange a CT

a.o: Dr. Mervat called Mr. Kamel's chest pain a simple muscle strain.
a.x: He needed a fluid sample, a CT and a chest clinic referral.
a.w: Chest pain, weight loss, fluid and a thickened lining after asbestos work point to mesothelioma.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked Mr. Kamel about his years of work in the shipyard.
a.x: His work in the shipyard was off topic for his chest pain.
a.w: Asbestos causes lung disease.

a.o: Dr. Mervat did a chest X-ray on Mr. Kamel as part of the work-up.
a.x: The chest X-ray was unnecessary for a man with a muscle strain.
a.w: It shows the fluid.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mr. Kamel's blood tests as part of the work-up.
a.x: Blood tests were unnecessary for a man with a muscle strain.
a.w: Anemia can be a sign of cancer.

t: Thrush from a steroid inhaler without rinse advice
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 44, has asthma and started a higher-dose steroid inhaler two months ago. Her asthma is much better. She now has a sore mouth with white patches and a hoarse voice.

Dr. Ghada looked in her mouth and saw white patches that came off easily, leaving red spots.

She checked her inhaler technique and saw she did not use a spacer.

Mrs. Nadia is a singer in a choir and was upset about her voice.

She has no diabetes and takes no antibiotics. She had not had thrush before. She was worried the steroid inhaler was dangerous and wanted to stop it, but Dr. Ghada explained it was keeping her asthma under control.

Dr. Ghada prescribed antifungal drops, without advice on rinsing or using a spacer.
h: Dr. Ghada prescribed antifungal drops, without advice on rinsing or using a spacer

a.o: Dr. Ghada treated Mrs. Nadia's thrush with no prevention advice.
a.x: She needed to rinse her mouth after each use and use a spacer.
a.w: Rinsing and a spacer reduce the steroid left in the mouth, preventing thrush and a hoarse voice.

a.o: Dr. Ghada looked inside Mrs. Nadia's mouth during the visit.
a.x: Looking in her mouth was unnecessary for a sore throat like this.
a.w: The look confirms thrush.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mrs. Nadia's inhaler technique during the visit.
a.x: Her inhaler technique was off topic for a sore mouth like this.
a.w: Poor technique leaves more steroid in the mouth.

a.o: Dr. Ghada prescribed antifungal drops for the thrush in her mouth.
a.x: Antifungal drops were unnecessary for a sore mouth like this.
a.w: Antifungals clear thrush.

s:
Mr. Sami, 66, has COPD and takes theophylline tablets. He was admitted with a urine infection, and the team started ciprofloxacin. On day three he felt sick, vomited and had a racing heart.

Dr. Ayman checked his heart tracing, which showed a fast rhythm. His potassium was low.

He gave him anti-sickness medicine and potassium.

Mr. Sami's son asked whether the infection had spread to his heart.

He also takes salbutamol and a steroid inhaler, and he still smokes a few cigarettes a day, though he had stopped since admission. He had no fever now, and his urine was clearing. The ward pharmacist was on leave that week.

Dr. Ayman continued both the theophylline and the ciprofloxacin, without checking a theophylline level.
h: Dr. Ayman continued both the theophylline and the ciprofloxacin, without checking a theophylline level

a.o: Dr. Ayman kept Mr. Sami on theophylline while giving ciprofloxacin.
a.x: He needed a level checked and a different antibiotic chosen.
a.w: Ciprofloxacin raises theophylline levels. Toxicity causes vomiting, fast heart rhythms, low potassium and fits.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked Mr. Sami's potassium level with his other bloods.
a.x: His potassium level was off topic for a man on these tablets.
a.w: Theophylline toxicity lowers potassium.

a.o: Dr. Ayman did a heart tracing on Mr. Sami when his pulse was fast.
a.x: The heart tracing was unnecessary for a man on these tablets.
a.w: Toxicity causes heart rhythm problems.

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave Mr. Sami anti-sickness medicine for his nausea.
a.x: Anti-sickness medicine was unnecessary for a man like him.
a.w: Vomiting is a common symptom.

s:
Mr. Tarek, 30, has a chest drain for a collapsed right lung after a fall from a ladder. The drain bottle is still bubbling with each breath. He was comfortable this morning, with an oxygen level of 96%.

Dr. Hala checked the drain site, which was clean, and the X-ray, which showed the lung partly up. She checked his pain relief and asked the physiotherapist to help with deep breathing.

She made sure the drain bottle was kept below the level of his chest and the water seal was correct.

Mr. Tarek wanted to walk to the hospital shop and asked whether the drain could be disconnected for a while. The nurse was worried about him tripping over the tube.

Dr. Hala clamped the drain so he could walk around without the bottle.
h: Dr. Hala clamped the drain so he could walk around without the bottle

a.o: Dr. Hala clamped Mr. Tarek's chest drain while it was bubbling.
a.x: His drain needed to stay open, with the bottle kept down low.
a.w: A bubbling drain means air is still leaking. Clamping it can cause a tension pneumothorax, which can kill.

a.o: Dr. Hala kept the drain bottle below the level of Mr. Tarek's chest.
a.x: The height of the drain bottle doesn't matter for the drain.
a.w: A raised bottle can siphon fluid back into the chest.

a.o: Dr. Hala checked Mr. Tarek's latest chest X-ray on the ward round.
a.x: The chest X-ray was unnecessary for a man with a chest drain.
a.w: The X-ray shows if the lung is up.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked the physiotherapist to help Mr. Tarek walk around.
a.x: Physiotherapy was unnecessary for a man with a chest drain.
a.w: Deep breathing helps the lung re-expand.

t: Large lung clot with low blood pressure not thrombolysed
s:
Mrs. Amira, 52, collapsed at home. She had been breathless for two days after a long flight. Her blood pressure was 78/40, her pulse 130 and her oxygen 85% on high-flow oxygen. A bedside heart scan showed a very swollen right side of the heart.

Dr. Nada started heparin and gave fluids carefully. She called intensive care.

A CT scan confirmed large clots in both lung arteries.

Mrs. Amira had no recent surgery, bleeding or stroke. Her husband asked whether she would survive.

She takes the combined pill and has no other illnesses. Her troponin was raised. The ward had a bed free, while the intensive care unit was nearly full.

Dr. Nada continued heparin and admitted her to the ward, without giving clot-busting treatment.
h: Dr. Nada continued heparin and admitted her to the ward, without giving clot-busting treatment

a.o: Dr. Nada gave Mrs. Amira heparin alone for a massive lung clot.
a.x: She needed clot-busting treatment at once, with ICU care.
a.w: A clot that drops the blood pressure is a massive PE. Without clot-busting treatment, the risk of death is very high.

a.o: Dr. Nada called the intensive care team to see Mrs. Amira early.
a.x: Intensive care was unnecessary for a woman with a lung clot.
a.w: A massive PE needs intensive care.

a.o: Dr. Nada did a bedside heart scan on Mrs. Amira in the department.
a.x: The bedside heart scan was unnecessary for a lung clot.
a.w: A swollen right heart supports a massive PE.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked Mrs. Amira about any bleeding problems in the past.
a.x: Past bleeding problems were off topic for a lung clot like hers.
a.w: Bleeding risk matters before clot-busting treatment.

t: Young man with emphysema not tested for a gene
s:
Mr. Sherif, 38, has emphysema on his CT scan, mostly at the bottom of his lungs. He smoked only lightly for five years in his twenties. His liver tests are mildly raised. His uncle died of lung disease at 45.

Dr. Fady checked his lung function tests, which showed COPD. He started inhalers and offered pulmonary rehab.

He advised him never to smoke again and to avoid dust and fumes at work.

Mr. Sherif has two children and works as a carpenter. He asked why he had lung disease so young.

His brother, 34, has a cough but has never been checked.

Dr. Fady said it was from smoking and did not test for alpha-1 antitrypsin.
h: Dr. Fady said it was from smoking and did not test for alpha-1 antitrypsin

a.o: Dr. Fady blamed smoking alone for Mr. Sherif's early emphysema.
a.x: He needed an alpha-1 antitrypsin level and a gene test too.
a.w: Emphysema under 45, at the lung bases, with liver changes and a family history, points to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised Mr. Sherif to avoid dust and fumes at work.
a.x: Dust and fumes were off topic for a young man with emphysema.
a.w: Dust worsens lung disease.

a.o: Dr. Fady offered Mr. Sherif a place on a pulmonary rehab course.
a.x: Pulmonary rehab is useless for a young man with emphysema.
a.w: Rehab improves breathing.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Sherif's lung function tests in the clinic.
a.x: Lung function tests were unnecessary for a man with emphysema.
a.w: They confirm COPD.

t: Swollen face in lung cancer given an antihistamine
s:
Mr. Hamed, 64, has lung cancer on the right side, found last month. For a week his face, neck and arms have become swollen, worse in the mornings. The veins on his chest are swollen. He is breathless when lying flat.

Dr. Inas found his face red and puffy, with swollen veins across his chest and neck. His oxygen was 93%. He had no rash or itch.

She asked him to sit up, gave oxygen and checked his blood tests.

Mr. Hamed's wife thought he was allergic to his new pillow. He had no hives or wheeze.

Dr. Inas diagnosed an allergic reaction, gave an antihistamine and sent him home.
h: Dr. Inas diagnosed an allergic reaction, gave an antihistamine and sent him home

a.o: Dr. Inas put Mr. Hamed's swollen face and neck down to allergy.
a.x: He needed urgent imaging and care for SVC obstruction.
a.w: Face, neck and arm swelling with swollen chest veins in lung cancer means the big vein to the heart is blocked.

a.o: Dr. Inas sat Mr. Hamed upright on the trolley when he arrived.
a.x: Sitting him up was unnecessary for a man with a swollen face.
a.w: Sitting up eases breathing and swelling.

a.o: Dr. Inas looked for any rash on Mr. Hamed's skin during the exam.
a.x: A rash was off topic for a man with a swollen face like his.
a.w: No rash or itch makes allergy unlikely.

a.o: Dr. Inas gave Mr. Hamed oxygen when he became short of breath.
a.x: Oxygen was unnecessary for a man with a swollen face like his.
a.w: His oxygen was low.

t: Sarcoidosis with high calcium given vitamin D
s:
Mrs. Samar, 40, has sarcoidosis in her lungs and skin. Her calcium was 2.9, high, and she had kidney stones last year. She feels tired and thirsty.

Dr. Mervat checked her kidney function, which was a little reduced, and her chest X-ray, which showed swollen glands in the chest.

She advised her to drink more water and avoid too much sun.

Mrs. Samar said her friend told her vitamin D helps tiredness. Her vitamin D level was low.

She works as an office manager and has two teenage sons. She takes no other medicines. Her eyes had been checked last month and were healthy. She said she felt foggy and forgetful, and her husband said she had become irritable.

Dr. Mervat prescribed high-dose vitamin D tablets to "fix the low vitamin D".
h: Dr. Mervat prescribed high-dose vitamin D tablets to "fix the low vitamin D"

a.o: Dr. Mervat gave vitamin D to Mrs. Samar, who has a high calcium.
a.x: She needed vitamin D avoided and her high calcium treated.
a.w: In sarcoidosis, the granulomas turn vitamin D into its active form. Extra vitamin D pushes calcium even higher.

a.o: Dr. Mervat advised Mrs. Samar to drink more water each day.
a.x: Drinking more water was off topic for a woman with sarcoidosis.
a.w: Water helps prevent kidney stones.

a.o: Dr. Mervat advised Mrs. Samar to avoid too much sun in the summer.
a.x: Sun exposure was off topic for a woman with sarcoidosis.
a.w: Sunlight raises vitamin D and calcium.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mrs. Samar's kidney function with her bloods.
a.x: Checking her kidney function was unnecessary for sarcoidosis.
a.w: High calcium can harm the kidneys.

t: Silent chest sent to the ward
s:
Miss Dina, 24, has asthma and came in after two days of worsening breathlessness. She could only say single words. Her peak flow was 30% of her best, her oxygen 91% and her pulse 128. Her chest was nearly silent, with very little wheeze.

Dr. Nada gave back-to-back salbutamol and ipratropium nebulizers and oral prednisolone. She started IV magnesium.

She checked a blood gas, which showed a normal carbon dioxide level of 5.6, and asked for a chest X-ray to look for a collapsed lung.

Miss Dina had been in intensive care once before with asthma. Her mother said she ran out of her preventer inhaler last month.

After an hour, she was a little better, and Dr. Nada sent her to the general ward, without calling a senior or intensive care.
h: Dr. Nada sent her to the general ward, without calling a senior or intensive care

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Miss Dina to the ward with no senior or ICU review.
a.x: She needed senior and ICU review at once, and close watching.
a.w: A silent chest, oxygen under 92% and a "normal" CO2 in a tired asthmatic mean life-threatening asthma. She can stop breathing suddenly.

a.o: Dr. Nada started IV magnesium for Miss Dina's severe asthma attack.
a.x: IV magnesium was unnecessary for an asthma attack like hers.
a.w: Magnesium helps severe asthma.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked for a chest X-ray for Miss Dina in the department.
a.x: The chest X-ray was unnecessary for an asthma attack like hers.
a.w: A collapsed lung can complicate asthma.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked Miss Dina about any past stays in intensive care.
a.x: Past stays in intensive care were off topic for this attack.
a.w: Past ICU stays raise the risk of a fatal attack.

t: Three liters drained from the chest at once
s:
Mr. Fikry, 66, has a large fluid collection around his left lung from a cancer. He was very breathless. Dr. Ayman put a drain into the chest under ultrasound to drain the fluid.

He checked his blood thinner, which he had stopped, and his platelets, which were normal. He used local anesthetic and drained the fluid into a bag.

He sent the fluid for tests and checked his oxygen, which improved from 89% to 95%.

Mr. Fikry felt much better and asked for all the fluid to be removed at once. His wife was relieved.

Dr. Ayman let 3 liters drain out in 30 minutes, then left the drain open.
h: Dr. Ayman let 3 liters drain out in 30 minutes, then left the drain open

a.o: Dr. Ayman drained 3 liters from Mr. Fikry's chest in 30 minutes.
a.x: The drain needed clamping after about 1.5 liters came out.
a.w: Draining a large effusion too fast can cause re-expansion pulmonary edema, filling the lung with fluid.

a.o: Dr. Ayman used ultrasound to guide the drain into Mr. Fikry's chest.
a.x: Ultrasound was unnecessary for putting in a chest drain.
a.w: Ultrasound makes drain insertion safer.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked Mr. Fikry's platelets before putting in the drain.
a.x: His platelets were off topic before putting in a chest drain.
a.w: Low platelets raise bleeding risk.

a.o: Dr. Ayman sent the fluid from Mr. Fikry's chest to the lab for tests.
a.x: Tests on the fluid were unnecessary for a man like Mr. Fikry.
a.w: Tests show the cause.

t: Coughing man with TB put on an open ward
s:
Mr. Sami, 45, came from a country where TB is common. He has had a cough for two months, night sweats and weight loss. His chest X-ray showed a cavity at the top of the right lung.

Dr. Fouad sent three sputum samples and an HIV test. He checked his liver tests before treatment.

He asked about family and work contacts.

Mr. Sami was tired and wanted to rest. The side rooms were all full.

He works in a restaurant kitchen and shares a flat with four other men. One of the patients in the open bay was on chemotherapy. The infection control nurse had gone home for the day.

Dr. Fouad admitted him to an open ward bay with five other patients, without a mask or isolation.
h: Dr. Fouad admitted him to an open ward bay with five other patients, without a mask or isolation

a.o: Dr. Fouad put Mr. Sami, who likely has TB, on an open general ward.
a.x: Mr. Sami needed a side room until his sputum samples were clear.
a.w: TB with a cavity spreads through the air and can infect other patients and staff.

a.o: Dr. Fouad sent an HIV test for Mr. Sami along with his other bloods.
a.x: An HIV test was off topic for a man with a cough and weight loss.
a.w: HIV and TB often go together.

a.o: Dr. Fouad checked Mr. Sami's liver tests before starting treatment.
a.x: His liver tests were unnecessary before starting any treatment.
a.w: TB drugs can harm the liver.

a.o: Dr. Fouad asked Mr. Sami about the people he lives and works with.
a.x: His contacts at home and work were off topic for his own care.
a.w: Contacts need screening.

t: Flu in a pregnant woman without antivirals
s:
Mrs. Rana, 30, is 28 weeks pregnant. She came in with a sudden fever of 39°C, aching muscles, headache and dry cough since yesterday. Flu is spreading in the area.

Dr. Ghada listened to her chest, which was clear, and checked her oxygen, which was 97%.

She advised rest, fluids and paracetamol.

Mrs. Rana works as a teacher and had not had her flu vaccine this year.

This is her first pregnancy and the baby had been moving well. She has mild asthma and uses an inhaler now and then. Two children in her class had been off sick with flu last week. Her husband had the same illness a few days earlier and was still in bed.

Dr. Ghada told her it was a virus that would pass, without offering oseltamivir.
h: Dr. Ghada told her it was a virus that would pass, without offering oseltamivir

a.o: Dr. Ghada gave Mrs. Rana no antivirals for flu in pregnancy.
a.x: She needed oseltamivir within 48 hours of her first symptoms.
a.w: Pregnant women are at high risk of severe flu and pneumonia. Antivirals lower the risk.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mrs. Rana's oxygen level with a finger probe.
a.x: Her oxygen level was off topic for a pregnant woman with flu.
a.w: Low oxygen shows severe illness.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised Mrs. Rana to take paracetamol for her fever.
a.x: Paracetamol is unsafe to take at any stage in pregnancy.
a.w: Paracetamol is safe in pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked whether Mrs. Rana had her flu vaccine this year.
a.x: Her flu vaccine was off topic for a pregnant woman with flu.
a.w: The vaccine protects pregnant women.

t: Lung nodule on a scan not followed up
s:
Mr. Hesham, 61, had a CT scan for kidney stones. The report also mentioned a 9 mm nodule in the right lung, with advice to follow up. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day.

Dr. Fady treated his kidney stones and checked his kidney function.

He advised him to drink more water and avoid salty food.

Mr. Hesham was pleased the stone had passed. He asked whether he needed more tests.

He works as a taxi driver and has a cough most mornings, which he puts down to smoking. His father died of lung cancer at 66. The kidney stone report was long, and the line about the lung was near the end. He had no weight loss and felt well.

Dr. Fady discharged him without acting on the lung nodule.
h: Dr. Fady discharged him without acting on the lung nodule

a.o: Dr. Fady ignored the lung nodule that was seen on Mr. Hesham's scan.
a.x: He needed referral to the chest team to follow it up properly.
a.w: A 9 mm lung nodule in a smoker can be an early lung cancer, which is curable if caught early.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Hesham's kidney function with a blood test.
a.x: Kidney tests were unnecessary for a man with a kidney stone.
a.w: A blocking stone can harm the kidney.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised Mr. Hesham to drink more water through the day.
a.x: Drinking more water was off topic for a man with a kidney stone.
a.w: Water prevents stones.

a.o: Dr. Fady treated the kidney stone that was causing Mr. Hesham's pain.
a.x: The kidney stone would have passed all by itself in time.
a.w: Painful stones need pain relief and a check that they pass.

t: Allopurinol stopped during a gout attack
s:
Mr. Hany, 56, has had gout for years and has taken allopurinol 300 mg daily for a year. His uric acid has come down well. He came in with a hot, swollen right ankle that started last night after a wedding feast.

Dr. Ghada examined the ankle, which was red and very tender, with no break in the skin. He had no fever. His kidney function was normal.

She prescribed colchicine 500 micrograms two to three times a day and advised rest, ice and plenty of water.

Mr. Hany works as a chef and was frustrated because he thought the allopurinol was supposed to stop attacks. He had read online that it can make attacks worse. He asked whether he should stop it.

Dr. Ghada told him to stop the allopurinol until the attack settled, then restart it.
h: Dr. Ghada told him to stop the allopurinol until the attack settled, then restart it

a.o: Dr. Ghada stopped Mr. Hany's allopurinol during his gout attack.
a.x: He needed allopurinol kept going, with colchicine for the attack.
a.w: Stopping and restarting allopurinol changes uric acid levels and can trigger more attacks. It should continue through a flare.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mr. Hany's kidney function with a blood test.
a.x: His kidney function was off topic for a man with an attack of gout.
a.w: Colchicine doses depend on the kidneys.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised Mr. Hany to drink plenty of water each day.
a.x: Drinking more water was off topic for a man with gout like him.
a.w: Water helps the kidneys clear uric acid.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mr. Hany about the big family feast before the attack.
a.x: The family feast was off topic for a man with an attack of gout.
a.w: Rich food and alcohol can trigger gout.

s:
Mr. Sherif, 48, has had a kidney transplant and takes azathioprine 100 mg daily and prednisolone. He has had three gout attacks this year. His uric acid is high and his kidney function is stable.

Dr. Mervat checked his blood count, which was normal, and his liver tests, which were fine.

She advised him to cut down on beer and red meat, and to drink plenty of water.

Mr. Sherif said the gout was stopping him from working as a delivery driver. He wanted a tablet to prevent it. He takes no other medicines.

Dr. Mervat started allopurinol 100 mg daily, without changing his azathioprine or checking his blood count soon after.
h: Dr. Mervat started allopurinol 100 mg daily, without changing his azathioprine or checking his blood count soon after

a.o: Dr. Mervat added allopurinol to azathioprine at the same dose.
a.x: He needed another gout drug, or his azathioprine cut sharply.
a.w: Allopurinol stops the breakdown of azathioprine, causing a dangerous drop in blood cells.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mr. Sherif's blood count with his other tests.
a.x: His blood count was off topic for a man starting a gout drug.
a.w: Azathioprine can lower the blood count.

a.o: Dr. Mervat advised Mr. Sherif to cut down on the beer he drinks.
a.x: Beer was off topic for a man with gout like Mr. Sherif.
a.w: Beer raises uric acid.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mr. Sherif's liver tests with his other bloods.
a.x: His liver tests were off topic for a man starting a gout drug.
a.w: Azathioprine can harm the liver.

t: Methotrexate without folic acid or blood tests
s:
Mrs. Nawal, 52, has rheumatoid arthritis affecting her hands and wrists. She has morning stiffness for two hours. Her CRP is high and her rheumatoid factor positive.

Dr. Fady examined her hands and found swollen knuckles. He checked her chest X-ray and her hepatitis tests, which were normal.

He explained that methotrexate is a weekly tablet and that she should avoid alcohol.

Mrs. Nawal works as a seamstress and could no longer hold her needles. She was keen to start treatment quickly. She lives far from the clinic.

Her kidney and liver tests were normal at the start.

Dr. Fady started methotrexate 15 mg weekly, without folic acid or any plan for blood tests.
h: Dr. Fady started methotrexate 15 mg weekly, without folic acid or any plan for blood tests

a.o: Dr. Fady started methotrexate with no folic acid or blood tests.
a.x: Mrs. Nawal needed weekly folic acid and regular blood tests.
a.w: Methotrexate can lower the blood count and harm the liver. Folic acid cuts side effects, and blood tests catch problems early.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Nawal's chest X-ray before her methotrexate.
a.x: The chest X-ray was off topic before starting methotrexate.
a.w: Methotrexate can affect the lungs.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised Mrs. Nawal to avoid alcohol while on methotrexate.
a.x: Alcohol was off topic for a woman starting on methotrexate.
a.w: Alcohol adds to liver damage.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Nawal's hepatitis tests before treatment.
a.x: Hepatitis tests were unnecessary before starting methotrexate.
a.w: Hepatitis raises liver risk.

s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 72, has polymyalgia rheumatica and has taken prednisolone for eight months. She started on 15 mg and is now on 7.5 mg. Her shoulder and hip pain is much better and her ESR is normal.

Dr. Ihab checked her blood pressure and sugar, which had risen a little on the steroids. He checked that she was on calcium and vitamin D.

He asked about headaches and jaw pain, which she did not have.

Mrs. Fawzia said she hated the steroids because they made her face round. She wanted to stop them as soon as possible. She has not had a bone scan.

Dr. Ihab told her to stop the prednisolone that day, as she was better.
h: Dr. Ihab told her to stop the prednisolone that day, as she was better

a.o: Dr. Ihab stopped Mrs. Fawzia's long-term steroids all at once.
a.x: She needed her prednisolone reduced slowly over some months.
a.w: After months of steroids, the body stops making its own. Stopping suddenly can cause an Addisonian crisis and a flare of polymyalgia.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mrs. Fawzia about any new headaches or jaw pain.
a.x: Headaches were off topic for a woman with stiff shoulders.
a.w: Giant cell arteritis can come with polymyalgia.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mrs. Fawzia's blood sugar given her steroids.
a.x: Her blood sugar was off topic for a woman on steroids like her.
a.w: Steroids raise sugar.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mrs. Fawzia's calcium and vitamin D levels.
a.x: Checking her calcium and vitamin D was unnecessary for her.
a.w: Steroids weaken bones.

t: Lupus with protein in the urine left for months
s:
Miss Yasmin, 26, has lupus with joint pains and a rash. She came for her review. Her ankles were swollen and her urine was frothy. Her blood pressure was 148/94, higher than usual.

Dr. Mervat checked her urine, which showed 3+ protein and blood. Her creatinine had risen a little.

She checked her complement levels, which were low, and her double-stranded DNA antibodies, which were high.

Miss Yasmin is a law student with exams soon. She said she felt fine and did not want a hospital stay. She takes hydroxychloroquine.

Her mother also has lupus.

Dr. Mervat booked a review in three months, without referring her to the kidney team.
h: Dr. Mervat booked a review in three months, without referring her to the kidney team

a.o: Dr. Mervat left Miss Yasmin's likely lupus nephritis for months.
a.x: She needed the kidney team urgently for a biopsy.
a.w: Protein and blood in the urine, high blood pressure and active lupus point to lupus nephritis, which can cause kidney failure.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Miss Yasmin's complement levels with her bloods.
a.x: Her complement levels were off topic for a woman with lupus.
a.w: Low complement shows active lupus.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Miss Yasmin's urine for protein and blood.
a.x: Her urine was off topic for a young woman with lupus like her.
a.w: Urine shows kidney involvement.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Miss Yasmin's blood pressure during the visit.
a.x: Checking her blood pressure was unnecessary for her lupus.
a.w: High blood pressure can be a sign of kidney disease.

t: Scleroderma kidney crisis without an ACE inhibitor
s:
Mrs. Samar, 45, has scleroderma with tight skin on her hands, face and arms, diagnosed a year ago. She was started on high-dose prednisolone last month by another doctor. Now she has a severe headache, blurred vision and blood pressure of 210/120. Her creatinine has doubled in a week.

Dr. Ayman checked her blood film, which showed broken red cells, and her platelets, which were low. Her urine showed a little protein.

He asked the nurses to check her blood pressure every 15 minutes and called the kidney team.

Mrs. Samar's husband said she had been very well until the steroids. She has Raynaud's and her fingertips have small ulcers.

Dr. Ayman started IV labetalol to lower her blood pressure, without an ACE inhibitor, and continued the steroids.
h: Dr. Ayman started IV labetalol to lower her blood pressure, without an ACE inhibitor, and continued the steroids

a.o: Dr. Ayman treated Mrs. Samar's kidney crisis without an ACE.
a.x: She needed an ACE inhibitor such as captopril, started at once.
a.w: Scleroderma renal crisis needs ACE inhibitors, which save kidneys and lives. High-dose steroids can trigger it.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked Mrs. Samar's blood film for broken red cells.
a.x: The blood film was unnecessary for a woman with high pressure.
a.w: Broken red cells show damage to small vessels.

a.o: Dr. Ayman called the kidney team to see Mrs. Samar on the ward.
a.x: The kidney team was unnecessary for a woman with high pressure.
a.w: She may need dialysis.

a.o: Dr. Ayman asked the nurses for frequent blood pressure checks.
a.x: Frequent blood pressure checks were unnecessary for her.
a.w: Blood pressure must be lowered carefully.

t: Reactive arthritis without a sexual health check
s:
Mr. Karim, 25, came in with a swollen, painful left knee and right ankle for a week. He also had sore red eyes and burning on passing urine two weeks ago, which got better by itself. He had a new partner a month ago.

Dr. Ihab examined him and found both joints swollen and warm. He checked his blood tests, which showed a raised CRP.

He asked about diarrhea, which Mr. Karim did not have, and about back pain, which he had a little.

Mr. Karim plays football and was worried about missing a match. He was embarrassed about the urine symptoms.

Dr. Ihab diagnosed reactive arthritis and prescribed naproxen, without testing for sexually transmitted infections.
h: Dr. Ihab diagnosed reactive arthritis and prescribed naproxen, without testing for sexually transmitted infections

a.o: Dr. Ihab treated Mr. Karim's arthritis with no STI check at all.
a.x: He needed chlamydia and gonorrhea tests, partner too.
a.w: Reactive arthritis after urine symptoms is often caused by chlamydia. Untreated, it can spread and harm his partner.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mr. Karim about any diarrhea in recent weeks.
a.x: Diarrhea was off topic for a young man with swollen joints.
a.w: Gut infections can also trigger reactive arthritis.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mr. Karim about any pain in his lower back.
a.x: Back pain was off topic for a young man with swollen joints.
a.w: Reactive arthritis can affect the spine.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Karim's CRP along with his other blood tests.
a.x: His CRP was off topic for a young man with swollen joints.
a.w: A raised CRP shows inflammation.

s:
Mr. Fathi, 50, has rheumatoid arthritis that has not responded to methotrexate. The team decided to start adalimumab, an anti-TNF injection. He grew up in a village where TB was common, and his father had TB.

Dr. Fady checked his blood count, liver tests and hepatitis tests, which were normal.

He advised him to avoid live vaccines and to report any fever.

Mr. Fathi was keen to start because his hands were very painful. He works as a farmer.

He has a mild cough every winter, which he blames on dust from the fields. He has diabetes, controlled with tablets. His wife had TB treatment years ago, which she finished.

Dr. Fady started adalimumab, without a TB test or chest X-ray.
h: Dr. Fady started adalimumab, without a TB test or chest X-ray

a.o: Dr. Fady started adalimumab for Mr. Fathi without TB screening.
a.x: He needed a TB blood test and a chest X-ray first.
a.w: Anti-TNF drugs can wake up hidden TB, which can spread through the body and kill.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Fathi's hepatitis tests before the biologic.
a.x: Hepatitis tests were unnecessary before starting a biologic.
a.w: Anti-TNF drugs can wake up hepatitis B.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised Mr. Fathi to avoid live vaccines on the biologic.
a.x: Vaccines were off topic for a man starting a biologic drug.
a.w: Live vaccines can cause infection on biologics.

a.o: Dr. Fady told Mr. Fathi to report any fever on his new treatment.
a.x: Advice about reporting a fever was excessive for this man.
a.w: Serious infections are a major risk on biologics.

t: Nosebleeds and coughing blood called a cold
s:
Mr. Raouf, 55, has had a blocked, crusty nose and nosebleeds for two months. Recently he has coughed up blood and his joints ache. He has lost 4 kg. His urine dipstick showed blood and protein.

Dr. Ghada looked in his nose and saw crusts and bleeding. His blood pressure was 152/96.

She sent blood tests, which showed a raised creatinine and CRP.

Mr. Raouf works as a bus driver and thought he had a bad cold. He takes no regular medicines.

His ears had also felt blocked. He had no fever. His chest X-ray from last year was normal.

Dr. Ghada prescribed a nasal spray and antibiotics and booked a review in a month.
h: Dr. Ghada prescribed a nasal spray and antibiotics and booked a review in a month

a.o: Dr. Ghada called Mr. Raouf's nosebleeds just a simple cold.
a.x: He needed an urgent ANCA blood test and a kidney review.
a.w: Nose crusting, coughing blood, joint pain and blood in the urine with rising creatinine point to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which can destroy the kidneys within weeks.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mr. Raouf's urine for blood during the visit.
a.x: His urine was off topic for a man with a cold and a cough.
a.w: Blood and protein show kidney involvement.

a.o: Dr. Ghada looked inside Mr. Raouf's nose for any crusting.
a.x: Looking in his nose was unnecessary for a man with a cold.
a.w: Nasal crusting is a sign of vasculitis.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mr. Raouf's blood pressure during the visit.
a.x: His blood pressure was off topic for a man with a cold.
a.w: Kidney disease raises blood pressure.

t: Propranolol for a woman with Raynaud's
s:
Miss Hala, 32, has Raynaud's, where her fingers turn white then blue in the cold. She also has migraines twice a month. She came asking for a tablet to prevent the migraines.

Dr. Ihab checked her blood pressure, which was normal, and examined her fingers, which had no ulcers.

He advised her to keep her hands warm with gloves and to stop smoking.

Miss Hala works in a supermarket freezer section. She said her fingers had been worse this winter.

Her migraines come with flashing lights and she takes the progestogen-only pill. Triptans help her attacks. She has no asthma. Her mother also has Raynaud's.

Dr. Ihab prescribed propranolol to prevent her migraines.
h: Dr. Ihab prescribed propranolol to prevent her migraines

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave propranolol to Miss Hala, though she has Raynaud's.
a.x: She needed another migraine preventer, such as amitriptyline.
a.w: Beta blockers narrow the small blood vessels and make Raynaud's worse.

a.o: Dr. Ihab advised Miss Hala to wear warm gloves in cold weather.
a.x: Warm gloves were unnecessary for a young woman with migraine.
a.w: Warmth prevents attacks.

a.o: Dr. Ihab advised Miss Hala to stop smoking as soon as she could.
a.x: Smoking was off topic for a young woman with migraine like her.
a.w: Smoking narrows blood vessels.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Miss Hala's fingers for any ulcers or color change.
a.x: Checking her fingers was unnecessary for a woman with migraine.
a.w: Ulcers show severe Raynaud's.

t: Knee arthritis told to rest and avoid exercise
s:
Mrs. Nabila, 63, has had aching knees for two years, worse after walking and at the end of the day. Her knees are stiff for ten minutes in the morning. Her X-ray showed narrowing of the joint space on both sides. Her BMI is 32.

Dr. Ghada examined her knees, which creaked but were not hot or swollen. She checked her kidney function, which was normal.

She prescribed paracetamol and an anti-inflammatory gel to rub on the knees, and talked about weight loss.

Mrs. Nabila used to walk to the market every day but has stopped because of the pain. She lives with her husband and enjoys gardening. She asked whether walking was wearing out her knees.

Dr. Ghada told her to rest her knees and avoid exercise to stop them wearing out.
h: Dr. Ghada told her to rest her knees and avoid exercise to stop them wearing out

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mrs. Nabila to rest and avoid exercise for her knees.
a.x: She needed to stay active, with strengthening exercises daily.
a.w: Exercise is a core treatment for osteoarthritis. It strengthens the muscles that protect the knee and eases pain. Rest makes it worse.

a.o: Dr. Ghada prescribed an anti-inflammatory gel for Mrs. Nabila's knees.
a.x: Anti-inflammatory gels don't work at all for knee arthritis.
a.w: Anti-inflammatory gels help knee pain with fewer side effects.

a.o: Dr. Ghada talked with Mrs. Nabila about losing some weight.
a.x: Her weight was off topic for a woman with arthritis in her knees.
a.w: Weight loss eases knee pain.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mrs. Nabila's kidney function with a blood test.
a.x: Her kidney function was off topic for a woman with sore knees.
a.w: Kidney function affects painkiller choice.

s:
Mrs. Rasha, 42, has had widespread pain all over her body for two years, with poor sleep and tiredness. Her blood tests, including thyroid and inflammation markers, were normal. She was diagnosed with fibromyalgia.

Dr. Fady explained the condition and that the pain is real but not caused by damage. He advised graded exercise like swimming and better sleep habits.

He referred her for talking therapy and started amitriptyline at a low dose at night.

Mrs. Rasha works as a teacher and was desperate for relief. She said codeine had not helped and asked for something stronger.

She has two teenage children.

Dr. Fady started oxycodone twice a day "to break the pain cycle".
h: Dr. Fady started oxycodone twice a day "to break the pain cycle"

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Mrs. Rasha strong oxycodone for her fibromyalgia.
a.x: She needed exercise, therapy and amitriptyline, no opioids.
a.w: Opioids don't help fibromyalgia, can make pain worse, and lead to dependence.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised Mrs. Rasha to take graded exercise each week.
a.x: Exercise only makes the pain of fibromyalgia worse over time.
a.w: Gentle exercise helps fibromyalgia.

a.o: Dr. Fady referred Mrs. Rasha for talking therapy for her pain.
a.x: Talking therapy is useless for a woman with fibromyalgia.
a.w: Therapy helps people cope with chronic pain.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Rasha's thyroid along with her other bloods.
a.x: Her thyroid was off topic for a woman with widespread pain.
a.w: An underactive thyroid can cause aches.

s:
Mr. Kamel, 68, has a lung disease that needs prednisolone 20 mg daily. He has taken it for six months and will need it for at least another year. He is otherwise well.

Dr. Mervat checked his blood pressure, which was a little high, and his sugar, which was borderline.

She advised him to carry a steroid card and never stop the steroids suddenly.

Mr. Kamel said he had broken his wrist last year when he tripped. He walks with a stick.

He had his vitamin D checked last year, which was low, but never started a supplement. His mother broke her hip in her seventies. He lives alone in a house with stairs.

Dr. Mervat continued the prednisolone, without bone protection or a bone scan.
h: Dr. Mervat continued the prednisolone, without bone protection or a bone scan

a.o: Dr. Mervat gave Mr. Kamel no bone protection on long-term steroids.
a.x: He needed a bisphosphonate, with calcium and vitamin D added.
a.w: Steroids for three months or more weaken bones. Over 65 or with a past fracture, bone protection should start at once.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mr. Kamel's blood sugar given his steroids.
a.x: His blood sugar was off topic for a man on long-term steroids.
a.w: Steroids can cause diabetes.

a.o: Dr. Mervat gave Mr. Kamel a steroid card to carry with him.
a.x: A steroid card was unnecessary for a man on steroid tablets.
a.w: The card warns doctors in an emergency.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked Mr. Kamel about the wrist fracture he had last year.
a.x: His old wrist fracture was off topic for his current treatment.
a.w: A past fracture shows weak bones.

t: Child with arthritis without eye screening
s:
Laila, 4, has juvenile idiopathic arthritis in her right knee and left ankle. She was diagnosed three months ago. Her ANA blood test was positive. She is on naproxen and doing well, with less swelling.

Dr. Rana examined her joints and found mild swelling. She checked her growth, which was normal.

She referred her to the physiotherapist and gave advice on keeping active.

Laila's mother said Laila's eyes looked fine and she had no complaints. Laila loves drawing and painting.

She is in nursery and her teacher said she runs around like the other children. Her vaccines are up to date. Her father has psoriasis.

Dr. Rana booked a review in six months, without arranging eye screening.
h: Dr. Rana booked a review in six months, without arranging eye screening

a.o: Dr. Rana didn't arrange any eye screening for Laila with JIA.
a.x: Laila needed slit-lamp eye checks every three months or so.
a.w: Children with JIA can get silent uveitis with no red eye or pain, which can cause blindness.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked Laila's growth on her chart during the visit.
a.x: Her growth was off topic for a young girl with arthritis.
a.w: Arthritis can affect growth.

a.o: Dr. Rana referred Laila to the physiotherapist for her joints.
a.x: Physiotherapy was unnecessary for a young girl with arthritis.
a.w: Physio keeps joints moving.

a.o: Dr. Rana gave Laila's parents advice on keeping her active.
a.x: Activity only makes arthritis in children worse over time.
a.w: Staying active keeps joints healthy.

s:
Mr. Sami, 60, has gout and came in with a red, swollen big toe since this morning. He has kidney disease with an eGFR of 40 and takes atorvastatin.

Dr. Ihab examined the toe and found it hot and swollen. He checked his kidney function.

He advised rest, ice and elevation.

Mr. Sami said the pain was the worst he had ever had and wanted the strongest treatment.

He also takes clarithromycin, started yesterday for a chest infection. He works as a security guard and stands all night. He has had two attacks this year and is not on allopurinol.

Dr. Ihab told him to take colchicine 500 micrograms every hour until the pain stopped or he got diarrhea.
h: Dr. Ihab told him to take colchicine 500 micrograms every hour until the pain stopped or he got diarrhea

a.o: Dr. Ihab told Mr. Sami to take colchicine every hour for gout.
a.x: He needed prednisolone instead, as colchicine was risky.
a.w: The old "hourly" plan causes colchicine poisoning, with diarrhea, organ failure and death. Weak kidneys, a statin and clarithromycin all raise the level.

a.o: Dr. Ihab advised Mr. Sami to keep his painful foot raised up.
a.x: Raising the foot was unnecessary for a man with gout like him.
a.w: Raising the foot eases swelling.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Sami's kidney function with a blood test.
a.x: Checking his kidney function was unnecessary for an attack.
a.w: Kidneys affect the colchicine dose.

a.o: Dr. Ihab advised Mr. Sami to put an ice pack on his painful toe.
a.x: Ice on the toe only makes an attack of gout worse.
a.w: Ice eases gout pain.

t: Muscle weakness and rash without a cancer search
s:
Mrs. Hanem, 58, has had weakness in her thighs and shoulders for two months. She struggles to climb stairs and lift her arms to brush her hair. She has a purple rash on her eyelids and red patches over her knuckles. Her CK is 4,500.

Dr. Mervat examined her and found weakness in the muscles near the trunk, with normal reflexes. She diagnosed dermatomyositis.

She started high-dose prednisolone and asked the physiotherapist to see her. She checked her swallowing, which was a little slow.

Mrs. Hanem had lost 6 kg without trying. She had stopped going for her breast screening two years ago. She smokes 10 cigarettes a day.

Dr. Mervat booked a review in a month, without any tests to look for an underlying cancer.
h: Dr. Mervat booked a review in a month, without any tests to look for an underlying cancer

a.o: Dr. Mervat didn't look for cancer in Mrs. Hanem.
a.x: She needed a CT scan and other screening for hidden cancer.
a.w: Dermatomyositis in adults is often linked to a hidden cancer, especially with weight loss.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked how well Mrs. Hanem was able to swallow food.
a.x: Her swallowing was off topic for a woman with weak muscles.
a.w: Weak throat muscles can cause choking and pneumonia.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked the physiotherapist to see Mrs. Hanem in clinic.
a.x: Physiotherapy was unnecessary for a woman with weak muscles.
a.w: Physio keeps muscles working.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mrs. Hanem's CK level along with her bloods.
a.x: Her CK level was off topic for a woman with weak muscles.
a.w: A high CK shows muscle damage.

t: Rheumatoid neck not checked before surgery
s:
Mrs. Samia, 66, has had severe rheumatoid arthritis for 25 years, with badly deformed hands. She is due for a hip replacement under general anesthetic tomorrow. She has had neck pain and tingling in her hands when she bends her head forward.

Dr. Hala checked her airway, heart and lungs. Her mouth opening was a little limited.

She checked her blood count and kidney tests, and planned to hold her methotrexate around surgery as advised by the rheumatologist.

Mrs. Samia said she had been dropping things recently. She takes prednisolone 5 mg daily.

She lives with her daughter.

Dr. Hala planned a standard intubation, without neck X-rays or a plan to protect the neck.
h: Dr. Hala planned a standard intubation, without neck X-rays or a plan to protect the neck

a.o: Dr. Hala didn't check Mrs. Samia's neck before her intubation.
a.x: She needed neck X-rays first, with the neck kept still.
a.w: Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis can loosen the top of the neck. Bending it during intubation can damage the spinal cord.

a.o: Dr. Hala checked how wide Mrs. Samia could open her mouth.
a.x: Her mouth opening was off topic before a general anesthetic.
a.w: A small mouth opening makes intubation hard.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked Mrs. Samia about the steroids she takes each day.
a.x: Her steroids were off topic before a general anesthetic.
a.w: Long-term steroids may need extra cover during surgery.

a.o: Dr. Hala checked Mrs. Samia's blood count before the operation.
a.x: Checking her blood count was unnecessary before surgery.
a.w: Anemia is common in rheumatoid arthritis.

t: Yellow fever vaccine on a biologic
s:
Mr. Waleed, 40, has psoriatic arthritis and takes etanercept injections every week. His joints are well controlled. He came to clinic asking about vaccines for a work trip to West Africa next month.

Dr. Fady checked his blood tests, which were normal. He gave him advice on malaria tablets and insect bites.

He arranged hepatitis A and typhoid injection vaccines, which are not live.

Mr. Waleed said the travel clinic told him he needed a yellow fever vaccine to enter the country. He asked whether he could have it.

He has two children and his wife is pregnant.

Dr. Fady said it was fine and arranged the yellow fever vaccine for next week.
h: Dr. Fady said it was fine and arranged the yellow fever vaccine for next week

a.o: Dr. Fady approved a yellow fever vaccine for a woman on etanercept.
a.x: He needed an exemption letter instead of the live vaccine.
a.w: Yellow fever vaccine is live. On a biologic, it can cause a severe, even fatal, infection.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Mr. Waleed advice about avoiding malaria on his trip.
a.x: Malaria was off topic for a man going on a trip like his.
a.w: West Africa has malaria.

a.o: Dr. Fady arranged the typhoid injection for Mr. Waleed's trip.
a.x: The typhoid injection was off topic for a trip like his.
a.w: The injection is safe on biologics.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Waleed's blood tests before his travel.
a.x: Blood tests were unnecessary before a trip like Mr. Waleed's.
a.w: Biologics can affect blood counts.

t: Leflunomide stopped for pregnancy without a washout
s:
Mrs. Nour, 31, has rheumatoid arthritis well controlled on leflunomide for three years. She and her husband want to start trying for a baby now. She is not pregnant and uses condoms.

Dr. Mervat checked her joints, which were quiet, and her blood tests, which were normal.

She talked about switching to a pregnancy-safe treatment like hydroxychloroquine or sulfasalazine, and started folic acid.

Mrs. Nour is a pharmacist and asked how long the leflunomide stays in the body. She was keen to try for a baby next month.

Her mother had two miscarriages.

Dr. Mervat stopped the leflunomide and told her she could try for a baby from next month, without a washout.
h: Dr. Mervat stopped the leflunomide and told her she could try for a baby from next month, without a washout

a.o: Dr. Mervat let Mrs. Nour try for a baby with no leflunomide washout.
a.x: She needed a colestyramine washout, with blood levels checked.
a.w: Leflunomide can stay in the body for up to two years and may harm a baby. A washout clears it in weeks.

a.o: Dr. Mervat started Mrs. Nour on folic acid before she tried for a baby.
a.x: Folic acid was off topic for a woman with rheumatoid arthritis.
a.w: Folic acid before pregnancy prevents spine defects.

a.o: Dr. Mervat discussed safer drugs for pregnancy with Mrs. Nour.
a.x: Safer drugs were off topic for a woman planning a pregnancy.
a.w: Hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine are safe in pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mrs. Nour's joints for any swelling in clinic.
a.x: Checking her joints was unnecessary for a woman like Mrs. Nour.
a.w: Joints show if the arthritis is active.

s:
Mrs. Asmaa, 38, has antiphospholipid syndrome. She had a stroke at 34 and a clot in her leg. All three of her antibody tests are strongly positive. She takes warfarin and has had no clots since.

Dr. Fady checked her INR records, which were mostly in range.

He checked her kidney function, which was normal, and asked about bleeding, which she had none.

Mrs. Asmaa said she was fed up with INR checks every two weeks and wanted a newer blood thinner. Her friend takes apixaban and loves it.

She works as a lawyer and travels for court cases.

Dr. Fady switched her from warfarin to apixaban 5 mg twice a day.
h: Dr. Fady switched her from warfarin to apixaban 5 mg twice a day

a.o: Dr. Fady switched Mrs. Asmaa from warfarin to apixaban last month.
a.x: She needed to stay on warfarin, with a home INR machine too.
a.w: In antiphospholipid syndrome with past artery clots and triple positive tests, newer blood thinners lead to more strokes and clots than warfarin.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Asmaa's INR records from the last few months.
a.x: Her old INR records were unnecessary for changing her tablets.
a.w: Records show how stable her treatment is.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked Mrs. Asmaa about any bleeding while on warfarin.
a.x: Bleeding was off topic for a woman changing her blood thinner.
a.w: Bleeding is the main risk of blood thinners.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Asmaa's kidney function with a blood test.
a.x: Her kidney function was off topic for changing her tablets.
a.w: Kidneys affect blood thinner choice.

s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 69, has osteoporosis found on a bone scan after she broke her wrist. Her calcium, vitamin D and kidney tests were normal. She has no trouble swallowing and no heartburn.

Dr. Ghada explained what osteoporosis means and how to lower the risk of falls at home. She started calcium and vitamin D tablets.

She asked about her teeth, which were healthy, and advised her to see her dentist regularly.

Mrs. Fawzia takes levothyroxine and amlodipine every morning with her tea and toast. She said she likes to take all her tablets together so she does not forget any.

Dr. Ghada started alendronic acid 70 mg once a week and told her to take it with her other tablets at breakfast.
h: told her to take it with her other tablets at breakfast

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mrs. Fawzia to take alendronic acid with her breakfast.
a.x: It should be taken fasting, upright, 30 minutes before food.
a.w: Food, tea and calcium stop alendronic acid being absorbed, and lying down can cause gullet ulcers.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mrs. Fawzia about her teeth and any dental work planned.
a.x: Her teeth were off topic for a woman starting a bone tablet.
a.w: Bisphosphonates rarely cause jaw bone problems, so good dental health matters.

a.o: Dr. Ghada talked with Mrs. Fawzia about how to avoid falls at home.
a.x: Falls at home were off topic for a woman with thin bones.
a.w: Preventing falls prevents fractures.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mrs. Fawzia's kidney tests before the bone tablet.
a.x: Her kidney tests were off topic for a woman starting a bone tablet.
a.w: Bisphosphonates are not used with very weak kidneys.

t: Lupus mother with anti-Ro antibodies not screened for baby heart block
s:
Mrs. Yasmin, 30, has lupus and is 16 weeks pregnant with her first baby. She takes hydroxychloroquine and low-dose aspirin. Her blood tests showed anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies.

Dr. Soha checked her blood pressure and urine, which were normal, and her kidney function, which was stable.

She told her to keep taking hydroxychloroquine, as it is safe in pregnancy and lowers the risk of flares.

Mrs. Yasmin works as a teacher and was excited about the baby. She asked whether her lupus could affect the baby. Her lupus has been quiet for two years.

Her husband came with her and asked how often she would need to be seen. Dr. Soha said she would see her every four weeks, like most mothers, and that a growth scan would be done later in the pregnancy.

Dr. Soha planned routine pregnancy scans only, without weekly checks of the baby's heart rhythm.
h: Dr. Soha planned routine pregnancy scans only, without weekly checks of the baby's heart rhythm

a.o: Dr. Soha gave Mrs. Yasmin no extra checks of the baby's heart.
a.x: She needed regular scans of the baby's heart rhythm in pregnancy.
a.w: Anti-Ro antibodies can cross the placenta and cause heart block in the baby. Early treatment may stop it becoming permanent.

a.o: Dr. Soha kept Mrs. Yasmin on her hydroxychloroquine in pregnancy.
a.x: Hydroxychloroquine should be stopped as soon as she is pregnant.
a.w: It is safe and protects against flares and possibly heart block.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked Mrs. Yasmin's urine for protein at the visit.
a.x: Her urine was off topic for a pregnant woman with lupus like her.
a.w: Protein can mean lupus kidney disease or pre-eclampsia.

a.o: Dr. Soha kept Mrs. Yasmin on low-dose aspirin during her pregnancy.
a.x: Aspirin is unsafe at any stage of a pregnancy and should stop.
a.w: Low-dose aspirin lowers the risk of pre-eclampsia in lupus.

t: Young man's morning back stiffness called mechanical
s:
Mr. Hossam, 24, has had low back pain for eight months. It is worse in the morning, with stiffness lasting over an hour, and better with exercise. It wakes him in the second half of the night. Ibuprofen helps a lot.

Dr. Ihab examined his back and found reduced bending. He also found tenderness over the joints at the base of the spine.

He asked about eye problems, and Mr. Hossam had a painful red eye last year that needed steroid drops.

Mr. Hossam is a software engineer and sits all day. He thought his chair was the problem. His uncle has a "bent back".

Dr. Ihab diagnosed mechanical back pain, advised a better chair and referred him for physiotherapy.
h: Dr. Ihab diagnosed mechanical back pain, advised a better chair and referred him for physiotherapy

a.o: Dr. Ihab called Mr. Hossam's inflammatory back pain mechanical.
a.x: He needed a rheumatologist for possible spondylitis now.
a.w: Back pain under 45, with morning stiffness, better with exercise, waking at night, uveitis and a family history, points to axial spondyloarthritis. Treatment can prevent the spine fusing.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mr. Hossam about any past red or painful eyes.
a.x: Eye problems were off topic for a young man with back pain.
a.w: Uveitis comes with spondyloarthritis.

a.o: Dr. Ihab noticed that ibuprofen helped Mr. Hossam's back pain a lot.
a.x: How well ibuprofen helped was unnecessary for back pain.
a.w: A good response to NSAIDs suggests inflammatory back pain.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about the back problems that Mr. Hossam's uncle had.
a.x: His uncle's back was off topic for his own back pain.
a.w: Spondyloarthritis runs in families.

t: Biologic injection given during a fever
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 46, has rheumatoid arthritis and takes adalimumab every two weeks. She came to clinic for her injection. She has had a fever of 38.5°C, a cough with green phlegm and breathlessness for three days.

Dr. Fady listened to her chest and heard crackles on the right. Her oxygen was 94%.

He sent a chest X-ray and blood tests, and started antibiotics.

Mrs. Nadia said she did not want to miss her injection because her joints get bad when she does. She has two children at home.

Her blood tests later showed a high CRP and a raised white cell count. The X-ray showed shadowing at the base of the right lung. She had no rash and no joint swelling that day.

Dr. Fady gave her the adalimumab injection as planned, writing "keep disease controlled".
h: Dr. Fady gave her the adalimumab injection as planned, writing "keep disease controlled"

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Mrs. Nadia her biologic during a chest infection.
a.x: Her adalimumab needed holding until the infection cleared.
a.w: Anti-TNF drugs weaken the immune system and can let an infection become severe.

a.o: Dr. Fady sent Mrs. Nadia for a chest X-ray to look for pneumonia.
a.x: The chest X-ray was unnecessary for a woman with a cough.
a.w: The X-ray shows pneumonia.

a.o: Dr. Fady started Mrs. Nadia on antibiotics for her chest infection.
a.x: Antibiotics were unnecessary for a woman with a chest infection.
a.w: Bacterial pneumonia needs antibiotics.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Nadia's oxygen level with a finger probe.
a.x: Her oxygen level was off topic for a woman with a cough.
a.w: Low oxygen shows severe illness.

t: Monthly steroid injections into the same knee
s:
Mr. Kamal, 66, has osteoarthritis in his right knee. He has had a steroid injection into the knee every month for eight months. Each one helps for about two weeks. He has diabetes.

Dr. Ihab examined the knee, which was swollen with fluid but not hot. He drained some fluid, which was clear.

He checked his sugar, which had been high after each injection.

Mr. Kamal said he did not want surgery and liked the injections. He walks with a stick.

His last HbA1c had risen from 58 to 71 over the past year. An X-ray of the knee six months ago showed narrowing of the joint space. He has not been referred to physiotherapy and has not tried to lose weight, though his BMI is 34.

Dr. Ihab gave another steroid injection and booked the next one in a month.
h: Dr. Ihab gave another steroid injection and booked the next one in a month

a.o: Dr. Ihab kept giving Mr. Kamal monthly steroid injections.
a.x: He needed three or four injections a year at most.
a.w: Frequent steroid injections can damage the cartilage, raise sugar and risk infection.

a.o: Dr. Ihab drained some fluid from Mr. Kamal's knee before injecting it.
a.x: Draining fluid from the knee was unnecessary before injecting.
a.w: Draining fluid eases pain and checks for infection.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Kamal's blood sugar after his steroid injection.
a.x: His blood sugar was off topic for a man having knee injections.
a.w: Steroid injections raise sugar.

a.o: Dr. Ihab looked closely at the fluid he drained from Mr. Kamal's knee.
a.x: The fluid from his knee was off topic for a man with arthritis.
a.w: Cloudy fluid would mean infection.

t: Pain relief held until the surgeon arrived
s:
Mr. Ziad, 22, came in with pain that started around his belly button and moved to the lower right side over a day. He felt sick and had not eaten. His temperature was 37.9°C and his pulse 104.

Dr. Karim examined him and found tenderness and guarding in the right lower belly. He sent blood tests, which showed a raised white cell count, and a urine test, which was clear.

He started a drip, kept him nil by mouth and called the surgical team, who said they would come within the hour.

Mr. Ziad was lying very still, scoring his pain 9 out of 10. He asked for something for the pain. His mother was angry that he was left in pain while they waited, and asked the nurse twice when he would get something.

Dr. Karim wrote "no analgesia until seen by surgeon, so as not to mask signs" and gave him nothing for the pain.
h: gave him nothing for the pain

a.o: Dr. Karim held Mr. Ziad's pain relief until the surgeon saw him.
a.x: He needed IV morphine or IV paracetamol for pain straight away.
a.w: Pain relief does not hide the signs of appendicitis or delay the diagnosis. Leaving him in pain helps no one.

a.o: Dr. Karim kept Mr. Ziad nil by mouth until the surgeons had seen him.
a.x: He should have been allowed to eat while waiting for the surgeons.
a.w: He may need surgery soon, so an empty stomach is safer for the anesthetic.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked a urine test on Mr. Ziad as part of his work-up.
a.x: The urine test was off topic for a man with belly pain like his.
a.w: A kidney stone or urine infection can look like appendicitis.

a.o: Dr. Karim called the surgeons early about Mr. Ziad's belly pain.
a.x: He should have waited for a scan before calling the surgeons.
a.w: Clear signs of appendicitis need a surgeon's review without delay.

s:
Mr. Sabry, 58, came in with sudden, severe pain in the upper belly that started two hours ago. He takes ibuprofen most days for his knees and smokes 20 a day. He has had indigestion on and off for months.

Dr. Tarek found him lying still, with a pulse of 112. His belly was rigid like a board and very tender all over. His temperature was 37.6°C.

He sent blood tests, including amylase, which was only slightly raised, and an ECG, which was normal apart from a fast rate.

Mr. Sabry said the pain was the worst of his life and he could hardly breathe deeply. His wife said he had eaten a big meal just before. He asked for something for the pain, and Dr. Tarek gave him morphine, which helped a little.

Dr. Tarek gave him an antacid and omeprazole, and planned to send him home if he settled, without an erect chest X-ray or a CT scan.
h: without an erect chest X-ray or a CT scan

a.o: Dr. Tarek treated Mr. Sabry's board-like belly as indigestion.
a.x: He needed imaging for free air and an urgent surgeon now.
a.w: Sudden severe pain with a rigid belly in a man on ibuprofen suggests a burst ulcer, which needs surgery fast.

a.o: Dr. Tarek checked Mr. Sabry's amylase along with his other bloods.
a.x: His amylase was off topic for a man with sudden belly pain.
a.w: Pancreatitis can cause sudden upper belly pain.

a.o: Dr. Tarek did a heart tracing on Mr. Sabry as part of his work-up.
a.x: His heart was off topic for a man with sudden belly pain.
a.w: A heart attack can cause upper belly pain.

a.o: Dr. Tarek gave Mr. Sabry morphine for his severe belly pain.
a.x: Morphine hides the signs and should not have been given.
a.w: Pain relief is right and does not hide a surgical belly.

t: Severe belly pain in atrial fibrillation called gastritis
s:
Mrs. Fathia, 76, came in with severe central belly pain for six hours. She has atrial fibrillation and stopped her apixaban two weeks ago because of a nosebleed. She has vomited twice and had one loose stool.

Dr. Hany examined her. Her belly was soft and only mildly tender, but she was writhing in pain and asking for more morphine. Her pulse was 118 and irregular.

Her blood tests showed a lactate of 4.8 and a raised white cell count. Her amylase was normal and her ECG showed atrial fibrillation with no new changes.

Mrs. Fathia's daughter said her mother never complains and had never been in pain like this. Mrs. Fathia had needed three doses of morphine in two hours. Her urine was clear and her bladder was not full on the scan.

Dr. Hany wrote "soft belly, likely gastritis" and started omeprazole, without a CT angiogram.
h: wrote "soft belly, likely gastritis" and started omeprazole, without a CT angiogram

a.o: Dr. Hany called Mrs. Fathia's pain gastritis with no CT scan.
a.x: She needed an urgent CT angiogram and surgical review.
a.w: Pain far worse than the belly feels, with AF off blood thinners and a high lactate, points to bowel losing its blood supply.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked Mrs. Fathia's amylase along with her other bloods.
a.x: Her amylase level was not needed for a woman with belly pain.
a.w: Pancreatitis can cause severe central pain.

a.o: Dr. Hany scanned Mrs. Fathia's bladder with the ward scanner.
a.x: Her bladder was off topic for a woman with severe belly pain.
a.w: A full bladder in an older woman can cause belly pain.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked Mrs. Fathia's heart tracing during his review.
a.x: The heart tracing was unnecessary for a woman with belly pain.
a.w: It confirmed the atrial fibrillation that can throw clots.

t: Jaundice with fever given oral antibiotics
s:
Mr. Adel, 64, came in with pain under his right ribs, fever and yellow eyes for two days. He has known gallstones and is waiting for his gallbladder to be removed. He had shivers at home.

Dr. Karim found him with a temperature of 39.2°C, a pulse of 110 and a blood pressure of 98/60. He was tender under the right ribs.

His blood tests showed a high bilirubin, a high ALP and a raised white cell count. An ultrasound showed a wide bile duct with a stone at its end.

Mr. Adel was a little muddled and kept asking where he was. His son said he was normally sharp and still drove. Dr. Karim sent blood cultures and gave him a litre of fluid, after which his blood pressure rose a little.

Dr. Karim started oral co-amoxiclav and planned an ERCP for the next routine list in a week.
h: started oral co-amoxiclav and planned an ERCP for the next routine list in a week

a.o: Dr. Karim gave Mr. Adel oral antibiotics and a routine ERCP only.
a.x: He needed IV antibiotics and an urgent ERCP to drain the duct.
a.w: Infection behind a blocked bile duct can kill fast. Low blood pressure and confusion mean the duct needs draining urgently.

a.o: Dr. Karim sent blood cultures from Mr. Adel before any antibiotics.
a.x: Blood cultures were unnecessary for a man with yellow skin.
a.w: They guide antibiotics in a septic patient.

a.o: Dr. Karim gave Mr. Adel IV fluids when his blood pressure dropped.
a.x: IV fluids were not needed for a man with yellow skin like him.
a.w: His blood pressure was low from sepsis.

a.o: Dr. Karim did an ultrasound of Mr. Adel's liver and bile ducts.
a.x: The ultrasound scan was unnecessary for a man with yellow skin.
a.w: It showed the stone blocking the duct.

s:
Mr. Raafat, 70, came in with a lump in his right groin that has been there for years. It always went back in when he lay down. Since this morning it has been hard, very painful and will not go back. He has vomited three times.

Dr. Tarek examined him and found a tense, tender, red lump in the groin that did not go back with gentle pressure. His belly was a little swollen.

He checked his blood tests, which showed a raised white cell count and lactate, and his heart and chest, which were normal.

Mr. Raafat said he had not passed wind since the morning. He lives alone and his daughter brought him in. He asked whether he could go home and come back for an operation later.

Dr. Tarek gave him pain relief and sent him home with a routine referral to the hernia clinic.
h: sent him home with a routine referral to the hernia clinic

a.o: Dr. Tarek sent Mr. Raafat home with a stuck and painful hernia.
a.x: He needed an urgent surgical review for emergency surgery now.
a.w: A hard, painful hernia that won't go back, with vomiting, may be strangulated. The bowel can die within hours.

a.o: Dr. Tarek checked Mr. Raafat's lactate level with his blood tests.
a.x: His lactate level was not needed for a man with a sore hernia.
a.w: A high lactate can mean the bowel is losing blood.

a.o: Dr. Tarek examined Mr. Raafat's belly for any swelling or tenderness.
a.x: His belly was off topic for a man with a lump in his groin.
a.w: A swollen belly can mean the bowel is blocked.

a.o: Dr. Tarek gave Mr. Raafat pain relief for his painful hernia.
a.x: Pain relief should have waited until a surgeon had seen him.
a.w: Pain relief is kind and safe.

t: Fever after bowel surgery called a chest infection
s:
Mr. Ehab, 61, had part of his bowel removed for cancer five days ago, with the two ends joined together. He was eating well on day three. Since yesterday he has had a fever of 38.4°C and a pulse of 118.

Dr. Hany found his belly more tender than the day before, with some swelling. His wound looked clean and dry. He heard a few crackles at the base of the left lung.

His CRP had gone up from 110 yesterday to 290 today. His urine output had fallen overnight. Dr. Hany checked his calves, which were soft, and his drip site, which was clean.

Mr. Ehab said he felt unwell, had stopped eating and had new pain across his belly. His wife said he seemed confused this morning. The nurse noted he had not opened his bowels since the operation.

Dr. Hany wrote "likely chest infection" and started oral antibiotics, without a CT scan of the belly.
h: wrote "likely chest infection" and started oral antibiotics, without a CT scan of the belly

a.o: Dr. Hany called Mr. Ehab's fever a chest infection, with no CT scan.
a.x: He needed an urgent belly CT scan and a senior surgical review.
a.w: Fever, a fast pulse, rising CRP and a worse belly around day five after bowel surgery suggest a leak, which can be deadly.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked Mr. Ehab's calves for any swelling or tenderness.
a.x: His calves were off topic for a man with a fever after surgery.
a.w: A clot is a common cause of fever after surgery.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked Mr. Ehab's drip site for any redness or swelling.
a.x: Checking the drip site was unnecessary for a fever after surgery.
a.w: An infected drip can cause fever.

a.o: Dr. Hany listened to Mr. Ehab's chest as part of looking for a cause.
a.x: His chest was off topic for a man with a fever after surgery.
a.w: A chest infection is a common cause of fever after surgery.

t: Warfarin carried on before a hip replacement
s:
Mrs. Aziza, 72, came to the pre-op clinic before a planned hip replacement next week. She has atrial fibrillation and takes warfarin. Her INR is usually 2 to 3. She has never had a stroke and her heart valves are normal.

Dr. Karim checked her blood pressure, which was normal, and her blood count and kidney tests, which were fine. Her ECG showed atrial fibrillation with a normal rate.

He asked about her teeth and any loose caps, and checked her skin over the hip for any sores.

Mrs. Aziza lives with her husband and was keen to get the operation done. She asked how long she would stay in hospital. Her husband asked if she needed to change anything before the day.

Dr. Karim told her to keep taking her warfarin as usual up to the day of surgery.
h: told her to keep taking her warfarin as usual up to the day of surgery

a.o: Dr. Karim told Mrs. Aziza to keep taking warfarin up to surgery.
a.x: She needed her warfarin stopped five days before, with an INR.
a.w: Warfarin left on causes heavy bleeding during a hip replacement. Most people with AF and no clot history don't need bridging.

a.o: Dr. Karim did a heart tracing on Mrs. Aziza before her operation.
a.x: The heart tracing was unnecessary before a hip replacement.
a.w: It checks her heart rate before an anesthetic.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked the skin over Mrs. Aziza's hip for any sores.
a.x: The skin over her hip was off topic before a hip replacement.
a.w: A sore near the wound can infect the new joint.

a.o: Dr. Karim asked Mrs. Aziza about her teeth and any recent infections.
a.x: Her teeth were off topic for a woman having a hip replacement.
a.w: Loose teeth can be knocked out when the breathing tube goes in.

t: Diabetes tablet not stopped before bowel surgery
s:
Mr. Medhat, 57, has type 2 diabetes and is booked for bowel surgery in two days. He takes metformin and dapagliflozin. His HbA1c is 58. He will need bowel preparation and will not eat for a day before the operation.

Dr. Hany checked his blood pressure, kidney tests and blood count, which were all normal. He told him to stop metformin on the morning of surgery.

He arranged blood sugar checks every two hours on the ward on the day of surgery, and planned to restart his tablets once he was eating.

Mr. Medhat works as an engineer and asked many questions about the operation. He said he was worried about his sugar going too low while he was not eating.

Dr. Hany told him to keep taking dapagliflozin as normal, including on the day of surgery.
h: told him to keep taking dapagliflozin as normal, including on the day of surgery

a.o: Dr. Hany told Mr. Medhat to keep dapagliflozin up to surgery.
a.x: He needed it stopped at least three days before surgery.
a.w: SGLT2 drugs with fasting and surgery can cause ketoacidosis even with a normal blood sugar, so it is easily missed.

a.o: Dr. Hany stopped Mr. Medhat's metformin on the day of his surgery.
a.x: Metformin should have been stopped a full week before surgery.
a.w: Stopping it on the day is enough for most people with normal kidneys.

a.o: Dr. Hany planned regular sugar checks for Mr. Medhat on the ward.
a.x: Sugar checks were unnecessary after an operation on the bowel.
a.w: Fasting and surgery can push sugar up or down.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked Mr. Medhat's kidney tests before his operation.
a.x: Kidney tests were off topic before an operation on the bowel.
a.w: Kidney function guides diabetes drug safety.

s:
Ms. Shereen, 34, is booked for a planned gallbladder removal at 2 pm tomorrow. She is healthy, with no heartburn or diabetes. She has had gallstone pain three times this year.
