Dr. Karim checked her blood tests, which were normal, and her pregnancy test, which was negative.

He explained the operation and its risks, including bile leak and injury to the bile duct, and she signed the consent form.

Ms. Shereen said she gets bad headaches and feels faint if she does not drink for a long time. She works as a teacher and had arranged a day off. She asked when she should stop eating and drinking.

Dr. Karim told her to have nothing to eat or drink at all from midnight, including water.
h: told her to have nothing to eat or drink at all from midnight, including water

a.o: Dr. Karim told Ms. Shereen to stop all fluids from midnight.
a.x: She could drink clear fluids up to two hours before.
a.w: Long fasting from fluids causes thirst, headache and dehydration, with no gain in safety.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked a pregnancy test for Ms. Shereen before surgery.
a.x: A pregnancy test was unnecessary before gallbladder surgery.
a.w: Surgery and anesthetic drugs can harm an early pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Karim explained the small risk of a bile duct injury to her.
a.x: Explaining the bile duct risk was far too frightening for her.
a.w: Serious risks must be explained for proper consent.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Ms. Shereen's blood tests before her operation.
a.x: Her blood tests were off topic before a gallbladder operation.
a.w: They give a baseline before surgery.

t: Burst wound covered with dry gauze
s:
Mrs. Hoda, 67, had an open operation on her bowel eight days ago. She is overweight and has diabetes. This morning the nurse found pink fluid soaking her dressing. When she coughed, the wound opened and bowel could be seen.

Dr. Tarek was called. Mrs. Hoda was frightened but her pulse and blood pressure were normal. He laid her flat with her knees bent and gave her pain relief.

He sent blood tests and a group and save, and told her not to eat or drink.

Mrs. Hoda said she had been coughing a lot for two days. Her husband was in the room and very upset. The nurse said the wound had looked red at the edges yesterday.

Dr. Tarek covered the open wound with dry gauze and booked her for the next routine theatre list in two days.
h: covered the open wound with dry gauze and booked her for the next routine theatre list in two days

a.o: Dr. Tarek covered Mrs. Hoda's burst wound with dry gauze only.
a.x: Her bowel needed warm, wet packs and urgent theatre time.
a.w: A burst wound needs urgent closure. Dry gauze sticks to and damages the bowel.

a.o: Dr. Tarek laid Mrs. Hoda flat with her knees bent up on the bed.
a.x: She should have sat up straight in the bed instead of lying.
a.w: This takes pressure off the wound.

a.o: Dr. Tarek told Mrs. Hoda not to eat or drink anything for now.
a.x: Eating and drinking were fine for her while she waited.
a.w: She will need an anesthetic soon.

a.o: Dr. Tarek sent a group and save blood sample for Mrs. Hoda.
a.x: A group and save was unnecessary for a burst wound like hers.
a.w: She may need blood in theatre.

t: Breast lump watched for three months
s:
Mrs. Laila, 47, found a lump in her left breast two weeks ago. It does not hurt. She has no family history of breast cancer. Her periods are regular.

Dr. Ghada examined both breasts and armpits. She found a hard, 2 cm lump in the upper outer part of the left breast that did not move easily. There were no lumps in the armpit.

She asked about nipple discharge, which Mrs. Laila did not have, and about skin changes, and saw a slight dimple over the lump when Mrs. Laila raised her arms.

Mrs. Laila said she was very busy with her three children and her job. She hoped it was nothing, and said her friend had a lump that turned out to be a cyst.

Dr. Ghada said it was probably a cyst and told her to come back in three months if it was still there.
h: told her to come back in three months if it was still there

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mrs. Laila to wait three months with a hard lump.
a.x: She needed an urgent breast clinic referral, seen within 2 weeks.
a.w: A hard, fixed lump with skin dimpling in a woman over 30 may be cancer and needs to be seen within two weeks.

a.o: Dr. Ghada examined both of Mrs. Laila's armpits for any lumps.
a.x: The armpits were off topic for a woman with a lump in her breast.
a.w: Breast cancer often spreads to the armpit glands first.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mrs. Laila about any discharge from the nipple.
a.x: Nipple discharge was off topic for a woman with a breast lump.
a.w: Bloody discharge can be a sign of cancer.

a.o: Dr. Ghada looked at Mrs. Laila's breasts with her arms raised up.
a.x: Looking with her arms raised was unnecessary for a breast lump.
a.w: Raising the arms can show skin dimpling over a cancer.

t: Hard testicle lump called a cyst
s:
Mr. Mostafa, 28, noticed a lump on his right testicle a month ago. It does not hurt. He has no fever and no urine symptoms. He had an undescended testicle as a baby that was fixed with surgery.

Dr. Ihab examined him and found a hard, painless lump within the right testicle itself. He could not feel above it as separate. The left side was normal.

He asked about sexual partners and sent a urine test, which was clear.

Mr. Mostafa was embarrassed and had waited before coming. He said he had read online that most lumps are harmless. He plays football and wondered if it was an injury.

Dr. Ihab said it was probably a cyst and told him to come back if it got bigger, without an ultrasound.
h: told him to come back if it got bigger, without an ultrasound

a.o: Dr. Ihab called Mr. Mostafa's testicle lump a cyst with no scan.
a.x: He needed an urgent ultrasound scan and an urgent urology referral.
a.w: A hard lump within the testicle in a young man may be cancer, and an undescended testicle raises the risk.

a.o: Dr. Ihab sent a urine test for Mr. Mostafa to look for infection.
a.x: The urine test was off topic for a man with a lump in his testicle.
a.w: A urine infection can spread to the testicle.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mr. Mostafa gently about his recent sexual partners.
a.x: Asking about his sexual partners was intrusive and off topic.
a.w: Sexual infections can cause testicle swelling.

a.o: Dr. Ihab examined Mr. Mostafa's left testicle as well as the right.
a.x: Examining the left side was unnecessary for a lump on the right.
a.w: Comparing both sides helps find what's abnormal.

t: Cold, pale leg sent for a routine clinic
s:
Mr. Salah, 71, came in with sudden pain in his left leg that started three hours ago. He has atrial fibrillation and does not take a blood thinner. He smokes. He walked fine yesterday.

Dr. Tarek found the left leg pale and cold from the knee down. He could not feel any pulses in the left foot. Mr. Salah had pins and needles in his toes but could still move them.

He checked the right leg, which had normal pulses, and did an ECG, which showed atrial fibrillation.

Mr. Salah said the pain was severe and constant. His wife said he had been thinking of seeing someone about his heart rhythm. He asked for something for the pain, and Dr. Tarek gave him morphine.

Dr. Tarek started aspirin and referred him to the vascular clinic for next week.
h: started aspirin and referred him to the vascular clinic for next week

a.o: Dr. Tarek sent Mr. Salah's pulseless leg to a routine clinic.
a.x: He needed IV heparin and emergency vascular surgery at once.
a.w: A sudden cold, pale, pulseless leg is a blocked artery. The leg can be lost within six hours.

a.o: Dr. Tarek checked the pulses in Mr. Salah's right leg as well.
a.x: Checking the right leg was unnecessary for a problem on the left.
a.w: Comparing both legs shows the problem is one-sided.

a.o: Dr. Tarek did a heart tracing on Mr. Salah as part of his work-up.
a.x: The heart tracing was off topic for a man with a cold leg.
a.w: AF is the likely source of the clot.

a.o: Dr. Tarek checked whether Mr. Salah could still move his toes.
a.x: Moving his toes was off topic for a man with a cold, pale leg.
a.w: Loss of movement or feeling means the leg is in danger.

s:
Mr. Waleed, 35, came in with a painful swelling next to his anus for four days. It hurts to sit and to open his bowels. He has a mild fever. He has no bowel problems usually and no weight loss.

Dr. Ghada examined him and found a hot, red, tender, swollen lump next to the anus that felt soft in the middle. She did not do an internal exam because of pain.

She checked his blood sugar, which was normal, and asked about bleeding, which he did not have.

Mr. Waleed works as a taxi driver and said he could not sit for his shifts. He was keen to avoid surgery and asked if tablets would be enough.

Dr. Ghada gave him a week of oral antibiotics and told him to come back if it did not get better.
h: gave him a week of oral antibiotics and told him to come back if it did not get better

a.o: Dr. Ghada treated Mr. Waleed's abscess with antibiotics alone.
a.x: He needed same-day referral for surgical drainage.
a.w: A soft, pus-filled abscess needs draining. Antibiotics alone don't reach it, and it can spread.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mr. Waleed's blood sugar during the visit.
a.x: His blood sugar was off topic for a man with an abscess there.
a.w: Diabetes raises the risk of abscesses.

a.o: Dr. Ghada skipped an internal exam because of Mr. Waleed's pain.
a.x: She should have done the internal exam anyway despite his pain.
a.w: It can be done under anesthetic if needed.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mr. Waleed about any bleeding from his bottom.
a.x: Bleeding was off topic for a man with an abscess on his bottom.
a.w: Bleeding may point to another bowel problem.

t: Left rib pain after a fall sent home
s:
Mr. Omar, 26, fell off his motorbike two hours ago and hit the left side of his chest. He has pain in his lower left ribs and his left shoulder tip. He had glandular fever last month.

Dr. Karim found his pulse was 112 and his blood pressure 108/70. His lower left ribs were tender, and his belly was a little tender on the left. His chest X-ray showed no broken ribs or collapsed lung.

He checked his neck and spine, which were not tender, and his pelvis, which was stable. He gave him paracetamol and ibuprofen.

Mr. Omar wanted to go home, saying he felt fine apart from the pain. He was pale but chatty. His friend said he would stay with him that night.

Dr. Karim said it was bruised ribs and sent him home, without a CT scan of the belly.
h: said it was bruised ribs and sent him home, without a CT scan of the belly

a.o: Dr. Karim sent Mr. Omar home after his left side injury at once.
a.x: He needed a belly CT and close watching for a spleen injury.
a.w: Shoulder tip pain and a fast pulse after a left side blow suggest a torn spleen, and glandular fever makes it fragile.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Mr. Omar's spine for tenderness after the fall.
a.x: His spine was off topic for a man with pain in his left ribs.
a.w: A motorbike fall can injure the spine.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Mr. Omar's pelvis for any pain or movement.
a.x: Checking his pelvis was unnecessary for pain in the left ribs.
a.w: A broken pelvis can bleed heavily.

a.o: Dr. Karim did a chest X-ray on Mr. Omar to look for broken ribs.
a.x: The chest X-ray was unnecessary for pain in the left ribs.
a.w: It rules out a collapsed lung.

t: Older man with broken ribs sent home on paracetamol
s:
Mr. Fouad, 79, slipped in his bathroom yesterday and hit his right side on the bath. He has COPD and uses inhalers. He lives alone. He came in because the pain made it hard to breathe.

Dr. Karim found four broken ribs on the right on the chest X-ray, with no collapsed lung or fluid. His oxygen was 91% on air and his breathing rate was 24. He could not take a deep breath or cough because of the pain.

He checked his head for injury, which was fine, and asked why he fell. Mr. Fouad said he slipped on a wet floor and did not black out.

Mr. Fouad said he wanted to go home to his cat. His neighbour usually checks on him once a day. He had not eaten since the fall because moving hurt so much.

Dr. Karim gave him paracetamol and sent him home with advice to rest.
h: gave him paracetamol and sent him home with advice to rest

a.o: Dr. Karim sent Mr. Fouad home with broken ribs on paracetamol.
a.x: He needed admission for strong pain relief and chest physio.
a.w: Older people with three or more broken ribs and lung disease often get pneumonia if pain stops them coughing.

a.o: Dr. Karim asked Mr. Fouad why he fell and whether he blacked out.
a.x: The cause of the fall was off topic for a man with broken ribs.
a.w: A blackout would change the plan.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Mr. Fouad's head for any injury from the fall.
a.x: His head was off topic for a man with broken ribs like his.
a.w: Older people often hit their head when they fall.

a.o: Dr. Karim did a chest X-ray on Mr. Fouad to look at his ribs.
a.x: The chest X-ray was unnecessary for a man with broken ribs.
a.w: It rules out a collapsed lung or bleeding.

t: Burns fluids given without working out the amount
s:
Mr. Sherif, 40, was burned in a kitchen fire an hour ago. He weighs 80 kg. His burns cover the front of his chest, belly and both arms, about 27% of his body, with deep and partial thickness burns. His face and voice are normal.

Dr. Tarek gave him oxygen and IV morphine. He checked his airway, which was clear, with no soot in his mouth and no hoarse voice.

He removed his rings and watch, cooled the burns with running water for 20 minutes and covered them with cling film. He put in a urine catheter.

Mr. Sherif was shivering and asked for a blanket. His wife was in the room, crying. He said he had tried to put out a pan fire with water.

Dr. Tarek started a litre of saline over eight hours and wrote "adjust later", without working out his fluid needs.
h: started a litre of saline over eight hours and wrote "adjust later", without working out his fluid needs

a.o: Dr. Tarek gave Mr. Sherif a guessed amount of burns fluid by eye.
a.x: He needed fluids worked out with the Parkland formula.
a.w: Large burns lose a lot of fluid. Too little causes shock and kidney failure. Parkland here is about 8.6 litres in 24 hours.

a.o: Dr. Tarek removed the rings from Mr. Sherif's burned fingers.
a.x: Removing the rings was unnecessary for a man with burns.
a.w: Swelling can cut off blood to the fingers.

a.o: Dr. Tarek put in a urinary catheter to measure Mr. Sherif's urine.
a.x: The urinary catheter was unnecessary for a man with burns.
a.w: Urine output guides the fluids.

a.o: Dr. Tarek covered Mr. Sherif's burns loosely with cling film.
a.x: Covering the burns with cling film was the wrong choice.
a.w: Cling film is clean, keeps heat in and doesn't stick.

t: Jaundice after gallbladder surgery called normal
s:
Mrs. Salwa, 49, had keyhole surgery to remove her gallbladder three days ago. The operation note says it was difficult because of swelling. Since yesterday she has had pain under her right ribs, a fever of 38.1°C and yellow eyes.

Dr. Hany checked her wounds, which were clean. Her blood tests showed a bilirubin of 70 and a high ALP, which were normal before surgery. Her white cell count was raised.

He checked her calves, which were soft, and listened to her chest, which was clear. He gave her paracetamol for the pain.

Mrs. Salwa said she was feeling worse each day and could not eat. Her urine had become very dark. Her daughter asked why she was still in pain when she had been told the operation would fix it.

Dr. Hany wrote "normal after surgery" and planned to send her home tomorrow, without a scan.
h: wrote "normal after surgery" and planned to send her home tomorrow, without a scan

a.o: Dr. Hany called Mrs. Salwa's jaundice after her surgery normal.
a.x: She needed an urgent scan and MRCP for a likely bile duct injury.
a.w: New jaundice, pain and fever after a hard gallbladder operation suggest the bile duct was damaged or clipped.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked Mrs. Salwa's calves for any swelling after surgery.
a.x: Her calves were unnecessary to check for a woman with jaundice.
a.w: A clot can cause fever after surgery.

a.o: Dr. Hany listened to Mrs. Salwa's chest as part of his review.
a.x: Her chest was off topic for a woman with jaundice after surgery.
a.w: A chest infection can cause fever after surgery.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked Mrs. Salwa's wounds for any redness or leakage.
a.x: Her wounds were off topic for a woman with jaundice after surgery.
a.w: A wound infection can cause fever.

s:
Mrs. Inas, 62, came in with pain in the lower left belly and fever for four days. She has known diverticular disease. Her temperature was 38.7°C and her pulse 106.

Dr. Karim found her tender in the lower left belly with a firm lump. Her CRP was 240. A CT scan showed inflamed diverticula with a 6 cm abscess next to the bowel. There was no free air.

He started a drip, gave her pain relief and sent blood cultures.

Mrs. Inas said she had felt worse each day despite antibiotics from her GP. She was shivering and had not eaten for two days. Her husband asked whether she would need an operation.

Dr. Karim continued oral co-amoxiclav and planned to send her home in the morning.
h: continued oral co-amoxiclav and planned to send her home in the morning

a.o: Dr. Karim kept Mrs. Inas on tablets with a large abscess.
a.x: She needed IV antibiotics and drainage under scan guidance.
a.w: Abscesses over about 4 cm rarely settle with antibiotics alone and can burst into the belly.

a.o: Dr. Karim did a CT scan of Mrs. Inas's belly to look at the bowel.
a.x: The CT scan was unnecessary for a woman with diverticulitis.
a.w: It showed the abscess and no burst bowel.

a.o: Dr. Karim sent blood cultures from Mrs. Inas when she had a fever.
a.x: Blood cultures were off topic for a woman with diverticulitis.
a.w: She had signs of sepsis.

a.o: Dr. Karim started a drip for Mrs. Inas as she was not drinking well.
a.x: The drip was unnecessary for a woman with diverticulitis.
a.w: She was dehydrated and not eating.

t: Baby with green vomiting sent home
s:
Baby Malak, 2 weeks old, was brought in with three episodes of green vomiting since the morning. She was born at full term and had been feeding well. She passed meconium on her first day.

Dr. Dina found her alert, with a soft belly that was not swollen. Her temperature was normal and her weight was the same as at birth. Her nappy was wet.

She checked her blood sugar, which was normal, and her hip and spine, which were normal.

Her mother said the vomit was dark green like spinach, not milky. She had changed formula last week. She asked if the new milk could be to blame. The baby was crying and drawing her legs up.

Dr. Dina said the new milk was to blame, told her to change back and sent her home.
h: Dr. Dina said the new milk was to blame, told her to change back and sent her home

a.o: Dr. Dina sent Baby Malak home after an episode of green vomiting.
a.x: She needed an urgent contrast study and surgical review.
a.w: Green vomiting in a newborn is twisted bowel until proven otherwise. The bowel can die within hours, even with a soft belly.

a.o: Dr. Dina checked Baby Malak's weight against her birth weight.
a.x: Her weight was off topic for a baby who was being sick like this.
a.w: Poor weight gain can mean a feeding problem.

a.o: Dr. Dina checked Baby Malak's nappy for any stool or blood.
a.x: The nappy was off topic for a baby who was being sick like this.
a.w: Wet nappies show she isn't dehydrated.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked Baby Malak's mother when the baby first passed meconium.
a.x: Meconium was off topic for a baby who was being sick like this.
a.w: Late meconium can point to a blocked bowel.

s:
Mr. Nabil, 81, lives in a care home and has Parkinson's disease. He has had a hugely swollen belly for two days and has not opened his bowels or passed wind. He has vomited once. He often gets constipated.

Dr. Hany found a tight, drum-like belly that was only mildly tender. His pulse was 98 and his temperature normal. A belly X-ray showed a huge loop of large bowel shaped like a coffee bean, rising out of the pelvis.

He sent blood tests, which showed a normal lactate, and checked his hernia sites, which were normal. He put in a drip.

The care home nurse said he had been more confused and was not eating. His son asked whether he would need a big operation at his age. Mr. Nabil was uncomfortable but able to talk.

Dr. Hany wrote "severe constipation" and gave him a phosphate enema and senna, without asking the surgeons to untwist the bowel.
h: wrote "severe constipation" and gave him a phosphate enema and senna, without asking the surgeons to untwist the bowel

a.o: Dr. Hany treated Mr. Nabil's sigmoid volvulus as constipation.
a.x: He needed urgent untwisting with a flexible scope.
a.w: A coffee bean loop is twisted bowel. Laxatives don't untwist it, and the bowel can die or burst.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked all of Mr. Nabil's hernia sites during the exam.
a.x: Hernias were off topic for an older man with a swollen belly.
a.w: A stuck hernia can block the bowel.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked Mr. Nabil's lactate level with his blood tests.
a.x: His lactate level was unnecessary for a man with constipation.
a.w: A high lactate can mean the bowel is dying.

a.o: Dr. Hany put in a drip for Mr. Nabil as he had stopped drinking.
a.x: The drip was unnecessary for an older man with constipation.
a.w: He was vomiting and not eating.

t: Low urine after surgery given furosemide
s:
Mr. Gamal, 74, had a hip replacement yesterday under a spinal anesthetic. He has an enlarged prostate and takes tamsulosin, which was stopped before surgery. He has passed only 40 ml of urine in the last eight hours.

Dr. Karim was called by the nurse. Mr. Gamal had lower belly pain and felt he needed to pass urine but could not. His blood pressure was normal and his pulse 92.

He checked his blood tests, which showed normal kidney function, and his fluid chart, which showed he had drunk well and had a drip running.

Mr. Gamal was restless and kept trying to get out of bed. His wife said he gets up three times a night to pass urine at home. The nurse felt a firm, tender swelling above his pubic bone.

Dr. Karim wrote "low urine output, likely fluid overload" and gave 40 mg of IV furosemide, without a bladder scan.
h: gave 40 mg of IV furosemide, without a bladder scan

a.o: Dr. Karim gave Mr. Gamal furosemide for low urine, with no scan.
a.x: He needed a bladder scan and then a catheter for retention.
a.w: Spinal anesthesia, a big prostate and a tender swollen bladder mean urine retention. Furosemide only makes the bladder fuller.

a.o: Dr. Karim looked at Mr. Gamal's fluid chart from the last day.
a.x: The fluid chart was off topic for a man passing little urine.
a.w: It shows if he is dry or overloaded.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Mr. Gamal's kidney function with a blood test.
a.x: Checking his kidney function was unnecessary for low urine.
a.w: Kidney damage can cause low urine.

a.o: Dr. Karim asked Mr. Gamal about any past problems with his prostate.
a.x: His prostate was off topic for a man passing little urine.
a.w: A big prostate raises the risk of retention.

t: Leg ulcer bandaged tight without checking the pulses
s:
Mrs. Nagwa, 73, has had an ulcer above her left ankle for three months. She has varicose veins and her ankle skin is brown and hard. She also smokes and has pain in her calf after walking 100 meters, which goes with rest.

Dr. Fady measured the ulcer and took a photo. It was shallow, with a clean base. He sent a swab, which grew skin bacteria only, and did not start antibiotics as there was no spreading redness.

He checked her blood sugar, which was normal, and gave advice about raising the leg when sitting.

Mrs. Nagwa said her legs feel cold at night. She lives with her daughter, who changes the dressing. She asked whether the ulcer would ever heal.

Dr. Fady started strong compression bandages, without checking the foot pulses or the ankle-brachial pressure index.
h: started strong compression bandages, without checking the foot pulses or the ankle-brachial pressure index

a.o: Dr. Fady started tight compression for Mrs. Nagwa unchecked.
a.x: She needed her foot pulses and ABPI checked first of all.
a.w: Calf pain on walking and cold legs suggest blocked arteries. Tight bandages on a leg with poor blood flow can cause gangrene.

a.o: Dr. Fady didn't give Mrs. Nagwa antibiotics for her clean leg ulcer.
a.x: Antibiotics were needed for every ulcer on the leg like hers.
a.w: A swab growing skin bacteria without spreading redness doesn't need treatment.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Nagwa's blood sugar during the visit.
a.x: Her blood sugar was off topic for a woman with a leg ulcer.
a.w: Diabetes slows healing and changes the plan.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised Mrs. Nagwa to raise her leg when she was sitting.
a.x: Raising the leg is useless for a woman with a leg ulcer.
a.w: It helps swelling from vein disease.

t: Child after surgery given dextrose-only fluids
s:
Rana, 7, had her appendix removed yesterday. She is still not drinking much and feels sick. She weighs 22 kg. She was put on a drip of 5% dextrose alone at full maintenance rate.

Dr. Karim saw her this morning. She had a headache and had vomited twice. Her wound was clean and her belly was soft. Her temperature was normal.

He checked her blood tests, which showed a sodium of 128, down from 138 before surgery. Her blood sugar was normal.

Her mother said Rana seemed sleepy and not herself. The nurse said she had passed less urine than expected. Rana was given anti-sickness medicine, which did not help.

Dr. Karim kept the 5% dextrose drip running at the same rate and planned to recheck her blood tests tomorrow.
h: kept the 5% dextrose drip running at the same rate and planned to recheck her blood tests tomorrow

a.o: Dr. Karim kept Rana on dextrose-only fluids as her sodium fell.
a.x: Rana needed an isotonic fluid instead, and a sodium recheck.
a.w: After surgery, children hold on to water. Dextrose-only fluids drop the sodium, which can cause brain swelling and fits.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Rana's blood sugar while she was on the drip.
a.x: Her blood sugar was unnecessary for a child on a fluid drip.
a.w: Dextrose drips and fasting can change blood sugar.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Rana's wound for any redness after surgery.
a.x: Her wound was off topic for a child with a falling sodium.
a.w: A wound infection can cause fever and sickness.

a.o: Dr. Karim gave Rana anti-sickness medicine when she started vomiting.
a.x: Anti-sickness medicine was unnecessary for a child like Rana.
a.w: Feeling sick is common after surgery.

t: Painful red finger tip treated with cream
s:
Mr. Kareem, 45, came in with a throbbing pain at the tip of his right index finger for three days. He cut it on a fish bone while cooking. He works as a chef.

Dr. Tarek found the pad of the fingertip swollen, tense, red and very tender. The pain kept him awake. There was no redness spreading up the hand or arm, and the finger could bend and straighten fully.

He asked about diabetes, which he does not have, and checked his tetanus status, which was up to date.

Mr. Kareem said he needed to get back to work because the restaurant was busy. He asked if he could have something to put on it.

Dr. Tarek gave him antibiotic cream and told him to come back if it got worse, without draining it.
h: gave him antibiotic cream and told him to come back if it got worse, without draining it

a.o: Dr. Tarek gave Mr. Kareem a cream for a tense fingertip abscess.
a.x: He needed the abscess drained under a nerve block, not a cream.
a.w: Pus in the fingertip pad is under pressure and can spread to the bone. Cream doesn't reach it.

a.o: Dr. Tarek checked how well Mr. Kareem could move the swollen finger.
a.x: Finger movement was off topic for a man with a sore fingertip.
a.w: Pain on moving the finger can mean infection of the tendon sheath.

a.o: Dr. Tarek checked Mr. Kareem's tetanus status during the visit.
a.x: Tetanus was off topic for a man with a sore, swollen fingertip.
a.w: A cut from a fish bone is a dirty wound.

a.o: Dr. Tarek asked Mr. Kareem whether he has diabetes or other illness.
a.x: Diabetes was off topic for a man with a sore, swollen fingertip.
a.w: Diabetes raises the risk of serious hand infections.

s:
It was almost five in the afternoon when Mr. Tarek rushed into the ER carrying his nephew Omar, a skinny nine-year-old with a towel pressed to his left arm. Omar had crashed his bicycle into broken glass outside the bakery. By the time they arrived the bleeding had stopped, but the towel was soaked and Omar was pale and crying.

Nurse Salma checked him quickly. His heart was racing at 112, but his blood pressure was fine and he was talking clearly, so she put him in the yellow area. Omar weighed 28 kg, had no allergies his uncle knew of, and had his last tetanus shot at six.

Dr. Hany unwrapped the towel and found a clean 5 cm cut on the inside of the forearm. Omar could move every finger. "We'll need stitches," Dr. Hany said. Mr. Tarek nodded. "His parents are at work, but go ahead, I'm responsible for him." Dr. Hany washed the wound, numbed it with lidocaine and closed it with six neat stitches. He gave Omar 420 mg of paracetamol for the pain and sent him home with his uncle and a wound-care leaflet.
h: "His parents are at work, but go ahead, I'm responsible for him."

a.o: Dr. Hany stitched Omar's arm on his uncle's say alone.
a.x: He should have phoned Omar's parents for consent first.
a.w: An uncle is not Omar's legal guardian. The bleeding had stopped, so this was not an emergency and there was time to reach a parent.

a.o: Nurse Salma sent Omar to the yellow area despite his racing heart.
a.x: Omar should have gone straight to the red area of the department.
a.w: Yellow was right: the bleeding had stopped, his blood pressure was normal and he was talking. A fast heart in a scared, crying child is not shock.

a.o: Dr. Hany gave Omar 420 mg of paracetamol, too much for a 28 kg boy.
a.x: Omar should have had 280 mg of paracetamol for his weight.
a.w: 420 mg is 15 mg/kg for a 28 kg child, a normal dose.

a.o: Omar went home with no tetanus shot after falling on dirty glass.
a.x: Omar should have had a tetanus booster before he left.
a.w: His last tetanus shot was three years ago. A dirty wound needs a booster only if the last one was more than 5 years ago.

t: Blood given to a Jehovah's Witness who refused it
s:
Mrs. Mona, 52, is a Jehovah's Witness. She came in with heavy bleeding from fibroids and her hemoglobin was 68. She was awake, calm and clear. She carries a signed card refusing blood, made last year.

Dr. Mervat explained the risks of refusing blood, including that she could die. Mrs. Mona repeated them back in her own words and still refused. She agreed to IV iron, tranexamic acid and other blood-free treatments.

Dr. Mervat asked to speak with her alone, away from her family, to check no one was pressuring her. Mrs. Mona said the choice was her own.

Her son, who is not a Witness, begged the team to give the blood. He said his mother would thank them later. The nurse wrote the refusal clearly in the notes.

When her hemoglobin fell to 60 the next day, Dr. Mervat gave two units of blood, writing "life comes first".
h: Dr. Mervat gave two units of blood, writing "life comes first"

a.o: Dr. Mervat gave blood to Mrs. Mona against her clear refusal.
a.x: She should have respected her refusal and used blood-free care.
a.w: An adult with capacity can refuse any treatment, even to save her life. Giving blood anyway is assault.

a.o: Dr. Mervat spoke with Mrs. Mona alone, away from her family.
a.x: Speaking to her alone was rude to the family who came with her.
a.w: Checking she wasn't pressured is part of a valid refusal.

a.o: Dr. Mervat started Mrs. Mona on IV iron to help build up her blood.
a.x: IV iron was pointless for a woman who was bleeding like this.
a.w: Blood-free ways to raise hemoglobin should be used.

a.o: Dr. Mervat told Mrs. Mona honestly that she could die without blood.
a.x: Telling her she could die was far too frightening for her.
a.w: A refusal is only valid if she knows the risks.

t: Patient with capacity kept from leaving
s:
Mr. Hamdy, 66, was admitted with a chest infection two days ago. He is improving on IV antibiotics. This morning he said he wanted to go home to look after his wife, who has dementia.

Dr. Ihab checked his oxygen, which was 95%, and his confusion score, which was normal. Mr. Hamdy knew where he was and the date.

He explained that leaving early could make the infection worse and even risk his life. Mr. Hamdy said he understood, repeated the risks back and weighed them against his wife being alone.

Mr. Hamdy said his neighbour could not stay with his wife after today. He asked for tablets to take home. His daughter lives abroad and agreed with his choice on the phone.

Dr. Ihab told the nurses not to let him leave and hid his clothes, writing "unsafe discharge".
h: told the nurses not to let him leave and hid his clothes

a.o: Dr. Ihab stopped Mr. Hamdy leaving even though he had capacity.
a.x: He should have respected the choice and made leaving safe.
a.w: An adult with capacity can make an unwise choice. Keeping him against his will is unlawful.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Hamdy's confusion score before he decided.
a.x: The confusion score was unnecessary for a man wanting to leave.
a.w: Confusion can affect capacity.

a.o: Dr. Ihab explained the risks of leaving clearly to Mr. Hamdy.
a.x: Explaining the risks put too much pressure on Mr. Hamdy.
a.w: He needs the facts to decide.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mr. Hamdy about his wife, who was ill at home.
a.x: His wife at home was off topic for his own treatment.
a.w: His reasons matter in his decision.

t: Do-not-resuscitate order made without telling the patient
s:
Mr. Sayed, 78, has advanced heart failure and kidney disease. He was admitted with breathlessness for the third time this year. He is awake, alert and able to talk about his care.

Dr. Fady reviewed him with the senior doctor. They agreed that CPR would be very unlikely to work and would likely cause harm. His oxygen and fluids were adjusted and he improved a little.

Dr. Fady checked whether Mr. Sayed had any written wishes. He had none. His daughter visits each evening.

Mr. Sayed asked the nurse that morning how long he had left and whether he would go home. The nurse passed the question to Dr. Fady, who was busy with a sick patient on another ward.

Dr. Fady signed a do-not-resuscitate form and filed it in the notes, without telling Mr. Sayed or his family.
h: without telling Mr. Sayed or his family

a.o: Dr. Fady made a no-CPR decision without telling Mr. Sayed.
a.x: He should have talked it over with Mr. Sayed and his wishes.
a.w: Patients have a right to know about a DNR decision unless telling them would cause real harm. He was able and asking.

a.o: Dr. Fady discussed CPR for Mr. Sayed with the senior doctor first.
a.x: The senior doctor was off topic for a decision about CPR.
a.w: DNR decisions should involve a senior doctor.

a.o: Dr. Fady looked for any written wishes that Mr. Sayed had made.
a.x: Looking for written wishes was unnecessary for this decision.
a.w: Advance wishes must be respected.

a.o: Dr. Fady made a decision about CPR for Mr. Sayed at all.
a.x: CPR must always be offered to every patient in hospital.
a.w: Doctors don't have to give CPR that won't work.

t: Diagnosis told to the patient's employer
s:
Mr. Nader, 41, works in a bank. He was diagnosed with HIV last month and is well on treatment. His viral load is now undetectable.

Dr. Ghada checked his blood tests and asked about side effects, which he did not have. She talked about safer sex and partner testing, and he said his wife had been tested and was negative.

She gave him a sick note for two days for a stomach bug, as he had asked.

His manager phoned the clinic to ask why Mr. Nader had been off work and whether there was anything they should know. Mr. Nader had not given consent to share any details with his employer.

Dr. Ghada told the manager that Mr. Nader has HIV but is well controlled.
h: told the manager that Mr. Nader has HIV but is well controlled

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mr. Nader's manager at work that he has HIV.
a.x: She should have shared nothing without his written consent.
a.w: Health details are confidential. Telling an employer without consent is a serious breach and can cost him his job.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mr. Nader about testing for his partner.
a.x: Asking about his partner was intrusive at a routine visit.
a.w: Partners at risk should be offered testing.

a.o: Dr. Ghada gave Mr. Nader a sick note for his time off work.
a.x: Giving him a sick note was a lie told to his employer.
a.w: A sick note for a real illness is correct.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mr. Nader for any side effects of his tablets.
a.x: Side effects of his tablets were off topic at this visit.
a.w: Side effects affect whether he keeps taking treatment.

s:
Mrs. Fatma, 55, moved from Sudan last year and speaks little English. She came to clinic with her 11-year-old son. She has been losing weight and has had blood in her stool.

Dr. Ihab checked her weight, which had fallen 6 kg, and her blood count, which showed anemia. He examined her belly, which was soft.

He needed to ask about her bowel habit, bleeding and family history of cancer, and to explain that a camera test was needed to look for cancer.

A phone interpreter was available within ten minutes. The son spoke English well and offered to help. He was missing school to be there.

Dr. Ihab asked the son to interpret the questions and to tell his mother she might have bowel cancer.
h: asked the son to interpret the questions and to tell his mother she might have bowel cancer

a.o: Dr. Ihab used Mrs. Fatma's 11-year-old son as the interpreter.
a.x: He should have used the phone interpreter instead.
a.w: Children should not interpret, especially bad news. They may leave things out, and it is a burden for them.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mrs. Fatma's weight during the clinic visit.
a.x: Her weight was off topic for a woman being told this news.
a.w: Weight loss is a red flag for bowel cancer.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mrs. Fatma's blood count with her other tests.
a.x: Checking her blood count was unnecessary at this visit.
a.w: Anemia can come from a bleeding bowel cancer.

a.o: Dr. Ihab planned a camera test for Mrs. Fatma in the coming weeks.
a.x: Planning a camera test was too much for Mrs. Fatma right now.
a.w: Bleeding, weight loss and anemia need a camera test.

t: Teenager's request for the pill told to her mother
s:
Nour, 15, came to the clinic alone and asked for the contraceptive pill. She has a boyfriend of 16 and they plan to have sex. She does not want her parents to know.

Dr. Ghada talked with her about the pill, condoms and sexual infections. Nour understood how the pill works and its risks, and could weigh them up. Dr. Ghada encouraged her to talk to a parent, but Nour refused.

She asked about the boyfriend's age and whether Nour felt pressured, to check for abuse. Nour said she did not and felt ready.

She checked her blood pressure, which was normal, and asked about migraines and clots in the family, which she did not have.

Dr. Ghada prescribed the pill, then phoned Nour's mother to tell her, saying "parents have a right to know".
h: phoned Nour's mother to tell her, saying "parents have a right to know"

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Nour's mother about the pill.
a.x: She should have kept Nour's visit confidential.
a.w: A competent teenager has the same right to confidentiality as an adult unless there is a risk of serious harm.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Nour about the age of her boyfriend.
a.x: Asking about her boyfriend's age was intrusive and off topic.
a.w: A much older partner can be a sign of abuse.

a.o: Dr. Ghada encouraged Nour to think about telling a parent.
a.x: Encouraging her to tell a parent was too much pressure.
a.w: Doctors should encourage it, but not force it.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Nour about any migraines or blood clots.
a.x: Migraines and clots were off topic for a girl wanting the pill.
a.w: Some migraines and clot history make the pill unsafe.

s:
Mrs. Asmaa, 34, came in with a vaginal discharge and pelvic pain for a week. She has one partner. Her pregnancy test was negative.

Dr. Ihab took a careful history and checked her temperature, which was 37.8°C. He felt her belly, which was tender low down.

He explained that he needed to do an internal examination and take swabs. Mrs. Asmaa agreed but looked nervous.

A female nurse was free in the next room. Mrs. Asmaa had come alone and said she had a male doctor before who made her uncomfortable.

She works as a pharmacist and said she wanted to get back to work quickly. She asked how long the exam would take and whether it would hurt. Dr. Ihab said it would take a few minutes and she could ask him to stop at any time.

Dr. Ihab did the internal exam on his own, without offering a chaperone.
h: Dr. Ihab did the internal exam on his own, without offering a chaperone

a.o: Dr. Ihab did an intimate exam on Mrs. Asmaa with no chaperone.
a.x: He should have offered a chaperone and noted her choice.
a.w: A chaperone protects the patient's comfort and dignity, and protects the doctor too. It must always be offered.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked a pregnancy test for Mrs. Asmaa before the exam.
a.x: A pregnancy test was off topic for a woman with this problem.
a.w: Ectopic pregnancy can cause pelvic pain.

a.o: Dr. Ihab felt Mrs. Asmaa's belly first before the internal exam.
a.x: Feeling her belly could have waited until after the exam.
a.w: Belly tenderness helps find pelvic infection.

a.o: Dr. Ihab explained the exam to Mrs. Asmaa before he started.
a.x: Explaining the exam only wasted time in a busy clinic.
a.w: She must agree before an intimate exam.

t: Cancer news given in a busy corridor
s:
Mr. Fawzy, 63, had a CT scan for weight loss and jaundice. The scan showed a cancer of the pancreas that has spread to the liver. He is on the ward and walks around a lot.

Dr. Hany reviewed the scan with the senior doctor and booked the cancer team to see him. He checked his blood tests and pain relief.

He asked the nurse who Mr. Fawzy wanted with him for big news. Mr. Fawzy had said he wanted his wife there.

Mr. Fawzy stopped Dr. Hany in the corridor near the nurses' desk and asked for his scan result. His wife was due to arrive in an hour. A quiet room was free.

Dr. Hany told him the cancer had spread, there and then in the corridor, and left to see another patient.
h: told him the cancer had spread, there and then in the corridor

a.o: Dr. Hany broke the bad news to Mr. Fawzy in a busy corridor.
a.x: He should have used the quiet room, with time and support.
a.w: Bad news should be given in private, with enough time and the people the patient wants, and with a plan.

a.o: Dr. Hany asked Mr. Fawzy who he wanted with him for the news.
a.x: Asking who he wanted there was unnecessary for the news.
a.w: Patients often want family with them for big news.

a.o: Dr. Hany booked an early appointment with the cancer team.
a.x: Booking the cancer team was far too early at that point.
a.w: Fast specialist care helps planning.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked that Mr. Fawzy's pain relief was working well.
a.x: His pain was off topic while giving him bad news like this.
a.w: Pancreas cancer is often painful.

t: Drug error kept from the patient
s:
Mrs. Somaya, 70, was admitted with pneumonia. She has a known allergy to penicillin, which gives her a rash. Last night she was given co-amoxiclav by mistake and developed an itchy rash.

Dr. Fady saw her. Her breathing and blood pressure were normal, with no swelling of the lips or throat. He stopped the co-amoxiclav and gave her an antihistamine.

He switched her antibiotic to clarithromycin and checked that her allergy band was on her wrist.

Mrs. Somaya asked why she had a rash. Her son asked whether something had gone wrong. The nurse filled in an incident form.

Dr. Fady told them it was "probably a viral rash" and did not mention the wrong antibiotic.
h: told them it was "probably a viral rash" and did not mention the wrong antibiotic

a.o: Dr. Fady hid the drug error from Mrs. Somaya and her son.
a.x: He should have told them openly and apologized.
a.w: Doctors have a duty of candour: patients must be told when something goes wrong in their care.

a.o: Dr. Fady switched Mrs. Somaya's antibiotic to clarithromycin.
a.x: She should have stayed on co-amoxiclav for her infection.
a.w: Clarithromycin is safe in penicillin allergy.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Mrs. Somaya an antihistamine for her rash.
a.x: Adrenaline was needed instead of an antihistamine for her.
a.w: With no airway or blood pressure problem, an antihistamine is enough.

a.o: The nurse filled in an incident form about the drug error.
a.x: Filling in an incident form only blamed the people involved.
a.w: Reporting errors helps stop them happening again.

t: Colleague smelling of alcohol on shift ignored
s:
Dr. Rasha was on a night shift with a colleague, Dr. Sameh, who was covering the surgical wards. At midnight she noticed he smelled strongly of alcohol, was slurring his words and dropped a syringe.

She had seen him the same way two weeks before. She checked the patient he had just seen, who was well. She made sure the prescription he had written was correct.

She asked Dr. Sameh if he was all right. He laughed it off and said he was just tired.

The senior doctor on call was in the hospital. Dr. Sameh was due to put in a central line in an hour. Dr. Rasha was worried about getting him into trouble, as they were friends.

Dr. Rasha decided to say nothing and let him carry on with his shift.
h: Dr. Rasha decided to say nothing and let him carry on with his shift

a.o: Dr. Rasha let a doctor who seemed drunk keep working.
a.x: She should have told the senior on call at once.
a.w: Patient safety comes first. A colleague who may be impaired must be stopped and reported, and he may need help too.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked on Dr. Sameh's patient after the incident.
a.x: Checking his patient was not her job on that shift at all.
a.w: Patients he saw may have been put at risk.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked the prescription Dr. Sameh had just written.
a.x: Checking his prescription was rude to a fellow doctor.
a.w: A drunk doctor may make drug errors.

a.o: Dr. Rasha asked Dr. Sameh quietly whether he was all right.
a.x: She should have kept quiet and said nothing to him at all.
a.w: Talking to him first is kind, but isn't enough alone.

t: Signs of elder abuse not acted on
s:
Mrs. Zeinab, 84, has moderate dementia and lives with her son, who is her carer. She was brought in for a chest infection. She is frail and has lost 5 kg in three months.

Dr. Ghada listened to her chest and heard crackles on the left. She started antibiotics and checked her oxygen, which was 95%.

While examining her, she found finger-shaped bruises on both upper arms and a healing burn on her hand. Mrs. Zeinab flinched when her son spoke loudly. She checked her blood count and clotting, which were normal.

Her son said she bruises easily and burned herself on the kettle. He answered every question for her and would not leave the room. Her pension is paid into his account and he said money was tight.

Dr. Ghada wrote "bruising, likely fragile skin" and sent her home with her son, without raising a safeguarding concern.
h: wrote "bruising, likely fragile skin" and sent her home with her son, without raising a safeguarding concern

a.o: Dr. Ghada raised no safeguarding concern for Mrs. Zeinab.
a.x: She should have seen her alone and made a referral.
a.w: Grip-shaped bruises, a burn, weight loss, fear and a controlling carer are warning signs of abuse of a vulnerable adult.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mrs. Zeinab's clotting given her many bruises.
a.x: Her clotting was off topic for an older woman with bruises.
a.w: A bleeding problem can cause easy bruising.

a.o: Dr. Ghada noted Mrs. Zeinab's weight loss since her last visit.
a.x: Her weight loss was off topic for an older woman with bruises.
a.w: Neglect can show as weight loss.

a.o: Dr. Ghada started Mrs. Zeinab on antibiotics for her infection.
a.x: Antibiotics could have waited until her next visit.
a.w: Her chest infection needed treatment.

s:
Mr. Rafik, 74, has motor neurone disease. Six months ago, while he had full capacity, he signed a written advance decision refusing a breathing tube and ventilation, even if his life is at risk. It was witnessed and is in his notes.

He was admitted with pneumonia and is now drowsy and cannot make decisions. His oxygen is 85% on a mask and his carbon dioxide is rising.

Dr. Fady read the advance decision and confirmed it covered this exact situation. He gave antibiotics, oxygen and medicine to ease his breathlessness.

Mr. Rafik's wife said he had talked about this often and had not changed his mind. His brother, who had not seen him for a year, demanded that everything be done.

Dr. Fady called the intensive care team to put in a breathing tube, writing "the family wants everything done".
h: called the intensive care team to put in a breathing tube, writing "the family wants everything done"

a.o: Dr. Fady ignored Mr. Rafik's valid advance decision about care.
a.x: He should have followed it and focused on comfort.
a.w: A valid advance decision refusing treatment is legally binding when it fits the situation, even if family disagree.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Mr. Rafik antibiotics for his chest infection.
a.x: Giving antibiotics broke his wishes for his own care.
a.w: He refused only the breathing tube, not other care.

a.o: Dr. Fady eased Mr. Rafik's breathlessness with medicine.
a.x: Giving comfort care meant giving up on Mr. Rafik.
a.w: Relieving distress is always right.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked exactly what Mr. Rafik's advance decision covered.
a.x: Checking what it covered was unnecessary for his care.
a.w: It must fit the exact treatment and situation to apply.

t: Photo of a patient's X-ray posted online
s:
Mr. Atef, 31, came into the ER after swallowing a small toy car while drunk at a party. He was well, with no pain or vomiting.

Dr. Karim sent an X-ray, which showed the toy in his stomach. He explained that it would likely pass by itself and gave him safety advice to come back with pain or vomiting.

He checked his alcohol level and his breathing, which were fine, and made sure a friend would take him home.

Dr. Karim thought the X-ray was funny. The toy car was clear and the X-ray showed the date and the hospital name. Mr. Atef had not given consent for any photos.

Dr. Karim took a photo of the X-ray on his phone and posted it on his social media with a joke.
h: took a photo of the X-ray on his phone and posted it on his social media with a joke

a.o: Dr. Karim posted Mr. Atef's X-ray on social media.
a.x: He should not have shared it without written consent.
a.w: Patient images are confidential. Dates and places can identify him, and mocking patients breaks trust.

a.o: Dr. Karim gave Mr. Atef safety advice before he went home.
a.x: Safety advice was unnecessary for a man with a broken bone.
a.w: A swallowed object can block the bowel.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked who would take Mr. Atef home from hospital.
a.x: Checking who would take him home was not the doctor's job.
a.w: A drunk patient needs someone safe with him.

a.o: Dr. Karim sent Mr. Atef for an X-ray of his injured arm.
a.x: The X-ray was unnecessary for a man with an injury like his.
a.w: It shows where the object is.

t: Strong painkillers prescribed for the doctor's brother
s:
Dr. Ihab's brother, Mahmoud, 40, phoned him about back pain after lifting a sofa. He is not one of Dr. Ihab's patients and has his own GP, who had a free appointment the next day.

Dr. Ihab asked about red flags over the phone. Mahmoud had no leg weakness, numbness or problems with his bladder or bowels.

He advised him to keep moving and use heat. He suggested taking regular paracetamol and ibuprofen.

Mahmoud said the pain was bad and asked for something stronger. He said he did not want to wait to see his own GP.

Dr. Ihab wrote him a prescription for oxycodone without examining him or telling his GP.
h: wrote him a prescription for oxycodone without examining him or telling his GP

a.o: Dr. Ihab prescribed oxycodone for his own brother.
a.x: He should have sent his brother to his own GP.
a.w: Doctors should avoid treating close family, especially with strong opioids, except in emergencies.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked his brother about any red flag symptoms.
a.x: Asking about red flags was unnecessary for back pain.
a.w: Red flags point to serious back problems.

a.o: Dr. Ihab advised his brother to keep moving with his back pain.
a.x: He should have advised his brother to rest in bed instead.
a.w: Staying active helps back pain heal.

a.o: Dr. Ihab suggested paracetamol and ibuprofen for his brother.
a.x: Paracetamol and ibuprofen were far too weak for his pain.
a.w: Simple painkillers come first for back pain.

t: Emergency pill refused without passing her on
s:
Ms. Reem, 23, came to the clinic the morning after a condom split. She had sex 14 hours ago. She is not on other contraception and her period is regular.

Dr. Sameh checked when her last period was and whether she had any other times of unprotected sex. She had not.

He asked about her medicines, which included none that affect the emergency pill, and checked her weight, which was normal.

Dr. Sameh has a personal belief against emergency contraception. Ms. Reem was anxious and said she had driven a long way. Another doctor in the clinic was free.

Dr. Sameh told her he would not help with emergency contraception and sent her away, without telling her where to get it.
h: told her he would not help with emergency contraception and sent her away, without telling her where to get it

a.o: Dr. Sameh refused Ms. Reem the pill and didn't refer her.
a.x: He should have had the other doctor see her at once.
a.w: Doctors may object on belief, but must make sure the patient gets care quickly. Emergency contraception works best early.

a.o: Dr. Sameh checked Ms. Reem's other medicines before deciding.
a.x: Her other medicines were off topic for the emergency pill.
a.w: Some drugs make the emergency pill less effective.

a.o: Dr. Sameh checked Ms. Reem's weight before deciding on the pill.
a.x: Her weight was off topic for a woman wanting the emergency pill.
a.w: A high weight can change the best choice.

a.o: Dr. Sameh asked Ms. Reem about any other unprotected sex.
a.x: Asking about other unprotected sex was intrusive.
a.w: Earlier unprotected sex changes the risk and choice.

s:
Mr. Hassan, 38, has had a cough for two months, with night sweats and weight loss. He lives in a crowded flat with five family members and works in a factory.

Dr. Fady sent a chest X-ray, which showed a cavity in the right upper lobe. His sputum test was positive for TB bacteria.

He started him on four TB drugs and checked his liver tests, which were normal. He offered an HIV test, which was negative.

Mr. Hassan asked that no one at work find out, as he was afraid of losing his job. Dr. Fady explained how to cover his cough and that he should stay home for two weeks.

Dr. Fady did not report the TB to public health, so that Mr. Hassan's family and workmates were not traced.
h: Dr. Fady did not report the TB to public health

a.o: Dr. Fady didn't report Mr. Hassan's TB to the public health team.
a.x: He should have notified public health at once.
a.w: TB is a notifiable disease. Reporting is a legal duty, and contacts can be tested without naming him at work.

a.o: Dr. Fady offered Mr. Hassan an HIV test as part of his care.
a.x: An HIV test was off topic for a man who has TB like him.
a.w: HIV is common with TB and changes treatment.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Hassan's liver tests before his treatment.
a.x: Checking his liver tests was unnecessary before treatment.
a.w: TB drugs can damage the liver.

a.o: Dr. Fady told Mr. Hassan to stay at home for the first two weeks.
a.x: Telling him to stay at home was far too strict for him.
a.w: Infectious TB needs about two weeks of treatment before it's safe.

t: HIV kept from a wife at risk
s:
Mr. Samir, 45, was diagnosed with HIV three months ago. He has not started treatment and his viral load is high. He is married and does not use condoms with his wife, who is also a patient at the clinic.

Dr. Ghada explained the risk to his wife many times. She offered to help him tell her and offered partner notification without naming him. He refused each time and said he would never tell her.

She talked with a senior colleague and the clinic's legal adviser about the case.

Mr. Samir said his wife would leave him if she knew. His wife came in last week asking for a pregnancy test because they were trying for a baby.

Dr. Ghada decided she could never break his confidentiality and did not tell his wife.
h: Dr. Ghada decided she could never break his confidentiality and did not tell his wife

a.o: Dr. Ghada didn't tell Mr. Samir's wife about her HIV risk.
a.x: She should have made sure his wife was told and was tested.
a.w: Confidentiality can be broken to protect someone from serious harm when the patient refuses, after trying to get consent.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked a senior colleague and a legal adviser for help.
a.x: Asking a senior and a legal adviser broke his confidence.
a.w: Advice is right before a hard decision like this.

a.o: Dr. Ghada offered to help Mr. Samir tell his wife himself.
a.x: Offering to help him tell his wife was too much pressure.
a.w: Getting his consent first is the best route.

a.o: Dr. Ghada offered Mr. Samir the clinic's partner notification.
a.x: Partner notification was useless for a man like Mr. Samir.
a.w: Partners can be told without naming the patient.

t: Students examined a patient under anesthetic without consent
s:
Mrs. Hanaa, 42, was having a planned operation to remove her womb for fibroids. She was fully asleep under a general anesthetic in theatre.

Dr. Mervat checked the patient's name and the consent form for the operation, which Mrs. Hanaa had signed. The team did the surgical safety checklist.

Three medical students were in theatre to learn. Mrs. Hanaa had agreed to students being present to watch, but had not been asked about being examined by them.

Dr. Mervat thought it was a good chance for the students to learn how to do an internal exam. The operation list was running late.

Dr. Mervat let each student do an internal exam on Mrs. Hanaa while she was asleep.
h: Dr. Mervat let each student do an internal exam on Mrs. Hanaa while she was asleep

a.o: Dr. Mervat let students examine Mrs. Hanaa asleep, without consent.
a.x: She should have allowed only exams agreed to beforehand.
a.w: Intimate exams under anesthetic for teaching need specific written consent. Agreeing to students watching is not enough.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mrs. Hanaa's consent form before the operation.
a.x: Checking the consent form was unnecessary before surgery.
a.w: The operation must match what she agreed to.

a.o: The team did the full safety checklist before Mrs. Hanaa's surgery.
a.x: The safety checklist only wasted time before the operation.
a.w: The checklist prevents wrong-site and wrong-patient errors.

a.o: Dr. Mervat had medical students in theatre for the operation.
a.x: Medical students should never be in the theatre at all.
a.w: She agreed to students watching.

t: Cancer hidden from a patient who asked
s:
Mrs. Sanaa, 69, had a biopsy that showed stomach cancer. She is alert and fully able to make decisions. She has been asking the team about her results every day.

Dr. Hany met her two sons first, as they asked. They begged him not to tell their mother, saying she would lose hope and stop eating.

He listened to their worries and explained that he could not lie to her if she asked. He booked the cancer team.

Mrs. Sanaa asked him directly that afternoon, "Is it cancer? I want to know the truth." Her sons were in the room and shook their heads.

Dr. Hany told her it was "just an ulcer" and that she would be fine.
h: Dr. Hany told her it was "just an ulcer" and that she would be fine

a.o: Dr. Hany lied to Mrs. Sanaa about her cancer when she asked.
a.x: He should have told her the truth gently, with support.
a.w: A patient with capacity who asks has the right to know. Family can't decide that for her, and she needs it to make choices.

a.o: Dr. Hany listened to Mrs. Sanaa's sons about their worries.
a.x: He should have refused to meet her sons about her care.
a.w: Family worries should be heard kindly.

a.o: Dr. Hany booked an appointment with the cancer team for her.
a.x: Booking the cancer team should have waited for a while.
a.w: She needs specialist care quickly.

a.o: Dr. Hany told Mrs. Sanaa's sons that he could not lie to her.
a.x: Telling the sons he could not lie to her was far too harsh.
a.w: Being honest with family early prevents conflict later.

t: Notes changed after a missed result
s:
Mr. Yasser, 60, was admitted with chest pain. Two days ago his potassium came back at 6.8, but Dr. Fady did not see the result until the next morning. Mr. Yasser then had a dangerous heart rhythm and needed treatment.

Dr. Fady treated the high potassium and the rhythm settled. He checked his kidney tests and stopped his ramipril and spironolactone.

He told the senior doctor what had happened. The hospital started a review of the incident.

The night before the review meeting, Dr. Fady was worried about being blamed. He knew the notes would be read.

Dr. Fady went back and added a line to the notes, dated two days earlier, saying "potassium noted, recheck planned".
h: added a line to the notes, dated two days earlier, saying "potassium noted, recheck planned"

a.o: Dr. Fady added a back-dated line to Mr. Yasser's notes.
a.x: He should have left the notes and added a dated entry.
a.w: Changing records to hide a mistake is dishonest and can end a career. Honest reporting helps everyone learn.

a.o: Dr. Fady stopped Mr. Yasser's ramipril when his kidney test came back.
a.x: His ramipril should have carried on at the same dose.
a.w: Ramipril raises potassium.

a.o: Dr. Fady told the senior doctor about the missed blood result.
a.x: He should have kept the missed result quiet from his senior.
a.w: Errors must be reported openly.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Yasser's kidney tests again the next day.
a.x: His kidney tests were off topic for a man on ramipril.
a.w: Kidney problems cause high potassium.

t: Tablets hidden in food without a best interests decision
s:
Mrs. Kawthar, 86, has severe dementia and lives in a care home. She was admitted with a urine infection and has been refusing her tablets, spitting them out. She needs her antibiotics and her heart tablets.

Dr. Ihab assessed her capacity and found she could not understand or weigh up information about her tablets. He checked whether she had a lasting power of attorney, and she did not.

He asked the pharmacist which of her tablets could safely be crushed. He checked her swallowing, which was fine with soft food.

Her daughter visits daily and knows her mother's wishes well. The care home has a policy for hidden medicines. The nurse said Mrs. Kawthar likes yoghurt.

Dr. Ihab told the nurse to hide all her tablets in yoghurt from now on, without a best interests meeting or asking her daughter.
h: told the nurse to hide all her tablets in yoghurt from now on, without a best interests meeting or asking her daughter

a.o: Dr. Ihab hid tablets in her food with no best interests decision.
a.x: He needed a best interests meeting, recorded and reviewed.
a.w: Hiding medicines takes away a patient's choice. It is only allowed after a recorded best interests process, for the fewest drugs needed.

a.o: Dr. Ihab assessed the patient's capacity to refuse her tablets.
a.x: Her lack of capacity was obvious without any assessment.
a.w: Capacity must be assessed for each decision.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked the pharmacist about mixing the tablets with food.
a.x: Asking the pharmacist was unnecessary for a plan like this.
a.w: Some tablets are unsafe to crush.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked whether anyone had a power of attorney for her.
a.x: A power of attorney was off topic for her medicines.
a.w: An attorney would make the decision for her.

t: Dementia taken to mean no capacity
s:
Mr. Mahrous, 79, has mild Alzheimer's dementia and lives with his wife. He was admitted with a hip fracture after a fall and needs surgery.

Dr. Karim explained the operation, its risks and what would happen without it, using simple words and a drawing. Mr. Mahrous asked sensible questions about the anesthetic and how long he would be in hospital.

He checked his memory score, which showed mild problems with dates, and his pain, which was well controlled.

Mr. Mahrous said he wanted the operation so he could walk again. His wife was at home and would come in the afternoon.

Dr. Karim wrote "dementia, lacks capacity" and planned to wait for his wife to sign the consent form.
h: wrote "dementia, lacks capacity" and planned to wait for his wife to sign the consent form

a.o: Dr. Karim assumed Mr. Mahrous lacked capacity due to dementia.
a.x: He should have assessed his capacity for this one decision.
a.w: A diagnosis doesn't remove capacity. He understood, weighed and stated his choice, so he can consent himself.

a.o: Dr. Karim used a simple drawing to explain the operation to him.
a.x: Using a drawing was childish for a grown man like Mr. Mahrous.
a.w: Simple aids help people understand.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Mr. Mahrous's pain before talking to him.
a.x: His pain was off topic for a talk about consent like this.
a.w: Bad pain can make it harder to decide.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Mr. Mahrous's memory score in his notes.
a.x: Checking his memory score was unnecessary for consent.
a.w: It shows how his dementia affects him.

t: Consent signed after the sedative was given
s:
Mr. Nabih, 55, was booked for a planned hernia repair this morning. He had been seen in clinic a month ago, where the operation was explained, but he did not sign a form then.

On the ward, the nurse gave him his premedication of midazolam at 8 am, as written on his chart. He became sleepy and relaxed.

Dr. Tarek checked his name band, his allergy status and the side of the hernia, which was marked on the skin.

The theatre team called for Mr. Nabih at 8:30. Dr. Tarek realized the consent form had not been signed. Mr. Nabih was drowsy and his speech was slow.

Dr. Tarek read the risks quickly and asked Mr. Nabih to sign the consent form there and then.
h: asked Mr. Nabih to sign the consent form there and then

a.o: Dr. Tarek took Mr. Nabih's consent just after he had a sedative.
a.x: He should have waited until Mr. Nabih was fully awake again.
a.w: Consent is not valid if the patient is sedated and can't weigh up the information. It should be taken before premedication.

a.o: Dr. Tarek checked the marked side before Mr. Nabih's operation.
a.x: Checking the marked side was unnecessary before surgery.
a.w: Marking prevents wrong-side surgery.

a.o: Dr. Tarek checked Mr. Nabih's allergies before his operation.
a.x: His allergies were off topic before an operation like this.
a.w: Allergies affect anesthetic drugs and antibiotics.

a.o: The nurse gave Mr. Nabih his premedication as it was written.
a.x: The nurse should have refused to give the premedication.
a.w: It was prescribed and given on time.

t: Expensive gift accepted from a patient
s:
Mrs. Ilham, 72, has been Dr. Ghada's patient for ten years. She has heart failure and was recently changed to a new medicine that has helped her a lot.

Dr. Ghada checked her weight, which was steady, and her kidney tests, which were fine. She reviewed her tablets and booked a follow-up in three months.

She thanked Mrs. Ilham for bringing a box of homemade biscuits for the staff, which she shared with the team.

At the end of the visit, Mrs. Ilham handed her a gold necklace worth several thousand pounds. She said she wanted to say thank you. She mentioned she was changing her will and might leave something to "her doctor".

Dr. Ghada accepted the necklace and thanked her, without telling anyone or writing it down.
h: Dr. Ghada accepted the necklace and thanked her, without telling anyone or writing it down

a.o: Dr. Ghada accepted a very expensive necklace from Mrs. Ilham.
a.x: She should have kindly refused it and recorded the offer.
a.w: Large gifts can affect a doctor's judgment and how others see their care, especially from an older, vulnerable patient.

a.o: Dr. Ghada accepted the box of biscuits Mrs. Ilham brought in.
a.x: She should have refused the biscuits as well as the necklace.
a.w: Small gifts shared with the team are fine.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mrs. Ilham's kidney tests at the same visit.
a.x: Checking her kidney tests was unnecessary at that visit.
a.w: Heart failure drugs can affect the kidneys.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mrs. Ilham's weight during the same visit.
a.x: Her weight was off topic for a visit like Mrs. Ilham's.
a.w: Weight gain can mean fluid build-up.

s:
Mrs. Samia, 64, was admitted with a chest infection and is ready to go home. She has rheumatoid arthritis and takes methotrexate 15 mg once a week on Mondays, with folic acid on Thursdays.

Dr. Fady checked her blood count and liver tests, which were normal. He finished her antibiotic course and checked she could walk safely on the stairs.

He went through each of her medicines with her and wrote them on the discharge letter. He sent a copy to her GP and her pharmacy.

Mrs. Samia said she was a little confused by all her tablets and that her daughter usually fills her pill box. Her daughter was not there that day.

Dr. Fady wrote "methotrexate 15 mg once daily" on her discharge letter and medicine list.
h: wrote "methotrexate 15 mg once daily" on her discharge letter and medicine list

a.o: Dr. Fady wrote Mrs. Samia's weekly methotrexate as a daily dose.
a.x: He should have written it as once a WEEK, on Mondays.
a.w: Daily methotrexate is a well-known deadly error. It wipes out the bone marrow within days.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Samia's blood count before she went home.
a.x: Her blood count was off topic for a woman with a chest infection.
a.w: Methotrexate can lower blood counts.

a.o: Dr. Fady sent a copy of her medicine list to her own pharmacy.
a.x: Sending a copy to her pharmacy only added paperwork.
a.w: The pharmacy can catch and fix errors.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Samia could manage the stairs before discharge.
a.x: The stairs were off topic for a woman going home after an infection.
a.w: A safe discharge includes checking she can manage at home.

s:
Mr. Mohsen, 58, has type 2 diabetes and is on the ward with a foot infection. His sugars have been high, between 14 and 18. He takes long-acting insulin at night.

Dr. Rasha checked his sugar chart and his kidney tests, which were normal. She looked at his foot, which was improving on antibiotics.

She decided to raise his night insulin from 6 to 8 units and asked the nurse to keep checking his sugar before meals and at bedtime.

It was a busy night shift and the drug chart was written by hand. The nurse said she sometimes found handwriting hard to read.

Dr. Rasha wrote the new dose on the drug chart as "insulin glargine 8U at night".
h: wrote the new dose on the drug chart as "insulin glargine 8U at night"

a.o: Dr. Rasha wrote "U" for units on Mr. Mohsen's new insulin dose.
a.x: She should have written the word "units" in full on the chart.
a.w: A handwritten "U" can be read as a zero, so 8U becomes 80 units, a ten times overdose that can kill.

a.o: Dr. Rasha raised Mr. Mohsen's night insulin from 6 to 8 units.
a.x: His insulin dose should have stayed at 6 units for now.
a.w: His sugars were too high on the old dose.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mr. Mohsen's kidney tests along with his sugars.
a.x: His kidney tests were off topic for a man with high sugars.
a.w: Poor kidneys make insulin last longer.

a.o: Dr. Rasha asked for Mr. Mohsen's sugar to be checked before meals.
a.x: Checking his sugar before every meal was far too often for him.
a.w: Checks show if the new dose is safe.

t: Feeding started without checking the tube position
s:
Mr. Hamed, 71, had a stroke three days ago and cannot swallow safely. The speech therapist advised feeding through a nose tube. He is drowsy but rousable.

Dr. Hany asked the nurse to put in a fine-bore nasogastric tube. The nurse put it in and Mr. Hamed coughed a little during the procedure.

Dr. Hany checked his blood tests before feeding, including phosphate, which was normal, and asked the dietitian to plan his feeds.

The nurse tried to draw back fluid to test it, but nothing came. The X-ray department was busy and said a film would take two hours. Mr. Hamed had not eaten for three days.

Dr. Hany told the nurse to start the feed anyway, since "the tube went in easily".
h: told the nurse to start the feed anyway, since "the tube went in easily"

a.o: Dr. Hany started the feed without confirming where the tube was.
a.x: He should have waited for a pH test or an X-ray before any feed.
a.w: A tube in the lung is easy to miss, and feed in the lung can cause deadly pneumonia.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked Mr. Hamed's phosphate level before any feeding.
a.x: Phosphate was off topic for a man about to start tube feeds.
a.w: Feeding after starvation can drop phosphate dangerously.

a.o: Dr. Hany asked the dietitian to plan Mr. Hamed's tube feeds.
a.x: The dietitian was unnecessary for a simple standard feed like this.
a.w: Feeds must match his needs.

a.o: Dr. Hany followed the speech therapist's advice not to feed by mouth.
a.x: He should have let Mr. Hamed try soft food by mouth first.
a.w: Unsafe swallowing can cause choking and pneumonia.

s:
Mr. Sabry, 62, was booked for a right knee replacement. His left knee is also arthritic but less painful. His consent form says "right total knee replacement".

Dr. Tarek checked his name band, his blood tests and his ECG, which were fine. He confirmed his allergies with him.

He asked Mr. Sabry which knee was being operated on, and Mr. Sabry pointed to the right one.

The ward was busy and theatre was waiting. Dr. Tarek did not have a skin marker with him. Both knees looked the same, and the X-rays were on the computer in theatre.

Dr. Tarek sent him to theatre without marking the operation site, writing "side confirmed verbally".
h: sent him to theatre without marking the operation site

a.o: Dr. Tarek didn't mark the side of Mr. Sabry's knee before theatre.
a.x: He should have marked the right knee with an arrow on the ward.
a.w: Wrong-side surgery is a "never event". Marking, with consent and checklist, is a simple way to stop it.

a.o: Dr. Tarek asked Mr. Sabry himself which knee was being operated on.
a.x: Asking him was unnecessary, as the consent form said which side.
a.w: Asking the patient is part of checking the side.

a.o: Dr. Tarek checked Mr. Sabry's allergies before he went to theatre.
a.x: His allergies were off topic for a planned knee replacement.
a.w: Allergies matter for drugs used in theatre.

a.o: Dr. Tarek checked Mr. Sabry's ECG and blood tests before surgery.
a.x: The ECG was unnecessary for a fit man having a knee operation.
a.w: It is part of checking fitness for an anesthetic.

t: Swab count skipped at the end of surgery
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 45, had an open operation to remove her womb. It was long, with heavy bleeding, and many swabs were used to soak up blood. The scrub nurse had changed halfway through.

Dr. Mervat stopped the bleeding and checked the bladder and bowel, which were not injured. The anesthetist gave two units of blood.

Dr. Mervat checked the drain and the wound edges before closing.

At the end, the new scrub nurse said she was not sure of the count from before her shift. The theatre was running late and the next patient was waiting.

Dr. Mervat closed the belly without waiting for a full swab and instrument count, saying "I'm sure we have everything".
h: closed the belly without waiting for a full swab and instrument count

a.o: Dr. Mervat closed Mrs. Nadia's belly without a full swab count.
a.x: She should have waited for a correct swab and instrument count.
a.w: A swab left inside causes infection, pain and more surgery. Long, bloody operations with staff changes carry the highest risk.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mrs. Nadia's bladder and bowel for any injury.
a.x: Checking her bladder and bowel only made a long operation longer.
a.w: These can be injured during a womb operation.

a.o: The anesthetist gave Mrs. Nadia two units of blood during surgery.
a.x: Blood was not needed, as fluids alone would have been enough.
a.w: She had heavy bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked the drain and wound edges before closing.
a.x: The drain was off topic once the bleeding had been stopped.
a.w: A working drain shows if bleeding continues.

t: Paracetamol given twice in two forms
s:
Mrs. Dalia, 77, weighs 45 kg and is on the ward after a fall with a broken wrist. She is frail and eats little. She was prescribed co-codamol 30/500, two tablets four times a day, for pain.

Dr. Rasha checked her wrist, which was in a cast, and her fingers, which were warm and moved well. She checked her kidney and liver tests, which were normal.

She also prescribed a laxative to prevent constipation from the codeine.

Mrs. Dalia said she still had pain at night. The nurse asked if she could have something extra. Mrs. Dalia had already had four doses of co-codamol that day.

Dr. Rasha added paracetamol 1 g four times a day on top of the co-codamol.
h: added paracetamol 1 g four times a day on top of the co-codamol

a.o: Dr. Rasha added paracetamol 1 g on top of Mrs. Dalia's co-codamol.
a.x: She needed a different extra painkiller, not more paracetamol.
a.w: Co-codamol already has paracetamol. This doubles the dose to 8 g a day, which can destroy the liver.

a.o: Dr. Rasha prescribed Mrs. Dalia a laxative to go with her codeine.
a.x: A laxative was unnecessary for a woman who eats so little.
a.w: Codeine causes constipation.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked that Mrs. Dalia's fingers were warm and moving.
a.x: Her fingers were off topic for a woman whose wrist was in a cast.
a.w: A tight cast can cut off blood to the hand.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mrs. Dalia's liver tests along with her kidneys.
a.x: Her liver tests were unnecessary after a simple fall like hers.
a.w: Paracetamol is broken down in the liver.

t: Phone order for a drug not read back
s:
Mr. Atef, 69, is on the ward with heart failure. At night the nurse phoned Dr. Karim because his blood pressure had dropped to 92/58 and he felt dizzy. He takes furosemide, ramipril and bisoprolol.

Dr. Karim asked for his pulse, which was 64, his urine output and his latest kidney tests, which showed his creatinine had risen.

He asked the nurse to lie him flat for a while and to check his blood pressure every hour.

Dr. Karim was in the ER with a sick patient and could not come to the ward. The line was noisy. He told the nurse to hold the ramipril and lower the bisoprolol to "one point two five" milligrams.

Dr. Karim gave the orders over the phone and hung up, without asking the nurse to read them back.
h: gave the orders over the phone and hung up, without asking the nurse to read them back

a.o: Dr. Karim gave phone orders without asking for a read-back.
a.x: He should have had the nurse read the drug names and doses back.
a.w: "One point two five" and "twelve point five" sound alike on a noisy line. Read-back catches mistakes before they reach the patient.
