a.o: The page sends the facial nerve out of the skull through the jugular foramen with IX, X and XI.
a.x: The facial nerve leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen.
a.w: The facial nerve passes through the internal acoustic meatus and facial canal and exits at the stylomastoid foramen. The jugular foramen carries IX, X and XI.

a.o: The page puts the maxillary nerve in foramen rotundum and the mandibular nerve in foramen ovale.
a.x: The maxillary nerve should pass through foramen ovale and the mandibular through rotundum.
a.w: V2 leaves through foramen rotundum and V3 through foramen ovale. The page has them the right way round.

a.o: The page lists the abducent nerve among the nerves in the superior orbital fissure with III and IV.
a.x: The abducent nerve should be listed in the optic canal with the optic nerve.
a.w: Cranial nerves III, IV, VI and the branches of V1 all enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.

a.o: The page has the spinal roots of the accessory nerve passing up through the foramen magnum.
a.x: The accessory nerve's spinal roots should be shown entering through the hypoglossal canal.
a.w: The spinal roots of XI rise through the foramen magnum, then leave the skull through the jugular foramen with IX and X.

s:
Osteology lab notebook, page 12, student Hana Farouk. Task: sort a box of loose vertebrae into regions and count them against a full skeleton. Hana wrote that the cervical vertebrae have a foramen in each transverse process for the vertebral artery.

She recorded the thoracic vertebrae as having facets for ribs on their bodies and transverse processes, and long spinous processes pointing downwards. In her summary she wrote that a normal spine has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic and 7 lumbar vertebrae, followed by the sacrum and the coccyx.

She also noted that the atlas has no body and no spinous process, and that the axis has the dens, which acts as a pivot for turning the head. The lab assistant initialled the page and returned the box to the cabinet.
h: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic and 7 lumbar vertebrae

a.o: Hana's summary gives a normal spine seven lumbar vertebrae, as many as the cervical ones.
a.x: A normal spine has five lumbar vertebrae.
a.w: The usual count is 7 cervical, 12 thoracic and 5 lumbar vertebrae, then 5 fused sacral segments and the coccyx.

a.o: Hana records the atlas as a vertebra that has neither a body nor a spinous process.
a.x: The atlas should be recorded with a small body and a short spine.
a.w: The atlas is a ring of two lateral masses joined by arches. It has no body and only a small posterior tubercle instead of a spine.

a.o: Hana notes a foramen in each cervical transverse process that carries the vertebral artery.
a.x: The vertebral artery should pass through the vertebral bodies instead.
a.w: Cervical vertebrae have foramina transversaria. The vertebral artery runs through those of C6 to C1 on its way to the skull.

a.o: The notebook gives thoracic vertebrae rib facets on both the bodies and the transverse processes.
a.x: Rib facets should be found only on the lumbar vertebrae.
a.w: Thoracic vertebrae carry costal facets on their bodies for the rib heads and on most transverse processes for the rib tubercles.

s:
Short-answer exam, abdomen block, question 7: "Give the relations of the right kidney." Student Ahmed Lotfy writes that the right kidney sits a little lower than the left because the liver lies above it.

He lists the anterior relations as the liver, the second part of the duodenum, the right colic flexure and loops of small bowel. For the posterior relations he gives the diaphragm, psoas major, quadratus lumborum and the twelfth rib. He then writes that the right renal vein is longer than the left and crosses in front of the aorta to reach the inferior vena cava.

He ends by saying the right adrenal gland sits on the upper pole of the kidney and that the ureter leaves the renal pelvis at the hilum. The examiner wrote "good structure" in the margin.
h: the right renal vein is longer than the left and crosses in front of the aorta

a.o: Ahmed makes the right renal vein the long one that crosses in front of the aorta to the vena cava.
a.x: The left renal vein is the long one that crosses the aorta.
a.w: The vena cava lies on the right, so the right renal vein is short. The left renal vein is long and crosses anterior to the aorta.

a.o: Ahmed lists the second part of the duodenum among the anterior relations of the right kidney.
a.x: The duodenum should be listed among the posterior relations instead.
a.w: The descending part of the duodenum lies in front of the hilum of the right kidney, so it is an anterior relation.

a.o: Ahmed writes that the right kidney sits a little lower than the left because of the liver.
a.x: The right kidney should sit higher than the left, under the diaphragm.
a.w: The large right lobe of the liver pushes the right kidney down, so it lies slightly lower than the left.

a.o: Ahmed gives psoas major and quadratus lumborum as posterior relations of the right kidney.
a.x: These should be given as anterior relations of the kidney.
a.w: The kidneys lie on the posterior abdominal wall, on psoas major, quadratus lumborum and the diaphragm, with the twelfth rib behind.

s:
Draft textbook page "The wrist and hand", written for first-year students. The page starts with the carpal bones in two rows and explains that the flexor retinaculum bridges the carpal arch to form the carpal tunnel.

A box lists the contents of the tunnel: the median nerve, the four tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, the four tendons of flexor digitorum profundus, the tendon of flexor pollicis longus and the ulnar nerve. It explains that swelling in the tunnel squeezes the nerves inside it.

A clinical note says that in carpal tunnel syndrome patients feel tingling in the thumb, index, middle and half of the ring finger, and may later have weak, wasted thenar muscles. The page ends by saying that the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve passes over the retinaculum, so sensation over the thenar eminence is often spared.
h: flexor pollicis longus and the ulnar nerve

a.o: The page lists the ulnar nerve among the structures running through the carpal tunnel.
a.x: The ulnar nerve passes through Guyon's canal, outside the tunnel.
a.w: The carpal tunnel holds the median nerve and nine flexor tendons. The ulnar nerve and artery pass superficial to the retinaculum in Guyon's canal.

a.o: The page says the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve passes over the retinaculum.
a.x: That branch should pass through the tunnel with the main nerve.
a.w: The palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve above the wrist and crosses superficial to the retinaculum, so thenar skin often keeps feeling.

a.o: The page gives tingling in the thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger in carpal tunnel.
a.x: The tingling should cover the little finger and half the ring finger.
a.w: The median nerve supplies the palmar skin of the lateral three and a half digits, so that is where carpal tunnel symptoms are felt.

a.o: The page says carpal tunnel syndrome may later cause weak, wasted thenar muscles.
a.x: Wasting should be described in the hypothenar muscles instead.
a.w: The recurrent branch of the median nerve supplies the thenar muscles, so long compression weakens and wastes them.

s:
Handout for the lecture "Blood supply of the gut", hepatobiliary block. Part 1 explains that the coeliac trunk supplies the foregut, the superior mesenteric artery the midgut and the inferior mesenteric artery the hindgut.

Part 2 covers the venous drainage. It says the hepatic portal vein is formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric vein and the inferior mesenteric vein. It then notes that the portal vein carries nutrient-rich blood from the gut to the liver and supplies most of the blood that reaches the liver.

Part 3 describes the portosystemic anastomoses at the lower oesophagus, the rectum and around the umbilicus, and explains that these veins swell in portal hypertension. The last sentence says the hepatic veins drain the liver directly into the inferior vena cava.
h: the union of the superior mesenteric vein and the inferior mesenteric vein

a.o: The handout forms the portal vein from the superior and inferior mesenteric veins joining behind the pancreas.
a.x: The portal vein forms from the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
a.w: Behind the neck of the pancreas the superior mesenteric vein joins the splenic vein. The inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the splenic vein.

a.o: The handout says the portal vein brings most of the blood that reaches the liver, more than the hepatic artery.
a.x: The hepatic artery should be given as the main source of the liver's blood.
a.w: About 75% of the liver's blood comes through the portal vein and about 25% through the hepatic artery, as the handout says.

a.o: The handout names the lower oesophagus, rectum and umbilicus as places where portal and systemic veins meet.
a.x: The anastomoses should be listed at the stomach, spleen and kidney only.
a.w: The classic portosystemic anastomoses are at the lower oesophagus, the anorectal junction and the paraumbilical region.

a.o: The handout has the hepatic veins draining the liver straight into the inferior vena cava.
a.x: The hepatic veins should drain into the portal vein before the heart.
a.w: The hepatic veins leave the back of the liver and open directly into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm.

s:
Revision flashcards "Nerves of the upper limb", made by Nour for the anatomy viva. Card 1 says the median nerve supplies most of the forearm flexors and the thenar muscles, and that damage at the elbow gives the "hand of benediction" when the patient tries to make a fist.

Card 2 says the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle, where people feel the "funny bone" tingle, and that a cut at the wrist gives a claw hand. Card 3 says a fracture of the shaft of the humerus usually damages the ulnar nerve in the spiral groove, causing wrist drop.

Card 4 reminds her that the musculocutaneous nerve supplies the front of the arm: biceps, brachialis and coracobrachialis. The last card is a drawing of the brachial plexus with roots, trunks, divisions, cords and branches.
h: usually damages the ulnar nerve in the spiral groove

a.o: Card 3 puts the ulnar nerve in the humeral spiral groove and blames it for wrist drop.
a.x: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove and causes wrist drop.
a.w: The radial nerve winds round the humeral shaft in the spiral groove and supplies the wrist extensors, so its injury gives wrist drop.

a.o: Card 2 places the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle, at the "funny bone".
a.x: The ulnar nerve should pass in front of the lateral epicondyle.
a.w: The ulnar nerve runs in a groove behind the medial epicondyle, where a knock gives the familiar tingle down the little finger.

a.o: Card 4 gives biceps, brachialis and coracobrachialis to the musculocutaneous nerve.
a.x: The front of the arm should be given to the radial nerve instead.
a.w: The musculocutaneous nerve, from the lateral cord, supplies all three flexors in the anterior compartment of the arm.

a.o: Card 1 links median nerve damage at the elbow with the "hand of benediction" sign.
a.x: Median damage at the elbow should give a full claw of all five fingers.
a.w: A high median injury stops the index and middle fingers from flexing, so they stay straight when the patient tries to make a fist.

s:
Handout for the lecture "Nerves of the neck and thorax", head and neck block, written by Dr. Salma. Section 1 follows the vagus nerve down the neck inside the carotid sheath, between the internal jugular vein and the carotid artery.

Section 2 covers the recurrent laryngeal nerves. It explains that the right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the right subclavian artery, while the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the left subclavian artery before both climb in the groove between the trachea and the oesophagus.

Section 3 says these nerves supply all the muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve. A clinical box warns that the left nerve is at risk from a large aortic aneurysm or a lung tumour, and that a damaged nerve gives a hoarse voice.
h: the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the left subclavian artery

a.o: The handout has the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hook under the left subclavian artery.
a.x: The left nerve hooks under the arch of the aorta, by the ligamentum arteriosum.
a.w: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops below the aortic arch, which is why a big aortic aneurysm can stretch it.

a.o: The handout has the right recurrent laryngeal nerve hook under the right subclavian artery.
a.x: The right nerve should hook under the brachiocephalic vein instead.
a.w: On the right side the recurrent laryngeal nerve loops beneath the right subclavian artery, just as the handout says.

a.o: The handout leaves the cricothyroid to the external laryngeal nerve, not the recurrent ones.
a.x: The cricothyroid should be supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve too.
a.w: The cricothyroid is the one laryngeal muscle supplied by the external laryngeal nerve, a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

a.o: The handout places the vagus in the carotid sheath between the jugular vein and the carotid artery.
a.x: The vagus should lie outside the sheath, in front of the artery.
a.w: In the carotid sheath the vagus lies behind and between the internal jugular vein and the carotid artery.

s:
Long-answer exam, abdomen, question 2: "Compare direct and indirect inguinal hernias." Student Karim Nabil starts with the inguinal canal: about 4 cm long, running from the deep ring to the superficial ring, just above the medial half of the inguinal ligament.

He writes that an indirect hernia enters the deep ring and follows the canal, and may reach the scrotum in men. He then states that a direct hernia pushes through the posterior wall lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, while an indirect hernia begins medial to them.

Next he explains that Hesselbach's triangle is bounded by the inferior epigastric vessels, the lateral border of rectus abdominis and the inguinal ligament. He finishes by saying that indirect hernias are more common in children because of a patent processus vaginalis. The examiner gave him 14 out of 20.
h: a direct hernia pushes through the posterior wall lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels

a.o: Karim puts the direct hernia lateral and the indirect hernia medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
a.x: A direct hernia is medial to the vessels; an indirect one starts lateral.
a.w: The deep ring lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. A direct hernia bulges through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to them.

a.o: Karim says an indirect hernia enters the deep ring and may follow the canal down into the scrotum.
a.x: An indirect hernia should come out through the femoral canal instead.
a.w: An indirect hernia follows the path of the processus vaginalis through the deep ring, the canal and out of the superficial ring.

a.o: Karim bounds Hesselbach's triangle by the epigastric vessels, rectus abdominis and the inguinal ligament.
a.x: The triangle should be bounded by sartorius and adductor longus instead.
a.w: Hesselbach's triangle is bounded by the inferior epigastric vessels, the lateral edge of rectus and the inguinal ligament.

a.o: Karim links indirect hernias in children with a processus vaginalis that never closed.
a.x: Children's hernias should be put down to a weak posterior wall.
a.w: A patent processus vaginalis leaves a ready sac along the canal, so childhood inguinal hernias are almost always indirect.

s:
Draft page "Blood supply of the brain", neuroanatomy chapter. The page begins with the two internal carotid arteries and the two vertebral arteries, and explains that the vertebral arteries join at the lower border of the pons to form the basilar artery.

A diagram of the circle of Willis follows. The text under it says that the anterior communicating artery joins the two anterior cerebral arteries, and that each posterior communicating artery joins the anterior cerebral artery to the posterior cerebral artery on the same side.

The page then lists the territories: the middle cerebral artery supplies most of the lateral surface of the hemisphere, including the motor and sensory areas for the face and arm, and the anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface, including the leg area. A note says berry aneurysms most often arise at the anterior communicating artery.
h: each posterior communicating artery joins the anterior cerebral artery to the posterior cerebral artery

a.o: The page has each posterior communicating artery join the anterior cerebral to the posterior cerebral.
a.x: It joins the internal carotid artery to the posterior cerebral artery.
a.w: The posterior communicating artery links the internal carotid system with the posterior cerebral artery from the basilar.

a.o: The page gives the middle cerebral artery the face and arm areas on the lateral surface.
a.x: The middle cerebral artery should be given the leg area as well.
a.w: The leg area lies on the medial surface, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery. The middle cerebral supplies face and arm.

a.o: The page says the vertebral arteries join at the lower border of the pons to form the basilar artery.
a.x: The vertebral arteries should join at the upper border of the midbrain.
a.w: The two vertebral arteries unite at the lower border of the pons to form the basilar artery, which runs up the front of the pons.

a.o: The page names the anterior communicating artery as the commonest site of berry aneurysms.
a.x: The commonest site should be the basilar tip in most patients.
a.w: About a third of berry aneurysms arise at the anterior communicating artery, making it the most common site.

s:
Heart dissection notebook, sheep heart practical, student Dina Mostafa. We started by finding the front of the heart using the anterior interventricular groove and the thicker left ventricle, which felt firm compared with the right.

I opened the right atrium and found the opening of the coronary sinus and the fossa ovalis. Then I opened the left side and wrote: the tricuspid valve lies between the left atrium and the left ventricle, held by chordae tendineae and papillary muscles. The pulmonary valve and the aortic valve each had three semilunar cusps.

I measured the wall of the left ventricle at about three times the thickness of the right ventricle and wrote that this is because it pumps blood to the whole body. The fossa ovalis is the remains of the foramen ovale that let blood pass between the atria before birth.
h: the tricuspid valve lies between the left atrium and the left ventricle

a.o: Dina places the tricuspid valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle.
a.x: The mitral valve lies on the left; the tricuspid lies on the right.
a.w: The right atrioventricular valve has three cusps (tricuspid). The left one has two cusps and is the mitral (bicuspid) valve.

a.o: Dina found the fossa ovalis and the coronary sinus opening in the right atrium.
a.x: Both should be recorded in the left atrium instead.
a.w: The fossa ovalis lies on the interatrial septum seen from the right atrium, and the coronary sinus opens into the right atrium.

a.o: Dina records three semilunar cusps on both the pulmonary and the aortic valves.
a.x: The aortic valve should be recorded with two cusps only.
a.w: Both arterial valves normally have three semilunar cusps. A two-cusp aortic valve is a common birth defect, not the rule.

a.o: Dina measured the left ventricular wall at about three times the thickness of the right.
a.x: The two ventricular walls should be about the same thickness.
a.w: The left ventricle pumps against the much higher systemic pressure, so its wall is roughly three times thicker.

s:
Handout for "The thyroid and parathyroid glands", head and neck block. Part 1 describes the thyroid as two lobes joined by an isthmus over the second to fourth tracheal rings, wrapped in pretracheal fascia so that it moves up with swallowing.

Part 2 covers the blood supply. The superior thyroid artery is the first branch of the external carotid artery and runs with the external laryngeal nerve. The handout then states that the inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the external carotid artery and runs close to the recurrent laryngeal nerve near the lower pole.

Part 3 says there are usually four parathyroid glands on the back of the thyroid lobes, and that the inferior parathyroids develop from the third pharyngeal pouch with the thymus. The last line warns that the parathyroids can be removed by mistake during thyroid surgery, causing low calcium.
h: the inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the external carotid artery

a.o: The handout makes the inferior thyroid artery a branch of the external carotid artery.
a.x: It is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk from the subclavian artery.
a.w: The inferior thyroid artery comes from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery and passes behind the carotid sheath.

a.o: The handout says the thyroid moves up with swallowing because of the pretracheal fascia.
a.x: The gland should be said to stay still when the patient swallows.
a.w: The pretracheal fascia binds the thyroid to the larynx and trachea, so the gland rises with the larynx on swallowing.

a.o: The handout has the inferior parathyroids form from the third pharyngeal pouch with the thymus.
a.x: The inferior parathyroids should come from the fourth pharyngeal pouch.
a.w: The third pouch forms the thymus and inferior parathyroids. They migrate down below the fourth-pouch superior glands.

a.o: The handout makes the superior thyroid artery the first branch of the external carotid.
a.x: The superior thyroid artery should come from the internal carotid.
a.w: The superior thyroid artery is usually the first branch of the external carotid artery, given off just above the bifurcation.

s:
Practical report, surface anatomy session, student Mahmoud Gamal. The task was to mark safe intramuscular injection sites on a volunteer. Mahmoud first marked the deltoid site about three finger-breadths below the acromion, to avoid the axillary nerve lower down.

For the gluteal site he divided the buttock into four quarters using a vertical line through the ischial tuberosity and a horizontal line through the top of the natal cleft. He then wrote that the safe place for injections is the upper inner quadrant, because the sciatic nerve runs through the upper outer quadrant.

He also marked the vastus lateralis site on the outer thigh, between a hand-breadth below the greater trochanter and a hand-breadth above the knee, and noted it is a common site in babies. His partner checked the marks and took photos for the report.
h: the safe place for injections is the upper inner quadrant

a.o: Mahmoud picks the upper inner quadrant and says the sciatic nerve runs in the upper outer one.
a.x: The upper outer quadrant is safe; the sciatic runs in the lower inner part.
a.w: The sciatic nerve passes through the lower medial part of the buttock, so injections go into the upper outer quadrant.

a.o: Mahmoud places the deltoid site about three finger-breadths below the acromion.
a.x: The deltoid site should be at the lower end of the muscle, near its insertion.
a.w: Keeping high in the deltoid avoids the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex vessels that wind round the surgical neck.

a.o: Mahmoud marks the vastus lateralis site on the outer thigh and notes its use in babies.
a.x: The thigh site should be on the inner thigh over the adductors instead.
a.w: The vastus lateralis is thick, away from big nerves and vessels, and is a standard injection site in infants.

a.o: Mahmoud divides the buttock with lines through the natal cleft top and the ischial tuberosity.
a.x: The lines should be drawn through the umbilicus and the pubic bone.
a.w: The usual quadrants are made by a vertical line through the ischial tuberosity and a horizontal one through the top of the cleft.

s:
Flashcard set "Spinal cord and meninges" by Rana, for the neuroanatomy quiz. Card 1 says the spinal cord begins at the foramen magnum as the continuation of the medulla, and has cervical and lumbar enlargements for the limbs.

Card 2 says that in adults the spinal cord ends at the level of the fourth lumbar vertebra, so a lumbar puncture must be done below L5. Card 3 says the subarachnoid space, which holds the cerebrospinal fluid, continues down to the second sacral vertebra.

Card 4 names the filum terminale as a thread of pia that anchors the cord to the coccyx, and the cauda equina as the bundle of nerve roots below the end of the cord. Card 5 shows that the line joining the tops of the iliac crests crosses the spine at about L4, a landmark for the needle.
h: the spinal cord ends at the level of the fourth lumbar vertebra

a.o: Card 2 ends the adult spinal cord at L4 and sends the lumbar puncture needle below L5.
a.x: The adult cord ends at about L1-L2, so a puncture at L3-4 is safe.
a.w: In adults the conus medullaris lies at the L1-L2 disc. A needle at L3-4 or L4-5 enters the sac below it, among the cauda equina.

a.o: Card 3 runs the subarachnoid space down to the level of the second sacral vertebra.
a.x: The subarachnoid space should stop where the cord stops, at L1.
a.w: The dural sac and its subarachnoid space reach about S2, well below the end of the cord, which is what makes the tap safe.

a.o: Card 5 says the line between the tops of the iliac crests crosses the spine at about L4.
a.x: That line should be said to cross at the level of T12.
a.w: The supracristal line usually passes through the L4 spinous process or the L4-5 space, the landmark used for lumbar puncture.

a.o: Card 4 calls the filum terminale a thread of pia that anchors the cord to the coccyx.
a.x: The filum terminale should be called a thickening of the dura.
a.w: The filum terminale is a strand of pia mater from the conus that, wrapped in dura lower down, attaches to the coccyx.

s:
Draft revision page "The diaphragm", thorax chapter. The page explains that the diaphragm is the main muscle of breathing, is supplied by the phrenic nerves from C3, C4 and C5, and flattens when it contracts to draw air into the lungs.

A table lists its three large openings. It states that the aorta passes through the diaphragm at the level of T8, the oesophagus at T10 with the vagal trunks, and the inferior vena cava at T12 with the thoracic duct. The table also notes that the vena caval opening lies in the central tendon, so it is pulled open as the diaphragm contracts.

The page ends with a clinical note: pain from irritation of the diaphragm's central part can be felt at the tip of the shoulder, because the skin there shares the C4 segment with the phrenic nerve.
h: the aorta passes through the diaphragm at the level of T8

a.o: The table puts the aorta through at T8 and the inferior vena cava through at T12.
a.x: The vena cava passes at T8 and the aorta at T12, behind the diaphragm.
a.w: The caval opening is at T8 in the central tendon; the aortic hiatus is at T12, behind the median arcuate ligament with the thoracic duct.

a.o: The page says the phrenic nerves come from the C3, C4 and C5 spinal segments.
a.x: The phrenic nerves should come from the thoracic segments T7 to T12.
a.w: "C3, 4 and 5 keep the diaphragm alive": the phrenic nerves are the sole motor supply of the diaphragm.

a.o: The page has the oesophagus pass through the diaphragm at T10 together with the vagal trunks.
a.x: The oesophagus should pass at T12 with the sympathetic chain.
a.w: The oesophageal hiatus is at T10, in the right crus, and it carries the anterior and posterior vagal trunks.

a.o: The page links pain from the diaphragm's centre with pain at the tip of the shoulder.
a.x: That pain should be felt in the groin instead of the shoulder.
a.w: The central diaphragm is sensed through the phrenic nerve (C3-5); the shoulder tip skin is C4, so pain is referred there.

s:
Short-answer exam, gut block, question 3: "Describe the blood supply of the stomach." Student Yasmin Fathy begins by saying that the stomach is a foregut organ, so all its arteries come from branches of the coeliac trunk.

She lists the arteries along the lesser curvature: the left gastric artery, which she says is a branch of the splenic artery, and the right gastric artery from the common hepatic artery. Along the greater curvature she names the left gastroepiploic artery from the splenic artery and the right gastroepiploic artery from the gastroduodenal artery.

She ends with the short gastric arteries from the splenic artery to the fundus, and a note that a posterior duodenal ulcer can wear into the gastroduodenal artery and bleed heavily. The examiner circled one line and gave 8 out of 10.
h: the left gastric artery, which she says is a branch of the splenic artery

a.o: Yasmin makes the left gastric artery, on the lesser curvature, a branch of the splenic artery.
a.x: The left gastric artery comes directly from the coeliac trunk.
a.w: The coeliac trunk gives three branches: the left gastric, the splenic and the common hepatic. The left gastric is the smallest.

a.o: Yasmin gives the right gastroepiploic artery a source in the gastroduodenal artery.
a.x: It should come from the superior mesenteric artery instead.
a.w: The gastroduodenal artery runs behind the first part of the duodenum and ends as the right gastroepiploic artery.

a.o: Yasmin links a posterior duodenal ulcer with heavy bleeding from the gastroduodenal artery.
a.x: An anterior ulcer should be linked with that bleeding instead.
a.w: The gastroduodenal artery lies right behind the first part of the duodenum, so a posterior ulcer can erode it.

a.o: Yasmin sends short gastric arteries from the splenic artery up to the fundus of the stomach.
a.x: Short gastric arteries should come from the left gastric artery.
a.w: Several short gastric arteries leave the splenic artery near the spleen and pass in the gastrosplenic ligament to the fundus.

s:
Handout for "The knee joint", lower limb block, by Dr. Wael. Page 1 covers the bones: the femoral condyles sit on the tibial plateau, and the patella glides in the groove at the front of the femur.

Page 2 covers the ligaments. The handout explains that the anterior cruciate ligament stops the tibia sliding forward on the femur, and that the posterior cruciate ligament stops it sliding backward. It then says that the anterior drawer test, pulling the tibia forward with the knee bent, checks the posterior cruciate ligament.

Page 3 describes the menisci as C-shaped cartilage pads that deepen the tibial surface, and notes that the medial meniscus is attached to the tibial collateral ligament, so it tears more often. It ends with the "unhappy triad" of ACL, medial collateral and medial meniscus injury.
h: the anterior drawer test, pulling the tibia forward with the knee bent, checks the posterior cruciate ligament

a.o: The handout says the anterior drawer test, pulling the tibia forward, checks the posterior cruciate.
a.x: The anterior drawer test checks the anterior cruciate ligament.
a.w: The ACL stops the tibia moving forward, so excess forward glide in the anterior drawer test means an ACL tear.

a.o: The handout says the medial meniscus tears more often because it is fixed to the collateral ligament.
a.x: The lateral meniscus should be given as the one that tears more often.
a.w: The medial meniscus is attached to the tibial collateral ligament and moves less, so it is caught and torn more easily.

a.o: The handout has the anterior cruciate ligament stop the tibia from sliding forward on the femur.
a.x: The ACL should be said to stop the tibia from sliding backward.
a.w: The anterior cruciate runs from the front of the tibia to the back of the femur and resists forward shift of the tibia.

a.o: The handout lists ACL, medial collateral and medial meniscus injury as the "unhappy triad".
a.x: The triad should list the posterior cruciate and lateral meniscus.
a.w: A blow to the outside of the bent knee classically tears the ACL, the medial collateral ligament and the medial meniscus together.

s:
Practical report, dissection of the popliteal fossa, student Ziad Hamdy. The aim was to name the borders and contents of the fossa and their order from superficial to deep. Ziad describes the diamond-shaped space behind the knee, bounded by biceps femoris above and laterally, semimembranosus and semitendinosus above and medially, and the two heads of gastrocnemius below.

In the results he writes that the popliteal artery is the most superficial structure in the fossa, with the popliteal vein deep to it and the tibial nerve deepest, lying on the joint capsule. He adds that a pulse in the fossa is easy to feel because the artery lies just under the skin.

In the discussion he notes that a Baker's cyst is a swelling of a bursa in the fossa and that the common fibular nerve leaves the fossa along the medial border of biceps femoris. The demonstrator wrote "check your layers" at the bottom.
h: the popliteal artery is the most superficial structure in the fossa

a.o: Ziad makes the popliteal artery the most superficial structure, with the tibial nerve deepest.
a.x: The tibial nerve is most superficial and the artery is deepest.
a.w: From superficial to deep: tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery. The artery lies on the capsule, so its pulse is hard to feel.

a.o: Ziad sends the common fibular nerve out of the fossa along the medial border of biceps femoris.
a.x: It should leave along the lateral border of semimembranosus instead.
a.w: The common fibular nerve follows the medial edge of biceps femoris down to the neck of the fibula, as the report says.

a.o: Ziad bounds the fossa with biceps femoris above and laterally and the gastrocnemius heads below.
a.x: Gastrocnemius should form the upper borders of the diamond instead.
a.w: The hamstrings form the upper borders and the two gastrocnemius heads form the lower borders of the popliteal fossa.

a.o: Ziad calls a Baker's cyst a swelling of a bursa in the fossa behind the knee.
a.x: A Baker's cyst should be called a swelling of the popliteal artery.
a.w: A Baker's cyst is a fluid-filled swelling of a bursa, often the one under semimembranosus, linked to the knee joint.

s:
Flashcards "Muscles of the eye", made by Malak before her head and neck exam. Card 1 lists the six extraocular muscles: four recti (superior, inferior, medial and lateral) and two obliques (superior and inferior), plus levator palpebrae superioris, which lifts the upper eyelid.

Card 2 gives the nerve supply with the memory aid "LR6 SO4": the lateral rectus by the abducent nerve and the superior oblique by the oculomotor nerve, with all the others by the trochlear nerve. Card 3 says the superior oblique turns the eye down and out, and is tested by asking the patient to look down while the eye is turned in.

Card 4 says a third nerve palsy leaves the eye "down and out" with a drooping lid and a large pupil. Card 5 shows the tendon of the superior oblique passing through the trochlea, a fibrous pulley at the front of the orbit roof.
h: the superior oblique by the oculomotor nerve, with all the others by the trochlear nerve

a.o: Card 2 gives the superior oblique to the oculomotor nerve and the rest to the trochlear nerve.
a.x: SO4 is the trochlear; the rest take the oculomotor.
a.w: The trochlear nerve (IV) supplies only the superior oblique. The oculomotor (III) supplies the other recti, inferior oblique and levator.

a.o: Card 3 has the superior oblique move the eye down and out, tested with the eye turned in.
a.x: The superior oblique should move the eye up and in instead.
a.w: The superior oblique depresses, abducts and intorts the eye. It is the main depressor when the eye is turned inward.

a.o: Card 4 leaves the eye "down and out" with ptosis and a large pupil in a third nerve palsy.
a.x: A third nerve palsy should turn the eye "up and in" instead.
a.w: With III gone, the lateral rectus and superior oblique act unopposed, the levator fails and the pupil loses its constrictor.

a.o: Card 5 sends the superior oblique tendon through the trochlea, a pulley at the front of the orbit.
a.x: The tendon should pass through the optic canal instead.
a.w: The superior oblique tendon hooks through the trochlea near the front of the orbit roof, then turns back to the eyeball.

s:
Short-answer exam, head and neck block, question 5: "Describe the nerve supply of the tongue." Student Mohamed Sherif divides the tongue into its anterior two-thirds and posterior third at the sulcus terminalis, with the vallate papillae lying just in front of the sulcus.

For the anterior two-thirds he writes that general sensation comes from the lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular nerve, and that taste comes from the glossopharyngeal nerve. For the posterior third he gives both general sensation and taste to the glossopharyngeal nerve.

For the muscles he writes that all the muscles of the tongue are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve except palatoglossus, which is supplied by the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus. He ends by saying that a lesion of the hypoglossal nerve makes the protruded tongue point toward the damaged side. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: taste comes from the glossopharyngeal nerve

a.o: Mohamed gives taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue to the glossopharyngeal nerve.
a.x: That taste runs in the chorda tympani of the facial nerve.
a.w: The chorda tympani (VII) joins the lingual nerve to carry taste from the front two-thirds. IX carries taste from the back third.

a.o: Mohamed leaves palatoglossus out of the hypoglossal muscles and gives it to the vagus.
a.x: Palatoglossus should be supplied by the hypoglossal nerve too.
a.w: Palatoglossus is the one tongue muscle supplied by the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus. All others are supplied by XII.

a.o: Mohamed has the protruded tongue point toward the side of the damaged hypoglossal nerve.
a.x: The tongue should point away from the side of the lesion.
a.w: The healthy genioglossus pushes its side forward unopposed, so the tongue deviates toward the paralysed side.

a.o: Mohamed has the lingual nerve, from the mandibular nerve, carry general feeling from the front.
a.x: The front two-thirds should take general sensation from the vagus.
a.w: The lingual nerve, a branch of V3, carries touch, pain and temperature from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

s:
Handout for "Surface anatomy of the abdomen", for second-year students. It starts with the nine regions made by two vertical midclavicular lines and two horizontal lines, the subcostal and the transtubercular planes.

A section on the appendix says the base of the appendix lies at McBurney's point, which is found one-third of the way along a line from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine, measured from the umbilicus. It adds that the appendix itself is most often retrocaecal, behind the caecum.

The handout then explains that early appendicitis pain is felt around the umbilicus, because the appendix is a midgut organ supplied by the T10 segment, and only moves to the right iliac fossa when the parietal peritoneum is irritated. It ends with the transpyloric plane at L1, passing through the pylorus and the hila of the kidneys.
h: measured from the umbilicus

a.o: The handout measures McBurney's point one-third of the way along from the umbilicus.
a.x: It lies one-third along the line, measured from the iliac spine.
a.w: McBurney's point is two-thirds of the way from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine, so one-third up from the spine.

a.o: The handout says the appendix most often lies retrocaecal, tucked behind the caecum.
a.x: The commonest position should be given as in front of the bladder.
a.w: Studies find a retrocaecal appendix in about two-thirds of people, making it the most common position.

a.o: The handout explains that early appendix pain is felt around the umbilicus through the T10 segment.
a.x: Early pain should be felt in the right shoulder instead of the umbilicus.
a.w: Visceral pain from the midgut appendix is referred to the T10 dermatome around the umbilicus before the peritoneum is involved.

a.o: The handout puts the transpyloric plane at L1, through the pylorus and the hila of the kidneys.
a.x: The transpyloric plane should be placed at the level of L4.
a.w: The transpyloric plane lies at L1, halfway between the jugular notch and the pubic symphysis, crossing the pylorus and renal hila.

s:
Draft page "The pelvic ureter and its relations", reproductive anatomy chapter. The page follows the ureter from the pelvic brim, where it crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, down the side wall of the pelvis in front of the internal iliac artery.

In the female pelvis, the text says, the ureter runs in the base of the broad ligament. It states that the ureter passes above the uterine artery about 2 cm lateral to the cervix, so it is safe when the artery is clamped during a hysterectomy. Near the bladder it runs close to the lateral fornix of the vagina.

The page lists three narrow points where stones get stuck: the pelviureteric junction, the pelvic brim and where the ureter enters the bladder wall. It ends by noting that the ureter enters the bladder obliquely, which acts like a valve against backflow of urine.
h: the ureter passes above the uterine artery about 2 cm lateral to the cervix, so it is safe

a.o: The page runs the ureter above the uterine artery, safe when the artery is clamped.
a.x: The ureter passes under the uterine artery, at risk of the clamp.
a.w: "Water under the bridge": the ureter runs below the uterine artery beside the cervix, where it can be clamped or cut in hysterectomy.

a.o: The page has the ureter cross the bifurcation of the common iliac artery at the pelvic brim.
a.x: It should cross the bifurcation of the aorta in the midline.
a.w: At the pelvic brim the ureter usually crosses the end of the common iliac artery, where it splits into external and internal.

a.o: The page lists the pelviureteric junction, pelvic brim and bladder wall as the narrow points.
a.x: The narrow points should be the kidney cortex, the hilum and the urethra.
a.w: A ureteric stone tends to lodge at these three narrowings: the pelviureteric junction, the pelvic brim and the bladder wall.

a.o: The page says the oblique path of the ureter through the bladder wall works like a valve.
a.x: The ureter should enter the bladder straight on to let urine flow freely.
a.w: As the bladder fills, its wall squeezes the oblique intramural ureter shut, which helps stop urine flowing back up.

s:
Hand practical notebook, student Farida Kamal. Task: test the small muscles of the hand on a partner and record what each one does. I started with the thenar muscles and found that opponens pollicis brings the thumb across the palm to touch the little finger.

Next I tested the interossei with cards between the fingers. I wrote that the dorsal interossei adduct the fingers toward the middle finger and the palmar interossei abduct them away from it, and that the ulnar nerve supplies all of the interossei. My partner could hold a card between the fingers tightly.

Last I tested the lumbricals by asking my partner to bend the knuckles while keeping the fingers straight, the "tabletop" position. I wrote that the lumbricals start on the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus, bend the knuckles and straighten the finger joints.
h: the dorsal interossei adduct the fingers toward the middle finger and the palmar interossei abduct them

a.o: Farida writes that the dorsal interossei adduct the fingers and the palmar interossei abduct them.
a.x: The dorsal interossei abduct; the palmar ones adduct.
a.w: "PAD and DAB": palmar interossei adduct the fingers toward the middle finger, dorsal interossei abduct them away from it.

a.o: Farida gives all the interossei to the ulnar nerve.
a.x: The interossei should be given to the median nerve.
a.w: The deep branch of the ulnar nerve supplies all palmar and dorsal interossei, which is why ulnar injury weakens finger spreading.

a.o: Farida has the lumbricals start on the profundus tendons, bend the knuckles and straighten the fingers.
a.x: The lumbricals should arise from the superficialis tendons instead.
a.w: The lumbricals arise from the flexor digitorum profundus tendons and flex the MCP joints while extending the IP joints.

a.o: Farida has opponens pollicis bring the thumb across the palm to meet the little finger.
a.x: That movement should belong to adductor pollicis instead.
a.w: Opponens pollicis rotates the first metacarpal and brings the thumb pad across to face the fingers in opposition.

s:
Practical report, clinical skills lab, thorax block, student Hossam Reda. The task was to mark the site for a chest drain on a manikin and explain each step from the anatomy. Hossam first marks the "safe triangle", bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi and a line at the level of the nipple.

He chooses the fifth intercostal space in the midaxillary line. In the method he writes that the needle should pass just below the lower border of the rib above, because the intercostal vessels and nerve run along the upper border of each rib.

He lists the layers the needle crosses: skin, fat, serratus anterior, the three intercostal muscles and the parietal pleura. He ends by noting that the long thoracic nerve runs on serratus anterior in the midaxillary line and should not be cut.
h: the needle should pass just below the lower border of the rib above

a.o: Hossam passes the needle just under the rib above the chosen space.
a.x: The needle should go just over the top of the rib below.
a.w: The intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the costal groove under each rib, so the needle should hug the top of the lower rib.

a.o: Hossam bounds the safe triangle by pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi and a line at the nipple.
a.x: The triangle should be bounded by trapezius and the scapula instead.
a.w: The safe triangle is bounded by the edges of pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi and a horizontal line through the nipple.

a.o: Hossam warns that the long thoracic nerve runs on serratus anterior near the midaxillary line.
a.x: The long thoracic nerve should be placed on the back of the scapula.
a.w: The long thoracic nerve runs down the outer surface of serratus anterior, and cutting it causes a winged scapula.

a.o: Hossam picks the fifth intercostal space in the midaxillary line for the drain.
a.x: The drain should go in the second space at the midclavicular line.
a.w: The fifth space in the midaxillary line sits in the safe triangle, above the diaphragm and away from the big vessels.

s:
Flashcards "Arteries of the head and neck" made by Omar for a group quiz. Card 1 says the common carotid artery divides at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, around C4, into the internal and external carotid arteries.

Card 2 says the carotid sinus at the bifurcation senses blood pressure and the carotid body senses oxygen in the blood. Card 3 says the internal carotid artery gives several branches in the neck, such as the facial and lingual arteries, before it enters the skull through the carotid canal.

Card 4 lists the eight branches of the external carotid artery and says it ends in the parotid gland by dividing into the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries. The last card reminds him that the superficial temporal pulse can be felt in front of the ear.
h: the internal carotid artery gives several branches in the neck, such as the facial and lingual arteries

a.o: Card 3 has the internal carotid give the facial and lingual branches in the neck.
a.x: Those branches come from the external carotid instead.
a.w: The internal carotid normally gives no branches in the neck. The facial and lingual arteries are branches of the external carotid.

a.o: Card 1 splits the common carotid at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, about C4.
a.x: The split should be placed at the level of the cricoid cartilage, C6.
a.w: The common carotid artery usually divides at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, at about the level of C4.

a.o: Card 2 says the carotid sinus senses pressure and the carotid body senses oxygen.
a.x: The roles should be swapped between the sinus and the body.
a.w: The carotid sinus holds baroreceptors in the vessel wall; the carotid body is a chemoreceptor that senses low oxygen.

a.o: Card 4 ends the external carotid in the parotid as the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.
a.x: It should end in the orbit as the ophthalmic artery instead.
a.w: The external carotid ends inside the parotid gland by splitting into the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.

s:
Long-answer exam, neuroscience block, question 1: "Describe the cortical areas for language." Student Salma Adel writes that in most people language is based in the left hemisphere, including most left-handed people.

She writes that Broca's area lies in the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere and controls the production of speech, and that damage there leaves a patient who understands but speaks slowly with great effort. She places Wernicke's area at the back of the same region and says damage there gives fluent speech that makes little sense.

She then describes the arcuate fasciculus as the bundle of fibres joining the two areas, and says a lesion there causes conduction aphasia, where the patient cannot repeat a phrase. She ends with the blood supply: both areas lie in the territory of the middle cerebral artery. The examiner gave 15 out of 20.
h: Broca's area lies in the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere

a.o: Salma places Broca's area in the superior temporal gyrus, the same region as Wernicke's.
a.x: Broca's area lies in the inferior frontal gyrus of the same side.
a.w: Broca's area is in the inferior frontal gyrus, near the motor area for the face. Wernicke's lies in the posterior superior temporal gyrus.

a.o: Salma places language in the left hemisphere in most people, including most left-handers.
a.x: Language should be placed in the right hemisphere for all left-handers.
a.w: About 95% of right-handers and roughly 70% of left-handers have language based in the left hemisphere.

a.o: Salma says a lesion of the arcuate fasciculus causes conduction aphasia with poor repetition.
a.x: That lesion should cause complete loss of hearing in both ears.
a.w: The arcuate fasciculus links Wernicke's and Broca's areas, so cutting it leaves speech and understanding but ruins repetition.

a.o: Salma puts both language areas in the territory of the middle cerebral artery.
a.x: Both areas should be put in the posterior cerebral territory instead.
a.w: Broca's and Wernicke's areas lie on the lateral surface of the hemisphere, which is supplied by the middle cerebral artery.

s:
Handout for "The spleen and upper left quadrant", abdomen block. Part 1 says the spleen is the largest lymphoid organ, lies in the left hypochondrium and is protected by the left 5th to 7th ribs, with its long axis along the line of the 6th rib.

Part 2 lists its relations: the stomach in front, the left kidney behind and below, the left colic flexure below and the diaphragm above. It notes that the splenic artery runs a winding course along the upper border of the pancreas.

Part 3 explains that a normal spleen cannot be felt below the costal margin, and that an enlarged spleen grows down and toward the right iliac fossa, with a notch on its upper border that can be felt. A clinical box warns that fractures of the lower left ribs can tear the spleen and cause bleeding into the abdomen.
h: protected by the left 5th to 7th ribs, with its long axis along the line of the 6th rib

a.o: The handout places the spleen under the left 5th to 7th ribs, its long axis on the 6th.
a.x: It lies under the left 9th to 11th ribs, along the 10th.
a.w: The spleen lies deep to ribs 9, 10 and 11 on the left, which is why lower rib fractures, not upper ones, can tear it.

a.o: The handout runs the splenic artery in a winding course along the upper border of the pancreas.
a.x: The splenic artery should run along the lower border of the stomach.
a.w: The tortuous splenic artery runs to the left along the upper border of the pancreas, giving pancreatic branches on its way.

a.o: The handout says an enlarged spleen grows down and toward the right iliac fossa with a notch.
a.x: An enlarged spleen should be said to grow straight up into the chest.
a.w: The spleen enlarges down and medially toward the right iliac fossa, and its notched border helps tell it from a kidney.

a.o: The handout lists the left kidney behind and the left colic flexure below as relations.
a.x: The left kidney should be listed in front of the spleen instead.
a.w: The spleen lies on the left kidney behind, with the left colic flexure at its lower end and the stomach in front.

s:
Draft page "Gallbladder and bile ducts", hepatobiliary chapter. The page describes the gallbladder in a fossa on the underside of the liver, with its fundus at the tip of the right ninth costal cartilage, where the linea semilunaris meets the costal margin.

It then describes the triangle of Calot, bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the underside of the liver. It states that the cystic artery usually arises from the left gastric artery and enters the triangle from the left before reaching the gallbladder neck.

The page explains that the common bile duct is formed by the cystic duct joining the common hepatic duct, and that it runs behind the first part of the duodenum and the head of the pancreas to open at the major duodenal papilla. The last line says gallbladder pain can spread to the right shoulder blade.
h: the cystic artery usually arises from the left gastric artery

a.o: The page has the cystic artery come off the left gastric artery and enter from the left.
a.x: It usually comes from the right hepatic artery in Calot's triangle.
a.w: The cystic artery normally branches from the right hepatic artery in Calot's triangle, which surgeons dissect to find it.

a.o: The page places the fundus of the gallbladder at the tip of the right ninth costal cartilage.
a.x: The fundus should be placed under the left fifth rib instead.
a.w: The gallbladder fundus lies where the right linea semilunaris crosses the costal margin, at the ninth costal cartilage tip.

a.o: The page bounds the triangle of Calot by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct and the liver.
a.x: The triangle should be bounded by the duodenum and the pancreas.
a.w: Calot's triangle is bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the inferior surface of the liver.

a.o: The page runs the common bile duct behind the duodenum and pancreatic head to the major papilla.
a.x: The bile duct should run in front of the stomach to the minor papilla.
a.w: The common bile duct passes behind the first part of the duodenum and the pancreatic head to the major duodenal papilla.

s:
Handout for "Anatomy of the breast", thorax block. The first section describes the breast lying on pectoralis major and serratus anterior, from the second to the sixth rib, with an axillary tail that reaches up into the armpit.

The second section covers the suspensory (Cooper's) ligaments, which run from the skin to the deep fascia and pull the skin in when a cancer shortens them. The third section deals with lymph drainage. It says most lymph from the breast, about 75%, drains to the parasternal nodes along the internal thoracic artery, and only a small part goes to the axillary nodes.

A final box explains that cancer cells blocking the skin lymphatics give the skin an orange-peel look, and that the sentinel node is the first node to receive lymph from a tumour, so it is checked first during surgery.
h: about 75%, drains to the parasternal nodes along the internal thoracic artery

a.o: The handout sends most of the breast's lymph, about 75%, to the parasternal nodes.
a.x: About 75% of the lymph drains to the axillary nodes.
a.w: Most breast lymph, especially from the lateral half, goes to the axillary nodes. The parasternal nodes take much of the rest.

a.o: The handout says shortened suspensory ligaments pull the skin inward over a cancer.
a.x: Cooper's ligaments should be said to push the skin outward instead.
a.w: A cancer that involves Cooper's ligaments shortens them, so they tether and dimple the overlying skin.

a.o: The handout places the breast on pectoralis major and serratus anterior from rib 2 to rib 6.
a.x: The breast should be placed on the rectus abdominis below the ribs.
a.w: The breast lies on the deep fascia over pectoralis major and serratus anterior, from about the second to sixth ribs.

a.o: The handout links blocked skin lymphatics with the orange-peel look of the breast skin.
a.x: Orange-peel skin should be linked with a blocked artery instead.
a.w: Blocked dermal lymphatics cause skin oedema around the hair follicles, which gives the pitted peau d'orange look.

s:
Short-answer exam, lower limb block, question 6: "Explain why a fracture of the neck of the femur may lead to death of the femoral head." Student Adham Samir starts by saying the femoral head is covered by cartilage apart from a small pit, the fovea, where the ligament of the head is attached.

He writes that in adults the main blood supply of the femoral head is the artery of the ligament of the head, a branch of the obturator artery, and that the retinacular branches play only a small part. He then says that a fracture inside the joint capsule tears these vessels and can cut off the blood to the head.

He ends by saying the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries form a ring around the base of the neck, and that the hip joint is very stable because of its deep socket and strong iliofemoral ligament. The examiner wrote "check the main supply" in red.
h: the main blood supply of the femoral head is the artery of the ligament of the head

a.o: Adham calls the artery of the ligament of the head the main blood supply of the adult femoral head.
a.x: It comes mainly from retinacular branches of the medial circumflex.
a.w: In adults the artery in the ligament of the head is small. Most of the head's blood comes from retinacular branches of the medial circumflex.

a.o: Adham says a fracture inside the joint capsule can tear the vessels and starve the femoral head.
a.x: A fracture inside the capsule should be said to spare the blood supply.
a.w: Retinacular arteries run up the neck under the capsule, so an intracapsular fracture is the one that risks avascular necrosis.

a.o: Adham has the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries form a ring at the base of the neck.
a.x: The ring should be formed by the superior and inferior gluteal arteries.
a.w: The two circumflex femoral arteries form an arterial ring at the base of the femoral neck, which sends up the retinacular arteries.

a.o: Adham puts the stability of the hip down to its deep socket and strong iliofemoral ligament.
a.x: The hip should be called unstable, like the shoulder joint.
a.w: The deep acetabulum, the labrum and the strong iliofemoral ligament make the hip one of the most stable joints in the body.

s:
Practical report, surface anatomy and joints of the foot, student Reem Hassan. The task was to feel the ankle ligaments on a partner and explain common sprains. Reem first found the medial malleolus of the tibia and the lateral malleolus of the fibula, and noted the lateral one reaches lower.

She then wrote that the most common ankle sprain is an inversion injury, when the sole turns inward, and that it usually tears the deltoid ligament on the medial side. She added that the anterior talofibular ligament on the lateral side is rarely hurt because it is the strongest ligament of the ankle.

In the last part she felt the tendons behind the lateral malleolus, fibularis longus and brevis, and noted that they evert the foot. She also felt the dorsalis pedis pulse lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus.
h: it usually tears the deltoid ligament on the medial side

a.o: Reem says an inversion sprain usually tears the deltoid ligament on the inner side.
a.x: It usually tears the anterior talofibular ligament.
a.w: Turning the sole inward stretches the lateral ligaments. The weak anterior talofibular ligament is the one torn most often.

a.o: Reem notes that the lateral malleolus reaches lower than the medial malleolus.
a.x: The medial malleolus should be noted as the lower of the two.
a.w: The lateral malleolus of the fibula extends further down than the medial malleolus, which helps limit eversion.

a.o: Reem has fibularis longus and brevis pass behind the lateral malleolus and evert the foot.
a.x: These tendons should be said to invert the foot instead.
a.w: Fibularis longus and brevis run behind the lateral malleolus and are the main evertors of the foot.

a.o: Reem feels the dorsalis pedis pulse just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.
a.x: The pulse should be felt behind the medial malleolus instead.
a.w: The dorsalis pedis artery runs on the dorsum of the foot just lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus.

s:
Draft page "The pterion and extradural haemorrhage", head chapter. The page explains that the pterion is the H-shaped junction of the frontal, parietal, temporal and greater wing of the sphenoid bones, about 4 cm above the middle of the zygomatic arch.

It states that the bone is thin there and that the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery runs just deep to it. The page then says that the middle meningeal artery is a branch of the internal carotid artery and enters the skull through the foramen spinosum.

In the clinical part it describes a blow to the side of the head that tears the artery, so blood collects between the skull and the dura. The patient may wake up for a short time, the "lucid interval", before getting worse as the clot grows. The page notes that on a CT scan the clot looks like a lens because the dura is stuck firmly to the sutures.
h: the middle meningeal artery is a branch of the internal carotid artery

a.o: The page makes the middle meningeal artery a branch of the internal carotid artery.
a.x: It is a branch of the maxillary artery from the external carotid.
a.w: The middle meningeal artery arises from the first part of the maxillary artery, a terminal branch of the external carotid.

a.o: The page sends the middle meningeal artery into the skull through the foramen spinosum.
a.x: It should enter the skull through the foramen magnum instead.
a.w: The middle meningeal artery passes up through the foramen spinosum, just behind the foramen ovale.

a.o: The page gives the pterion as the meeting point of the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones.
a.x: The pterion should be given as the meeting of the occipital and parietal bones.
a.w: The pterion is where the frontal, parietal, squamous temporal and the greater wing of the sphenoid meet.

a.o: The page says the clot looks like a lens on CT because the dura is stuck to the sutures.
a.x: The clot should look like a crescent that crosses the sutures freely.
a.w: An extradural clot cannot spread past the sutures, where the dura is firmly attached, so it bulges into a lens shape.

s:
Flashcards "The autonomic nervous system", made by Hazem for the neuroanatomy exam. Card 1 says the sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar, from the lateral horn of the spinal cord between T1 and L2, and that its ganglia lie in the sympathetic chain beside the vertebrae.

Card 2 says the parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral: from cranial nerves III, V, IX and X, and from the sacral segments S2 to S4. Card 3 says the vagus carries parasympathetic fibres to the heart, lungs and the gut as far as the left colic flexure.

Card 4 says both systems use acetylcholine at the ganglia, and that most sympathetic fibres release noradrenaline at their targets, except the fibres to the sweat glands, which release acetylcholine. Card 5 says the pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2 to S4 empty the bladder.
h: from cranial nerves III, V, IX and X

a.o: Card 2 gives the trigeminal nerve (V) a parasympathetic outflow along with III, IX and X.
a.x: The cranial parasympathetic nerves are III, VII, IX and X.
a.w: The parasympathetic cranial outflow is in III, VII, IX and X. The trigeminal carries none of its own but its branches carry hitchhiking fibres.

a.o: Card 3 sends the vagus's parasympathetic fibres along the gut as far as the left colic flexure.
a.x: The vagus should be said to supply the whole colon down to the anus.
a.w: The vagus supplies the gut to about two-thirds of the way along the transverse colon. The pelvic splanchnics supply beyond it.

a.o: Card 4 says sympathetic fibres to sweat glands release acetylcholine, not noradrenaline.
a.x: Sweat gland fibres should release noradrenaline like other sympathetic ones.
a.w: Sweat glands are the classic exception: their sympathetic postganglionic fibres are cholinergic and release acetylcholine.

a.o: Card 1 puts the sympathetic outflow in the lateral horn from T1 to L2.
a.x: The sympathetic outflow should come from the brainstem and S2 to S4.
a.w: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons sit in the lateral grey horn of segments T1 to L2, hence "thoracolumbar".

s:
Handout for "The rectum and anal canal", pelvis block. Part 1 says the pectinate line divides the anal canal into an upper part that came from the hindgut and a lower part that came from the ectoderm of the proctodeum.

Part 2 compares the two halves. Above the line, the lining is mucosa, the nerve supply is autonomic, so it is not sensitive to pain, and the veins drain to the portal system. Below the line, the lining is skin, the nerve supply is from the inferior rectal nerve, so it is very painful, and the handout states that the lymph drains to the internal iliac nodes.

Part 3 says internal haemorrhoids form above the line and are usually painless, while external haemorrhoids below the line can be very painful. A last note warns that a cancer of the lower anal canal may first show as a lump in the groin.
h: the lymph drains to the internal iliac nodes

a.o: The handout drains lymph from below the pectinate line to the internal iliac nodes.
a.x: Lymph below the line drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.
a.w: Below the pectinate line the anal canal drains with the skin of the perineum to the superficial inguinal nodes, so a groin lump can appear.

a.o: The handout says the lining above the pectinate line is not sensitive to pain.
a.x: The upper part should be called very sensitive to pain.
a.w: Above the line the nerve supply is autonomic and visceral, so internal haemorrhoids and biopsies there are usually painless.

a.o: The handout says the veins above the line drain to the portal system.
a.x: Those veins should drain straight into the inferior vena cava.
a.w: Above the line the superior rectal vein drains to the inferior mesenteric vein and so to the portal system.

a.o: The handout says the lower part of the anal canal comes from the ectoderm of the proctodeum.
a.x: The lower part should come from the endoderm of the hindgut instead.
a.w: The part below the pectinate line forms from the proctodeum, an ingrowth of ectoderm, which explains its skin lining.

s:
Draft page "Muscles of the face and jaw", head chapter. The page divides the muscles into two groups: the muscles of facial expression, which lie in the superficial fascia and move the skin, and the muscles of mastication, which move the lower jaw.

It says the muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis and the two pterygoids) all come from the first pharyngeal arch and are supplied by the mandibular nerve. It then states that buccinator, the muscle of the cheek, is supplied by the buccal nerve of the mandibular nerve, since it helps with chewing by keeping food between the teeth.

The page notes that the lateral pterygoid is the only muscle of mastication that opens the mouth, and that a facial nerve palsy leaves the patient unable to close the eye or smile on that side, with food collecting in the cheek.
h: buccinator, the muscle of the cheek, is supplied by the buccal nerve of the mandibular nerve

a.o: The page gives buccinator to the buccal nerve of the mandibular nerve because it helps chewing.
a.x: Buccinator is supplied by the facial nerve instead.
a.w: Buccinator is a muscle of facial expression from the second arch, supplied by the buccal branches of VII. The buccal nerve of V3 is sensory.

a.o: The page has all the muscles of mastication come from the first arch and the mandibular nerve.
a.x: They should come from the second arch and the facial nerve.
a.w: The first pharyngeal arch forms the muscles of mastication, so all of them are supplied by its nerve, the mandibular division of V.

a.o: The page names the lateral pterygoid as the one muscle of mastication that opens the mouth.
a.x: The masseter should be named as the muscle that opens the mouth.
a.w: The lateral pterygoid pulls the head of the mandible forward onto the articular eminence, which opens the jaw.

a.o: The page says a facial palsy leaves food collecting in the cheek on the weak side.
a.x: Food should collect in the cheek only after a trigeminal palsy.
a.w: With buccinator paralysed after a facial nerve palsy, the cheek can no longer press food back between the teeth.

s:
Short-answer exam, upper limb block, question 9: "A baby is born after a difficult delivery in which the head was pulled away from the shoulder. Describe the likely injury." Student Lina Wagdy writes that the brachial plexus is formed from the anterior rami of C5 to T1.

She writes that pulling the head away from the shoulder stretches the lower roots of the plexus, C8 and T1, which is called Erb's palsy. She describes the arm hanging by the side, turned inward, with the elbow straight and the forearm turned so the palm faces backward, the "waiter's tip" position.

She adds that the muscles affected include the deltoid, the biceps and the shoulder rotators, and that in a different injury, when the arm is pulled up over the head, the lower roots are torn and the small muscles of the hand are weak. The examiner gave her 6 out of 10.
h: stretches the lower roots of the plexus, C8 and T1, which is called Erb's palsy

a.o: Lina says the pull stretches C8 and T1, and calls that Erb's palsy.
a.x: Erb's palsy is a stretch of the upper roots, C5 and C6.
a.w: Widening the neck-shoulder angle tears the upper trunk, C5 and C6. Erb's palsy gives the waiter's tip; C8-T1 injury is Klumpke's.

a.o: Lina forms the brachial plexus from the anterior rami of C5 to T1.
a.x: The plexus should be formed from the posterior rami of C1 to C4.
a.w: The brachial plexus arises from the anterior (ventral) rami of spinal nerves C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1.

a.o: Lina links pulling the arm up over the head with weak small muscles of the hand.
a.x: That injury should be linked with a weak deltoid and biceps instead.
a.w: Pulling the arm up tears the lower trunk, C8 and T1, which supplies the intrinsic hand muscles, as in Klumpke's palsy.

a.o: Lina describes the arm turned inward with a straight elbow and the palm facing backward.
a.x: The arm should be described as turned out with the elbow bent.
a.w: Loss of the deltoid, external rotators and biceps lets the arm hang adducted, medially rotated, extended and pronated.

s:
Handout for "The heart as a pump", cardiovascular physiology, by Dr. Rasha. Section 1 defines stroke volume as the blood pushed out by one ventricle in one beat, about 70 mL at rest, and cardiac output as stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.

Section 2 covers the three things that set stroke volume: preload, afterload and contractility. The handout explains the Frank-Starling law and states that when more blood fills the ventricle in diastole, the muscle fibres are overstretched and the stroke volume falls, so the heart pumps less of what it receives.

Section 3 says that a higher afterload, such as raised aortic pressure, makes it harder for the ventricle to eject blood, and that sympathetic nerves raise contractility through noradrenaline acting on beta-1 receptors. A last box notes that this law lets the two ventricles keep their outputs matched beat by beat.
h: the muscle fibres are overstretched and the stroke volume falls

a.o: The handout says more filling overstretches the fibres so that stroke volume falls.
a.x: More filling stretches the fibres further and stroke volume rises.
a.w: Within the normal range, a bigger end-diastolic volume stretches the fibres toward their best length, so the heart contracts harder.

a.o: The handout says sympathetic nerves raise contractility through beta-1 receptors.
a.x: Sympathetic nerves should lower contractility through alpha-1 receptors.
a.w: Noradrenaline on cardiac beta-1 receptors raises calcium entry, so each beat is stronger at any given filling.

a.o: The handout says a higher afterload makes it harder for the ventricle to eject its blood.
a.x: A higher afterload should be said to make ejection easier.
a.w: Afterload is the pressure the ventricle must beat to open the aortic valve, so a higher afterload lowers stroke volume.

a.o: The handout says the law keeps the outputs of the two ventricles matched beat by beat.
a.x: The law should be said to make the right ventricle pump more.
a.w: If one ventricle pumps a little more, the other fills more and so pumps more, keeping both outputs equal over time.

s:
Practical report, cardiovascular lab, student Hadeer Ali. The aim was to estimate cardiac output at rest from heart rate and an ultrasound measure of stroke volume. Hadeer lay on a couch for five minutes before the readings, then her partner counted her pulse for a full minute.

Results: heart rate 72 beats per minute and stroke volume 70 mL. Using the formula cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume, she writes that her cardiac output is 50.4 litres per minute, which is "inside the normal range for a healthy adult at rest".

In the discussion she says that during exercise the heart rate and the stroke volume both rise, so cardiac output can go up four to five times. She adds that lying down raises venous return compared with standing. The demonstrator asked her to check her units.
h: her cardiac output is 50.4 litres per minute

a.o: Hadeer works out a resting cardiac output of 50.4 L/min from 72 beats and 70 mL.
a.x: 72 x 70 mL is 5,040 mL, so the output is about 5 L/min.
a.w: 72 beats x 70 mL is 5,040 mL per minute, which is 5.04 L/min. That is the normal resting value. 50.4 L/min is ten times too high.

a.o: Hadeer rests lying on a couch for five minutes before her partner takes the readings.
a.x: The readings should be taken straight after walking into the lab.
a.w: Resting first lets the heart rate settle, so the reading is a true resting value and not raised by the walk in.

a.o: Hadeer says cardiac output can rise four to five times in hard exercise.
a.x: Cardiac output should be said to stay the same in exercise.
a.w: In fit adults cardiac output rises from about 5 L/min to 20-25 L/min, as both heart rate and stroke volume increase.

a.o: Hadeer says lying down raises the venous return to the heart compared with standing up.
a.x: Lying down should be said to lower the venous return.
a.w: Lying flat removes the pooling of blood in the leg veins, so more blood returns to the heart than when standing.

s:
Flashcards "Oxygen transport", made by Bassant for the respiratory physiology quiz. Card 1 shows the S-shaped oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve and notes that haemoglobin is about 97% saturated at a PO2 of 100 mmHg.

Card 2 lists what shifts the curve to the right, so haemoglobin lets go of oxygen more easily: higher carbon dioxide, more acid (lower pH) and more 2,3-BPG. Card 3 says that a rise in body temperature shifts the curve to the left, so working muscle, which is warm, gets less oxygen.

Card 4 explains the P50, the oxygen pressure at which haemoglobin is half saturated, about 27 mmHg in adults, and says a right shift raises the P50. Card 5 says carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin over 200 times more strongly than oxygen.
h: a rise in body temperature shifts the curve to the left

a.o: Card 3 says warm working muscle gets less oxygen because heat shifts the curve left.
a.x: Heat shifts the curve to the right, releasing more.
a.w: Heat lowers haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, so the curve moves right and warm active muscle gets more oxygen.

a.o: Card 4 says a right shift of the curve raises the P50 above about 27 mmHg.
a.x: A right shift should be said to lower the P50.
a.w: A right shift means lower affinity, so a higher PO2 is needed to half saturate haemoglobin: the P50 rises.

a.o: Card 2 lists more carbon dioxide, more acid and more 2,3-BPG as right shifts.
a.x: These should be listed as causes of a left shift.
a.w: CO2, acid and 2,3-BPG all lower the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen, which is the Bohr effect and its partners.

a.o: Card 5 says carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin over 200 times more strongly than oxygen.
a.x: It should bind about half as strongly as oxygen does.
a.w: Carbon monoxide has roughly 200-250 times the affinity of oxygen for haemoglobin, so small amounts block oxygen transport.

s:
Draft page "The resting membrane potential", nerve and muscle chapter. The page opens by saying that a typical nerve cell at rest is about -70 mV inside compared with outside, and that the sodium-potassium pump moves 3 sodium ions out for every 2 potassium ions in.

It then says the main cause of the resting potential is sodium leaking out of the cell through open leak channels, which leaves the inside negative. It adds that the membrane at rest is far more permeable to sodium than to potassium, which is why the resting potential sits close to the sodium equilibrium potential.

The last section says that raising potassium outside the cell makes the resting potential less negative, which is why high blood potassium is dangerous for the heart. A diagram shows the Nernst potentials for potassium (-90 mV) and sodium (+60 mV).
h: the main cause of the resting potential is sodium leaking out of the cell

a.o: The page blames sodium leaking out, and calls the resting membrane more open to sodium.
a.x: Potassium leaking out sets it; the membrane is most open to K+.
a.w: At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K+, so potassium leaving the cell sets a potential near -90 mV, pulled up a little by sodium.

a.o: The page says the sodium-potassium pump moves 3 sodium ions out for every 2 potassium ions in.
a.x: The pump should be said to move 2 sodium out and 3 potassium in.
a.w: The Na+/K+ ATPase moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in for each ATP, adding a small direct negative charge inside.

a.o: The page says high potassium outside the cell makes the resting potential less negative.
a.x: High outside potassium should make the cell more negative.
a.w: Raising extracellular K+ lowers the gradient for K+ to leave, so the membrane depolarises, a risk for the heart.

a.o: The page gives the Nernst potentials as -90 mV for potassium and +60 mV for sodium.
a.x: The two Nernst values should be swapped between the ions.
a.w: With K+ high inside its equilibrium potential is about -90 mV; with Na+ high outside its potential is about +60 mV.

s:
