Short-answer exam, physiology block, question 2: "Describe the phases of a nerve action potential." Student Tarek Amin starts by saying a stimulus must bring the membrane to a threshold of about -55 mV before an action potential fires.

He writes that the rapid upstroke is caused by potassium rushing into the cell through voltage-gated channels, which takes the inside up to about +30 mV. He then says repolarisation happens when the sodium channels close and potassium channels open, letting potassium leave the cell.

He describes a short hyperpolarisation below the resting level, and an absolute refractory period when no new action potential can start, which keeps the signal running in one direction. He ends by saying the action potential is "all or none". The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the rapid upstroke is caused by potassium rushing into the cell

a.o: Tarek puts the rapid upstroke down to potassium ions rushing into the cell.
a.x: The upstroke is caused by sodium rushing into the cell.
a.w: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open fast at threshold, and sodium entering the cell drives the membrane up to about +30 mV.

a.o: Tarek says the absolute refractory period keeps the impulse running one way.
a.x: The refractory period should be said to make the impulse go both ways.
a.w: The patch just behind the impulse cannot fire again yet because its sodium channels are inactivated, so it moves forward only.

a.o: Tarek gives a threshold of about -55 mV before an action potential fires.
a.x: The threshold should be about +55 mV inside the cell.
a.w: A typical neuron fires once the membrane reaches about -55 mV, when enough sodium channels open to feed themselves.

a.o: Tarek describes a short dip below the resting level after repolarisation.
a.x: The membrane should go straight back to rest with no dip.
a.w: Potassium channels close slowly, so extra K+ leaves for a moment and the membrane briefly overshoots below rest.

s:
Renal physiology lab notebook, student Mariam Saber. Today we learned how the kidney filters blood and how we measure it. I wrote that blood enters the glomerulus through the afferent arteriole and leaves through the efferent arteriole, and that filtration happens because glomerular capillary pressure is higher than in other capillaries.

I copied the normal values from the board: renal blood flow is about 1.2 L per minute, about 20% of the cardiac output, and the normal glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is about 125 L per minute, or 180 L a day.

Then we used the formula GFR = (urine creatinine x urine flow) / plasma creatinine to estimate GFR from our own samples. I also noted that constricting the efferent arteriole raises glomerular pressure and so keeps up filtration when blood flow is low.
h: the normal glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is about 125 L per minute

a.o: Mariam writes the normal glomerular filtration rate as about 125 litres a minute.
a.x: Normal GFR is about 125 mL a minute, about 180 L a day.
a.w: 125 mL/min x 1,440 minutes is about 180 L a day. 125 L/min would be about a hundred times the renal blood flow.

a.o: Mariam writes that efferent constriction raises glomerular pressure and keeps up filtration.
a.x: Efferent constriction should be said to lower glomerular pressure.
a.w: Narrowing the outflow vessel holds blood in the glomerulus, raising capillary pressure and so the filtration rate.

a.o: Mariam gives renal blood flow as about 1.2 L a minute, around 20% of cardiac output.
a.x: Renal blood flow should be about 5% of cardiac output.
a.w: The kidneys receive about 1-1.2 L of blood a minute, roughly a fifth of the resting cardiac output.

a.o: Mariam uses urine creatinine times urine flow divided by plasma creatinine.
a.x: The formula should divide urine creatinine by urine flow instead.
a.w: Clearance = (U x V) / P. Creatinine is filtered and barely secreted, so its clearance is close to the GFR.

s:
Handout for "Water balance", renal physiology, by Dr. Khaled. Part 1 says ADH (vasopressin) is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary when plasma osmolality rises or blood volume falls.

Part 2 explains its action. ADH binds V2 receptors on the collecting duct cells and moves aquaporin-2 water channels into the cell membrane. The handout then says that ADH therefore increases the volume of urine and makes it more dilute, helping the body get rid of extra water.

Part 3 covers diabetes insipidus: when ADH is missing or the kidney cannot respond, the patient passes large volumes of dilute urine and is always thirsty. A box notes that alcohol blocks ADH release, which is why drinking causes frequent urination.
h: ADH therefore increases the volume of urine and makes it more dilute

a.o: The handout says ADH increases the volume of urine and makes it more dilute.
a.x: ADH lowers urine volume and makes the urine more concentrated.
a.w: Aquaporins let water leave the collecting duct into the salty medulla, so less, more concentrated urine is passed.

a.o: The handout says ADH puts aquaporin-2 water channels into the collecting duct cells.
a.x: ADH should be said to put sodium channels into the loop of Henle.
a.w: Through V2 receptors and cAMP, ADH moves aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane of collecting duct cells.

a.o: The handout says alcohol blocks ADH release, which is why drinking makes people pass urine.
a.x: Alcohol should be said to boost ADH and hold water back.
a.w: Alcohol suppresses ADH from the posterior pituitary, so the collecting ducts stay closed to water and urine output rises.

a.o: The handout links missing ADH with large volumes of dilute urine and constant thirst.
a.x: Missing ADH should be linked with small amounts of dark urine.
a.w: Without ADH action the collecting ducts reabsorb little water, so diabetes insipidus gives a lot of dilute urine.

s:
Flashcards "Blood sugar control", made by Ahmed for the endocrine physiology exam. Card 1 says insulin is made by the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans and released when blood glucose rises after a meal.

Card 2 says insulin moves glucose into muscle and fat cells through GLUT4 channels. Card 3 says that glucagon, from the alpha cells, is released between meals and stores glucose as glycogen in the liver, so it lowers blood sugar between meals.

Card 4 says that adrenaline, cortisol and growth hormone all raise blood sugar, so they are called counter-regulatory hormones. Card 5 reminds him that the brain takes up glucose without needing insulin, so it can keep working when insulin levels are low.
h: stores glucose as glycogen in the liver, so it lowers blood sugar

a.o: Card 3 has glucagon store glucose as glycogen and lower blood sugar.
a.x: Glucagon breaks glycogen down and raises blood sugar.
a.w: Glucagon drives glycogen breakdown and new glucose making in the liver between meals. Insulin is the hormone that stores glycogen.

a.o: Card 2 says insulin brings glucose into muscle and fat through GLUT4 transporters.
a.x: Insulin should open GLUT2 channels in the brain instead.
a.w: Insulin moves GLUT4 transporters to the surface of muscle and fat cells, which is how it pulls glucose in after a meal.

a.o: Card 4 calls adrenaline, cortisol and growth hormone counter-regulatory hormones.
a.x: These hormones should be listed as lowering blood sugar.
a.w: All three oppose insulin by raising blood glucose, so they are grouped with glucagon as counter-regulatory.

a.o: Card 5 says the brain takes in glucose without needing insulin.
a.x: The brain should be said to need insulin for every bit of glucose.
a.w: Neurons use GLUT1 and GLUT3, which do not depend on insulin, so the brain keeps its glucose supply when insulin is low.

s:
Short-answer exam, cardiovascular block, question 4: "Explain the baroreceptor reflex." Student Rawan Nasser writes that the baroreceptors are stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and the aortic arch, and that the carotid sinus signals travel in the glossopharyngeal nerve.

She explains that when blood pressure suddenly rises, the receptors are stretched more, the brainstem cuts vagal tone and boosts sympathetic output, so the heart rate goes up. When blood pressure falls, she writes, the opposite happens and the heart slows.

She ends by saying the reflex works over seconds to minutes and is mainly for short changes, such as standing up from lying down, and that the kidney controls blood pressure over the long term through salt and water. The examiner gave 6 out of 10.
h: the brainstem cuts vagal tone and boosts sympathetic output, so the heart rate goes up

a.o: Rawan has a sudden rise in blood pressure cut vagal tone and speed up the heart.
a.x: A rise should raise vagal tone and slow the heart.
a.w: The baroreflex opposes the change: more stretch raises vagal and lowers sympathetic drive, so heart rate and pressure fall back.

a.o: Rawan sends carotid sinus signals to the brainstem in the glossopharyngeal nerve.
a.x: Carotid sinus signals should travel in the hypoglossal nerve.
a.w: The carotid sinus nerve is a branch of IX. The aortic arch receptors send their signals in the vagus nerve.

a.o: Rawan uses standing up from lying down as an example of what the reflex corrects.
a.x: The reflex should be said to handle only changes over many weeks.
a.w: On standing, blood pools in the legs and pressure falls; the baroreflex corrects this within seconds.

a.o: Rawan gives long-term blood pressure control to the kidney through salt and water.
a.x: Long-term control should be given to the baroreceptors alone.
a.w: Baroreceptors reset within days, so long-term pressure is set by the kidney's handling of sodium and water.

s:
Practical report, respiratory lab, student Mostafa Ibrahim. The aim was to work out alveolar ventilation from a spirometer trace. Mostafa breathed quietly through the mouthpiece for three minutes with a nose clip on.

Results: tidal volume 500 mL, respiratory rate 12 breaths a minute, and an estimated anatomical dead space of 150 mL. He wrote that his alveolar ventilation is tidal volume times rate, 500 x 12 = 6 L per minute, and that this is the air that reaches the alveoli for gas exchange.

In the discussion he notes that shallow fast breathing wastes more of each breath on the dead space than slow deep breathing, and that the nose clip was needed so that no air escaped around the spirometer. The demonstrator wrote "you have given minute ventilation" next to the result.
h: 500 x 12 = 6 L per minute

a.o: Mostafa calls tidal volume times rate, 6 L a minute, his alveolar ventilation.
a.x: Alveolar ventilation is (500 - 150) x 12, about 4.2 L/min.
a.w: Tidal volume times rate is minute ventilation. The first 150 mL of each breath stays in the dead space, so only 350 mL reaches alveoli.

a.o: Mostafa says shallow fast breathing wastes more of each breath on the dead space.
a.x: Shallow fast breathing should be said to waste less air.
a.w: With a fixed 150 mL dead space, a smaller tidal volume leaves a smaller share of each breath to reach the alveoli.

a.o: Mostafa wore a nose clip so that no air escaped around the spirometer.
a.x: The nose clip should be removed so he can breathe normally.
a.w: With the nose open, part of each breath would bypass the mouthpiece and the measured volumes would be too low.

a.o: Mostafa breathed quietly for three minutes before the trace was read.
a.x: The trace should be taken from his very first breath.
a.w: A few minutes of quiet breathing gives a steady pattern, so the tidal volume and rate reflect his normal breathing.

s:
Draft page "Control of breathing", respiratory physiology chapter. The page explains that the rhythm of breathing is generated in the medulla, and that the pons smooths the pattern. It then turns to the chemoreceptors that adjust breathing to the blood gases.

It says the central chemoreceptors, on the front surface of the medulla, respond mainly to a fall in arterial oxygen, while the peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies respond mainly to a rise in carbon dioxide. It adds that carbon dioxide crosses the blood-brain barrier easily, while hydrogen ions do not.

A clinical box explains that in some patients with long-standing high carbon dioxide, breathing comes to depend on low oxygen, so too much oxygen therapy can reduce their drive to breathe. The page ends by noting that the carotid bodies have a very high blood flow for their size.
h: respond mainly to a fall in arterial oxygen

a.o: The page has central chemoreceptors sense low oxygen and peripheral ones sense CO2.
a.x: Central ones sense CO2 via brain fluid pH; peripheral, low oxygen.
a.w: Central chemoreceptors sense the H+ made when CO2 enters brain fluid. Only the peripheral carotid and aortic bodies respond to low PO2.

a.o: The page says carbon dioxide crosses the blood-brain barrier easily but hydrogen ions do not.
a.x: Hydrogen ions should cross the barrier more easily than CO2.
a.w: CO2 is lipid-soluble and diffuses into the CSF, where it forms H+. Charged H+ from the blood crosses the barrier poorly.

a.o: The page warns that too much oxygen can lower the breathing drive of some patients with high CO2.
a.x: Extra oxygen should be said to always increase their breathing drive.
a.w: With chronic CO2 retention the central drive is blunted, so the hypoxic drive matters more and high oxygen can reduce breathing.

a.o: The page says the carotid bodies have a very high blood flow for their size.
a.x: The carotid bodies should be said to have a very low blood flow.
a.w: Their huge flow per gram keeps their own oxygen use from changing the blood they sample, so they read arterial PO2.

s:
Handout for "Secretion in the stomach", gut physiology, by Dr. Mona. Part 1 lists the cells of the gastric glands. It says the chief cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, the parietal cells secrete pepsinogen, and the G cells in the antrum release gastrin into the blood.

Part 2 describes the three phases of acid secretion: the cephalic phase, set off by the sight, smell and thought of food through the vagus; the gastric phase, when food stretches the stomach; and the intestinal phase, which mostly slows secretion down.

Part 3 says acid turns pepsinogen into active pepsin, which starts protein digestion, and that intrinsic factor is needed to absorb vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum. The handout ends by saying proton pump inhibitors block the final step of acid secretion.
h: the chief cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, the parietal cells secrete pepsinogen

a.o: The handout gives acid to the chief cells and pepsinogen to the parietal cells.
a.x: Parietal cells make the acid; chief cells make pepsinogen.
a.w: Parietal (oxyntic) cells carry the proton pump and make intrinsic factor. Chief cells make pepsinogen, the precursor of pepsin.

a.o: The handout says the cephalic phase is set off by the sight and smell of food via the vagus.
a.x: The cephalic phase should start only when food reaches the duodenum.
a.w: Thinking of, seeing or smelling food sends vagal signals that start acid secretion before any food is eaten.

a.o: The handout says intrinsic factor is needed to absorb vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum.
a.x: B12 should be said to be absorbed in the stomach without help.
a.w: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor is taken up by receptors in the terminal ileum.

a.o: The handout says proton pump inhibitors block the final step of acid secretion.
a.x: These drugs should be said to block the first step, gastrin release.
a.w: PPIs block the H+/K+ ATPase in parietal cells, the last common step whatever the stimulus.

s:
Short-answer exam, gut block, question 6: "Describe how fat is digested and absorbed." Student Nada Fouad starts by saying that fat enters the duodenum as large droplets and that this triggers release of cholecystokinin, which makes the gallbladder contract.

She writes that bile contains lipase, which breaks fat down into fatty acids and monoglycerides. She then says the products are carried to the gut wall inside micelles formed with bile salts, absorbed into the cells and rebuilt into triglycerides.

Finally she explains that the triglycerides are packed into chylomicrons, which are too large for the blood capillaries and so enter the lacteals of the lymphatic system. She adds that most bile salts are taken back in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver. The examiner gave her 7 out of 10.
h: bile contains lipase, which breaks fat down

a.o: Nada says bile carries lipase, the enzyme that breaks fat down into fatty acids.
a.x: Bile has no lipase; pancreatic lipase digests the fat.
a.w: Bile salts only emulsify fat and form micelles. The digestive enzyme is pancreatic lipase, helped by colipase.

a.o: Nada sends chylomicrons into the lacteals because they are too large for blood capillaries.
a.x: Chylomicrons should go straight into the portal vein.
a.w: Chylomicrons are too big to cross capillary walls, so they enter the lacteals and reach the blood through the thoracic duct.

a.o: Nada says most bile salts are taken back in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver.
a.x: Most bile salts should be said to leave the body in the stool.
a.w: About 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and recycled through the enterohepatic circulation.

a.o: Nada says fat entering the duodenum triggers cholecystokinin and gallbladder contraction.
a.x: The trigger should be secretin from stomach acid instead.
a.w: Fats and amino acids in the duodenum release CCK, which contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi.

s:
Flashcards "Skeletal muscle contraction", made by Hesham for the physiology quiz. Card 1 says an action potential spreads along the muscle membrane and down the T-tubules, which makes the sarcoplasmic reticulum release calcium.

Card 2 says the calcium binds to tropomyosin, which then rolls off the binding sites on actin so the myosin heads can attach. Card 3 says ATP is needed for the myosin head to let go of actin, which is why muscles stay stiff after death (rigor mortis).

Card 4 says relaxation happens when calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which also uses ATP. Card 5 shows a sarcomere: during contraction the A band stays the same length while the I band and H zone get shorter.
h: the calcium binds to tropomyosin

a.o: Card 2 has calcium bind to tropomyosin, which then rolls off actin.
a.x: Calcium binds troponin C, which then moves tropomyosin aside.
a.w: Calcium binds troponin C. That changes troponin's shape, and troponin pulls tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin.

a.o: Card 3 says ATP lets the myosin head release actin, which explains rigor mortis.
a.x: ATP should be said to make the head bind actin more tightly.
a.w: Without ATP after death, myosin heads stay locked onto actin, so the muscles become stiff until proteins break down.

a.o: Card 5 keeps the A band the same length while the I band and H zone shorten.
a.x: The A band should be said to shorten most in contraction.
a.w: Filaments slide past each other without changing length, so the A band (the myosin length) stays the same.

a.o: Card 4 says pumping calcium back into the reticulum also uses ATP.
a.x: Calcium should be said to return to the reticulum with no energy.
a.w: The SERCA pump uses ATP to move calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which lets the muscle relax.

s:
Draft page "The thyroid axis", endocrine physiology chapter. The page explains that the hypothalamus releases TRH, which makes the anterior pituitary release TSH, and that TSH makes the thyroid produce T4 and a little T3.

It says T4 is mostly turned into the more active T3 in the tissues. It then states that high levels of thyroid hormone in the blood act on the pituitary to raise TSH release, so the gland keeps making more hormone.

The clinical section uses this to explain blood tests: in primary hypothyroidism, when the thyroid itself fails, T4 is low and TSH is high; in Graves' disease, antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor, so T4 is high and TSH is low. The page ends by saying iodine is needed to make the hormones.
h: act on the pituitary to raise TSH release

a.o: The page says high thyroid hormone pushes the pituitary to raise TSH.
a.x: High thyroid hormone lowers TSH release: negative feedback.
a.w: T3 and T4 feed back on the pituitary and hypothalamus to cut TRH and TSH, which is why TSH is low when hormone is high.

a.o: The page gives primary hypothyroidism a low T4 with a high TSH.
a.x: Primary hypothyroidism should give both a low T4 and a low TSH.
a.w: When the thyroid fails, the low T4 removes feedback, so the pituitary pours out more TSH and the TSH rises.

a.o: The page says antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor in Graves' disease.
a.x: Graves' antibodies should be said to block the TSH receptor.
a.w: Graves' disease antibodies switch on the TSH receptor, so the thyroid overworks and TSH is suppressed.

a.o: The page says T4 is mostly turned into the more active T3 in the tissues.
a.x: T3 should be said to turn into T4 in the tissues.
a.w: Deiodinase enzymes in tissues remove one iodine from T4 to make T3, which binds the receptor more strongly.

s:
Endocrine lab notebook, student Shahd Magdy. Topic: the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. I wrote that renin is released from the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney when blood pressure in the afferent arteriole falls.

Renin turns angiotensinogen into angiotensin I, and ACE in the lungs turns that into angiotensin II, which narrows blood vessels and releases aldosterone. In my notes I wrote that aldosterone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct to reabsorb sodium and keep potassium in the body.

At the end I noted that ACE inhibitors lower blood pressure by blocking angiotensin II formation, and that they can raise blood potassium. The tutor told us to draw the whole system as a flow chart for next week.
h: reabsorb sodium and keep potassium in the body

a.o: Shahd says aldosterone makes the tubule reabsorb sodium and keep potassium in the body.
a.x: It keeps sodium and makes the tubule excrete potassium.
a.w: Aldosterone opens ENaC channels and boosts the Na+/K+ pump, so sodium is kept and potassium is secreted into the urine.

a.o: Shahd says renin comes from juxtaglomerular cells when afferent arteriole pressure falls.
a.x: Renin should come from the macula densa when pressure rises.
a.w: The juxtaglomerular cells sense stretch in the afferent arteriole and release renin when perfusion pressure drops.

a.o: Shahd says ACE in the lungs turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II.
a.x: ACE should be said to work mostly in the liver.
a.w: ACE is found on endothelium everywhere, but most conversion happens in the large lung capillary bed.

a.o: Shahd notes that ACE inhibitors can raise the potassium in the blood.
a.x: ACE inhibitors should be said to lower potassium.
a.w: Less angiotensin II means less aldosterone, so less potassium is excreted and serum potassium can rise.

s:
Handout for "The cardiac cycle", cardiovascular physiology, by Dr. Sherif. The first part follows the left ventricle through one beat. In late diastole the atria contract and top up the ventricles with about the last fifth of their filling.

The handout then says that in isovolumetric contraction, the ventricle squeezes with the mitral valve closed and the aortic valve open, so pressure rises quickly. When ventricular pressure passes aortic pressure, ejection begins, and when it falls below aortic pressure at the end of systole, the aortic valve shuts.

The last part links the heart sounds to the valves: the first sound when the mitral and tricuspid valves close, and the second sound when the aortic and pulmonary valves close. A note says the dicrotic notch in the aortic pressure trace marks the aortic valve closing.
h: the mitral valve closed and the aortic valve open

a.o: The handout keeps the aortic valve open while the ventricle squeezes in isovolumetric contraction.
a.x: Both the mitral and aortic valves are closed in this phase.
a.w: "Isovolumetric" means the volume does not change: with all valves closed, pressure rises until it forces the aortic valve open.

a.o: The handout says atrial contraction adds about the last fifth of ventricular filling at rest.
a.x: Atrial contraction should add about four-fifths of the filling.
a.w: At rest most filling is passive. The atrial kick adds about 20%, more at fast heart rates.

a.o: The handout links the first heart sound with closing of the mitral and tricuspid valves.
a.x: The first sound should be linked with the aortic and pulmonary valves.
a.w: S1 is the closure of the atrioventricular valves at the start of systole. S2 is the closure of the semilunar valves.

a.o: The handout says the dicrotic notch on the aortic trace marks the aortic valve closing.
a.x: The dicrotic notch should mark the mitral valve opening.
a.w: When the aortic valve snaps shut, a short backflow causes the small notch seen on the aortic pressure curve.

s:
Short-answer exam, cardiovascular block, question 8: "Explain the waves of a normal ECG." Student Ali Mahmoud starts by saying that the heartbeat starts in the sinoatrial node and the ECG records the electrical activity of the heart from the skin.

He writes that the P wave shows the atria depolarising, the QRS complex shows the ventricles depolarising, and the T wave shows the atria repolarising. He adds that the PR interval is the time taken for the signal to pass from the atria through the AV node to the ventricles, normally 0.12 to 0.20 seconds.

He ends with the paper speed: at 25 mm per second, one small square is 0.04 seconds and one large square 0.2 seconds, so a heart rate can be found by dividing 300 by the number of large squares between two R waves. The examiner gave 8 out of 10.
h: the T wave shows the atria repolarising

a.o: Ali says the T wave on the ECG shows the atria repolarising.
a.x: The T wave should show the ventricles repolarising.
a.w: The T wave is ventricular repolarisation. Atrial repolarisation happens during the QRS and is hidden by it.

a.o: Ali gives a normal PR interval of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds.
a.x: The normal PR interval should be 0.5 to 1.0 seconds.
a.w: The PR interval, from the start of P to the start of QRS, is normally 0.12-0.20 s, three to five small squares.

a.o: Ali finds the heart rate by dividing 300 by the large squares between two R waves.
a.x: The rate should be 1,500 divided by the number of large squares.
a.w: At 25 mm/s there are 300 large squares a minute, so 300 divided by the large squares per beat gives the rate.

a.o: Ali says the heartbeat starts in the sinoatrial node.
a.x: The beat should be said to start in the AV node.
a.w: The sinoatrial node fires fastest of all the pacemaker cells, so it normally sets the heart rate.

s:
Practical report, exercise physiology lab, student Kareem Wael. The aim was to measure how blood pressure and heart rate change with exercise. Kareem walked up four flights of stairs to the lab, sat down, and his partner took his "resting" blood pressure and pulse straight away.

He then cycled on an exercise bike for six minutes at a steady load. Readings were taken at the end of each minute with an automatic cuff on the left arm, held at heart level. Systolic pressure rose from 130 to 165 mmHg while diastolic stayed close to 80 mmHg.

In the discussion he concludes that exercise raises systolic pressure only by about 35 mmHg, a smaller change than the textbook predicts. He explains that diastolic pressure stays the same because the arteries in working muscle widen. The demonstrator asked him how he chose his baseline.
h: walked up four flights of stairs to the lab, sat down, and his partner took his "resting" blood pressure and pulse straight away

a.o: Kareem's "resting" reading was taken right after he climbed four flights of stairs.
a.x: He should sit and rest for five minutes before the baseline.
a.w: The stairs had already raised his pressure and pulse, so the baseline was too high and the measured rise looks too small.

a.o: Kareem keeps the cuffed arm at the level of the heart for each reading.
a.x: The arm should hang down by his side for each reading.
a.w: An arm below heart level reads falsely high because of the extra column of blood, so heart level is correct.

a.o: Kareem says diastolic pressure holds steady because the arteries in working muscle widen.
a.x: Diastolic pressure should be said to rise as much as systolic.
a.w: Vessels in exercising muscle dilate, so peripheral resistance falls and diastolic pressure changes little.

a.o: Kareem takes readings at the end of each minute at a steady cycling load.
a.x: The readings should be taken only once, after he stops cycling.
a.w: Repeated readings at a fixed load show how pressure settles, and avoid the quick fall after stopping.

s:
Draft page "How we hear", sensory physiology chapter. The page follows sound from the outer ear to the eardrum, then through the three ossicles, which act as a lever and raise the pressure at the oval window about 20 times.

It explains that the basilar membrane inside the cochlea is narrow and stiff at the base, near the oval window, and wide and floppy at the apex. It then states that high-pitched sounds make the apex vibrate most and low-pitched sounds make the base vibrate most, so each pitch has its own place along the membrane.

The page says the hair cells turn the movement into nerve signals when their stereocilia bend, and that loud noise over years damages the hair cells at the base first, so high tones are lost early in noise-induced hearing loss.
h: high-pitched sounds make the apex vibrate most and low-pitched sounds make the base vibrate most

a.o: The page has high pitches peak at the apex and low pitches peak at the base.
a.x: High pitches peak at the base; low ones at the apex.
a.w: The narrow stiff base resonates with high frequencies and the wide floppy apex with low ones, matching the noise-loss pattern.

a.o: The page says the ossicles raise the pressure at the oval window about 20 times.
a.x: The ossicles should be said to lower the pressure at the window.
a.w: The large eardrum and the ossicle lever focus force on the small oval window, raising pressure about 20-fold.

a.o: The page says hair cells make nerve signals when their stereocilia bend.
a.x: The signals should be made when the eardrum touches the nerve.
a.w: Bending the stereocilia opens channels that let potassium in, which depolarises the hair cell and releases transmitter.

a.o: The page says years of loud noise damage the basal hair cells first, so high tones are lost early.
a.x: Noise should be said to remove the low tones first.
a.w: Noise-induced hearing loss shows a typical notch around 4 kHz, from damage near the base of the cochlea.

s:
Flashcards "Vision", made by Jana for the special senses exam. Card 1 says light passes through the cornea, aqueous humour, lens and vitreous before reaching the retina, and that the cornea does most of the focusing.

Card 2 says rods work in dim light and give black-and-white vision, while cones work in bright light and give colour and fine detail. Card 3 says the fovea is packed with rods, which is why we see the finest detail when we look straight at something.

Card 4 says the optic disc has no rods or cones, so it forms the blind spot. Card 5 says vitamin A is needed to make rhodopsin in the rods, so a lack of it causes night blindness.
h: the fovea is packed with rods

a.o: Card 3 packs the fovea with rods and links them to our sharpest vision.
a.x: The fovea is packed with cones and has almost no rods.
a.w: The fovea holds tightly packed cones, each with its own nerve path, giving the sharpest vision. Rods lie mostly outside it.

a.o: Card 1 says the cornea does most of the focusing of light.
a.x: The lens should be said to do most of the focusing.
a.w: The air-cornea surface bends light most, about two-thirds of the eye's power. The lens fine-tunes focus.

a.o: Card 4 says the optic disc has no rods or cones and forms the blind spot.
a.x: The blind spot should be at the fovea instead.
a.w: Where the nerve fibres leave the eye at the optic disc there are no photoreceptors, so that patch of the field is blind.

a.o: Card 5 links a lack of vitamin A with night blindness through rhodopsin.
a.x: Lack of vitamin A should be linked with colour blindness.
a.w: Retinal, made from vitamin A, is part of rhodopsin, so without it rods fail first and dim-light vision suffers.

s:
Handout for "Pain pathways", neurophysiology, by Dr. Amr. Part 1 describes the two waves of pain after a sudden injury, such as stubbing a toe: a first sharp, well-localised pain, and then a second dull, burning pain that is hard to place.

Part 2 matches the waves to the nerve fibres. It says the first sharp pain is carried by thin unmyelinated C fibres, which conduct quickly, and the second dull pain by thinly myelinated A-delta fibres, which are slower.

Part 3 says both types enter the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, cross to the other side and run up in the spinothalamic tract. It ends with the gate control theory: rubbing the skin activates large A-beta fibres, which can reduce pain signals in the dorsal horn.
h: the first sharp pain is carried by thin unmyelinated C fibres, which conduct quickly

a.o: The handout gives the fast sharp pain to unmyelinated C fibres and the dull pain to A-delta.
a.x: A-delta fibres carry the sharp pain; C fibres the dull.
a.w: Myelin speeds conduction. Myelinated A-delta fibres (5-30 m/s) bring the first pain; unmyelinated C fibres (under 2 m/s) bring the second.

a.o: The handout has pain fibres enter the dorsal horn, cross and rise in the spinothalamic tract.
a.x: They should rise on the same side in the dorsal columns.
a.w: Pain fibres synapse in the dorsal horn; second neurons cross within a segment or two and ascend in the spinothalamic tract.

a.o: The handout says rubbing the skin can damp pain through large A-beta fibres.
a.x: Rubbing should be said to increase pain through C fibres.
a.w: Gate control: touch input from A-beta fibres excites inhibitory interneurons that reduce pain transmission in the dorsal horn.

a.o: The handout describes a first sharp, well-placed pain and a second dull, burning one.
a.x: Both pains should be described as dull and hard to place.
a.w: After a sudden injury people first feel a sharp pricking pain, then a slower aching or burning pain.

s:
Practical report, lung function lab, student Habiba Samy. The aim was to read spirometry results from three patient sheets and decide the pattern. Each patient blew out as hard and fast as possible after a full breath in, three times, and the best result was used.

Patient A had an FEV1 of 1.4 L and an FVC of 3.5 L, a ratio of 40%. Habiba wrote that a low FEV1/FVC ratio like this shows a restrictive pattern, such as lung fibrosis. Patient B had an FEV1 of 2.0 L and an FVC of 2.4 L, a ratio of 83%, both volumes small for his height.

For patient B she wrote "small lungs, ratio normal or high, restrictive". In the discussion she notes that a ratio below 70% is the usual cut-off, and that asthma often improves after a bronchodilator while COPD improves less. The demonstrator ticked her patient B answer only.
h: a low FEV1/FVC ratio like this shows a restrictive pattern

a.o: Habiba reads patient A's ratio of 40% as a restrictive pattern like fibrosis.
a.x: A 40% ratio shows an obstructive pattern, like COPD.
a.w: Narrowed airways slow the out-breath, so FEV1 falls much more than FVC and the ratio drops below 70%: obstruction.

a.o: Habiba calls patient B's small lungs with a normal ratio a restrictive pattern.
a.x: Patient B should be called obstructive because of the small FEV1.
a.w: In restriction both FEV1 and FVC fall together, so the ratio stays normal or rises, exactly as patient B shows.

a.o: Habiba says asthma often improves after a bronchodilator, while COPD improves less.
a.x: COPD should be said to improve more than asthma does.
a.w: Asthma airway narrowing is largely reversible, while COPD narrowing is mostly fixed, so bronchodilators help asthma more.

a.o: Habiba uses the best of three hard, fast blows after a full breath in.
a.x: Only the first blow should be used, whatever its quality.
a.w: Several good attempts are needed to make sure the patient gave a full, maximal effort, and the best one is reported.

s:
Short-answer exam, physiology block, question 7: "How does the fetus get enough oxygen from the mother?" Student Youssef Hany writes that oxygen crosses the placenta by diffusion from maternal blood to fetal blood, because the oxygen pressure is higher on the mother's side.

He then writes that fetal haemoglobin (HbF) has a lower affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin, so it releases oxygen more easily to the fetal tissues. He adds that HbF is made of two alpha and two gamma chains and binds 2,3-BPG less well than adult haemoglobin does.

He ends by saying that the fetus has a high haemoglobin level and that the ductus arteriosus lets most blood skip the lungs, which do not take part in gas exchange before birth. The examiner gave 6 out of 10.
h: fetal haemoglobin (HbF) has a lower affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin

a.o: Youssef gives fetal haemoglobin a lower oxygen affinity than adult haemoglobin.
a.x: HbF has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult blood.
a.w: HbF binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so its curve lies to the left. It loads oxygen at the placenta where the PO2 is low.

a.o: Youssef says HbF has two alpha and two gamma chains.
a.x: HbF should have two beta and two delta chains.
a.w: Fetal haemoglobin is alpha2 gamma2. Adult HbA is alpha2 beta2, and the minor HbA2 is alpha2 delta2.

a.o: Youssef says the ductus arteriosus lets most blood bypass the fetal lungs.
a.x: The ductus should be said to send all the blood through the lungs.
a.w: The ductus arteriosus joins the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, so most right ventricular output skips the airless lungs.

a.o: Youssef says oxygen crosses the placenta by diffusion, down a pressure gradient.
a.x: Oxygen should be said to cross by active transport.
a.w: Oxygen moves by simple diffusion from the higher PO2 of maternal blood to the lower PO2 of fetal blood.

s:
Renal lab notebook, student Ola Nabil. Topic: clearance. I wrote that the clearance of a substance is the volume of plasma that is completely cleared of it per minute, worked out as (urine concentration x urine flow) / plasma concentration.

The tutor explained two markers. I recorded that PAH is freely filtered and not reabsorbed or secreted, so its clearance equals the GFR, and that inulin is filtered and almost fully secreted, so its clearance measures renal plasma flow. I noted inulin must be given by drip because the body does not make it.

At the end I wrote that glucose has a clearance of zero in a healthy person, because all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, and that glucose appears in the urine once the blood level is above about 10 mmol/L.
h: PAH is freely filtered and not reabsorbed or secreted, so its clearance equals the GFR

a.o: Ola uses PAH clearance for the GFR and inulin clearance for renal plasma flow.
a.x: Inulin gives the GFR; PAH gives renal plasma flow.
a.w: Inulin is only filtered, so its clearance equals GFR. PAH is filtered and secreted almost completely, so it measures plasma flow.

a.o: Ola notes that inulin must be given by drip because the body does not make it.
a.x: Inulin should be said to be made by the kidney itself.
a.w: Inulin is a plant sugar, so it has to be infused to keep a steady plasma level for the test.

a.o: Ola gives glucose a clearance of zero in health because the proximal tubule takes it all back.
a.x: Glucose should have a clearance equal to the GFR.
a.w: All filtered glucose is reabsorbed by SGLT transporters in the proximal tubule, so none is cleared into the urine.

a.o: Ola says glucose spills into the urine once blood glucose passes about 10 mmol/L.
a.x: Glucose should spill over at about 3 mmol/L.
a.w: The renal threshold for glucose is about 10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL), above which the transporters are saturated.

s:
Handout for "Blood groups", haematology physiology, by Dr. Nermeen. Part 1 explains that the ABO groups depend on the A and B antigens on red cells, and that the plasma holds antibodies against the antigens that are missing.

Part 2 gives the table: group A has anti-B, group B has anti-A, group AB has no antibodies and group O has both. It then says group AB is the universal red cell donor, because its red cells carry both antigens, and group O is the universal recipient.

Part 3 covers the Rhesus system: an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive baby can make anti-D antibodies, which may harm a later Rh-positive baby. The handout says anti-D is given to the mother to prevent this.
h: group AB is the universal red cell donor, because its red cells carry both antigens, and group O is the universal recipient

a.o: The handout makes AB the universal donor and O the universal recipient.
a.x: Group O is the universal donor; AB, the recipient.
a.w: O red cells carry no A or B antigen, so no recipient's antibodies attack them. AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B, so AB accepts all.

a.o: The handout says group O plasma holds both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.
a.x: Group O plasma should be said to hold no antibodies.
a.w: People make antibodies against the ABO antigens they lack, and group O lacks both, so it has anti-A and anti-B.

a.o: The handout says an Rh-negative mother can make anti-D against an Rh-positive baby.
a.x: The risk should be with an Rh-positive mother and negative baby.
a.w: Fetal Rh-positive cells entering an Rh-negative mother can sensitise her, and her anti-D may then cross into the next baby.

a.o: The handout says anti-D is given to the mother to prevent the problem.
a.x: Anti-D should be given to the newborn baby instead.
a.w: Giving anti-D to the Rh-negative mother clears fetal cells before her immune system can make its own antibodies.

s:
Short-answer exam, physiology block, question 10: "How does the body lose heat on a hot day?" Student Marwan Adel writes that the temperature set point lies in the hypothalamus, which compares the core temperature with the set point and starts the right responses.

He writes that in heat the blood vessels of the skin constrict, which pushes warm blood to the surface so heat can leave. He adds that sweat glands, supplied by sympathetic nerves, produce sweat, and that the evaporation of sweat is the main way of losing heat when the air is hotter than the body.

He ends by saying that in very humid air sweat cannot evaporate well, so heat stroke is more likely, and that drinking water replaces the fluid lost in sweat. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the blood vessels of the skin constrict, which pushes warm blood to the surface

a.o: Marwan says skin vessels constrict in the heat to bring warm blood to the surface.
a.x: In heat the skin vessels dilate instead.
a.w: Skin vasodilation increases blood flow to the skin, so more heat is lost. Constriction keeps heat in, as happens in the cold.

a.o: Marwan says evaporation of sweat is the main heat loss when the air is hotter than the body.
a.x: Radiation should be the main loss when the air is that hot.
a.w: When air is warmer than the skin, the body gains heat by radiation and conduction, so evaporation is the only way left to lose it.

a.o: Marwan says very humid air stops sweat evaporating, so heat stroke is more likely.
a.x: Humid air should be said to help sweat evaporate.
a.w: Evaporation depends on the difference in water vapour, so in humid air sweat drips off instead of cooling the skin.

a.o: Marwan puts the temperature set point in the hypothalamus.
a.x: The set point should lie in the medulla oblongata.
a.w: The preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus holds the thermostat that compares core temperature with the set point.

s:
Flashcards "Sleep and body rhythms", made by Rana for the physiology exam. Card 1 says the body clock sits in the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus and runs on a cycle of about 24 hours.

Card 2 says light reaching special cells in the retina resets the clock each day. Card 3 says the pineal gland releases melatonin mostly in daylight and very little at night, which keeps us awake during the day.

Card 4 says cortisol peaks in the early morning, soon after waking, and is lowest around midnight. Card 5 says jet lag happens when the body clock is out of step with the local day and night, and that it often takes about a day to adjust for each time zone crossed.
h: the pineal gland releases melatonin mostly in daylight and very little at night

a.o: Card 3 has the pineal gland release melatonin mostly in daylight.
a.x: Melatonin rises in darkness and peaks at night.
a.w: Light reaching the retina switches melatonin off through the suprachiasmatic nucleus, so levels rise after dark and help bring on sleep.

a.o: Card 1 places the body clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus.
a.x: The body clock should be placed in the cerebellum.
a.w: The suprachiasmatic nucleus, just above the optic chiasm, is the master clock that sets daily rhythms.

a.o: Card 4 says cortisol peaks soon after waking and is lowest around midnight.
a.x: Cortisol should peak at midnight and dip in the morning.
a.w: Cortisol has a strong daily rhythm: it peaks in the early morning and is lowest in the first half of the night.

a.o: Card 5 allows about a day to adjust for each time zone crossed.
a.x: Jet lag should be said to clear in a single hour.
a.w: The body clock can shift about one hour a day, so a six-hour flight shift can take close to a week to settle.

s:
Draft page "Calcium balance", endocrine physiology chapter. The page says that about half the calcium in the blood is free (ionised) and that this is the part that matters for nerves and muscle. It notes that a low ionised calcium makes nerves fire too easily, causing tingling and muscle spasms.

It explains that parathyroid hormone (PTH) raises blood calcium by releasing calcium from bone, increasing calcium reabsorption in the kidney and switching on vitamin D in the kidney. It then says that calcitonin from the thyroid raises blood calcium in the same way, and is the main hormone that protects against low calcium.

The page ends by saying that active vitamin D (calcitriol) increases calcium absorption from the gut, and that PTH makes the kidney excrete more phosphate.
h: calcitonin from the thyroid raises blood calcium in the same way

a.o: The page says calcitonin raises blood calcium and is the main guard against low calcium.
a.x: Calcitonin lowers calcium and plays a minor role.
a.w: Calcitonin from thyroid C cells slows bone breakdown and lowers calcium. PTH is the main hormone that protects against low calcium.

a.o: The page says PTH makes the kidney excrete more phosphate.
a.x: PTH should be said to make the kidney keep phosphate.
a.w: PTH blocks phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, so the phosphate released from bone is lost in the urine.

a.o: The page says a low ionised calcium makes nerves fire too easily, with tingling and spasms.
a.x: Low calcium should be said to make the nerves slow and numb.
a.w: Low ionised calcium lowers the threshold of sodium channels, so nerves fire too easily, causing tingling and tetany.

a.o: The page says active vitamin D increases the absorption of calcium from the gut.
a.x: Vitamin D should be said to block calcium absorption.
a.w: Calcitriol switches on calcium-binding proteins in the gut lining, raising the absorption of dietary calcium.

s:
Practical report, reflexes lab, student Rowan Tamer. The aim was to test the deep tendon reflexes on a partner and link each one to its spinal segment. Rowan asked her partner to sit with legs hanging freely and to look away while she tapped.

Results table: biceps jerk C5-C6, triceps jerk C7, knee jerk S1-S2 and ankle jerk S1-S2. She describes the stretch reflex as monosynaptic: the tap stretches the muscle spindle, the sensory fibre synapses directly on the motor neuron and the muscle contracts.

In the discussion she notes that clenching the teeth or pulling the hands apart (the Jendrassik manoeuvre) can bring out a weak reflex. She adds that a brisk reflex can point to an upper motor neuron lesion, while an absent reflex can point to a problem in the reflex arc.
h: knee jerk S1-S2

a.o: Rowan's table gives the knee jerk the same segments as the ankle jerk, S1-S2.
a.x: The knee jerk belongs to segments L3 and L4.
a.w: The patellar tendon reflex runs through the femoral nerve and segments L3-L4. The ankle jerk is S1-S2.

a.o: Rowan describes the stretch reflex as monosynaptic, sensory fibre straight onto the motor neuron.
a.x: The stretch reflex should have at least three synapses in the cord.
a.w: In the stretch reflex the Ia spindle fibre synapses directly on the alpha motor neuron, making it monosynaptic.

a.o: Rowan uses clenched teeth or pulled hands to bring out a weak reflex.
a.x: The partner should be told to tense the tested leg instead.
a.w: The Jendrassik manoeuvre distracts the patient and raises spinal excitability, so a weak reflex can appear.

a.o: Rowan links a brisk reflex with an upper motor neuron lesion.
a.x: A brisk reflex should be linked with a cut peripheral nerve.
a.w: Loss of descending inhibition after an upper motor neuron lesion leaves stretch reflexes exaggerated.

s:
Handout for "Haemostasis", blood physiology, by Dr. Hala. Part 1 says that after a vessel is cut it first narrows, then platelets stick to exposed collagen with the help of von Willebrand factor and form a soft plug.

Part 2 covers the clotting cascade. The extrinsic pathway starts when tissue factor from damaged tissue meets factor VII. The intrinsic pathway starts with factor XII on contact with a surface. Both meet at factor X, which turns prothrombin into thrombin, and thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin. The handout then says that the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) tests the extrinsic pathway and is used to monitor warfarin.

Part 3 says vitamin K is needed to make factors II, VII, IX and X in the liver, and that warfarin works by blocking vitamin K recycling. The last line says antithrombin, boosted by heparin, switches off thrombin.
h: the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) tests the extrinsic pathway and is used to monitor warfarin

a.o: The handout uses the aPTT to test the extrinsic pathway and monitor warfarin.
a.x: The PT/INR tests the extrinsic pathway and is used for warfarin.
a.w: The PT starts with tissue factor and is sensitive to factor VII, so it tracks warfarin. The aPTT tests the intrinsic pathway.

a.o: The handout says platelets stick to collagen with the help of von Willebrand factor.
a.x: Platelets should be said to stick with the help of factor VIII alone.
a.w: Von Willebrand factor bridges exposed collagen and the platelet GPIb receptor, starting platelet adhesion.

a.o: The handout lists II, VII, IX and X as the factors that need vitamin K.
a.x: The vitamin K factors should be listed as I, V, VIII and XII.
a.w: The liver needs vitamin K to add carboxyl groups to factors II, VII, IX and X, and to proteins C and S.

a.o: The handout says antithrombin, boosted by heparin, switches off thrombin.
a.x: Heparin should be said to work by blocking vitamin K.
a.w: Heparin binds antithrombin and speeds its action against thrombin and factor Xa a thousandfold.

s:
Practical report, exercise lab, student Ziad Mohsen. The aim was to measure how fast heart rate returns to resting after a step test. Ziad's resting rate was 68 beats per minute. After three minutes of stepping, his partner recorded his pulse every 30 seconds for six minutes.

His graph shows 150 at the end of exercise, 120 at 1 minute, 100 at 2 minutes, 85 at 3 minutes, 76 at 4 minutes, 70 at 5 minutes and 68 at 6 minutes. In the results he writes that his heart rate was back to resting within one minute of stopping, which shows very good fitness.

In the discussion he explains that the fast early fall in heart rate after exercise comes mostly from the vagus nerve switching back on. He notes that recovery time is a useful simple measure of fitness, and that the test should be done at the same time of day when repeated.
h: his heart rate was back to resting within one minute of stopping

a.o: Ziad reads his graph as back to rest within a minute, when it takes about six.
a.x: The graph shows 120 at one minute; rest is reached at about six.
a.w: His own data fall from 150 to 120 in the first minute and only reach 68 at six minutes, so the conclusion does not fit the graph.

a.o: Ziad credits the vagus nerve switching back on for the quick early fall.
a.x: The early fall should be credited to adrenaline being released.
a.w: Fast heart rate recovery in the first minute is mainly vagal reactivation, which is why it reflects fitness.

a.o: Ziad says the test should be done at the same time of day when it is repeated.
a.x: The time of day should be said to make no difference.
a.w: Heart rate varies over the day with meals, caffeine and body rhythms, so repeat tests should match the time.

a.o: Ziad's partner records the pulse every 30 seconds for six minutes after stepping.
a.x: The pulse should be recorded only once, at the end of the six minutes.
a.w: Frequent readings show the shape of the recovery curve, not just its end point.

s:
Flashcards "Hormones of pregnancy", made by Mennatullah for the reproductive block. Card 1 says that after fertilisation the embryo implants in the uterus about a week later, and the outer layer of the embryo starts to make hCG.

Card 2 says hCG keeps the corpus luteum alive, so it keeps making progesterone in early pregnancy, and that hCG is what home pregnancy tests detect. Card 3 says the placenta takes over progesterone production at about 10 to 12 weeks.

Card 4 says that progesterone makes the uterus contract strongly, which helps keep the pregnancy safe. Card 5 says that human placental lactogen raises the mother's blood sugar so more glucose reaches the baby.
h: progesterone makes the uterus contract strongly, which helps keep the pregnancy safe

a.o: Card 4 says progesterone makes the uterus contract strongly to protect the pregnancy.
a.x: Progesterone relaxes the uterus and keeps it quiet.
a.w: Progesterone calms the uterine muscle, which is why it is called the hormone that keeps the pregnancy. Strong contractions would expel it.

a.o: Card 2 says hCG keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone in early pregnancy.
a.x: hCG should be said to break down the corpus luteum.
a.w: hCG acts like LH on the corpus luteum, keeping it alive and making progesterone until the placenta takes over.

a.o: Card 3 says the placenta takes over making progesterone at about 10 to 12 weeks.
a.x: The placenta should take over only in the last week of pregnancy.
a.w: The luteal-placental shift happens around the end of the first trimester, after which the corpus luteum can fade.

a.o: Card 5 says placental lactogen raises the mother's blood sugar to feed the baby.
a.x: Placental lactogen should be said to lower the mother's sugar.
a.w: hPL makes the mother's tissues less sensitive to insulin, leaving more glucose in her blood for the fetus.

s:
Short-answer exam, reproductive block, question 3: "Describe the hormone changes of the menstrual cycle." Student Aya Hamed starts with the follicular phase, when FSH from the pituitary makes several follicles grow, and one becomes dominant.

She writes that the growing follicle makes more and more oestrogen, and that high oestrogen for about two days switches to positive feedback on the pituitary. She then writes that this causes a sudden fall in FSH, and that this FSH drop is what makes the follicle burst and release the egg.

For the luteal phase she says the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum and makes progesterone, which prepares the endometrium. If there is no pregnancy, the corpus luteum fades after about 14 days, progesterone falls and menstruation starts. The examiner gave 6 out of 10.
h: this causes a sudden fall in FSH, and that this FSH drop is what makes the follicle burst

a.o: Aya says positive feedback causes a sudden FSH fall, and that the fall triggers ovulation.
a.x: Positive feedback causes an LH surge, which triggers ovulation.
a.w: High oestrogen switches the pituitary to positive feedback and an LH surge follows. Ovulation comes about 36 hours after it starts.

a.o: Aya says FSH makes several follicles grow in the follicular phase, and one becomes dominant.
a.x: FSH should make only a single follicle grow from the start.
a.w: A group of follicles is recruited each cycle under FSH, and the one most sensitive to it becomes dominant.

a.o: Aya says the corpus luteum fades after about 14 days if there is no pregnancy.
a.x: The corpus luteum should last for about three months every cycle.
a.w: Without hCG the corpus luteum lives about 14 days, so the luteal phase is the more constant part of the cycle.

a.o: Aya says the corpus luteum makes progesterone to prepare the lining of the uterus.
a.x: The corpus luteum should be said to make only FSH.
a.w: Progesterone from the corpus luteum turns the endometrium secretory, ready for an embryo to implant.

s:
Renal lab notebook, student Habiba Gaber. Topic: plasma osmolality. I wrote that osmolality measures the number of dissolved particles per kilogram of water, and that sodium and its partner ions account for most of it.

From the board I copied the estimate: calculated osmolality = 2 x sodium + glucose + urea, all in mmol/L. Then I worked out my sample: sodium 140, glucose 5 and urea 5, which gives 290. I wrote that the normal range of plasma osmolality is 28.5 to 29.5 mOsm/kg, so my sample is very high.

At the end I noted that the gap between measured and calculated osmolality is normally under 10, and that a large gap suggests another substance, such as alcohol or a toxic alcohol. The tutor initialled the page.
h: the normal range of plasma osmolality is 28.5 to 29.5 mOsm/kg

a.o: Habiba writes the normal plasma osmolality as 28.5 to 29.5 mOsm/kg.
a.x: Normal plasma osmolality is about 285-295 mOsm/kg.
a.w: The normal range is about 285-295 mOsm/kg, so her result of 290 is normal. Her range is ten times too small.

a.o: Habiba calculates 2 x 140 + 5 + 5 and gets 290 for her sample.
a.x: The sum should be 140 + 5 + 5, giving 150.
a.w: Sodium is doubled to include its partner anions, so 2 x 140 + 5 + 5 = 290 is the right calculated value.

a.o: Habiba says a big gap between measured and calculated osmolality points to another substance.
a.x: A big gap should be said to mean only a lab error.
a.w: An osmolar gap above about 10 suggests unmeasured particles such as ethanol, methanol or ethylene glycol.

a.o: Habiba says sodium and its partner ions make up most of the plasma osmolality.
a.x: Most plasma osmolality should come from glucose.
a.w: Sodium with chloride and bicarbonate accounts for the large majority of plasma osmoles. Glucose and urea add a little.

s:
Draft page "Acid-base balance", renal and respiratory physiology chapter. The page explains that the body keeps blood pH near 7.4 using buffers, the lungs and the kidneys, and that the bicarbonate buffer links carbon dioxide and bicarbonate.

It then gives the four simple disorders. In respiratory acidosis, for example after an opioid overdose or in severe COPD, carbon dioxide builds up and the pH falls. The page says the body compensates for respiratory acidosis by breathing faster to blow off carbon dioxide.

For metabolic acidosis, such as diabetic ketoacidosis, the page says the patient breathes deeply and quickly (Kussmaul breathing) to lower carbon dioxide. It ends by saying kidney compensation takes days, while breathing compensation starts within minutes.
h: the body compensates for respiratory acidosis by breathing faster to blow off carbon dioxide

a.o: The page has respiratory acidosis compensated by faster breathing to blow off CO2.
a.x: The kidneys compensate by keeping more bicarbonate.
a.w: The lungs are the problem in respiratory acidosis, so they cannot fix it. The kidneys retain bicarbonate and excrete acid over days.

a.o: The page says Kussmaul breathing in ketoacidosis lowers the carbon dioxide.
a.x: Ketoacidosis should be said to slow the breathing down.
a.w: In metabolic acidosis the acid stimulates breathing, and deep, fast Kussmaul breaths lower CO2 to raise the pH.

a.o: The page says kidney compensation takes days but breathing changes start in minutes.
a.x: Kidney compensation should be said to start within seconds.
a.w: The lungs can change CO2 almost at once, but the kidney needs days to raise bicarbonate reabsorption and acid excretion.

a.o: The page gives opioid overdose and severe COPD as causes of respiratory acidosis.
a.x: Opioid overdose should be given as a cause of alkalosis.
a.w: Both reduce ventilation, so CO2 builds up in the blood and the pH falls: respiratory acidosis.

s:
Handout for "Gas transport in blood", respiratory physiology, by Dr. Adel. Part 1 says that oxygen is carried in two forms. It states that most oxygen in the blood is dissolved in the plasma, and only a small part is bound to haemoglobin in the red cells.

Part 2 says each gram of haemoglobin can carry about 1.34 mL of oxygen, so with 15 g/dL of haemoglobin, fully saturated arterial blood holds about 20 mL of oxygen per 100 mL. Part 3 says carbon dioxide is carried mainly as bicarbonate, with smaller amounts bound to proteins and dissolved.

A clinical box says that in anaemia the PO2 and saturation can be normal while the oxygen content is low, because there is less haemoglobin to carry it.
h: most oxygen in the blood is dissolved in the plasma, and only a small part is bound to haemoglobin

a.o: The handout says most blood oxygen is dissolved in plasma, not on haemoglobin.
a.x: About 98% of oxygen is carried bound to haemoglobin.
a.w: Only about 0.3 mL of oxygen dissolves in 100 mL of plasma at normal PO2, against about 20 mL carried on haemoglobin.

a.o: The handout says each gram of haemoglobin carries about 1.34 mL of oxygen.
a.x: Each gram should carry about 13.4 mL of oxygen.
a.w: Fully saturated haemoglobin binds about 1.34 mL O2 per gram, which gives about 20 mL per 100 mL of normal blood.

a.o: The handout says carbon dioxide travels in the blood mainly as bicarbonate.
a.x: Carbon dioxide should travel mainly dissolved in the plasma.
a.w: About 70% of CO2 is carried as bicarbonate, made in red cells by carbonic anhydrase, the rest bound or dissolved.

a.o: The handout says anaemia can lower oxygen content with a normal PO2 and saturation.
a.x: Anaemia should be said to always lower the PO2.
a.w: PO2 depends on the lungs, not on haemoglobin, so with less haemoglobin the content falls while PO2 stays normal.

s:
Flashcards "Gut hormones", made by Islam for the gastrointestinal block. Card 1 says gastrin comes from G cells in the stomach antrum and increases acid secretion. Card 2 says somatostatin from D cells switches off the release of many gut hormones.

Card 3 says secretin is released from the duodenum when acid arrives from the stomach, and makes the gallbladder contract and empty its bile. Card 4 says cholecystokinin is released when fat and protein enter the duodenum, and makes the pancreas release bicarbonate-rich fluid.

Card 5 says GIP is released when glucose reaches the small intestine and boosts insulin release, which is why oral glucose gives a bigger insulin rise than the same glucose given into a vein.
h: makes the gallbladder contract and empty its bile

a.o: Islam's cards swap secretin and CCK: secretin contracts the gallbladder, CCK sends bicarbonate.
a.x: Secretin releases bicarbonate; CCK contracts the gallbladder.
a.w: Acid in the duodenum releases secretin, which brings bicarbonate from the pancreas. Fat brings CCK, which empties the gallbladder.

a.o: Card 1 says gastrin from antral G cells increases acid secretion.
a.x: Gastrin should be said to come from the duodenum and block acid.
a.w: Gastrin from G cells in the antrum stimulates parietal cells, both directly and through histamine.

a.o: Card 5 says GIP is why oral glucose gives a bigger insulin rise than glucose in a vein.
a.x: The effect should be credited to secretin instead of GIP.
a.w: GIP and GLP-1 from the gut boost insulin release after oral glucose, the incretin effect.

a.o: Card 2 says somatostatin from D cells switches off many gut hormones.
a.x: Somatostatin should be said to boost gastrin release.
a.w: Somatostatin is a broad inhibitor: it lowers gastrin, acid secretion and many other gut hormones.

s:
Draft page "Fluid exchange in capillaries", cardiovascular physiology chapter. The page explains that fluid moves across capillary walls depending on four Starling forces: capillary and tissue hydrostatic pressure, and capillary and tissue oncotic pressure.

It says that at the arterial end of a capillary the hydrostatic pressure is about 35 mmHg and pushes fluid out, while the plasma oncotic pressure of about 25 mmHg pulls fluid in. It then states that the oncotic pressure comes mostly from sodium in the plasma, since proteins are too large to have much effect.

The page explains that at the venous end hydrostatic pressure falls to about 15 mmHg, so fluid comes back in, and that the lymphatics return the small extra amount of filtered fluid. It ends by linking low albumin, as in liver disease, with swelling of the legs.
h: the oncotic pressure comes mostly from sodium in the plasma, since proteins are too large to have much effect

a.o: The page puts plasma oncotic pressure down to sodium and says proteins add little.
a.x: Plasma proteins, mostly albumin, create the oncotic pressure.
a.w: Sodium crosses the capillary wall freely, so it creates no oncotic gradient. Albumin cannot cross, and that is what holds water in.

a.o: The page says hydrostatic pressure falls to about 15 mmHg at the venous end.
a.x: The pressure should rise to about 50 mmHg at the venous end.
a.w: Pressure drops along the capillary, so at the venous end the oncotic pull wins and fluid moves back in.

a.o: The page says the lymphatics return the small extra amount of filtered fluid.
a.x: The lymphatics should be said to carry only fat.
a.w: Filtration slightly exceeds reabsorption, and the lymphatics return this few litres a day to the blood.

a.o: The page links low albumin, as in liver disease, with swelling of the legs.
a.x: Low albumin should be linked with dehydration of the legs.
a.w: With less albumin the oncotic pull falls, so more fluid stays in the tissues and gathers in the legs.

s:
Short-answer exam, neuroscience block, question 4: "Describe the formation and flow of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)." Student Omar Adel writes that CSF is made by the choroid plexus in the ventricles of the brain.

He writes that the adult makes about 50 mL of CSF a day, and that the total volume in the system at any time is about 150 mL. He then describes the flow: from the lateral ventricles through the interventricular foramina to the third ventricle, then through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle, and out into the subarachnoid space.

He ends by saying CSF is absorbed into the venous sinuses through the arachnoid granulations, and that a blocked aqueduct causes hydrocephalus with large lateral and third ventricles. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the adult makes about 50 mL of CSF a day

a.o: Omar says an adult makes about 50 mL of CSF a day, a third of its volume.
a.x: An adult makes about 500 mL of CSF every day.
a.w: About 500 mL is made each day while about 150 mL is present, so the fluid is replaced three or four times daily.

a.o: Omar runs the CSF from the third ventricle through the aqueduct to the fourth ventricle.
a.x: The flow should go from the fourth ventricle up to the third.
a.w: CSF flows from the lateral ventricles to the third, then through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle.

a.o: Omar says CSF is absorbed into the venous sinuses through the arachnoid granulations.
a.x: CSF should be said to drain into the lymph nodes of the neck.
a.w: Arachnoid granulations push into the dural venous sinuses and let CSF pass into the venous blood.

a.o: Omar says a blocked aqueduct enlarges the lateral and third ventricles.
a.x: A blocked aqueduct should enlarge only the fourth ventricle.
a.w: Fluid builds up above the block, so the lateral and third ventricles swell while the fourth stays normal.

s:
Handout for "Glycolysis", metabolism block, by Dr. Tamer. Part 1 says glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm of every cell and breaks one glucose into two pyruvate molecules, with no need for oxygen.

Part 2 sums up the energy. The first half of the pathway uses 2 ATP to trap and split glucose, and the second half makes 4 ATP and 2 NADH. The handout then says that the net gain from one glucose is therefore 4 ATP, which is why red cells can live on glycolysis alone.

Part 3 says that without oxygen, pyruvate is turned into lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can keep going. A last note says red blood cells have no mitochondria, so they depend fully on glycolysis for energy.
h: the net gain from one glucose is therefore 4 ATP

a.o: The handout gives a net gain of 4 ATP from each glucose, after spending 2.
a.x: 4 ATP made minus 2 ATP used gives a net gain of 2 ATP.
a.w: Glycolysis makes 4 ATP but spends 2 on hexokinase and PFK-1, so the net yield is 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose.

a.o: The handout says lactate making regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can keep going.
a.x: Lactate making should be said to use up the cell's ATP.
a.w: Lactate dehydrogenase uses NADH to reduce pyruvate, freeing NAD+ for the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate step.

a.o: The handout says red cells depend fully on glycolysis because they lack mitochondria.
a.x: Red cells should be said to rely on fatty acid oxidation.
a.w: Without mitochondria red cells cannot use the Krebs cycle or oxidative phosphorylation, so glycolysis is their only ATP source.

a.o: The handout says glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and needs no oxygen.
a.x: Glycolysis should be placed inside the mitochondria.
a.w: All ten glycolytic enzymes work in the cytosol, and none of them needs oxygen to function.

s:
Flashcards "Control of glycolysis", made by Malak for the biochemistry quiz. Card 1 says hexokinase traps glucose in the cell as glucose-6-phosphate and is inhibited by its own product. Card 2 says glucokinase, in liver and pancreatic beta cells, has a high Km, so it works mainly after a meal.

Card 3 says the rate-limiting step of glycolysis is hexokinase, which is why the pathway is controlled mainly at its first step. Card 4 says PFK-1 is switched on by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and switched off by ATP and citrate.

Card 5 says pyruvate kinase is the last step and makes ATP, and that a lack of pyruvate kinase causes haemolytic anaemia because red cells run out of energy.
h: the rate-limiting step of glycolysis is hexokinase

a.o: Card 3 names hexokinase as the rate-limiting step of glycolysis.
a.x: PFK-1 is the rate-limiting, committed step of glycolysis.
a.w: PFK-1 makes fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, the first step committed to glycolysis, and is the main point of control.

a.o: Card 2 says glucokinase has a high Km and works mainly after a meal.
a.x: Glucokinase should have a very low Km and work in fasting.
a.w: A high Km means glucokinase only works fast when glucose is high, so the liver takes up glucose after meals.

a.o: Card 4 says AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate switch PFK-1 on, and ATP and citrate switch it off.
a.x: ATP should be said to switch PFK-1 on instead.
a.w: When energy is low (AMP high) PFK-1 speeds up; when ATP and citrate are high the cell has enough and it slows down.

a.o: Card 5 says pyruvate kinase lack causes haemolytic anaemia.
a.x: Pyruvate kinase lack should be said to cause liver failure.
a.w: Red cells need glycolytic ATP for their pumps, so pyruvate kinase deficiency makes them rigid and they break early.

s:
Short-answer exam, biochemistry block, question 3: "Explain enzyme kinetics and inhibition." Student Hager Sobhy writes that Vmax is the maximum rate when all the enzyme is saturated with substrate, and that Km is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half Vmax.

She explains that a low Km means high affinity of the enzyme for its substrate. She then writes that a competitive inhibitor lowers Vmax but leaves Km unchanged, because it binds to a site away from the active site.

She adds that a non-competitive inhibitor cannot be overcome by adding more substrate. She ends by giving methotrexate, which looks like folic acid and competes with it at dihydrofolate reductase, as an example of competitive inhibition. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: a competitive inhibitor lowers Vmax but leaves Km unchanged

a.o: Hager says a competitive inhibitor lowers Vmax and binds away from the site.
a.x: It raises Km, leaves Vmax and binds the active site.
a.w: It competes for the active site, so more substrate overcomes it: Vmax is reached, but more substrate is needed (Km rises).

a.o: Hager says a low Km means the enzyme has a high affinity for its substrate.
a.x: A low Km should be said to mean low affinity.
a.w: If half the maximum rate is reached at a low substrate level, the enzyme binds its substrate tightly.

a.o: Hager says adding more substrate cannot overcome a non-competitive inhibitor.
a.x: More substrate should fully reverse this kind of inhibition.
a.w: A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and lowers the active enzyme, so Vmax falls whatever the substrate level.

a.o: Hager gives methotrexate at dihydrofolate reductase as competitive inhibition.
a.x: Methotrexate should be given as an inhibitor of DNA ligase.
a.w: Methotrexate resembles folate and competes with it for the active site of dihydrofolate reductase.

s:
Molecular biology lab notebook, student Nour Elhady. We studied the structure of DNA. I wrote that DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands held together by hydrogen bonds between bases, with adenine pairing with thymine by two bonds and guanine with cytosine by three.

Then we did a Chargaff exercise. The sample had 20% adenine. I wrote that thymine is also 20%, and so guanine is also 20%, and cytosine makes up the remaining 40%.

At the end I noted that DNA rich in G-C pairs needs a higher temperature to separate, because of the extra hydrogen bond, and that RNA uses uracil in place of thymine. The tutor asked us to check our answers before the quiz.
h: guanine is also 20%, and cytosine makes up the remaining 40%

a.o: Nour gives guanine 20% and cytosine 40% in a sample with 20% adenine.
a.x: Guanine and cytosine should each be 30% of the bases.
a.w: A = T = 20% leaves 60% for G and C. Since G always pairs with C, each is 30%. G and C cannot differ in double-stranded DNA.

a.o: Nour pairs adenine with thymine by two hydrogen bonds and guanine with cytosine by three.
a.x: A-T should have three bonds and G-C two bonds.
a.w: A-T pairs form two hydrogen bonds and G-C pairs form three, which is why G-C rich DNA is more stable.

a.o: Nour says DNA rich in G-C pairs needs a higher temperature to separate.
a.x: G-C rich DNA should separate at a lower temperature.
a.w: The third hydrogen bond and stronger stacking of G-C pairs raise the melting temperature of the DNA.

a.o: Nour notes that RNA uses uracil in place of thymine.
a.x: RNA should be said to use cytosine in place of thymine.
a.w: RNA has uracil, which pairs with adenine like thymine does, but lacks thymine's methyl group.

s:
Draft page "Getting rid of nitrogen", amino acid metabolism chapter. The page explains that when amino acids are broken down, their amino groups are removed and become ammonia, which is toxic to the brain.

It states that the urea cycle takes place mainly in the kidney, using enzymes in both the mitochondria and the cytoplasm, and that carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I is the first and rate-limiting step. Each turn of the cycle makes one urea molecule from two nitrogen atoms.

The page then says urea is carried in the blood and passed in the urine. A clinical box explains that in liver failure ammonia builds up and can cause confusion and coma (hepatic encephalopathy), and that a lack of ornithine transcarbamylase is the most common inherited urea cycle disorder.
h: the urea cycle takes place mainly in the kidney

a.o: The page places the urea cycle, which removes ammonia, mainly in the kidney.
a.x: The urea cycle runs mainly in the liver cells.
a.w: Liver cells hold the full set of urea cycle enzymes. The kidney only excretes the urea, which is why liver failure raises ammonia.

a.o: The page names carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I as the first, rate-limiting step.
a.x: The rate-limiting step should be arginase, the last step.
a.w: CPS I in the mitochondria joins ammonia and bicarbonate to make carbamoyl phosphate. It needs N-acetylglutamate.

a.o: The page names ornithine transcarbamylase lack as the commonest inherited urea cycle disorder.
a.x: The commonest should be arginase deficiency.
a.w: OTC deficiency is X-linked and is the most common of the urea cycle disorders, often showing with high ammonia in baby boys.

a.o: The page says each turn of the cycle makes one urea from two nitrogen atoms.
a.x: Each turn should make two urea molecules from four nitrogens.
a.w: One nitrogen comes from ammonia via carbamoyl phosphate and one from aspartate, giving one urea per turn.

s:
Flashcards "Water-soluble vitamins", made by Rahma for the nutrition block. Card 1 says vitamin B1 (thiamine) is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and that its lack causes beriberi, with heart failure or nerve damage.

Card 2 says Wernicke's encephalopathy, with confusion, unsteady walking and eye movement problems, is caused by a lack of vitamin B12, and is common in people who drink a lot of alcohol. Card 3 says a lack of niacin (B3) causes pellagra, with the three Ds: dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.

Card 4 says folate and vitamin B12 are both needed for DNA synthesis, so a lack of either causes a megaloblastic anaemia. Card 5 says vitamin C is needed to make collagen, and its lack causes scurvy with bleeding gums.
h: is caused by a lack of vitamin B12

a.o: Card 2 blames a lack of vitamin B12 for Wernicke's in drinkers.
a.x: It is caused by a lack of thiamine, vitamin B1, instead.
a.w: Alcohol lowers thiamine intake and absorption. The brain depends on thiamine-using enzymes, so their failure causes Wernicke's.

a.o: Card 3 links a lack of niacin with pellagra and its three Ds.
a.x: Pellagra should be linked with a lack of riboflavin.
a.w: Niacin (B3) is needed to make NAD and NADP. Its lack gives dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.

a.o: Card 4 says a lack of folate or B12 gives a megaloblastic anaemia.
a.x: Their lack should give a small-cell anaemia instead.
a.w: Both are needed for DNA synthesis, so red cell precursors grow but cannot divide, making large cells.

a.o: Card 1 makes thiamine a cofactor of pyruvate dehydrogenase.
a.x: Thiamine should be the cofactor for lactate dehydrogenase.
a.w: Thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase.

s:
Practical report, carbohydrate tests, student Hossam Mahmoud. The aim was to identify four unknown sugar solutions: glucose, fructose, sucrose and starch. Hossam used iodine, Benedict's reagent and a water bath at 100 degrees C.
