Results: tube 1 turned blue-black with iodine, so he called it starch. Tubes 2, 3 and 4 all turned brick-red with Benedict's after heating. He wrote that tube 4 must be sucrose, because sucrose is a reducing sugar and gives a strong red colour with Benedict's.

In the discussion he explains that Benedict's test works because reducing sugars change blue copper(II) ions to red copper(I) oxide. He adds that a fair test needs equal volumes of each sample and the same heating time. The demonstrator wrote "check your sucrose" on the report.
h: sucrose is a reducing sugar and gives a strong red colour with Benedict's

a.o: Hossam calls sucrose a reducing sugar that turns Benedict's reagent red.
a.x: Sucrose is non-reducing, so Benedict's stays blue.
a.w: In sucrose the reducing ends of glucose and fructose are joined, so it gives no red colour. A red tube 4 means another sugar.

a.o: Hossam calls tube 1 starch because it turned blue-black with iodine.
a.x: Iodine should turn starch bright yellow instead.
a.w: Iodine slips into the starch helix and gives a blue-black colour, the standard test for starch.

a.o: Hossam says reducing sugars turn blue copper(II) into red copper(I) oxide.
a.x: The colour should come from copper turning into copper sulfate.
a.w: Reducing sugars give electrons to Cu2+, forming a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide.

a.o: Hossam uses equal sample volumes and the same heating time in each tube.
a.x: Each tube should be heated for a different time.
a.w: Keeping volume and heating time the same means the colour depends only on the sugar in the tube.

s:
Practical report, enzyme lab, student Lina Saad. The aim was to find the effect of temperature on the activity of amylase. Lina set up five tubes of starch at 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 degrees C and added amylase to each, then tested drops with iodine every minute until the blue colour was gone.

In the method she writes that because the higher temperature tubes worked faster, she also used a stronger amylase solution in the 20 and 30 degree tubes "so that all the tubes would finish in the lesson". She kept a sixth tube with boiled amylase as a control, which stayed blue throughout.

She concludes that amylase works best at about 40 degrees C and that it stops at 60 degrees C because the enzyme is denatured. The demonstrator asked her which results she could still trust.
h: she also used a stronger amylase solution in the 20 and 30 degree tubes

a.o: Lina used a stronger amylase solution in the cooler tubes as well.
a.x: The same enzyme strength should be used in every tube.
a.w: Changing enzyme strength as well as temperature makes the cool tubes look faster than they really are, so the curve cannot be trusted.

a.o: Lina keeps a boiled amylase tube as a control, and it stays blue.
a.x: The control should use amylase at room temperature instead.
a.w: A boiled enzyme shows that the colour change needs active enzyme, not just heat or time.

a.o: Lina says amylase stops at 60 degrees because the enzyme is denatured.
a.x: The stop at 60 degrees should be put down to the starch breaking.
a.w: High heat breaks the bonds that hold the enzyme's shape, so the active site no longer fits starch.

a.o: Lina tests drops with iodine every minute until the blue colour is gone.
a.x: The iodine test should be done only once at the start.
a.w: Repeated iodine tests show when the starch is used up, which gives the time for each temperature.

s:
Handout for "Fasting metabolism", metabolism block, by Dr. Nabila. Part 1 says that after the glycogen in the liver runs low, usually within a day of fasting, the liver makes new glucose by gluconeogenesis to supply the brain and red cells.

Part 2 lists the sources of new glucose: lactate from muscle and red cells, glycerol from broken-down fat, and amino acids such as alanine from muscle protein. It then says that even-chain fatty acids are also turned into glucose in large amounts, since they give acetyl-CoA, which can be made into pyruvate.

Part 3 says that in longer fasting the liver makes ketone bodies from fatty acids, and that the brain adapts to use them, which saves muscle protein. The last box says glucagon and cortisol drive gluconeogenesis, while insulin blocks it.
h: even-chain fatty acids are also turned into glucose in large amounts, since they give acetyl-CoA, which can be made into pyruvate

a.o: The handout says acetyl-CoA from fatty acids can be made into new glucose.
a.x: Acetyl-CoA cannot become pyruvate, so no new glucose.
a.w: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is one-way, so acetyl-CoA cannot be turned back into pyruvate. Only the glycerol part of fat feeds glucose.

a.o: The handout lists lactate, glycerol and alanine as sources of new glucose.
a.x: Glycerol should be left off the list of glucose sources.
a.w: Lactate (Cori cycle), glycerol from fat and amino acids like alanine are the main gluconeogenic substrates.

a.o: The handout says the brain adapts to burn ketone bodies, which saves muscle protein.
a.x: The brain should be said never to use ketone bodies.
a.w: In long fasting the brain takes up ketones, so less glucose is needed and less muscle is broken down for it.

a.o: The handout says glucagon and cortisol drive gluconeogenesis while insulin blocks it.
a.x: Insulin should be said to drive gluconeogenesis too.
a.w: Glucagon and cortisol switch on gluconeogenic enzymes, while insulin switches them off after a meal.

s:
Short-answer exam, metabolism block, question 7: "Describe von Gierke disease." Student Mohamed Tarek writes that it is a glycogen storage disease, passed on in an autosomal recessive way, and that babies present with a big liver and severe low blood sugar between feeds.

He writes that it is caused by a lack of muscle glycogen phosphorylase, so the liver cannot release glucose from glycogen. He adds that the patients have high lactate, high uric acid and high blood fats.

He ends by saying that treatment is frequent feeds, including uncooked cornstarch at night to give a slow release of glucose, and that the liver keeps storing glycogen because glucose-6-phosphate cannot leave the cell as glucose. The examiner gave 6 out of 10.
h: a lack of muscle glycogen phosphorylase

a.o: Mohamed blames von Gierke disease on a lack of the muscle phosphorylase.
a.x: It is caused by a lack of glucose-6-phosphatase.
a.w: Without glucose-6-phosphatase the liver cannot turn G6P into free glucose, so glycogen piles up and fasting sugar falls.

a.o: Mohamed lists high lactate, uric acid and blood fats in these patients.
a.x: These patients should have low lactate and low uric acid.
a.w: Trapped G6P is pushed into glycolysis and the pentose pathway, raising lactate, uric acid and triglycerides.

a.o: Mohamed gives uncooked cornstarch at night for a slow release of glucose.
a.x: Night feeds should be stopped to rest the liver.
a.w: Uncooked cornstarch is digested slowly, giving steady glucose and preventing night-time hypoglycaemia.

a.o: Mohamed says von Gierke disease is passed on in an autosomal recessive way.
a.x: It should be said to pass only from father to son.
a.w: Like most enzyme deficiency disorders, glycogen storage disease type I is autosomal recessive.

s:
Draft page "Phenylketonuria", inborn errors chapter. The page says PKU is an autosomal recessive disease found in about 1 in 10,000 births, and is one of the conditions checked on the newborn heel-prick test.

It states that classic PKU is caused by a lack of tyrosinase, the enzyme that turns phenylalanine into tyrosine, so phenylalanine builds up in the blood and brain. It adds that untreated children develop severe learning disability, seizures and a musty smell.

The page explains that because tyrosine is needed to make melanin, children with PKU often have fair skin and hair. Treatment is a diet low in phenylalanine, and the page warns that the sweetener aspartame contains phenylalanine. It ends by saying tyrosine becomes an essential amino acid in PKU.
h: a lack of tyrosinase, the enzyme that turns phenylalanine into tyrosine

a.o: The page blames PKU on a lack of the enzyme tyrosinase.
a.x: Classic PKU is a lack of phenylalanine hydroxylase.
a.w: Phenylalanine hydroxylase makes tyrosine. Tyrosinase works later, turning tyrosine toward melanin, and its lack causes albinism.

a.o: The page says children with PKU often have fair skin and hair.
a.x: Children with PKU should be said to have darker skin.
a.w: With little tyrosine made, less melanin is produced, so untreated children often have fair skin, hair and eyes.

a.o: The page warns that aspartame contains phenylalanine.
a.x: The warning should be about table sugar instead.
a.w: Aspartame is a dipeptide of aspartate and phenylalanine methyl ester, so it adds phenylalanine to the diet.

a.o: The page says tyrosine becomes an essential amino acid in PKU.
a.x: Tyrosine should be said to become harmful in PKU.
a.w: The body normally makes tyrosine from phenylalanine, so when that step fails tyrosine must come from food.

s:
Flashcards "The electron transport chain", made by Shady for the biochemistry quiz. Card 1 says NADH gives its electrons to complex I and FADH2 to complex II, and the electrons pass along to oxygen.

Card 2 says that as electrons move, complexes I, III and IV pump protons into the space between the two mitochondrial membranes, and ATP synthase uses the flow back to make ATP. Card 3 says oxygen is the final electron acceptor and is turned into water at complex IV.

Card 4 says cyanide blocks complex I, which is why it stops cells using oxygen so quickly. Card 5 says uncouplers such as the fat-soluble chemical DNP let protons leak back without making ATP, so the energy is lost as heat.
h: cyanide blocks complex I

a.o: Card 4 says cyanide stops cells using oxygen by blocking complex I first.
a.x: Cyanide blocks complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase.
a.w: Cyanide binds the ferric iron of cytochrome a3 in complex IV, so electrons cannot reach oxygen and the whole chain stops.

a.o: Card 3 makes oxygen the final electron acceptor, turned into water at complex IV.
a.x: Oxygen should be the first acceptor at complex I.
a.w: Complex IV passes electrons to O2, which picks up protons to form water at the end of the chain.

a.o: Card 5 says uncouplers let protons leak back, so energy is lost as heat.
a.x: Uncouplers should be said to make more ATP.
a.w: DNP carries protons across the inner membrane, so the gradient runs down without passing through ATP synthase.

a.o: Card 2 has complexes I, III and IV pump protons between the two membranes.
a.x: Complex II should be the main proton pump.
a.w: Complexes I, III and IV pump protons into the intermembrane space. Complex II passes electrons but pumps none.

s:
Short-answer exam, biochemistry block, question 9: "Describe the structure of haemoglobin and how it binds oxygen." Student Mai Hosny writes that adult haemoglobin (HbA) is made of four chains, two alpha and two beta, each holding a haem group.

She writes that the iron in haem must be in the ferric (Fe3+) state to bind oxygen, and that each haemoglobin molecule can carry four oxygen molecules. She explains that once one oxygen binds, the others bind more easily, which gives the S-shaped curve.

She ends by saying that methaemoglobin, which can form after some drugs, cannot carry oxygen and makes the patient look blue, and that it is treated with methylene blue. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the iron in haem must be in the ferric (Fe3+) state to bind oxygen

a.o: Mai says haem iron must be ferric (Fe3+) to bind oxygen.
a.x: Haem iron must be ferrous (Fe2+) to bind oxygen.
a.w: Oxygen binds ferrous iron. When iron is oxidised to ferric, the molecule becomes methaemoglobin and can no longer carry oxygen.

a.o: Mai says each haemoglobin carries four oxygen molecules.
a.x: Each haemoglobin should carry only one oxygen molecule.
a.w: There is one haem per chain and one oxygen per haem, so a full haemoglobin molecule carries four O2.

a.o: Mai says oxygen binding to one site makes the others bind more easily.
a.x: Each bound oxygen should make the next one harder to bind.
a.w: Cooperative binding shifts haemoglobin from the tense to the relaxed state, which gives the sigmoid curve.

a.o: Mai says methaemoglobinaemia is treated with methylene blue.
a.x: It should be treated with vitamin K by mouth.
a.w: Methylene blue helps the NADPH-dependent reductase turn ferric iron back to ferrous iron.

s:
Handout for "Haem synthesis and porphyrias", biochemistry block, by Dr. Waleed. Part 1 says haem is made partly in the mitochondria and partly in the cytoplasm, mostly in the bone marrow and the liver.

Part 2 says the first and rate-limiting step joins glycine and succinyl-CoA to make delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), using the enzyme ALA synthase, which needs vitamin B6. The last step puts iron into protoporphyrin using ferrochelatase.

Part 3 covers lead poisoning. The handout states that lead acts mainly by blocking ALA synthase, the first enzyme, so ALA levels in the urine fall. It adds that lead poisoning gives a small-cell anaemia with basophilic stippling of red cells, and that children may have abdominal pain and learning problems.
h: lead acts mainly by blocking ALA synthase, the first enzyme, so ALA levels in the urine fall

a.o: The handout says lead blocks ALA synthase, so less ALA appears in the urine.
a.x: Lead blocks ALA dehydratase, so ALA rises instead.
a.w: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase. ALA builds up and spills into the urine, and protoporphyrin rises in red cells.

a.o: The handout says the first step joins glycine and succinyl-CoA using a B6-dependent enzyme.
a.x: The first step should join alanine and acetyl-CoA.
a.w: ALA synthase joins glycine and succinyl-CoA and needs pyridoxal phosphate, from vitamin B6, as its cofactor.

a.o: The handout says ferrochelatase puts iron into protoporphyrin as the last step.
a.x: Iron should be added as the very first step of haem making.
a.w: Ferrochelatase in the mitochondria adds ferrous iron to protoporphyrin IX to complete haem.

a.o: The handout links lead poisoning with basophilic stippling of the red cells.
a.x: Lead should be linked with large red cells and no stippling.
a.w: Lead inhibits the enzyme that clears RNA from red cells, so leftover ribosomes show as blue dots.

s:
Short-answer exam, biochemistry block, question 4: "Describe how bilirubin is handled by the body." Student Laila Osman writes that bilirubin comes mainly from the breakdown of haemoglobin from old red cells in the spleen.

She writes that unconjugated bilirubin is fat-soluble and travels in the blood bound to albumin. In the liver it is joined to glucuronic acid by the enzyme UDP-glucuronyl transferase, which makes it water-soluble. She then writes that in haemolysis unconjugated bilirubin rises and passes into the urine, making it dark.

She ends by saying that gut bacteria turn bilirubin into urobilinogen, part of which is reabsorbed and passed in the urine, and that stercobilin gives stool its brown colour. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: in haemolysis unconjugated bilirubin rises and passes into the urine, making it dark

a.o: Laila says unconjugated bilirubin passes into the urine in haemolysis.
a.x: Unconjugated bilirubin is never filtered by the kidney.
a.w: Only water-soluble conjugated bilirubin can appear in urine. Haemolytic jaundice is "acholuric": the urine has no bilirubin.

a.o: Laila says UDP-glucuronyl transferase makes bilirubin water-soluble in the liver.
a.x: The enzyme should be said to make bilirubin fat-soluble.
a.w: Adding glucuronic acid makes bilirubin water-soluble so it can be excreted in bile.

a.o: Laila says unconjugated bilirubin is carried in the blood bound to albumin.
a.x: It should be said to travel freely dissolved in plasma.
a.w: Unconjugated bilirubin is poorly soluble in water, so it rides on albumin to reach the liver.

a.o: Laila says stercobilin gives stool its brown colour.
a.x: Stool colour should come from biliverdin instead.
a.w: Gut bacteria turn bilirubin into urobilinogen and then stercobilin, the brown pigment of faeces.

s:
Flashcards "Lipids", made by Ahmed Fathy for the nutrition and biochemistry exam. Card 1 says triglycerides are made of glycerol and three fatty acids and are the main store of energy in the body.

Card 2 lists the essential fatty acids that must come from food: oleic acid and linoleic acid, because the body cannot make them. Card 3 says saturated fatty acids have no double bonds, while unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds that put kinks in the chain.

Card 4 says phospholipids form cell membranes because they have a water-loving head and two water-fearing tails. Card 5 says omega-3 fatty acids, found in oily fish, can lower blood triglycerides.
h: oleic acid and linoleic acid, because the body cannot make them

a.o: Card 2 lists oleic acid as an essential fatty acid along with linoleic acid.
a.x: The essential pair is linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid.
a.w: Humans can make oleic acid (omega-9). They cannot add double bonds beyond carbon 9, so linoleic and alpha-linolenic are essential.

a.o: Card 3 says unsaturated fatty acids have double bonds that kink the chain.
a.x: Unsaturated fats should be said to have no double bonds.
a.w: Cis double bonds bend the chain, so unsaturated fats pack loosely and stay liquid at room temperature.

a.o: Card 4 says phospholipids have a water-loving head and two water-fearing tails.
a.x: Phospholipids should have three tails and no head group.
a.w: The polar head faces water and the two fatty acid tails face inward, forming the lipid bilayer.

a.o: Card 5 says omega-3 fatty acids from oily fish can lower triglycerides.
a.x: Omega-3 fats should be said to raise blood triglycerides.
a.w: Omega-3 fatty acids reduce liver production of VLDL, which lowers triglyceride levels in the blood.

s:
Practical report, molecular biology lab, student Seif Ashraf. The aim was to copy a short gene from a DNA sample using PCR. Seif mixed the template DNA, two primers, the four nucleotides, a buffer with magnesium and a heat-stable Taq polymerase.

In the method he lists each cycle: denature at 95 degrees C to separate the strands, anneal the primers at 95 degrees C so they stick to the single strands, then extend at 72 degrees C so Taq can build the new strands. He ran 30 cycles.

In the discussion he explains that the number of copies doubles with each cycle, and that he ran a tube with no template DNA as a negative control to check for contamination. The demonstrator circled one temperature in his method.
h: anneal the primers at 95 degrees C so they stick to the single strands

a.o: Seif anneals the primers at 95 degrees C, like the first step.
a.x: Primers should anneal lower, at about 50-65 degrees C.
a.w: At 95 degrees C the strands stay apart and primers cannot bind. Cooling to around 55 degrees C lets them pair with their targets.

a.o: Seif says the number of copies doubles with each PCR cycle.
a.x: The number of copies should rise by one with each cycle.
a.w: Each cycle copies every strand present, so the target doubles each time, about a billion copies after 30 cycles.

a.o: Seif runs a tube with no template DNA as a negative control.
a.x: The control should contain twice the template DNA instead.
a.w: A no-template control should stay blank; a band there shows contamination of the reagents.

a.o: Seif uses Taq polymerase because it survives the heating steps.
a.x: A human DNA polymerase should be used for PCR instead.
a.w: Taq comes from a bacterium that lives in hot springs, so it is not destroyed by the 95-degree steps.

s:
Handout for "From gene to protein", molecular biology block, by Dr. Heba. Part 1 says that in transcription RNA polymerase reads the template DNA strand and builds mRNA, using uracil in place of thymine.

Part 2 explains the genetic code: each codon of three bases codes for one amino acid, and the code is "degenerate", meaning most amino acids have more than one codon. The handout then lists AUG, UAA and UAG as the three stop codons, and says UGA codes for methionine and starts every protein.

Part 3 says translation takes place on ribosomes, where tRNA brings each amino acid and its anticodon pairs with the codon. A last box explains that a point mutation that turns a codon into a stop codon is called a nonsense mutation.
h: lists AUG, UAA and UAG as the three stop codons, and says UGA codes for methionine

a.o: The handout makes AUG a stop codon and UGA the methionine start codon instead.
a.x: AUG is the start codon; UAA, UAG and UGA are stops.
a.w: AUG codes for methionine and starts translation. The three stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA, which code for no amino acid.

a.o: The handout says the code is degenerate, with most amino acids having several codons.
a.x: Each amino acid should have exactly one codon.
a.w: There are 61 sense codons for 20 amino acids, so most amino acids are coded by two to six codons.

a.o: The handout calls a change that creates a stop codon a nonsense mutation.
a.x: Such a change should be called a silent mutation.
a.w: A nonsense mutation turns a sense codon into a stop, cutting the protein short; a silent one changes no amino acid.

a.o: The handout says the tRNA anticodon pairs with the codon on the ribosome.
a.x: The anticodon should pair with the DNA in the nucleus.
a.w: Each tRNA carries an anticodon that base-pairs with the matching mRNA codon at the ribosome.

s:
Draft page "Gout and purine breakdown", metabolism chapter. The page explains that uric acid is the end product of the breakdown of pyrimidines such as cytosine and thymine, and that humans cannot break uric acid down further because they lack the enzyme uricase.

It states that the enzyme xanthine oxidase turns hypoxanthine into xanthine and then xanthine into uric acid, and that allopurinol blocks this enzyme to lower uric acid levels. The page adds that uric acid crystals form in cool joints, which is why gout often starts in the big toe.

A box explains that cancer treatment can release a lot of nucleic acid from dying cells, causing tumour lysis syndrome with very high uric acid. The page ends by describing Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, caused by a lack of the salvage enzyme HGPRT.
h: the end product of the breakdown of pyrimidines such as cytosine and thymine

a.o: The page calls uric acid the end product of breaking down the pyrimidines.
a.x: Uric acid is the end product of purine breakdown.
a.w: Uric acid comes from purines: adenine and guanine pass through hypoxanthine and xanthine. Pyrimidines break down to soluble products.

a.o: The page says allopurinol lowers uric acid by blocking xanthine oxidase.
a.x: Allopurinol should be said to work by blocking uricase.
a.w: Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, so less hypoxanthine and xanthine become uric acid.

a.o: The page says crystals form in cool joints, so gout often starts in the big toe.
a.x: Gout should be said to start in the warm spine.
a.w: Uric acid is less soluble at lower temperatures, so cooler joints at the ends of the limbs are hit first.

a.o: The page blames Lesch-Nyhan syndrome on a lack of the salvage enzyme HGPRT.
a.x: Lesch-Nyhan should be blamed on too much uricase.
a.w: HGPRT recycles purine bases. Without it purines are broken down instead, so uric acid rises sharply.

s:
Flashcards "Collagen", made by Farah for the connective tissue block. Card 1 says collagen is the most common protein in the body and gives strength to skin, bone, tendon and cartilage.

Card 2 says each collagen molecule is a triple helix of three chains, and that proline is found at every third position, because it is the smallest amino acid and fits in the tight centre of the helix. Card 3 says vitamin C is needed to add hydroxyl groups to proline and lysine, which makes the helix stable.

Card 4 says type I collagen is found in bone, skin and tendon, and that faulty type I collagen causes osteogenesis imperfecta, with bones that break easily. Card 5 says Ehlers-Danlos syndrome gives stretchy skin and loose joints.
h: proline is found at every third position, because it is the smallest amino acid

a.o: Card 2 puts proline, as the smallest amino acid, every third position.
a.x: Glycine, the smallest amino acid, is every third one here.
a.w: Glycine has only a hydrogen side chain, so it alone fits inside the tight triple helix. Proline is common but bulky.

a.o: Card 3 says vitamin C is needed to hydroxylate proline and lysine.
a.x: Vitamin C should be said to break collagen down instead.
a.w: Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need vitamin C; without it collagen is weak and scurvy follows.

a.o: Card 4 links faulty type I collagen with osteogenesis imperfecta.
a.x: Osteogenesis imperfecta should be linked with type IV collagen.
a.w: Type I collagen is the main protein of bone, so mutations in it cause brittle bones that fracture easily.

a.o: Card 5 says Ehlers-Danlos syndrome gives stretchy skin and loose joints.
a.x: It should be said to give stiff skin and fused joints.
a.w: Ehlers-Danlos syndromes come from faulty collagen processing, giving very elastic skin and hypermobile joints.

s:
Short-answer exam, biochemistry block, question 6: "Describe how hormones signal to cells." Student Karim Samy writes that steroid hormones such as cortisol are fat-soluble, cross the cell membrane and bind receptors inside the cell that act on genes.

He writes that adrenaline binds a G protein-coupled receptor, which switches on adenylate cyclase and raises cAMP. He then writes that the insulin receptor is also a G protein-coupled receptor that raises cAMP inside the cell, just like glucagon.

He ends by saying that the effect of a hormone that acts through cAMP is switched off when phosphodiesterase breaks cAMP down, and that caffeine blocks this enzyme. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the insulin receptor is also a G protein-coupled receptor that raises cAMP

a.o: Karim calls the insulin receptor a G protein-coupled receptor that raises cAMP.
a.x: The insulin receptor is a tyrosine kinase, not a GPCR.
a.w: Insulin binding makes the receptor phosphorylate itself on tyrosines, starting the IRS and PI3K pathway. Insulin actually lowers cAMP.

a.o: Karim says steroid hormones cross the membrane and bind receptors inside the cell.
a.x: Steroids should bind receptors on the cell surface only.
a.w: Steroids are lipid-soluble, so they diffuse in and bind cytoplasmic or nuclear receptors that change gene transcription.

a.o: Karim says adrenaline acts through a G protein receptor that raises cAMP.
a.x: Adrenaline should act through a tyrosine kinase receptor.
a.w: Beta receptors couple to Gs, which switches on adenylate cyclase and raises cAMP inside the cell.

a.o: Karim says phosphodiesterase ends cAMP signals and caffeine blocks it.
a.x: Caffeine should be said to speed up phosphodiesterase.
a.w: Phosphodiesterase turns cAMP into AMP. Caffeine and theophylline inhibit it, which prolongs cAMP signals.

s:
Handout for "The pentose phosphate pathway", metabolism block, by Dr. Sameh. Part 1 says the pathway runs in the cytoplasm and starts from glucose-6-phosphate, and that its first enzyme, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), is the rate-limiting step.

Part 2 states that the main products are ATP and NADH, which red cells use for energy, and ribose-5-phosphate for making nucleotides. Part 3 explains that red cells use the pathway to keep glutathione in its reduced form, which protects them from oxidant damage.

A clinical box describes G6PD deficiency, an X-linked disorder that is common in the Mediterranean. Eating fava beans or taking some drugs can trigger haemolysis, with Heinz bodies and bite cells on the blood film.
h: the main products are ATP and NADH

a.o: The handout names ATP and NADH as the main products formed by this pathway.
a.x: The main products are NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate.
a.w: The pentose phosphate pathway makes no ATP. Its key product is NADPH, used to keep glutathione reduced and to build fats.

a.o: The handout names G6PD as the first and rate-limiting enzyme of the pathway.
a.x: The rate-limiting enzyme should be transketolase.
a.w: G6PD makes the first NADPH and controls flow through the pathway, which is why its lack matters so much.

a.o: The handout calls G6PD deficiency X-linked and common in the Mediterranean.
a.x: G6PD deficiency should be said to be autosomal dominant.
a.w: The G6PD gene is on the X chromosome, so mostly males are affected; it is common where malaria was.

a.o: The handout links fava beans with haemolysis, Heinz bodies and bite cells.
a.x: Fava beans should be said to protect against haemolysis.
a.w: Fava beans and some drugs create oxidant stress; without NADPH, haemoglobin clumps (Heinz bodies) and cells are cleared.

s:
Biochemistry lab notebook, student Mohab Raafat. Topic: cholesterol. I wrote that cholesterol is made in the liver from acetyl-CoA, and that it is used to build cell membranes, bile acids, steroid hormones and vitamin D.

I wrote that the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis is HMG-CoA synthase, and that statin drugs block this enzyme, so the liver makes less cholesterol. I added that the liver cells then make more LDL receptors and pull more LDL out of the blood.

At the end I noted that familial hypercholesterolaemia is caused by faulty LDL receptors, so LDL stays high from birth, and that cholesterol synthesis is highest at night, so some statins are taken in the evening.
h: the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis is HMG-CoA synthase

a.o: Mohab names HMG-CoA synthase as the rate-limiting step and the statin target.
a.x: HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting step instead.
a.w: HMG-CoA reductase turns HMG-CoA into mevalonate, the main control step. Statins inhibit it; the synthase acts one step earlier.

a.o: Mohab says liver cells make more LDL receptors when statins lower their cholesterol.
a.x: Statins should be said to cut the number of LDL receptors.
a.w: Low cholesterol inside the cell switches on SREBP, which raises LDL receptors and clears more LDL from the blood.

a.o: Mohab blames familial hypercholesterolaemia on faulty LDL receptors.
a.x: It should be blamed on too much HDL in the blood.
a.w: Mutations in the LDL receptor stop the liver clearing LDL, so levels are high from birth.

a.o: Mohab says cholesterol synthesis peaks at night, so some statins are taken in the evening.
a.x: All statins should be taken first thing in the morning.
a.w: Short-acting statins work best at night, when HMG-CoA reductase activity is highest.

s:
Practical report, spectrophotometry lab, student Nada Hamdy. The aim was to make a standard curve for protein using the biuret reagent and read the concentration of an unknown sample. Nada zeroed the spectrophotometer with a blank tube that held biuret reagent and water.

She measured the absorbance of five standards at 540 nm and drew a straight line. In the discussion she explains the Beer-Lambert law and writes that when the concentration of the protein doubles, the absorbance halves, because more of the light is blocked.

She read the unknown from the curve as 4.5 g/dL and noted that it fell inside the range of her standards, so the value could be trusted. She ends by saying the same cuvette was used for every reading so the path length stayed the same.
h: when the concentration of the protein doubles, the absorbance halves

a.o: Nada says doubling the protein concentration halves the absorbance.
a.x: Doubling the concentration doubles the absorbance.
a.w: Beer-Lambert: absorbance = e x c x l, so absorbance rises in step with concentration. It is the light passing through that falls.

a.o: Nada zeroes the machine with a blank of biuret reagent and water.
a.x: The blank should contain the unknown sample instead.
a.w: The blank removes the colour of the reagent itself, so the reading shows only the colour made by protein.

a.o: Nada trusts the unknown because it falls inside the range of her standards.
a.x: Values outside the standards should be trusted more.
a.w: A standard curve is only proven inside its range, so reading within it avoids guessing beyond the data.

a.o: Nada uses the same cuvette for every reading to keep the path length fixed.
a.x: A different cuvette should be used for each reading.
a.w: Path length is part of the Beer-Lambert law, so keeping it constant lets absorbance track concentration alone.

s:
Handout for "Iron metabolism", biochemistry and nutrition block, by Dr. Sahar. Part 1 says the body holds about 3 to 4 g of iron, most of it in haemoglobin, and that there is no active way to excrete iron, so absorption is tightly controlled.

Part 2 says dietary iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum. The handout states that iron is best absorbed in the ferric (Fe3+) form, and that vitamin C reduces absorption by turning ferrous iron into ferric. It adds that haem iron from meat is absorbed better than iron from plants.

Part 3 explains that iron is carried in the blood by transferrin and stored as ferritin, and that the liver hormone hepcidin lowers iron absorption when stores are full. A last box says that low ferritin is the most specific blood test for iron deficiency.
h: iron is best absorbed in the ferric (Fe3+) form, and that vitamin C reduces absorption by turning ferrous iron into ferric

a.o: The handout says ferric iron is absorbed best and that vitamin C lowers absorption.
a.x: Ferrous iron absorbs best, and vitamin C helps it.
a.w: The gut transporter DMT1 carries Fe2+. Vitamin C keeps iron in that reduced form, so it improves absorption.

a.o: The handout says hepcidin from the liver lowers iron absorption when stores are full.
a.x: Hepcidin should be said to raise iron absorption.
a.w: Hepcidin breaks down ferroportin, the iron exporter on gut cells, so less iron enters the blood.

a.o: The handout says low ferritin is the most specific blood test for iron deficiency.
a.x: A high ferritin should be the sign of iron deficiency.
a.w: Ferritin reflects iron stores, so a low level confirms deficiency. It can be falsely normal in inflammation.

a.o: The handout says haem iron from meat is absorbed better than plant iron.
a.x: Plant iron should be said to absorb better than meat iron.
a.w: Haem iron is taken up through its own pathway and is less affected by other foods than non-haem iron.

s:
Flashcards "Diabetes lab tests", made by Hamza for the biochemistry quiz. Card 1 says glucose sticks to haemoglobin without an enzyme, forming glycated haemoglobin, HbA1c.

Card 2 says that HbA1c shows the average blood glucose over the last 2 to 3 days, because glucose is only stuck to haemoglobin for a short time. Card 3 says an HbA1c of 6.5% or higher can be used to diagnose diabetes.

Card 4 says that conditions that shorten red cell life, such as haemolysis, can make the HbA1c falsely low. Card 5 says fasting glucose of 7.0 mmol/L or higher on two occasions also diagnoses diabetes. Hamza adds a note in red at the bottom of the set: "Ask Dr. Nadia which test is best for checking control in a patient who already has diabetes."
h: shows the average blood glucose over the last 2 to 3 days

a.o: Card 2 says HbA1c shows the average glucose over the last 2 to 3 days.
a.x: HbA1c reflects the average over about 2 to 3 months.
a.w: Red cells live about 120 days and glucose stays bound for their whole life, so HbA1c reflects the last 2-3 months.

a.o: Card 3 says an HbA1c of 6.5% or higher can diagnose diabetes.
a.x: The cut-off should be an HbA1c of 4.5% or higher.
a.w: An HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or more is the accepted diagnostic threshold for diabetes.

a.o: Card 4 says haemolysis can make the HbA1c falsely low.
a.x: Haemolysis should be said to make the HbA1c falsely high.
a.w: With shorter red cell lives, cells have less time to collect glucose, so the HbA1c reads lower than the true average.

a.o: Card 5 says a fasting glucose of 7.0 mmol/L or more twice diagnoses diabetes.
a.x: The fasting cut-off should be 4.0 mmol/L or more.
a.w: A fasting plasma glucose of 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or more on two tests diagnoses diabetes.

s:
Short-answer exam, nutrition block, question 2: "What are essential amino acids?" Student Rana Fawzy writes that essential amino acids are those the body cannot make, so they must come from food, and that there are nine of them in adults.

She lists them: leucine, isoleucine, valine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and alanine. She adds that leucine, isoleucine and valine are the branched-chain amino acids, which are broken down mostly in muscle.

She ends by saying that tryptophan is used to make serotonin and niacin, and that a meal with all the essential amino acids, such as eggs, is called a complete protein. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: tryptophan and alanine

a.o: Rana lists alanine among the nine essential amino acids.
a.x: Histidine is the ninth; alanine is non-essential.
a.w: Alanine is easily made from pyruvate by transamination. The nine essentials include histidine, not alanine.

a.o: Rana says leucine, isoleucine and valine are branched-chain amino acids.
a.x: Glycine and alanine should be listed as branched-chain.
a.w: Leucine, isoleucine and valine have branched side chains and are mostly broken down in muscle.

a.o: Rana says tryptophan is used to make serotonin and niacin.
a.x: Tryptophan should be said to make dopamine instead.
a.w: Tryptophan is the precursor of serotonin and melatonin, and can be turned into niacin.

a.o: Rana calls a food with all the essential amino acids a complete protein.
a.x: Such a food should be called an incomplete protein.
a.w: Eggs, milk and meat give all nine essential amino acids in good amounts, so they are complete proteins.

s:
Draft page "Reading enzyme graphs", enzymes chapter. The page explains that the Michaelis-Menten curve is hard to read at high substrate levels, so the Lineweaver-Burk plot of 1/rate against 1/[substrate] gives a straight line.

It states that on this plot the y-intercept is equal to 1/Km and the x-intercept is equal to -1/Vmax. It then shows that a competitive inhibitor makes the line steeper but keeps the same y-intercept, while a non-competitive inhibitor raises the y-intercept and keeps the x-intercept the same.

The page warns that the plot gives extra weight to points at low substrate levels, which can be less accurate, and ends by saying the slope of the line is Km/Vmax.
h: the y-intercept is equal to 1/Km and the x-intercept is equal to -1/Vmax

a.o: The page sets the y-intercept as 1/Km and the x-intercept as -1/Vmax.
a.x: The y-intercept is 1/Vmax and the x-intercept is -1/Km.
a.w: At infinite substrate 1/[S] is zero, so the y-intercept gives 1/Vmax. The line crosses the x-axis at -1/Km.

a.o: The page says a competitive inhibitor keeps the same y-intercept on the plot.
a.x: A competitive inhibitor should raise the y-intercept.
a.w: A competitive inhibitor does not change Vmax, so the lines all cross the y-axis at the same 1/Vmax.

a.o: The page says the slope of the double reciprocal line is Km/Vmax.
a.x: The slope should be Vmax/Km instead.
a.w: 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax, so the slope of the line is Km divided by Vmax.

a.o: The page warns the plot gives extra weight to the less accurate low-substrate points.
a.x: The plot should be said to weigh all points equally.
a.w: Taking reciprocals spreads out low-substrate points, where errors are largest, so they pull the line.

s:
Biochemistry lab notebook, student Amr Selim. Topic: disaccharides. I wrote that a disaccharide is made of two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond, which is broken by enzymes on the brush border of the small intestine.

I listed three: maltose is glucose plus glucose, sucrose is glucose plus fructose, and lactose is glucose plus fructose too, which is why both taste sweet. I wrote that lactase breaks lactose down, and that people who lose lactase after childhood get bloating and diarrhoea after milk.

At the end I noted that undigested lactose reaches the colon, where bacteria ferment it to make gas and acids, and that the water drawn into the gut causes the diarrhoea. The tutor said we will test lactose next week.
h: lactose is glucose plus fructose too

a.o: Amr makes lactose out of glucose and fructose, the same as sucrose.
a.x: Lactose is glucose plus galactose.
a.w: Lactose, the sugar of milk, is made of galactose and glucose joined by a beta-1,4 bond. Sucrose is glucose plus fructose.

a.o: Amr says lactase is lost after childhood in many people, giving symptoms after milk.
a.x: Lactase should be said to rise with age in everyone.
a.w: In most of the world lactase activity falls after weaning, so many adults cannot digest large amounts of milk.

a.o: Amr says colon bacteria ferment undigested lactose into gas and acids.
a.x: The colon should be said to absorb the lactose fully.
a.w: Bacteria ferment lactose to hydrogen, CO2 and short-chain acids, causing bloating and gas.

a.o: Amr says water drawn into the gut by the lactose causes the diarrhoea.
a.x: The diarrhoea should be put down to a bacterial toxin.
a.w: Unabsorbed lactose holds water in the gut by osmosis, so the stool becomes loose.

s:
Flashcards "Vitamins: an overview", made by Esraa for the nutrition exam. Card 1 says vitamins are split into two groups: water-soluble ones, which are not stored much and are lost in urine, and fat-soluble ones, which are stored in the body.

Card 2 lists the fat-soluble vitamins as A, C, D and K, and says they can build up to toxic levels if too much is taken. Card 3 says the fat-soluble vitamins need bile and fat for absorption, so their levels can drop in diseases that cause fatty stools.

Card 4 says vitamin K is needed for clotting factors and that newborns are given a vitamin K injection at birth. Card 5 says too much vitamin A in pregnancy can harm the baby.
h: A, C, D and K

a.o: Card 2 lists vitamin C among the fat-soluble vitamins.
a.x: The fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E and K.
a.w: Vitamin C is water-soluble and lost in urine. The four fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E and K, which are stored in the liver and fat.

a.o: Card 3 says fat-soluble vitamins need bile and fat for absorption.
a.x: They should be said to need intrinsic factor instead.
a.w: Fat-soluble vitamins enter micelles with dietary fat, so poor bile flow or fat malabsorption lowers their uptake.

a.o: Card 4 says newborns are given vitamin K at birth.
a.x: Newborns should be given vitamin C at birth instead.
a.w: Babies have little vitamin K at birth, so an injection prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

a.o: Card 5 says too much vitamin A in pregnancy can harm the baby.
a.x: Extra vitamin A should be said to protect the baby.
a.w: High doses of vitamin A, and drugs like isotretinoin, can cause birth defects, so high doses are avoided in pregnancy.

s:
Short-answer exam, metabolism block, question 8: "Describe the Cori cycle." Student Moaz Khaled writes that during hard exercise muscle makes ATP by glycolysis faster than oxygen can be supplied, so pyruvate is turned into lactate.

He writes that the lactate leaves the muscle and travels in the blood to the kidney, where it is turned back into glucose, which then returns to the muscle. He adds that the cycle costs energy: making one glucose from two lactates uses 6 ATP, while glycolysis gives only 2.

He ends by saying the glucose-alanine cycle is a similar loop that also carries nitrogen from muscle to be turned into urea. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: travels in the blood to the kidney, where it is turned back into glucose

a.o: Moaz sends lactate from muscle to the kidney to be turned back into glucose.
a.x: Lactate goes to the liver to become glucose.
a.w: The liver takes up lactate and makes glucose by gluconeogenesis, then returns it to the muscle. That loop is the Cori cycle.

a.o: Moaz says making one glucose from two lactates uses 6 ATP while glycolysis gives 2.
a.x: Making glucose should be said to release 6 ATP.
a.w: Gluconeogenesis costs about 6 high-energy phosphates per glucose, so the cycle as a whole uses energy.

a.o: Moaz says the glucose-alanine cycle also carries nitrogen from muscle to make urea.
a.x: The alanine cycle should be said to carry fat instead.
a.w: Muscle passes amino groups to pyruvate as alanine; the liver makes glucose from it and turns the nitrogen into urea.

a.o: Moaz says hard exercise turns pyruvate into lactate when oxygen falls short.
a.x: Pyruvate should be said to become ethanol in muscle.
a.w: When glycolysis outpaces oxygen use, lactate dehydrogenase turns pyruvate into lactate to regenerate NAD+.

s:
Handout for "Mitochondria and disease", biochemistry block, by Dr. Yasser. Part 1 explains that mitochondria have their own small circular DNA, which codes for some proteins of the electron transport chain.

Part 2 says mitochondrial DNA is passed on from the father, because sperm carry many mitochondria in their midpiece into the egg. It adds that a cell can hold a mix of normal and faulty mitochondrial DNA, called heteroplasmy, so the severity can vary even within one family.

Part 3 says mitochondrial diseases most often affect organs that need a lot of energy, such as the brain, muscle and eyes. A last box says mitochondrial DNA mutates faster than nuclear DNA because it is close to the free radicals made by the electron transport chain.
h: mitochondrial DNA is passed on from the father

a.o: The handout says mitochondrial DNA is passed down from the father.
a.x: Mitochondrial DNA is passed on from the mother.
a.w: The egg supplies almost all the mitochondria. Sperm mitochondria are destroyed after fertilisation, so mitochondrial DNA is maternal.

a.o: The handout says heteroplasmy lets severity vary even within one family.
a.x: Heteroplasmy should be said to make every relative the same.
a.w: Cells hold a mix of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA in changing proportions, so relatives can be affected differently.

a.o: The handout says mitochondrial diseases hit high-energy organs like brain, muscle and eyes.
a.x: These diseases should be said to hit mainly the skin.
a.w: Organs that depend most on oxidative phosphorylation suffer first when the electron transport chain is faulty.

a.o: The handout says mitochondrial DNA mutates faster because it sits near free radicals.
a.x: It should be said to mutate more slowly than nuclear DNA.
a.w: Mitochondrial DNA lies near the electron transport chain's free radicals and has weaker repair, so it mutates faster.

s:
Draft page "Lysosomal storage disorders", inborn errors chapter. The page explains that lysosomes hold enzymes that break down large molecules, and that when one enzyme is missing, its substrate builds up inside the lysosome and the cell swells.

It lists two examples. It states that Tay-Sachs disease is caused by a lack of glucocerebrosidase, while Gaucher disease is caused by a lack of hexosaminidase A. Tay-Sachs gives a baby who loses skills, has a cherry-red spot in the eye and an exaggerated startle response; Gaucher disease gives a big liver and spleen, bone pain and "crumpled tissue paper" cells.

The page ends by saying most of these disorders are autosomal recessive, apart from Fabry disease and Hunter syndrome, which are X-linked, and that enzyme replacement treatment works well for Gaucher disease.
h: Tay-Sachs disease is caused by a lack of glucocerebrosidase, while Gaucher disease is caused by a lack of hexosaminidase A

a.o: The page gives Tay-Sachs a lack of glucocerebrosidase, Gaucher hexosaminidase A.
a.x: Tay-Sachs lacks hexosaminidase A; Gaucher, glucocerebrosidase.
a.w: Hexosaminidase A breaks down GM2 ganglioside in neurons (Tay-Sachs). Glucocerebrosidase breaks down glucocerebroside (Gaucher).

a.o: The page names Fabry disease and Hunter syndrome as X-linked.
a.x: Both should be named as autosomal dominant instead.
a.w: Fabry (alpha-galactosidase A) and Hunter (iduronate sulfatase) are the X-linked lysosomal disorders.

a.o: The page says enzyme replacement works well for Gaucher disease.
a.x: Enzyme replacement should be said to help only Tay-Sachs.
a.w: Gaucher type 1 responds well to infused enzyme, which reaches the macrophages of the liver, spleen and bone.

a.o: The page gives Tay-Sachs a cherry-red spot and an exaggerated startle response.
a.x: Tay-Sachs should be given a large liver and spleen instead.
a.w: Ganglioside builds up in the retina and brain, giving the cherry-red macula and a strong startle to noise.

s:
Practical report, DNA lab, student Malak Hamed. The aim was to separate DNA fragments by agarose gel electrophoresis. Malak loaded the samples into wells at the negative end of the gel and ran the gel at 100 volts for 40 minutes, next to a ladder of fragments of known size.

In the results she explains that DNA moves toward the positive electrode because its phosphate backbone carries a negative charge. She then writes that the larger fragments move faster and further down the gel, because they carry more charge.

In the discussion she notes that a higher percentage of agarose makes smaller pores and separates small fragments better, and that the ladder lets her estimate the size of each band. She stained the gel with a DNA dye and viewed it under UV light.
h: the larger fragments move faster and further down the gel, because they carry more charge

a.o: Malak says larger fragments travel faster and further because they carry more charge.
a.x: Smaller fragments move faster and further through the gel.
a.w: Charge rises with length, so charge per size is about the same. The gel acts as a sieve, holding back long fragments more.

a.o: Malak loads the samples at the negative end, so DNA runs toward the positive electrode.
a.x: The wells should be placed at the positive end.
a.w: DNA is negatively charged along its phosphate backbone, so it moves away from the negative electrode.

a.o: Malak says a higher percentage of agarose separates small fragments better.
a.x: A higher percentage should separate large fragments better.
a.w: More agarose makes a tighter mesh, which spreads out small fragments while large ones barely move.

a.o: Malak runs a ladder of known sizes next to the samples to estimate band size.
a.x: The ladder should be run on a separate day.
a.w: A size ladder on the same gel lets each band be compared directly, since running conditions are the same.

s:
Handout for "Ketone bodies", metabolism block, by Dr. Reem. Part 1 says that in fasting, starvation and uncontrolled type 1 diabetes, the liver breaks down large amounts of fatty acids to acetyl-CoA, more than the Krebs cycle can use.

Part 2 says the liver turns the extra acetyl-CoA into acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, the ketone bodies, and releases them into the blood. The handout then says that the liver itself is the main user of ketone bodies, which is why it makes them, and that the brain cannot use them at all.

Part 3 says that in diabetic ketoacidosis the ketones lower the blood pH, and that acetone, formed from acetoacetate, gives a fruity smell to the breath. A last note says the urine dipstick test mainly detects acetoacetate.
h: the liver itself is the main user of ketone bodies, which is why it makes them, and that the brain cannot use them at all

a.o: The handout makes the liver the main user of ketones and says the brain cannot use them.
a.x: The liver cannot use ketones; the brain and muscle can.
a.w: The liver lacks the enzyme thiophorase, so it exports ketones. The brain, heart and muscle use them, especially in long fasting.

a.o: The handout says acetone from acetoacetate gives the breath a fruity smell.
a.x: The fruity smell should come from beta-hydroxybutyrate.
a.w: Acetoacetate breaks down without an enzyme into acetone, which is volatile and breathed out with a fruity odour.

a.o: The handout says the urine dipstick mainly detects acetoacetate.
a.x: The dipstick should mainly detect beta-hydroxybutyrate.
a.w: The nitroprusside dipstick reacts with acetoacetate, and much less with acetone, but not beta-hydroxybutyrate.

a.o: The handout says the liver makes ketones when acetyl-CoA exceeds what the Krebs cycle can use.
a.x: Ketones should be said to form only after a large meal.
a.w: When oxaloacetate is used for gluconeogenesis, extra acetyl-CoA from fat is shunted into ketone body making.

s:
Flashcards "Lipoproteins", made by Yehia for the biochemistry exam. Card 1 says fats travel in the blood inside lipoproteins, which have a coat of phospholipid and protein around a core of triglyceride and cholesterol.

Card 2 says chylomicrons carry fat from the gut, and VLDL carries triglyceride made in the liver. Card 3 says HDL carries cholesterol from the liver to the tissues and the artery walls, which is why a high HDL raises the risk of heart attack, while LDL takes extra cholesterol back to the liver.

Card 4 says the LDL receptor takes LDL into cells by endocytosis. Card 5 says chylomicrons make the blood look milky after a fatty meal.
h: HDL carries cholesterol from the liver to the tissues and the artery walls

a.o: Card 3 has HDL carry cholesterol to the tissues and LDL bring it back.
a.x: LDL carries cholesterol out to tissues; HDL brings it back.
a.w: HDL does reverse cholesterol transport to the liver, which is why high HDL protects. LDL delivers cholesterol and can build plaques.

a.o: Card 2 says chylomicrons carry fat from the gut and VLDL carries liver fat.
a.x: VLDL should carry fat from the gut instead.
a.w: Chylomicrons transport dietary triglyceride from the intestine; VLDL exports triglyceride made in the liver.

a.o: Card 4 says the LDL receptor takes LDL into cells by endocytosis.
a.x: LDL should be said to cross membranes by simple diffusion.
a.w: LDL binds its receptor in coated pits, which fold in to bring the particle into the cell.

a.o: Card 5 says chylomicrons make the blood look milky after a fatty meal.
a.x: The milky look should come from HDL particles.
a.w: Chylomicrons are large enough to scatter light, so plasma looks milky for some hours after a fatty meal.

s:
Short-answer exam, biochemistry block, question 1: "Describe the levels of protein structure." Student Hana Mostafa writes that the primary structure is the order of amino acids, joined by peptide bonds.

She writes that the secondary structure includes the alpha-helix and the beta-pleated sheet, and that both are held together mainly by disulfide bonds between cysteines in the backbone. She then says the tertiary structure is the full 3D folding of one chain, held by hydrophobic interactions, ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds and disulfide bonds.

She ends by saying that the quaternary structure is the way two or more chains fit together, giving haemoglobin as an example, and that heat breaks the weak bonds and denatures the protein without breaking the peptide bonds. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: both are held together mainly by disulfide bonds between cysteines in the backbone

a.o: Hana holds the alpha-helix and beta-sheet together mainly by disulfide bonds.
a.x: They are held mainly by backbone hydrogen bonds.
a.w: In secondary structure the backbone C=O of one residue bonds with the N-H of another by hydrogen bonds. Disulfides help tertiary structure.

a.o: Hana gives haemoglobin as an example of quaternary structure.
a.x: Haemoglobin should be given as primary structure only.
a.w: Haemoglobin has four chains fitting together, which is exactly what quaternary structure means.

a.o: Hana says heat denatures a protein without breaking the peptide bonds.
a.x: Heat should be said to break all the peptide bonds.
a.w: Denaturing breaks the weak bonds that hold the shape; the amino acid sequence itself stays intact.

a.o: Hana lists hydrophobic, ionic, hydrogen and disulfide bonds in tertiary structure.
a.x: Tertiary structure should rely on peptide bonds only.
a.w: The 3D fold of one chain is held by many side-chain interactions, including hydrophobic, ionic and disulfide links.

s:
Metabolism lab notebook, student Ahmed Wahba. Topic: fatty acid oxidation. I wrote that long-chain fatty acids are first activated to fatty acyl-CoA in the cytoplasm, using ATP.

Then I wrote that the fatty acyl-CoA crosses the inner mitochondrial membrane freely, without any carrier, and that beta-oxidation then takes place in the cytoplasm, cutting two carbons off at a time as acetyl-CoA. Each turn also makes one FADH2 and one NADH.

At the end I noted that a lack of the enzyme that handles medium-chain fatty acids (MCAD deficiency) causes low blood sugar with low ketones during fasting in babies, and that the acetyl-CoA from beta-oxidation feeds the Krebs cycle. The tutor wrote "check where this happens" next to my notes.
h: crosses the inner mitochondrial membrane freely, without any carrier, and that beta-oxidation then takes place in the cytoplasm

a.o: Ahmed lets fatty acyl-CoA cross freely and puts beta-oxidation in the cytoplasm.
a.x: It needs carnitine; beta-oxidation is in the mitochondria.
a.w: Long-chain acyl groups cross the inner membrane on carnitine, via CPT I and II. Beta-oxidation takes place in the mitochondrial matrix.

a.o: Ahmed says each turn of beta-oxidation makes one FADH2 and one NADH.
a.x: Each turn should make two ATP directly and no NADH.
a.w: Each cycle removes one acetyl-CoA and makes one FADH2 and one NADH, which then feed the electron transport chain.

a.o: Ahmed links MCAD deficiency with low sugar and low ketones in fasting babies.
a.x: MCAD deficiency should give high ketones and high sugar.
a.w: Without fat oxidation, the liver cannot make ketones or fuel gluconeogenesis, so fasting gives hypoketotic hypoglycaemia.

a.o: Ahmed says fatty acids are first activated to fatty acyl-CoA in the cytoplasm.
a.x: Activation should take place in the nucleus.
a.w: Acyl-CoA synthetase on the outer mitochondrial membrane faces the cytoplasm and uses ATP to activate the fatty acid.

s:
Handout for "DNA replication", molecular biology block, by Dr. Omneya. Part 1 says replication is semi-conservative: each new DNA molecule keeps one old strand and one new strand.

Part 2 says helicase unwinds the helix, primase lays down a short RNA primer, and DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only in the 5' to 3' direction. The handout states that the leading strand is made in short pieces called Okazaki fragments, while the lagging strand is made in one continuous piece.

Part 3 says DNA ligase joins the fragments together, and that telomerase adds repeats to the ends of chromosomes in stem cells and many cancer cells. A last box says DNA polymerase can proofread and remove wrong bases.
h: the leading strand is made in short pieces called Okazaki fragments, while the lagging strand is made in one continuous piece

a.o: The handout makes the leading strand in Okazaki fragments and the lagging in one piece.
a.x: The lagging strand is the one made in Okazaki fragments.
a.w: Polymerase works only 5' to 3', so the strand running the other way is made backwards in short pieces: that is the lagging strand.

a.o: The handout says DNA ligase joins the fragments together.
a.x: The fragments should be joined by helicase instead.
a.w: DNA ligase seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments after the RNA primers are replaced with DNA.

a.o: The handout says telomerase adds repeats to chromosome ends in stem cells and cancers.
a.x: Telomerase should be said to remove the chromosome ends.
a.w: Telomerase carries its own RNA template and extends telomeres, which keeps stem cells and many cancers dividing.

a.o: The handout says replication is semi-conservative, one old and one new strand.
a.x: Each new molecule should hold two new strands.
a.w: Meselson and Stahl showed each daughter molecule keeps one parental strand and one newly made strand.

s:
Short-answer exam, biochemistry block, question 10: "Explain how buffers work, using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation." Student Omar Nagy writes that a buffer is a mix of a weak acid and its conjugate base that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.

He writes the equation as pH = pKa + log ([base] / [acid]). He then writes that when the pH equals the pKa, the acid is ten times more than the base, and that a buffer works best within one unit of its pKa.

He uses the bicarbonate system as an example: with a pKa of 6.1 and a normal ratio of bicarbonate to carbonic acid of 20 to 1, the log of 20 is about 1.3, giving a blood pH of about 7.4. He adds that the system is strong because the lungs and kidneys can each adjust one side of it. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: when the pH equals the pKa, the acid is ten times more than the base

a.o: Omar says that at pH equal to pKa there is ten times more acid than base.
a.x: At pH = pKa the acid and base are present in equal amounts.
a.w: If pH = pKa, then log([base]/[acid]) = 0, so the ratio is 1. A tenfold excess of acid would put the pH one unit below the pKa.

a.o: Omar works out a blood pH of about 7.4 from 6.1 plus the log of 20.
a.x: The blood pH should come out at about 6.1 instead.
a.w: 6.1 + log 20 = 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4, which is exactly the normal arterial pH.

a.o: Omar says a buffer works best within one unit of its pKa.
a.x: A buffer should work best five units from its pKa.
a.w: Within about one pH unit of the pKa both forms are present in useful amounts, so added acid or base is absorbed.

a.o: Omar says the lungs and the kidneys can each adjust one side of the bicarbonate system.
a.x: The bicarbonate system should be said to be fixed and closed.
a.w: The lungs set CO2 (the acid side) and the kidneys set bicarbonate (the base side), which makes the system powerful.

s:
Handout for "Cell death", general pathology, by Dr. Nermin. Part 1 says necrosis is the death of cells in living tissue after severe injury, and that the cells swell, burst and set off inflammation.

Part 2 lists the patterns of necrosis. Coagulative necrosis keeps the outline of the dead cells for some days and is typical of infarcts in the heart and kidney. The handout then says a brain infarct also shows coagulative necrosis, keeping the outline of the neurons for weeks. Caseous necrosis, with a cheese-like centre, is typical of tuberculosis.

Part 3 says fat necrosis is seen in acute pancreatitis, where released enzymes digest fat and form chalky white spots with calcium. It ends by noting that fibrinoid necrosis is seen in the walls of blood vessels in severe hypertension and vasculitis.
h: a brain infarct also shows coagulative necrosis

a.o: The handout gives a brain infarct coagulative necrosis that keeps neuron outlines.
a.x: A brain infarct shows liquefactive necrosis.
a.w: Brain tissue has little structural protein and many enzymes, so it liquefies after an infarct and later leaves a fluid-filled cyst.

a.o: The handout says caseous necrosis with a cheese-like centre is typical of TB.
a.x: Caseous necrosis should be called typical of a heart infarct.
a.w: The soft, white, cheese-like centre of TB granulomas is caseous necrosis, a mix of coagulative and liquefactive.

a.o: The handout says fat necrosis in pancreatitis forms chalky white spots with calcium.
a.x: Fat necrosis should be said to form black spots of iron.
a.w: Lipase frees fatty acids that bind calcium (saponification), leaving chalky white areas in the fat.

a.o: The handout says fibrinoid necrosis is seen in vessel walls in severe hypertension.
a.x: Fibrinoid necrosis should be placed in the brain tissue.
a.w: Immune complexes or very high pressure damage vessel walls, and fibrin-like material leaks into them.

s:
Flashcards "Apoptosis", made by Hazem for the general pathology quiz. Card 1 says apoptosis is a planned, energy-using cell death that removes old, damaged or unwanted cells, such as the webs between the fingers of an embryo.

Card 2 says that in apoptosis the cell shrinks, the chromatin clumps and the cell breaks up into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies. Card 3 says that apoptotic cells spill their contents and cause strong inflammation in the nearby tissue, much like necrosis.

Card 4 says caspases are the enzymes that carry out apoptosis, and that the protein BCL-2 blocks it. Card 5 says cytotoxic T cells kill virus-infected cells by triggering apoptosis, and asks the reader to compare this with necrosis.
h: apoptotic cells spill their contents and cause strong inflammation in the nearby tissue

a.o: Card 3 has apoptotic cells spill their contents and cause strong inflammation.
a.x: Apoptotic cells stay sealed and cause no swelling.
a.w: Apoptotic bodies are wrapped in membrane and eaten quickly by macrophages, so the contents never leak and no inflammation follows.

a.o: Card 2 says the cell shrinks and breaks up into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies.
a.x: The cell should swell and burst in apoptosis.
a.w: Shrinkage, chromatin clumping and budding into apoptotic bodies are the hallmarks of apoptosis.

a.o: Card 4 makes caspases the enzymes of apoptosis and says BCL-2 blocks it.
a.x: BCL-2 should be said to switch apoptosis on.
a.w: BCL-2 guards the mitochondria against releasing cytochrome c, so it inhibits apoptosis; too much of it helps some lymphomas.

a.o: Card 5 says cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells by triggering apoptosis.
a.x: T cells should be said to kill by causing necrosis.
a.w: CD8 T cells use perforin, granzymes and Fas ligand, which switch on caspases inside the target cell.

s:
Short-answer exam, general pathology, question 3: "Describe the events of acute inflammation." Student Rana Saleh lists the five signs: redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function, and explains that the arterioles widen and the small vessels become leaky.

She writes that the first white cells to arrive in the first few hours are macrophages, and that neutrophils follow later, after about 48 hours. She explains that the white cells roll along the vessel wall using selectins, stick firmly using integrins and then move out through the wall toward the injury.

She ends by saying that chemical signals such as histamine cause the early leakiness, and that the result can be healing, abscess formation or chronic inflammation. The examiner gave 6 out of 10.
h: the first white cells to arrive in the first few hours are macrophages, and that neutrophils follow later

a.o: Rana says macrophages arrive first and neutrophils come after about 48 hours.
a.x: Neutrophils arrive first; macrophages take over after 48 hours.
a.w: Neutrophils dominate the first 6-24 hours of acute inflammation. Monocytes arrive later and become macrophages by 24-48 hours.

a.o: Rana has white cells roll on selectins, then stick with integrins before leaving.
a.x: Cells should stick with selectins first and roll on integrins.
a.w: Selectins give loose rolling, then integrins on the white cells bind firmly to the endothelium before the cells leave the vessel.

a.o: Rana says histamine causes the early leakiness of the vessels.
a.x: The early leak should be put down to collagen.
a.w: Histamine from mast cells makes venule endothelial cells contract, causing the immediate, short-lived leak.

a.o: Rana lists healing, abscess or chronic inflammation as outcomes.
a.x: The only outcome should be said to be cancer.
a.w: Acute inflammation may resolve, form pus and an abscess, heal by scarring or pass into chronic inflammation.

s:
Pathology practical notebook, student Seif Mahmoud. Today we looked at slides of chronic inflammation. I wrote that a granuloma is a small collection of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), often with giant cells and a rim of lymphocytes.

Slide 1 was a lung with tuberculosis. Slide 2 was a lymph node from a patient with sarcoidosis. I wrote that TB granulomas have no central necrosis, while sarcoid granulomas typically have caseous necrosis in the centre.

I also noted that the giant cells in TB are Langhans giant cells, with nuclei in a horseshoe around the edge, and that the TB bacteria can be seen with the Ziehl-Neelsen stain as red rods. The tutor asked us to label every slide for next week.
h: TB granulomas have no central necrosis, while sarcoid granulomas typically have caseous necrosis

a.o: Seif gives TB granulomas no necrosis and sarcoid granulomas caseous centres.
a.x: TB granulomas caseate; sarcoid ones usually do not.
a.w: Caseous necrosis in the centre is the hallmark of TB granulomas. Sarcoid granulomas are typically tight and non-caseating.

a.o: Seif describes Langhans giant cells with nuclei in a horseshoe at the edge.
a.x: Langhans cells should have one huge central nucleus.
a.w: Langhans giant cells are fused macrophages whose nuclei line up around the edge in a horseshoe or ring.

a.o: Seif says TB bacteria show as red rods with the Ziehl-Neelsen stain.
a.x: TB should be said to stain blue with Gram stain.
a.w: Mycobacteria hold the red carbol fuchsin even after acid-alcohol, so they are acid-fast red rods.

a.o: Seif describes a granuloma as epithelioid macrophages with a rim of lymphocytes.
a.x: A granuloma should be described as a sheet of neutrophils.
a.w: Epithelioid macrophages, giant cells and a cuff of lymphocytes make up the granuloma of chronic inflammation.

s:
Handout for "Thrombosis", circulatory pathology, by Dr. Hesham. Part 1 says a thrombus is a solid mass of blood formed inside a living vessel, unlike a clot that forms in a tube or after death.

Part 2 lists Virchow's triad, the three factors that lead to thrombosis: high blood pressure, slow or stopped blood flow, and a blood that clots too easily. It gives long flights and bed rest as causes of stasis, and pregnancy, cancer and the pill as causes of a blood that clots too easily.

Part 3 explains that arterial thrombi are pale and rich in platelets, while venous thrombi are dark red with many red cells. The handout ends by saying the main danger of a leg vein thrombus is that a piece breaks off and lodges in the lungs.
h: high blood pressure, slow or stopped blood flow, and a blood that clots too easily

a.o: The handout lists high blood pressure as one of the three parts of Virchow's triad.
a.x: The triad is vessel injury, stasis and easy clotting.
a.w: Virchow's triad is damage to the vessel lining, abnormal (slow) flow and a blood that clots too easily. Hypertension is not one of them.

a.o: The handout says arterial thrombi are pale and platelet-rich, venous ones dark red.
a.x: Venous thrombi should be pale and arterial ones red.
a.w: In fast arterial flow platelets build the clot; in slow venous flow red cells get trapped in fibrin, making it red.

a.o: The handout gives pregnancy, cancer and the pill as causes of easy clotting.
a.x: These should be given as causes of bleeding instead.
a.w: All three raise clotting factors or lower natural anticoagulants, tipping blood toward clotting.

a.o: The handout says a leg vein thrombus is dangerous because it can lodge in the lungs.
a.x: The danger should be a clot travelling to the leg arteries.
a.w: Leg vein clots travel through the right heart into the pulmonary arteries, causing pulmonary embolism.

s:
Practical report, gross pathology museum session, student Mona Farag. The task was to describe three infarcts in specimen pots. Mona wrote that an infarct is an area of tissue death caused by loss of blood supply, usually from a blocked artery.

Pot 1 was a kidney with a pale, wedge-shaped area under the capsule. Pot 2 was a heart with a pale, yellow area in the left ventricle wall. Pot 3 was a lung with a dark red, wedge-shaped area. She wrote that the lung infarct is pale because the lung has a single blood supply and little spare circulation.

In the discussion she notes that infarcts are wedge-shaped because the blocked artery branches out toward the surface, and that a red infarct also forms in organs with loose tissue where blood can collect. The demonstrator signed the report.
h: the lung infarct is pale because the lung has a single blood supply

a.o: Mona calls the lung infarct pale and gives the lung a single blood supply.
a.x: Lung infarcts are red, as the lung has a dual blood supply.
a.w: The lung gets both pulmonary and bronchial arteries, so blood keeps seeping into the dead area, making a red infarct.

a.o: Mona describes the kidney and heart infarcts as pale.
a.x: The kidney and heart infarcts should be red.
a.w: Solid organs with end arteries and dense tissue form pale (white) infarcts after an artery blocks.

a.o: Mona says infarcts are wedge-shaped because the artery branches toward the surface.
a.x: Infarcts should be said to be round like a ball.
a.w: The blocked vessel sits at the tip of the wedge and its territory fans out to the organ's surface.

a.o: Mona says red infarcts also form in loose tissues where blood can collect.
a.x: Loose tissue should be said to give pale infarcts only.
a.w: Loose organs such as the lung let blood pool in the dead area, which adds to the red colour.

s:
Draft page "Cellular adaptations", general pathology chapter. The page defines hypertrophy as an increase in the size of cells and hyperplasia as an increase in their number, and explains that both can happen together in tissues that can divide.

It gives the pregnant uterus as an example of both, and the enlarged prostate in older men as an example of hyperplasia. It then says that in long-standing high blood pressure the heart grows mainly by hyperplasia, with the heart muscle cells dividing to make more cells.

The page ends with atrophy, a shrinking of cells, such as in muscles after a long time in a plaster cast, and metaplasia, where one adult cell type is replaced by another, such as in the bronchi of smokers.
h: the heart grows mainly by hyperplasia, with the heart muscle cells dividing to make more cells

a.o: The page says the heart grows in hypertension mainly by its muscle cells dividing.
a.x: The heart grows by hypertrophy, with much bigger cells.
a.w: Adult heart muscle cells hardly divide, so they meet the extra workload by growing larger. This is hypertrophy, not hyperplasia.

a.o: The page gives the enlarged prostate in older men as an example of hyperplasia.
a.x: The enlarged prostate should be an example of atrophy.
a.w: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is an increase in the number of gland and stromal cells, driven by hormones.

a.o: The page gives the pregnant uterus as an example of both hypertrophy and hyperplasia.
a.x: The pregnant uterus should be an example of metaplasia.
a.w: Uterine smooth muscle cells both enlarge and divide under oestrogen in pregnancy.

a.o: The page gives muscle shrinking in a plaster cast as an example of atrophy.
a.x: The shrinking should be an example of hyperplasia instead.
a.w: Disuse removes the stimulus to maintain muscle, so the cells shrink: disuse atrophy.

s:
Short-answer exam, gut pathology, question 5: "What is Barrett's oesophagus?" Student Karim Lotfy writes that it develops in people with long-standing acid reflux, when stomach acid keeps damaging the lower oesophagus.

He writes that in Barrett's oesophagus the normal columnar lining of the oesophagus is replaced by stratified squamous epithelium, which is more resistant to acid. He adds that the new lining often contains goblet cells, like the intestine, and that this is called intestinal metaplasia.

He ends by saying that Barrett's oesophagus raises the risk of adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus, so patients are followed with regular endoscopy and biopsies, looking for dysplasia. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the normal columnar lining of the oesophagus is replaced by stratified squamous epithelium

a.o: Karim says Barrett's swaps a columnar lining for stratified squamous cells.
a.x: Barrett's turns a squamous lining into a columnar one.
a.w: The oesophagus is normally lined by stratified squamous epithelium. In Barrett's it changes to acid-resistant columnar cells.

a.o: Karim says the new lining often holds goblet cells, called intestinal metaplasia.
a.x: The goblet cells should be called squamous metaplasia.
a.w: Goblet cells are a feature of the intestine, so their presence in the oesophagus is intestinal metaplasia.

a.o: Karim says Barrett's raises the risk of adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus.
a.x: Barrett's should raise the risk of squamous carcinoma only.
a.w: The glandular metaplasia can progress through dysplasia to adenocarcinoma, the cancer of glandular cells.

a.o: Karim says patients with Barrett's are followed with regular endoscopy and biopsies.
a.x: They should be followed with yearly chest X-rays only.
a.w: Surveillance endoscopy looks for dysplasia so it can be treated before invasive cancer develops.

s:
Flashcards "Benign and malignant tumours", made by Salma for the pathology quiz. Card 1 says benign tumours usually grow slowly and are often surrounded by a capsule, which makes them easy to remove.

Card 2 says malignant tumours grow faster and invade the tissue around them. Card 3 says that both benign and malignant tumours can spread to distant organs, which is why every tumour needs a full body scan.

Card 4 says malignant cells often show large dark nuclei, many mitoses and loss of the normal structure, called anaplasia in the worst cases. Card 5 says a benign tumour can still be dangerous if it presses on something vital, such as a benign tumour in the skull.
h: both benign and malignant tumours can spread to distant organs

a.o: Card 3 says both benign and malignant tumours can spread to distant organs.
a.x: Only malignant tumours spread to distant organs.
a.w: Metastasis is the one sure sign of malignancy. Benign tumours stay where they started and never spread to distant sites.

a.o: Card 1 says benign tumours are often wrapped in a capsule that eases removal.
a.x: Benign tumours should be said never to have a capsule.
a.w: Many benign tumours push tissue aside and form a fibrous capsule, so they can be shelled out cleanly.

a.o: Card 4 links malignant cells with large dark nuclei, many mitoses and anaplasia.
a.x: Malignant cells should be said to look exactly like normal cells.
a.w: Pleomorphism, large dark nuclei, many and abnormal mitoses and loss of structure mark malignancy.

a.o: Card 5 warns that a benign tumour inside the skull can still be dangerous.
a.x: Benign tumours should be called harmless wherever they are.
a.w: In a closed space like the skull even a slow, benign mass can press on the brain and kill.

s:
Handout for "Naming tumours", neoplasia lecture, by Dr. Rasha. Part 1 explains the basic rule: benign tumours end in "-oma", such as lipoma (fat), fibroma (fibrous tissue) and adenoma (gland).

Part 2 says malignant tumours of epithelium are carcinomas, such as adenocarcinoma, and malignant tumours of connective tissue are sarcomas, such as osteosarcoma and liposarcoma. The handout then says that lymphoma, melanoma and seminoma end in "-oma", so they are benign tumours.

Part 3 says a teratoma contains tissues from all three germ layers, such as hair, teeth and skin, and is usually benign in the ovary. The last box says a hamartoma is a disorganised overgrowth of normal tissue for that site, not a true tumour.
h: lymphoma, melanoma and seminoma end in "-oma", so they are benign tumours

a.o: The handout calls lymphoma, melanoma and seminoma benign because they end in "-oma".
a.x: These three are malignant despite their "-oma" ending.
a.w: Lymphoma, melanoma and seminoma are exceptions to the naming rule: all three are malignant tumours.

a.o: The handout calls malignant connective tissue tumours sarcomas, like osteosarcoma.
a.x: They should be called carcinomas, like the epithelial ones.
a.w: Malignant tumours of mesenchymal tissue such as bone or fat are sarcomas; carcinomas come from epithelium.

a.o: The handout says an ovarian teratoma holds tissue from all three germ layers.
