a.x: A teratoma should hold tissue from one germ layer only.
a.w: Teratomas come from germ cells and can make hair, teeth, skin and other tissue from all three layers.

a.o: The handout calls a hamartoma a disorganised overgrowth of normal tissue for that site.
a.x: A hamartoma should be called a cancer of blood vessels.
a.w: A hamartoma is made of tissues normally found there, arranged in a jumbled way, and is not a true tumour.

s:
Draft page "Genes in cancer", neoplasia chapter. The page explains that cancer comes from a build-up of mutations in two main groups of genes. Oncogenes push the cell to divide when they are switched on, so one faulty copy is enough.

It gives RAS and MYC as oncogenes. It then states that p53 and RB are also oncogenes, since a mutation that switches them on makes the cell divide out of control. It adds that the "two-hit" idea of Knudson explains why inherited retinoblastoma appears early and often in both eyes.

The page describes p53 as "the guardian of the genome", which stops the cell cycle when DNA is damaged and starts apoptosis if repair fails. It ends by saying HPV proteins E6 and E7 work by switching off p53 and RB.
h: p53 and RB are also oncogenes, since a mutation that switches them on

a.o: The page calls p53 and RB oncogenes that cause cancer when switched on.
a.x: p53 and RB are tumour suppressors, not oncogenes.
a.w: Tumour suppressor genes brake the cell cycle. Losing both copies of p53 or RB lets damaged cells divide, as Knudson's two hits show.

a.o: The page gives RAS and MYC as oncogenes, where one faulty copy is enough.
a.x: RAS and MYC should need both copies lost to act.
a.w: Oncogenes act dominantly: one activating mutation or amplification of RAS or MYC is enough to drive growth.

a.o: The page says HPV E6 and E7 switch off p53 and RB.
a.x: E6 and E7 should be said to switch p53 and RB on.
a.w: E6 targets p53 for breakdown and E7 binds RB, removing both brakes on the cell cycle in cervical cells.

a.o: The page says inherited retinoblastoma appears early and often in both eyes.
a.x: Inherited cases should appear late and in one eye only.
a.w: Children who inherit one bad RB copy need only one more hit, so tumours come early and in both eyes.

s:
Practical report, special stains session, student Nada Shawky. The aim was to identify amyloid in a kidney biopsy. Nada first looked at the H&E slide, where the glomeruli contained pink, glassy material that had no cells in it.

She then stained a second section with Prussian blue, which she writes is the stain for amyloid, and saw blue deposits. She adds that under polarised light amyloid stained this way shows an apple-green colour.

In the discussion she explains that amyloid is a misfolded protein that forms beta-pleated sheets, and that in the kidney it often causes heavy protein loss in the urine. She lists myeloma and long-standing inflammation such as rheumatoid arthritis as common causes.
h: stained a second section with Prussian blue, which she writes is the stain for amyloid

a.o: Nada uses Prussian blue, the stain she names for amyloid, on the biopsy.
a.x: Amyloid is stained with Congo red.
a.w: Congo red stains amyloid red-pink and gives apple-green birefringence under polarised light. Prussian blue is the stain for iron.

a.o: Nada says amyloid is a misfolded protein forming beta-pleated sheets.
a.x: Amyloid should be called a type of fat deposit.
a.w: Amyloid proteins fold into beta-pleated sheets and stack into fibrils that tissues cannot break down.

a.o: Nada says amyloid in the kidney often causes heavy protein loss in the urine.
a.x: Kidney amyloid should be said to cause blood in the urine only.
a.w: Amyloid in the glomeruli damages the filter, so large amounts of protein leak: nephrotic syndrome.

a.o: Nada lists myeloma and rheumatoid arthritis as common causes of amyloid.
a.x: These should be listed as causes of iron overload.
a.w: Myeloma makes AL amyloid from light chains; long inflammation makes AA amyloid from serum amyloid A.

s:
Short-answer exam, pathology block, question 9: "Compare types of shock." Student Hassan Gamal defines shock as a failure of the circulation to supply enough blood to the tissues, leading to cell injury.

He writes that in hypovolaemic shock, such as after bleeding, the central venous pressure is high and the skin is cold and pale. In cardiogenic shock, such as after a big heart attack, the pump fails, so the central venous pressure is high and the skin is cold.

He writes that in septic shock the vessels widen, so the skin may be warm and flushed at first, and that the main problem is low vascular resistance. He ends by saying all types of shock lead to lactic acidosis. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: in hypovolaemic shock, such as after bleeding, the central venous pressure is high

a.o: Hassan gives hypovolaemic shock a high central venous pressure.
a.x: In hypovolaemic shock the central venous pressure is low.
a.w: After blood loss the veins are underfilled, so the CVP is low. A high CVP fits cardiogenic shock, where the failing pump backs blood up.

a.o: Hassan gives cardiogenic shock a high CVP and cold skin.
a.x: Cardiogenic shock should give a low CVP and warm skin.
a.w: The failing heart cannot clear venous return, so the CVP rises, and vessels constrict, leaving cold skin.

a.o: Hassan says septic shock can give warm skin at first, with low vascular resistance.
a.x: Septic shock should start with cold skin and high resistance.
a.w: Inflammatory mediators widen the vessels, so early septic shock often has warm skin and low resistance.

a.o: Hassan says every type of shock leads to lactic acidosis.
a.x: Shock should be said to cause alkalosis from the start.
a.w: Poorly perfused tissues switch to anaerobic glycolysis, so lactate builds up in all types of shock.

s:
Handout for "Atherosclerosis", cardiovascular pathology, by Dr. Sherine. Part 1 says atherosclerosis is a disease of the intima of large and medium-sized arteries, such as the aorta, coronary and carotid arteries, and that it is the main cause of heart attacks and strokes.

Part 2 describes the stages. The earliest lesion is the fatty streak, made of foam cells (macrophages full of fat), which can be seen even in children. Over years this grows into a fibrous plaque with a fat-rich core and a fibrous cap. The handout then says that plaques form most often in the large veins of the legs, where blood flow is slow.

Part 3 lists the risk factors: smoking, high LDL cholesterol, high blood pressure and diabetes. It ends by saying that a plaque with a thin cap can rupture, and the clot that forms on it can block the artery suddenly.
h: plaques form most often in the large veins of the legs, where blood flow is slow

a.o: The handout places plaques most often in the large leg veins, where flow is slow.
a.x: Plaques form in the arteries, never in the leg veins.
a.w: Atherosclerosis affects arteries under high pressure and disturbed flow. Slow flow in leg veins causes thrombosis, not atheroma.

a.o: The handout says fatty streaks of foam cells can be seen even in children.
a.x: Fatty streaks should be said to appear only after age 60.
a.w: Fatty streaks are found in the aorta of many children and teenagers, long before any symptoms appear.

a.o: The handout lists smoking, high LDL, high blood pressure and diabetes as risks.
a.x: High HDL should be listed as the biggest risk.
a.w: These four are the major changeable risk factors for atherosclerosis; HDL is protective.

a.o: The handout says a thin-capped plaque can rupture and a clot can block the artery.
a.x: A thin cap should be said to make a plaque safer.
a.w: Thin fibrous caps break easily, exposing the core, and a thrombus forms on top that can block the vessel.

s:
Short-answer exam, general pathology, question 6: "Describe healing of a clean surgical wound." Student Mai Adel writes that a clean, stitched wound heals by first intention, with little tissue lost and only a thin scar.

She writes that in the first days the gap fills with a clot, then neutrophils and macrophages clear debris, and by day 3 to 5 granulation tissue forms, with new capillaries and fibroblasts. She writes that the fibroblasts first lay down type I collagen, which is later replaced by type III collagen as the scar matures.

She ends by saying the wound has only about 10% of its normal strength at one week when the stitches are removed, and reaches about 70 to 80% by three months. She adds that vitamin C lack and steroids slow healing. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the fibroblasts first lay down type I collagen, which is later replaced by type III collagen

a.o: Mai says fibroblasts lay down type I collagen first, replaced later by type III.
a.x: Type III collagen comes first and is later replaced by type I.
a.w: Early granulation tissue holds weak type III collagen. As the scar remodels, it is replaced by strong type I collagen.

a.o: Mai says the wound has about 10% of its strength at one week.
a.x: The wound should be fully strong by the end of the first week.
a.w: When stitches come out at about one week, the wound has only about a tenth of normal strength.

a.o: Mai says vitamin C lack and steroids slow wound healing.
a.x: Steroids should be said to speed up wound healing.
a.w: Vitamin C is needed for collagen, and steroids blunt inflammation and fibroblast activity, so both delay healing.

a.o: Mai says granulation tissue with capillaries and fibroblasts forms by day 3 to 5.
a.x: Granulation tissue should appear only after a month.
a.w: Granulation tissue, with new vessels and fibroblasts, appears within days and fills the wound.

s:
Draft page "Metal storage diseases of the liver", liver pathology chapter. The page explains that Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of the ATP7B gene, which normally moves copper into bile.

It states that in Wilson disease iron builds up in the liver, brain and eye, and that a golden-brown ring in the cornea, the Kayser-Fleischer ring, is a key sign. It adds that the serum caeruloplasmin is usually low and that young patients may have liver disease, tremor or psychiatric changes.

The page then covers hereditary haemochromatosis, caused mostly by HFE gene mutations, where too much iron is absorbed and stored in the liver, pancreas, heart and skin. It says the iron shows blue with Perls' Prussian blue stain and that treatment is regular removal of blood.
h: in Wilson disease iron builds up in the liver, brain and eye

a.o: The page says iron builds up in the liver, brain and eye in Wilson disease.
a.x: Copper builds up in Wilson disease.
a.w: ATP7B moves copper into bile. When it fails, copper collects in the liver, brain and cornea, causing the Kayser-Fleischer ring.

a.o: The page says serum caeruloplasmin is usually low in Wilson disease.
a.x: Caeruloplasmin should be said to be high in Wilson disease.
a.w: Copper cannot be loaded onto caeruloplasmin in the liver, so less of it is released and blood levels are low.

a.o: The page says iron in haemochromatosis shows blue with Perls' Prussian blue stain.
a.x: Haemochromatosis iron should stain red with Congo red.
a.w: Perls' Prussian blue reacts with ferric iron in haemosiderin to give a bright blue colour.

a.o: The page says haemochromatosis is treated by regular removal of blood.
a.x: It should be treated by giving iron tablets.
a.w: Each unit of blood removed takes out about 200-250 mg of iron, slowly emptying the body's stores.

s:
Flashcards "Hepatitis B blood tests", made by Hager for the liver pathology block. Card 1 says HBsAg (surface antigen) in the blood means the person has hepatitis B infection now, either acute or chronic.

Card 2 says anti-HBs (surface antibody) means immunity, either from past infection or from vaccination. Card 3 says that anti-HBc (core antibody) on its own, with no other marker, means the person has been vaccinated against hepatitis B.

Card 4 says HBeAg is a sign that the virus is multiplying a lot and the person is highly infectious. Card 5 says HBsAg lasting more than six months means chronic infection, which can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer.
h: anti-HBc (core antibody) on its own, with no other marker, means the person has been vaccinated

a.o: Card 3 says core antibody alone means the person was vaccinated.
a.x: The vaccine gives anti-HBs only, never core.
a.w: The vaccine holds only surface antigen, so it never makes core antibody. Anti-HBc shows exposure to the whole virus.

a.o: Card 2 says anti-HBs means immunity from infection or vaccination.
a.x: Anti-HBs should be said to mean active infection.
a.w: Surface antibody neutralises the virus, so it marks immunity, after recovery or after the vaccine.

a.o: Card 4 says HBeAg marks a lot of virus and high infectivity.
a.x: HBeAg should be said to mean the virus is cleared.
a.w: HBeAg is released when the virus is replicating actively, so its presence means high infectivity.

a.o: Card 5 says HBsAg for more than six months means chronic infection.
a.x: Chronic infection should need HBsAg for six years.
a.w: Persistence of surface antigen beyond six months defines chronic hepatitis B.

s:
Practical report, museum pots of the liver, student Islam Fathy. The task was to describe and explain three liver specimens. Pot 1 was a liver with a speckled cut surface of dark red and pale yellow areas, which looked like a cut nutmeg.

Islam wrote that this "nutmeg liver" is caused by left heart failure, which raises the pressure in the pulmonary veins and pushes blood back into the liver. He explained that the dark areas are the congested centres of the lobules and the pale areas are fatty cells at the edges.

Pot 2 was a small liver with nodules throughout, which he called cirrhosis. Pot 3 had a single large pale mass that he called a secondary tumour, noting that the liver is a common site for spread from the bowel through the portal vein. The demonstrator asked him to explain the colour pattern again.
h: this "nutmeg liver" is caused by left heart failure, which raises the pressure in the pulmonary veins

a.o: Islam blames the nutmeg liver on left heart failure.
a.x: Nutmeg liver comes from right heart failure instead.
a.w: Right heart failure raises pressure in the vena cava and hepatic veins, congesting the centres of the liver lobules.

a.o: Islam calls the small, nodular liver in pot 2 a case of cirrhosis.
a.x: A small nodular liver should be called a fatty liver instead.
a.w: Cirrhosis is fibrosis that splits the liver into regenerating nodules, often leaving it small and lumpy.

a.o: Islam says bowel cancers often spread to the liver through the portal vein.
a.x: Bowel cancer should be said to reach the liver through the lymph.
a.w: Blood from the bowel drains through the portal vein, so the liver is the first organ to catch spreading cells.

a.o: Islam says the dark areas are the congested centres of the lobules.
a.x: The dark areas should be the edges of the lobules.
a.w: Back pressure fills the central veins first, so the centre of each lobule is dark and the edge is pale.

s:
Handout for "Oedema and effusions", general pathology, by Dr. Wael. Part 1 says oedema is extra fluid in the tissues, and an effusion is extra fluid in a body cavity, such as the pleural space.

Part 2 compares the two kinds of fluid. The handout says a transudate is cloudy, rich in protein and cells, and comes from inflammation, while an exudate is clear, low in protein and comes from raised pressure or low blood protein, as in heart failure.

Part 3 says Light's criteria compare pleural fluid with blood: a pleural fluid to serum protein ratio above 0.5 suggests one type of fluid. A last box says that pneumonia, TB and cancer give one kind of effusion, while heart failure and nephrotic syndrome give the other.
h: a transudate is cloudy, rich in protein and cells, and comes from inflammation, while an exudate is clear

a.o: The handout calls the transudate protein-rich and inflammatory, the exudate clear.
a.x: The exudate is the protein-rich, cloudy one.
a.w: Inflamed, leaky vessels let protein and cells out: an exudate. Raised pressure or low protein pushes out a clear, low-protein transudate.

a.o: The handout says a fluid to serum protein ratio above 0.5 marks one type of fluid.
a.x: The cut-off should be a ratio above 5.0 instead.
a.w: In Light's criteria a pleural to serum protein ratio over 0.5 points to an exudate.

a.o: The handout pairs heart failure and nephrotic syndrome with one kind of effusion.
a.x: These should be paired with pneumonia and TB.
a.w: Raised pressure and low albumin both give transudates, so heart failure and nephrotic syndrome go together.

a.o: The handout calls an effusion extra fluid in a body cavity such as the pleura.
a.x: An effusion should be called fluid inside cells.
a.w: Effusions are collections in serous cavities like the pleural, pericardial or peritoneal spaces.

s:
Short-answer exam, immunopathology, question 2: "Classify hypersensitivity reactions with examples." Student Amira Saeed lists four types. Type I is immediate, IgE on mast cells, as in anaphylaxis and hay fever. Type II is antibodies against cells, as in a mismatched blood transfusion.

Type III is immune complexes depositing in tissues, as in lupus kidney disease. She then writes that the tuberculin skin test is an example of type I hypersensitivity, because the swelling is caused by IgE and appears within minutes.

For type IV she gives contact dermatitis from nickel, and says it is caused by T cells, not antibodies. She ends by noting that adrenaline is the first treatment for anaphylaxis. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the tuberculin skin test is an example of type I hypersensitivity

a.o: Amira calls the tuberculin skin test a type I, IgE reaction.
a.x: The tuberculin test is a type IV reaction.
a.w: The skin test swells over 48-72 hours as T cells and macrophages gather, the classic delayed type IV reaction.

a.o: Amira gives a mismatched blood transfusion as type II hypersensitivity.
a.x: A mismatched transfusion should be type I instead.
a.w: Antibodies bind antigens on the donor red cells and destroy them: a type II, antibody against cell reaction.

a.o: Amira gives lupus kidney disease as an immune complex type III reaction.
a.x: Lupus kidney disease should be type IV instead.
a.w: Complexes of antibody and nuclear antigen lodge in glomeruli and set off complement, a type III reaction.

a.o: Amira gives adrenaline as the first treatment for anaphylaxis.
a.x: Antihistamine tablets should be given first instead.
a.w: Intramuscular adrenaline reverses airway swelling and low blood pressure quickly, so it comes first.

s:
Handout for "Grading and staging of cancer", neoplasia lecture, by Dr. Lobna. Part 1 says both grade and stage guide treatment and outlook, but they measure different things.

Part 2 states that the stage describes how much the tumour cells look like the normal tissue, judged under the microscope, while the grade describes how far the tumour has spread in the body. It gives the TNM system as an example of grading, with T for tumour size, N for lymph nodes and M for distant metastases.

Part 3 says that, of the two, stage usually predicts outcome better. A final box says a well-differentiated tumour looks close to normal tissue and a poorly differentiated tumour looks very different from it.
h: the stage describes how much the tumour cells look like the normal tissue

a.o: The handout has stage describe the cells and grade the spread.
a.x: Grade is how the cells look; stage is the spread.
a.w: Grade is a microscope judgement of differentiation. Stage, such as TNM, measures size, nodes and metastases.

a.o: The handout says stage usually predicts outcome better than grade.
a.x: Grade should be said to predict outcome better than stage.
a.w: For most cancers, the extent of spread at diagnosis is the strongest predictor of survival.

a.o: The handout says a well-differentiated tumour looks close to normal tissue.
a.x: A well-differentiated tumour should look nothing like normal.
a.w: Well-differentiated means the cells still resemble their tissue of origin, usually a lower grade.

a.o: The handout spells out TNM as tumour size, lymph nodes and distant metastases.
a.x: TNM should stand for tissue, nucleus and mitosis.
a.w: T is the primary tumour, N regional nodes, M distant metastases: the standard staging system.

s:
Practical report, tumour spread tutorial, student Mostafa Lotfy. The task was to explain how three tumours seen in museum pots had spread. Mostafa wrote that malignant tumours spread by invasion, by lymph, by blood and across body cavities.

Pot 1 was a breast carcinoma with enlarged armpit lymph nodes. Pot 2 was an osteosarcoma of the femur with round deposits in the lungs. He wrote that sarcomas usually spread first through the lymph nodes, while carcinomas usually spread first through the blood.

Pot 3 was an ovarian carcinoma with many small nodules on the peritoneum, which he explained as spread across the abdominal cavity. In the discussion he noted that the lungs and liver are common sites of blood-borne spread because blood from most organs passes through them.
h: sarcomas usually spread first through the lymph nodes, while carcinomas usually spread first through the blood

a.o: Mostafa says sarcomas spread by lymph and carcinomas spread by blood first.
a.x: Carcinomas spread by lymph first; sarcomas spread by blood.
a.w: Carcinomas usually reach the lymph nodes first, as in pot 1. Sarcomas usually go by blood to the lungs, as in pot 2.

a.o: Mostafa explains the ovarian nodules as spread across the abdominal cavity.
a.x: The nodules should be explained as spread through the bones.
a.w: Ovarian cancer often seeds the peritoneal surfaces directly, giving many small nodules and fluid.

a.o: Mostafa says the lungs and liver catch blood-borne spread from many organs.
a.x: The spleen should be named as the most common site.
a.w: Venous blood from most organs passes through the lungs, and gut blood passes through the liver, so both trap cells.

a.o: Mostafa lists invasion, lymph, blood and body cavities as spread routes.
a.x: Spread should be limited to invasion only.
a.w: Malignant tumours spread locally, by lymphatics, by the blood and across serous cavities.

s:
Flashcards "Calcification", made by Rawan for the pathology quiz. Card 1 says abnormal calcium deposits in tissue come in two kinds: dystrophic and metastatic calcification.

Card 2 says dystrophic calcification happens in damaged or dead tissue, such as old TB lesions, atheroma and damaged heart valves. Card 3 says dystrophic calcification needs a high blood calcium to happen, and so is a sign of hyperparathyroidism.

Card 4 says metastatic calcification happens in normal tissue when blood calcium is high, for example in the kidneys, lungs and stomach. Card 5 says psammoma bodies, small round layered calcium bodies, are seen in papillary thyroid cancer. On the back of the last card Rawan has drawn a calcified heart valve next to a kidney full of calcium spots.
h: dystrophic calcification needs a high blood calcium to happen

a.o: Card 3 says dystrophic calcification needs a high blood calcium.
a.x: It happens with a normal blood calcium.
a.w: Dystrophic calcium settles in damaged tissue whatever the blood level. High calcium causes the metastatic kind, in normal tissue.

a.o: Card 2 places dystrophic calcification in old TB, atheroma and damaged valves.
a.x: It should be placed only in healthy bone.
a.w: Dead and damaged tissue attracts calcium salts, so old TB, plaques and scarred valves often calcify.

a.o: Card 4 places metastatic calcification in kidneys, lungs and stomach.
a.x: It should be placed only in old scars instead.
a.w: Tissues that lose acid, like kidney, lung and stomach, have an alkaline inside that helps calcium settle.

a.o: Card 5 links psammoma bodies with papillary thyroid cancer.
a.x: Psammoma bodies should be linked with follicular cancer.
a.w: Psammoma bodies are a classic finding in papillary thyroid carcinoma, as well as some ovarian and meningeal tumours.

s:
Pathology lab notebook, student Ahmed Shawky. Topic: cell injury. I wrote that cells under stress first go through reversible injury, and if the stress continues they reach irreversible injury and die.

From the slides I recorded the signs of injury. I wrote that cell swelling and fatty change are signs of irreversible injury, and that once a cell swells it can never recover. I then listed the nuclear changes of cell death: pyknosis (the nucleus shrinks and darkens), karyorrhexis (it breaks into pieces) and karyolysis (it fades away).

At the end I noted that damage to the cell membrane and to the mitochondria marks the point of no return, and that enzymes such as troponin leak into the blood when heart cells die. The tutor asked us to bring coloured pencils next week.
h: cell swelling and fatty change are signs of irreversible injury

a.o: Ahmed lists cell swelling and fatty change as signs of irreversible injury.
a.x: Swelling and fatty change are signs of reversible injury.
a.w: Cell swelling from pump failure and fatty change are the first signs of injury and can reverse if the stress stops.

a.o: Ahmed lists pyknosis, karyorrhexis and karyolysis as nuclear signs of death.
a.x: These should be listed as signs of healthy dividing cells.
a.w: The nucleus shrinks and darkens, breaks up and finally fades, the three classic nuclear signs of necrosis.

a.o: Ahmed says membrane and mitochondrial damage marks the point of no return.
a.x: Ribosome damage should mark the point of no return.
a.w: Severe mitochondrial damage and membrane breakdown let calcium flood in and enzymes leak out, so the cell cannot recover.

a.o: Ahmed says troponin leaks into the blood when heart cells die.
a.x: Troponin should be said to fall when heart cells die.
a.w: When heart muscle cells die their membranes leak, so troponin enters the blood and is measured to diagnose a heart attack.

s:
Long-answer exam, circulation pathology, question 1: "Describe the types of embolism." Student Farida Nabil defines an embolus as a mass carried in the blood to a site far from where it formed, and writes that most emboli are thrombi.

She describes pulmonary embolism from leg vein thrombi and arterial emboli from the left heart reaching the brain or legs. She then writes that fat embolism typically follows a severe head injury, and gives shortness of breath, confusion and a rash of small spots as its signs, appearing a day or two later.

She ends with air embolism, which can happen when a central line is opened to air, and amniotic fluid embolism during labour. The examiner gave 15 out of 20.
h: fat embolism typically follows a severe head injury

a.o: Farida says fat embolism typically follows a severe injury to the head.
a.x: It typically follows a broken femur or other long bone.
a.w: Fat droplets from the marrow of a broken femur or pelvis enter the torn veins and lodge in the lungs, brain and skin.

a.o: Farida gives breathlessness, confusion and a rash of small spots a day or two later.
a.x: These signs should appear within seconds of the injury.
a.w: Fat embolism syndrome classically shows 24-72 hours after the fracture with these three features.

a.o: Farida says air embolism can follow opening a central line to the air.
a.x: Air embolism should only follow deep-sea diving.
a.w: Air can be sucked into a large neck vein through an open central line, which is why lines are closed carefully.

a.o: Farida says arterial emboli from the left heart reach the brain or legs.
a.x: Left heart emboli should go to the lungs first.
a.w: Clots from the left atrium or ventricle pass into the aorta, so they lodge in systemic arteries such as the brain.

s:
Handout for "Myocardial infarction", cardiovascular pathology, by Dr. Nader. Part 1 says an infarct follows a blocked coronary artery, usually from a clot on a ruptured plaque, and that heart muscle starts to die after about 20 to 30 minutes.

Part 2 gives the timeline under the microscope. In the first day, the muscle shows wavy fibres and early coagulative necrosis. From days 1 to 3, neutrophils flood in. The handout then says that by day 3 a firm white scar has already replaced the dead muscle, so the wall is at its strongest by the end of the first week.

Part 3 lists complications: arrhythmias in the first hours, wall rupture between days 3 and 7, and a ventricular aneurysm months later. It ends by saying troponin starts to rise 3 to 4 hours after the attack.
h: by day 3 a firm white scar has already replaced the dead muscle

a.o: The handout has a firm scar replace dead heart muscle by day 3.
a.x: The scar takes about 6-8 weeks to form.
a.w: After neutrophils, macrophages clear the dead muscle in days 3-7, leaving the wall soft. Granulation and then scar follow over weeks.

a.o: The handout lists wall rupture between days 3 and 7 as a complication.
a.x: Rupture should be listed only in the first hour.
a.w: The wall is weakest when macrophages remove the dead tissue, around days 3-7, which is when rupture happens.

a.o: The handout says neutrophils flood in from days 1 to 3.
a.x: Neutrophils should arrive only after two weeks.
a.w: Dead muscle sets off acute inflammation, and neutrophils peak in the infarct at about 1-3 days.

a.o: The handout says troponin starts to rise 3 to 4 hours after the attack.
a.x: Troponin should rise only after three days.
a.w: Troponin leaks from dying cells within hours, peaks at about a day and stays high for up to two weeks.

s:
Draft page "Emphysema", lung pathology chapter. The page defines emphysema as permanent enlargement of the air spaces beyond the terminal bronchioles, with destruction of their walls and no obvious fibrosis.

It describes two main patterns. It states that smoking causes the panacinar type, mainly in the lower lobes, while alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes the centriacinar type, mainly in the upper lobes. It explains that elastase from neutrophils breaks down the alveolar walls, and that alpha-1 antitrypsin normally blocks this enzyme.

The page ends by saying that patients lose the elastic recoil of the lungs, so their airways collapse when they breathe out, trapping air and giving a barrel-shaped chest. A margin note asks which type is seen in young non-smokers.
h: smoking causes the panacinar type, mainly in the lower lobes, while alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes the centriacinar type

a.o: The page gives smoking panacinar and alpha-1 lack centriacinar.
a.x: Smoking is centriacinar; alpha-1 lack is panacinar.
a.w: Smoke hits the central acini of the upper lobes most. Alpha-1 antitrypsin lack affects whole acini, worst in the lower lobes.

a.o: The page says alpha-1 antitrypsin normally blocks neutrophil elastase.
a.x: Alpha-1 antitrypsin should be said to make elastase.
a.w: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is the main protease inhibitor of the lung, protecting the alveolar walls from elastase.

a.o: The page says loss of elastic recoil lets airways collapse on breathing out.
a.x: Loss of recoil should be said to widen the airways.
a.w: Elastic tissue holds small airways open; without it they close on expiration and air is trapped.

a.o: The page defines emphysema as enlarged air spaces with wall destruction.
a.x: It should be defined as thickened walls with fibrosis.
a.w: Emphysema is permanent airspace enlargement beyond the terminal bronchioles, with destroyed walls.

s:
Short-answer exam, renal pathology, question 4: "Compare nephrotic and nephritic syndrome." Student Hossam Adel writes that both are diseases of the glomeruli, but they show in different ways.

For nephrotic syndrome he lists heavy protein in the urine, more than 3.5 g a day, low blood albumin, swelling and high cholesterol. He then writes that the main features of nephrotic syndrome are blood in the urine, high blood pressure and a low urine output, with red cell casts.

He gives minimal change disease as the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis as a classic cause of nephritic syndrome, appearing one to three weeks after a sore throat. The examiner gave 6 out of 10.
h: the main features of nephrotic syndrome are blood in the urine, high blood pressure and a low urine output

a.o: Hossam gives nephrotic syndrome blood in the urine, high blood pressure and red cell casts.
a.x: Those are the features of nephritic syndrome.
a.w: Nephritic syndrome means inflamed glomeruli that leak blood: haematuria, red cell casts, hypertension and oliguria.

a.o: Hossam lists protein over 3.5 g a day, low albumin, swelling and high cholesterol.
a.x: The protein loss should be under 0.5 g a day.
a.w: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by heavy proteinuria above 3.5 g a day, with low albumin, oedema and raised lipids.

a.o: Hossam names minimal change disease as the commonest cause in children.
a.x: The commonest cause in children should be diabetes.
a.w: Minimal change disease causes most nephrotic syndrome in children and responds well to steroids.

a.o: Hossam says post-streptococcal disease follows a sore throat by one to three weeks.
a.x: It should appear on the same day as the sore throat.
a.w: The immune complexes take time to form, so the kidney disease starts one to three weeks after the infection.

s:
Flashcards "Polyps of the colon", made by Nour for the gut pathology quiz. Card 1 says a polyp is any growth that sticks out from the lining of the bowel into its lumen.

Card 2 says hyperplastic polyps are the ones that most often turn into cancer, so they must all be removed, while adenomatous polyps are harmless and can be left alone. Card 3 says the risk of cancer in a polyp rises with its size, a villous structure and the grade of dysplasia.

Card 4 says most colorectal cancers develop from a polyp over about 10 years, which is why screening colonoscopy can prevent cancer. Card 5 says familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) causes hundreds of polyps and almost always leads to cancer.
h: hyperplastic polyps are the ones that most often turn into cancer

a.o: Card 2 says hyperplastic polyps most often turn cancerous and adenomas are safe.
a.x: Adenomatous polyps are the pre-cancerous ones.
a.w: Adenomas carry dysplasia and are the usual start of colorectal cancer. Small hyperplastic polyps rarely become malignant.

a.o: Card 3 says cancer risk rises with size, villous structure and dysplasia.
a.x: Smaller polyps should be said to carry the most risk.
a.w: Large size, villous growth and high-grade dysplasia all raise the chance of cancer inside an adenoma.

a.o: Card 4 says most colorectal cancers grow from a polyp over about 10 years.
a.x: The change should take only a few weeks.
a.w: The adenoma to carcinoma sequence is slow, which gives screening time to find and remove polyps.

a.o: Card 5 says FAP causes hundreds of polyps and almost always leads to cancer.
a.x: FAP should be said to cause one polyp and no cancer.
a.w: APC gene mutations in FAP cause hundreds of adenomas, and without surgery cancer is almost certain.

s:
Practical report, breast pathology session, student Sara Hamdy. The task was to describe two breast biopsies. Biopsy 1 was from a 19-year-old woman with a smooth, rubbery, mobile lump. Under the microscope Sara saw both glands and loose stroma, neatly arranged, with a clear border.

She wrote that this is a fibroadenoma, the most common benign breast lump in young women. She added that fibroadenomas are usually found in women over 60, and that they often turn into cancer, so they must always be removed.

Biopsy 2 was from a 62-year-old woman with a hard, fixed lump and puckered skin. Sara saw irregular nests of cells invading fat and called it an invasive ductal carcinoma, the most common type of breast cancer.
h: fibroadenomas are usually found in women over 60, and that they often turn into cancer

a.o: Sara says fibroadenomas occur mostly over age 60 and often turn into cancer.
a.x: Fibroadenomas occur in young women and are benign.
a.w: Fibroadenomas peak in women in their teens to thirties and are benign, with a very low risk. Many are watched, not removed.

a.o: Sara calls biopsy 1 a fibroadenoma, the commonest benign lump in young women.
a.x: A rubbery mobile lump should be called a carcinoma.
a.w: A smooth, mobile "breast mouse" in a young woman, with glands and stroma, is a fibroadenoma.

a.o: Sara calls the invading nests of cells an invasive ductal carcinoma.
a.x: Cells invading fat should be called benign.
a.w: Irregular cell nests invading the fat are typical of invasive ductal carcinoma, the most common breast cancer.

a.o: Sara describes a hard, fixed lump with puckered skin in the older woman.
a.x: A malignant lump should be said to be soft and mobile.
a.w: Cancer infiltrates and tethers tissue, so it feels hard, fixed and can pull the skin inward.

s:
Handout for "Thyroid tumours", endocrine pathology, by Dr. Hoda. Part 1 says most thyroid nodules are benign, and that a fine-needle aspiration is used to look at the cells of a suspicious nodule.

Part 2 describes the cancers. The handout says follicular carcinoma is the most common type and is known by its "Orphan Annie eye" nuclei, nuclear grooves and psammoma bodies. It says papillary carcinoma spreads mainly through the blood to bone and lung.

Part 3 says medullary carcinoma comes from the C cells and makes calcitonin, and can be part of the MEN 2 syndromes. The last box says anaplastic carcinoma is rare, affects older people, and grows very fast with a very poor outlook.
h: follicular carcinoma is the most common type and is known by its "Orphan Annie eye" nuclei

a.o: The handout gives follicular carcinoma the Orphan Annie nuclei and psammoma bodies.
a.x: These belong to papillary carcinoma, the commonest.
a.w: Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer, with clear "Orphan Annie" nuclei, grooves and psammoma bodies.

a.o: The handout says medullary carcinoma comes from C cells and makes calcitonin.
a.x: Medullary carcinoma should come from follicular cells.
a.w: Medullary carcinoma arises from the parafollicular C cells, which secrete calcitonin, a useful tumour marker.

a.o: The handout links medullary carcinoma with the MEN 2 syndromes.
a.x: It should be linked with MEN 1 only.
a.w: RET mutations cause MEN 2A and 2B, both of which include medullary thyroid carcinoma.

a.o: The handout says anaplastic carcinoma grows very fast in older people.
a.x: Anaplastic carcinoma should be called slow and harmless.
a.w: Anaplastic carcinoma is undifferentiated, grows within weeks and has one of the worst outlooks of any cancer.

s:
Draft page "Lymphomas", haematopathology chapter. The page divides lymphomas into Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin types, and says Hodgkin lymphoma often starts in a single group of neck nodes and spreads to the next group in order.

It states that the key cell of Burkitt lymphoma is the Reed-Sternberg cell, a large cell with two mirror-image nuclei that look like "owl's eyes". It describes Hodgkin lymphoma as having a "starry sky" pattern, with many macrophages among sheets of small cells.

The page ends by saying B symptoms (fever, night sweats and weight loss) suggest a worse outlook, and that Hodgkin lymphoma has a peak in young adults and a second peak in older people.
h: the key cell of Burkitt lymphoma is the Reed-Sternberg cell

a.o: The page makes the Reed-Sternberg cell the key cell of Burkitt lymphoma.
a.x: Reed-Sternberg cells mark Hodgkin lymphoma instead.
a.w: Owl's-eye Reed-Sternberg cells define Hodgkin lymphoma. The "starry sky" of macrophages among sheets of cells is Burkitt's.

a.o: The page says Hodgkin lymphoma spreads from one node group to the next in order.
a.x: Hodgkin should be said to skip around the body at random.
a.w: Hodgkin lymphoma typically spreads in a predictable way to nearby node groups, which helps staging.

a.o: The page says B symptoms suggest a worse outlook.
a.x: B symptoms should be said to mean a cure is likely.
a.w: Fever, drenching night sweats and weight loss over 10% mark more active disease and a higher stage.

a.o: The page gives Hodgkin lymphoma a peak in young adults and another in older people.
a.x: Hodgkin should be said to affect only infants.
a.w: Hodgkin lymphoma has a bimodal age pattern, with peaks in the twenties and after about 55.

s:
Haematology practical notebook, student Yasmin Ali. Today we looked at blood films and full blood counts from three patients with anaemia. I wrote that anaemia means low haemoglobin, and that the MCV tells us the average size of the red cells.

Patient 1 had an MCV of 68 fL, with small pale red cells and pencil cells. I wrote that this is a macrocytic anaemia, most likely from a lack of vitamin B12. Patient 2 had an MCV of 112 fL and large oval cells with hypersegmented neutrophils.

For patient 2 I wrote "folate or B12 lack". Patient 3 had a normal MCV, with a recent heavy bleed. At the end I noted that iron deficiency is the most common cause of anaemia in the world.
h: this is a macrocytic anaemia, most likely from a lack of vitamin B12

a.o: Yasmin calls an MCV of 68 fL a macrocytic anaemia from B12 lack.
a.x: An MCV of 68 fL is microcytic, from iron lack.
a.w: Normal MCV is about 80-100 fL. Small pale cells with pencil cells point to iron deficiency, not B12, which makes cells large.

a.o: Yasmin links large oval cells and hypersegmented neutrophils with folate or B12 lack.
a.x: These should be linked with iron deficiency instead.
a.w: Megaloblastic changes, oval macrocytes and neutrophils with six or more lobes come from folate or B12 lack.

a.o: Yasmin gives a recent heavy bleed a normal MCV.
a.x: A fresh bleed should give a very small MCV.
a.w: After an acute bleed the remaining red cells are normal, so the anaemia is normocytic at first.

a.o: Yasmin says iron deficiency is the commonest cause of anaemia worldwide.
a.x: The commonest cause should be B12 lack.
a.w: Iron deficiency, from poor diet, blood loss and pregnancy, is the leading cause of anaemia in the world.

s:
Flashcards "Sickle cell disease", made by Kareem for the blood pathology quiz. Card 1 says sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive, and that carriers (sickle trait) are partly protected from severe malaria.

Card 2 says it is caused by a point mutation in the alpha-globin gene that puts valine in place of glutamic acid at position 6. Card 3 says that when HbS loses its oxygen it sticks together in long chains that bend the red cells into sickles.

Card 4 says sickled cells block small vessels, causing painful crises, stroke and damage to the spleen, which often shrinks away by adulthood. Card 5 says hydroxyurea helps by raising fetal haemoglobin.
h: a point mutation in the alpha-globin gene

a.o: Card 2 puts the sickle mutation in the alpha-globin gene.
a.x: The mutation is in the beta-globin gene instead.
a.w: HbS comes from a single base change in the beta-globin gene, putting valine for glutamic acid at the sixth position.

a.o: Card 1 says sickle trait carriers are partly protected from severe malaria.
a.x: Carriers should be said to catch malaria more easily.
a.w: Red cells with HbS sickle and are cleared when infected, so carriers get less severe malaria.

a.o: Card 4 says the spleen often shrinks away by adulthood.
a.x: The spleen should be said to grow huge by adulthood.
a.w: Repeated small infarcts scar the spleen until it shrinks (autosplenectomy), raising the risk of infection.

a.o: Card 5 says hydroxyurea helps by raising fetal haemoglobin.
a.x: Hydroxyurea should be said to lower fetal haemoglobin.
a.w: HbF does not join HbS chains, so more HbF in each cell means less sickling and fewer crises.

s:
Autopsy practical report, forensic and neuropathology session, student Marwan Fathy. The case was a 38-year-old woman who collapsed after a sudden "worst headache of her life". At autopsy the brain was covered in fresh blood spread over its surface and into the sulci and the cisterns at its base.

Marwan wrote that the cause of death was a subdural haemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm on the circle of Willis. He found the aneurysm at the junction of the anterior communicating artery, about 7 mm across, with a tear at its tip.

In the discussion he noted that berry aneurysms are linked with adult polycystic kidney disease and high blood pressure, and that the blood irritates the meninges, causing neck stiffness. The tutor marked his report and asked him to name the space correctly.
h: the cause of death was a subdural haemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm

a.o: Marwan calls blood from a ruptured berry aneurysm a subdural haemorrhage.
a.x: A ruptured berry aneurysm bleeds into the subarachnoid space.
a.w: Circle of Willis arteries run in the subarachnoid space, so blood spreads into the sulci and cisterns. Subdural bleeds come from veins.

a.o: Marwan links berry aneurysms with polycystic kidney disease and high blood pressure.
a.x: These should be linked with low blood pressure.
a.w: Adult polycystic kidney disease and hypertension both raise the risk of berry aneurysms.

a.o: Marwan finds the aneurysm at the anterior communicating artery junction.
a.x: It should be placed in the middle of the basilar artery.
a.w: The anterior communicating artery is the most common site of berry aneurysms on the circle of Willis.

a.o: Marwan says blood irritating the meninges causes neck stiffness.
a.x: Neck stiffness should be put down to a neck sprain.
a.w: Blood in the subarachnoid space inflames the meninges, giving meningism with a stiff neck.

s:
Handout for "Cervical cancer", gynaecological pathology, by Dr. Rania. Part 1 says nearly all cervical cancers are caused by long-lasting infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), which is passed on through sexual contact.

Part 2 says HPV types 6 and 11 are the high-risk types that cause most cervical cancers, while types 16 and 18 cause genital warts. It explains that the virus infects the transformation zone, where the columnar and squamous linings meet.

Part 3 says the precancerous changes are called cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), which can be found by a smear test or HPV test before cancer develops. The handout ends by saying the HPV vaccine given to young people prevents most of these cancers.
h: HPV types 6 and 11 are the high-risk types that cause most cervical cancers, while types 16 and 18 cause genital warts

a.o: The handout makes HPV 6 and 11 the cancer types and 16 and 18 the wart types.
a.x: HPV 16 and 18 cause most cancers; 6 and 11 cause warts.
a.w: HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk and cause about 70% of cervical cancers. Low-risk types 6 and 11 cause most genital warts.

a.o: The handout says the virus infects the transformation zone where the two linings meet.
a.x: The virus should infect the top of the uterus instead.
a.w: The transformation zone has dividing metaplastic cells, which makes it the site HPV infects and where CIN develops.

a.o: The handout says a smear or HPV test can find CIN before cancer develops.
a.x: CIN should be said to be found only after cancer forms.
a.w: Screening detects precancerous CIN, which can be treated so invasive cancer never develops.

a.o: The handout says the HPV vaccine given to young people prevents most of these cancers.
a.x: The vaccine should be said to work only after cancer starts.
a.w: Vaccinating before exposure prevents infection with the high-risk types and so most cervical cancers.

s:
Short-answer exam, general pathology, question 8: "Compare dry and wet gangrene." Student Ali Hassan writes that gangrene is death of a large area of tissue, usually a limb, with changes on top of necrosis.

He writes that dry gangrene is caused mainly by bacteria growing in the tissue, which makes the foot dry, black and shrunken. He says it has a clear line between dead and living tissue and spreads slowly.

For wet gangrene he writes that it happens when bacteria infect dead tissue, often when venous blood flow is also blocked, so the tissue is swollen, soft and smelly, and that it spreads fast and can cause sepsis. He ends by saying diabetes raises the risk of both. The examiner gave 6 out of 10.
h: dry gangrene is caused mainly by bacteria growing in the tissue

a.o: Ali blames dry gangrene mainly on bacteria growing in the tissue.
a.x: It comes from arterial blockage, not bacteria.
a.w: Dry gangrene is coagulative necrosis from arterial blockage, with little infection. Bacterial growth is what makes gangrene wet.

a.o: Ali says dry gangrene has a clear line between dead and living tissue.
a.x: Dry gangrene should be said to have no clear border.
a.w: A line of demarcation forms with inflammation at its edge, separating the dry dead part from living tissue.

a.o: Ali says wet gangrene spreads fast and can cause sepsis.
a.x: Wet gangrene should be said to stay small and slow.
a.w: Infected, swollen tissue lets bacteria spread quickly and enter the blood, so wet gangrene is an emergency.

a.o: Ali says diabetes raises the risk of both types of gangrene.
a.x: Diabetes should be said to protect against gangrene.
a.w: Diabetes damages arteries and nerves and weakens defences, so both dry and wet gangrene are more common.

s:
Draft page "Multiple myeloma", haematopathology chapter. The page says myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow, usually in older adults, and that the cells make large amounts of one antibody, seen as an M band on electrophoresis.

It states that myeloma causes osteoblastic lesions, with dense white areas of new bone on X-ray, because the tumour cells make bone grow. It lists the CRAB features: high calcium, renal failure, anaemia and bone disease.

The page adds that free light chains, called Bence Jones proteins, can be found in the urine and can damage the kidney tubules. It ends by saying rouleaux (red cells stacked like coins) are seen on the blood film, and that amyloid can form from the light chains.
h: myeloma causes osteoblastic lesions, with dense white areas of new bone on X-ray

a.o: The page gives myeloma dense, bone-forming osteoblastic lesions.
a.x: Myeloma causes punched-out osteolytic lesions.
a.w: Myeloma cells switch on osteoclasts and switch off bone building, so X-rays show punched-out holes, often in the skull.

a.o: The page says Bence Jones light chains in the urine can damage kidney tubules.
a.x: Bence Jones proteins should be said to protect the kidney.
a.w: Light chains filtered in large amounts form casts in the tubules, causing myeloma kidney.

a.o: The page says rouleaux are seen on the blood film.
a.x: The film should show sickle cells instead of rouleaux.
a.w: The high antibody protein lowers the charge between red cells, so they stack like coins.

a.o: The page lists high calcium, renal failure, anaemia and bone disease as CRAB.
a.x: CRAB should stand for low calcium and raised blood pressure.
a.w: Bone breakdown, kidney damage, marrow failure and lytic lesions are the four CRAB features.

s:
Handout for "Pigmented skin lesions", skin pathology, by Dr. Tarek. Part 1 lists the ABCDE warning signs of melanoma: asymmetry, irregular border, uneven colour, diameter over 6 mm and evolution (change over time).

Part 2 says melanoma comes from melanocytes in the basal layer of the epidermis, and that sunburn in childhood raises the risk. The handout then says that the width of the lesion across the skin is the most important sign of the outlook in melanoma.

Part 3 says that melanoma can spread early to lymph nodes and distant organs, even when small, and that the sentinel lymph node is often checked. It ends by saying a mole with a sudden change should always be checked by a doctor.
h: the width of the lesion across the skin is the most important sign of the outlook in melanoma

a.o: The handout makes the lesion's width the key sign of outlook.
a.x: The depth of invasion (Breslow thickness) is the key sign.
a.w: Breslow thickness, measured in mm from the granular layer down, best predicts spread and survival in melanoma.

a.o: The handout says melanoma comes from melanocytes in the basal layer.
a.x: Melanoma should come from keratinocytes on the surface.
a.w: Melanocytes sit in the basal layer of the epidermis, and melanoma is their malignant tumour.

a.o: The handout says childhood sunburn raises the risk of melanoma.
a.x: Childhood sunburn should be said to protect the skin.
a.w: Intermittent intense sun exposure and blistering sunburn, especially in childhood, raise melanoma risk.

a.o: The handout says the sentinel lymph node is often checked in melanoma.
a.x: The sentinel node should be ignored in melanoma.
a.w: Melanoma can spread early by lymph, so the first draining node is sampled to guide staging.

s:
Pathology lab notebook, student Habiba Samir. Topic: alcohol and the liver. I wrote that alcohol damages the liver in three stages that often overlap: fatty liver, alcoholic hepatitis and cirrhosis.

For the first stage I wrote that fat droplets fill the liver cells within days of heavy drinking, making the liver large, yellow and greasy. I then wrote that fatty liver is already permanent, so stopping alcohol at this stage does not help the liver recover.

For alcoholic hepatitis I noted swollen liver cells, neutrophils and pink tangled clumps inside the cells called Mallory-Denk bodies. For cirrhosis I wrote that bands of scar tissue split the liver into small nodules, and that it can lead to portal hypertension and liver cancer. The tutor asked us to bring a drawing of each stage.
h: fatty liver is already permanent, so stopping alcohol at this stage does not help the liver recover

a.o: Habiba calls fatty liver permanent, so stopping alcohol would not help it recover.
a.x: Fatty liver is reversible if the person stops drinking.
a.w: Fat in liver cells clears within weeks of stopping alcohol. Only the scarring of cirrhosis is permanent.

a.o: Habiba records Mallory-Denk bodies inside the swollen liver cells of alcoholic hepatitis.
a.x: Mallory-Denk bodies should be placed in the bile ducts.
a.w: These pink clumps of damaged keratin filaments inside liver cells are typical of alcoholic hepatitis.

a.o: Habiba says scar bands split the cirrhotic liver into small nodules.
a.x: Cirrhosis should be said to leave the liver smooth and soft.
a.w: Cirrhosis is diffuse fibrosis with regenerating nodules, often small (micronodular) after alcohol.

a.o: Habiba says cirrhosis can lead to portal hypertension and liver cancer.
a.x: Cirrhosis should be said to lower portal pressure.
a.w: Scarring blocks blood flow through the liver, raising portal pressure, and the regenerating cells can turn cancerous.

s:
Handout for "Pharmacokinetics 2", by Dr. Ehab. Part 1 defines the half-life of a drug as the time it takes for its blood level to fall by half, and notes that it depends on both clearance and volume of distribution.

Part 2 covers regular dosing. When a drug is given at the same dose and interval, its level rises until the amount going in equals the amount going out. The handout then states that steady state is reached after about one half-life, whatever the drug.

Part 3 says that a loading dose can be used to reach the target level quickly when the half-life is long, as with amiodarone or digoxin. A last note says that after stopping a drug, it takes about four to five half-lives for nearly all of it to leave the body.
h: steady state is reached after about one half-life

a.o: The handout says steady state is reached after about one half-life of dosing.
a.x: Steady state takes about four to five half-lives.
a.w: After one half-life the level is only half way there. About 97% of the steady state is reached after five half-lives.

a.o: The handout says a loading dose reaches the target quickly when the half-life is long.
a.x: A loading dose should be said to slow the rise in level.
a.w: A large first dose fills the volume of distribution at once, so a long half-life drug works sooner.

a.o: The handout says a drug takes four to five half-lives to leave the body.
a.x: The drug should be gone after a single half-life.
a.w: Each half-life removes half of what is left, so after 4-5 half-lives about 94-97% has gone.

a.o: The handout says half-life depends on both clearance and volume of distribution.
a.x: Half-life should depend on the dose given alone.
a.w: t1/2 = 0.693 x Vd / clearance, so a bigger volume or slower clearance lengthens it.

s:
Short-answer exam, pharmacology block, question 1: "What is first-pass metabolism?" Student Rana Ashraf writes that a drug swallowed by mouth is absorbed from the gut into the portal vein and passes through the liver before reaching the rest of the body.

She writes that some of the drug is broken down in the gut wall and the liver on this first pass, so less reaches the circulation, and gives morphine and glyceryl trinitrate as examples. She then writes that drugs given into a vein also go through first-pass metabolism, which is why their bioavailability is about 50%.

She ends by saying that giving glyceryl trinitrate under the tongue avoids the first pass, because the veins there drain straight into the systemic circulation. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: drugs given into a vein also go through first-pass metabolism, which is why their bioavailability is about 50%

a.o: Rana says drugs given into a vein also go through first-pass metabolism.
a.x: IV drugs skip first pass; bioavailability is 100%.
a.w: An IV dose enters the systemic blood directly, so by definition its bioavailability is 100%. First pass applies to oral drugs.

a.o: Rana says sublingual glyceryl trinitrate avoids first-pass metabolism.
a.x: Sublingual drugs should pass through the liver first.
a.w: Veins under the tongue drain to the superior vena cava, so the drug reaches the heart before the liver.

a.o: Rana gives morphine and glyceryl trinitrate as drugs with heavy first pass.
a.x: These should be given as drugs with no first pass.
a.w: Both are largely broken down by the liver after oral dosing, which is why oral doses are higher.

a.o: Rana says some of the drug is broken down in the gut wall as well as the liver.
a.x: The gut wall should be said to play no part at all.
a.w: Enzymes such as CYP3A4 in the gut wall add to first-pass loss before the drug reaches the liver.

s:
Flashcards "Opioids", made by Hassan for the pharmacology quiz. Card 1 says morphine acts mainly on mu opioid receptors in the brain and spinal cord to relieve pain.

Card 2 lists the side effects: slow breathing, constipation, nausea, small "pinpoint" pupils and drowsiness. Card 3 says naloxone is a strong opioid agonist that is given in overdose to boost the body's own pain control and wake the patient up.

Card 4 says naloxone's action is shorter than many opioids, so the patient must be watched and the dose may need repeating. Card 5 says long-term opioid use causes tolerance and dependence, so stopping suddenly causes withdrawal. Hassan has added a star next to card 3 and written "check before the quiz".
h: naloxone is a strong opioid agonist

a.o: Card 3 calls naloxone a strong opioid agonist used in an overdose.
a.x: Naloxone is an opioid antagonist that blocks them.
a.w: Naloxone competes with opioids at mu receptors without switching them on, quickly reversing slow breathing and drowsiness.

a.o: Card 4 says naloxone wears off sooner than many opioids, so doses may need repeating.
a.x: Naloxone should be said to last much longer than morphine.
a.w: Naloxone acts for about 30-90 minutes, so a long-acting opioid can bring the overdose back.

a.o: Card 2 lists pinpoint pupils among the side effects of morphine.
a.x: Morphine should be said to make the pupils very large.
a.w: Opioids stimulate the Edinger-Westphal nucleus, so the pupils become very small.

a.o: Card 5 says stopping opioids suddenly after long use causes withdrawal.
a.x: Stopping should be said to be safe at any time.
a.w: Long use leads to physical dependence, so sudden stopping causes withdrawal with pain, sweating and diarrhoea.

s:
Handout for "Beta-blockers", cardiovascular pharmacology, by Dr. Magdy. Part 1 says beta-blockers slow the heart and reduce its force by blocking beta-1 receptors, and are used in angina, heart failure, high blood pressure and after a heart attack.

Part 2 compares the drugs. Propranolol blocks both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors, while bisoprolol and atenolol are more selective for beta-1. The handout then says that propranolol is the safest beta-blocker for patients with asthma, because blocking beta-2 receptors relaxes the airways.

Part 3 lists side effects: tiredness, cold hands and slow heart rate. It warns that beta-blockers can hide the warning signs of low blood sugar, such as a fast heartbeat, in diabetics on insulin.
h: propranolol is the safest beta-blocker for patients with asthma, because blocking beta-2 receptors relaxes the airways

a.o: The handout calls propranolol the safest beta-blocker for asthma patients.
a.x: Propranolol is avoided, as beta-2 block narrows airways.
a.w: Beta-2 receptors relax bronchial muscle. Blocking them can bring on severe bronchospasm, so propranolol is avoided in asthma.

a.o: The handout calls bisoprolol and atenolol more selective for beta-1 receptors.
a.x: These should be called more selective for beta-2 receptors.
a.w: Bisoprolol and atenolol are cardioselective, acting mostly on beta-1 receptors in the heart.

a.o: The handout says beta-blockers can hide the warning signs of low blood sugar.
a.x: They should be said to make low sugar signs stronger.
a.w: The fast heartbeat and tremor of hypoglycaemia come from adrenaline on beta receptors, so blocking them hides the warning.

a.o: The handout lists tiredness, cold hands and slow heart rate as side effects.
a.x: These should be listed as signs of an overdose of salt.
a.w: Lower cardiac output and peripheral vasoconstriction explain tiredness and cold hands; beta-1 block slows the heart.

s:
Pharmacology tutorial report, drug interactions, student Mohamed Gaber. The task was to predict the effect of adding a new drug to a patient stable on warfarin with an INR of 2.5.

Mohamed explains that warfarin is broken down by liver CYP450 enzymes. Case A: the patient starts clarithromycin, an enzyme inhibitor; he predicts the INR will rise and bleeding risk will go up. Case B: the patient starts rifampicin for TB. He writes that rifampicin is also an enzyme inhibitor, so the INR will rise even more and the warfarin dose should be lowered.

In his summary he notes that warfarin has a narrow therapeutic index, so small changes in its level matter, and that the INR should be checked more often whenever a drug is started or stopped.
h: rifampicin is also an enzyme inhibitor, so the INR will rise even more

a.o: Mohamed calls rifampicin an enzyme inhibitor and expects the INR to rise.
a.x: Rifampicin is an inducer, so the INR will fall.
a.w: Rifampicin induces CYP450, so warfarin is broken down faster, its level drops and the INR falls. The dose often needs raising.

a.o: Mohamed predicts clarithromycin will raise the INR and bleeding risk.
a.x: Clarithromycin should be predicted to lower the INR.
a.w: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and other enzymes, slowing warfarin breakdown, so its effect and the INR rise.

a.o: Mohamed says warfarin has a narrow therapeutic index.
a.x: Warfarin should be said to have a very wide margin.
a.w: The gap between the dose that works and the dose that causes bleeding is small, so small changes matter.

a.o: Mohamed says the INR should be checked more often when drugs are started or stopped.
a.x: The INR should be checked only once a year.
a.w: Starting or stopping an interacting drug can shift warfarin levels, so closer INR checks catch the change early.

s:
Short-answer exam, cardiovascular pharmacology, question 3: "Describe ACE inhibitors." Student Lina Zaki writes that ACE inhibitors, such as ramipril, block the enzyme that turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II, so the blood vessels relax and less aldosterone is made.

She lists their uses: high blood pressure, heart failure, after a heart attack and to protect the kidneys in diabetes. She then writes that their typical dry cough is caused by a build-up of angiotensin II in the lungs.

She ends by listing other side effects: high potassium, a fall in kidney function when starting, and rarely swelling of the face and lips (angioedema). She notes they must be avoided in pregnancy. The examiner gave 8 out of 10.
h: caused by a build-up of angiotensin II in the lungs

a.o: Lina blames the dry cough on angiotensin II piling up in the lungs.
a.x: The cough comes from a build-up of bradykinin instead.
a.w: ACE also breaks down bradykinin. When ACE is blocked, bradykinin builds up in the airways and causes the dry cough.

a.o: Lina lists high potassium among the side effects of ACE inhibitors.
a.x: ACE inhibitors should be said to lower potassium.
a.w: Less angiotensin II means less aldosterone, so the kidney keeps more potassium.

a.o: Lina says ACE inhibitors must be avoided in pregnancy.
a.x: They should be called the first choice in pregnancy.
a.w: ACE inhibitors damage the developing fetal kidneys, especially in the second and third trimesters.

a.o: Lina lists angioedema as a rare side effect.
a.x: Angioedema should be called the most common side effect.
a.w: Swelling of the face and lips is rare but serious, also linked to bradykinin build-up.

s:
Flashcards "Antiplatelet drugs", made by Nada for the haematology pharmacology block. Card 1 says platelets make thromboxane A2 through the COX-1 enzyme, and thromboxane makes platelets stick together.

Card 2 says low-dose aspirin blocks COX-1 reversibly, so its effect on platelets wears off within a few hours of the last dose. Card 3 says clopidogrel blocks the P2Y12 receptor for ADP on platelets.

Card 4 says aspirin is used after heart attacks and strokes to prevent new clots, and that its main side effects are stomach ulcers and bleeding. Card 5 says aspirin should not be given to children because of the risk of Reye's syndrome. Nada's last note reminds her to learn the usual doses before the exam.
h: blocks COX-1 reversibly, so its effect on platelets wears off within a few hours

a.o: Card 2 has aspirin block COX-1 reversibly, wearing off within hours.
a.x: Aspirin blocks COX-1 for the platelet's whole life.
a.w: Aspirin acetylates COX-1 permanently. Platelets have no nucleus to make new enzyme, so the effect lasts 7-10 days.

a.o: Card 3 says clopidogrel blocks the platelet P2Y12 receptor for ADP.
a.x: Clopidogrel should be said to block COX-2.
a.w: Clopidogrel's active metabolite blocks the ADP P2Y12 receptor, stopping platelets from activating.

a.o: Card 4 gives stomach ulcers and bleeding as aspirin's main side effects.
a.x: The main side effect should be weight gain.
a.w: Blocking COX-1 in the stomach reduces protective prostaglandins, and less platelet action adds to bleeding risk.

a.o: Card 5 warns against aspirin in children because of Reye's syndrome.
a.x: Aspirin should be called the best fever drug for children.
a.w: Aspirin in children with viral illness is linked to Reye's syndrome, with liver and brain damage.

s:
Handout for "Common poisonings", clinical pharmacology, by Dr. Hanan. Part 1 says paracetamol is safe at normal doses, but in overdose the normal liver pathways are full, so more is turned into a toxic product called NAPQI.

Part 2 explains that NAPQI is normally made safe by glutathione, but in overdose glutathione runs out and NAPQI damages the liver cells, with liver failure after two to four days. The handout then says the antidote for paracetamol overdose is naloxone, which should be started as soon as possible.

Part 3 says the treatment decision uses a blood level plotted against the time since the overdose, and that people who drink a lot of alcohol or are starving may be at higher risk.
h: the antidote for paracetamol overdose is naloxone

a.o: The handout names naloxone as the antidote for paracetamol overdose.
a.x: The antidote is N-acetylcysteine, given early.
a.w: N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione so NAPQI is made safe again. Naloxone reverses opioids and does nothing for paracetamol.

a.o: The handout says liver failure comes two to four days after the overdose.
a.x: Liver failure should be said to start within an hour.
a.w: Liver cell death builds up over days, so patients may feel well at first, then become very ill by days 2-4.

a.o: The handout says glutathione normally makes NAPQI safe.
a.x: Glutathione should be said to make NAPQI more toxic.
a.w: Glutathione binds NAPQI, so it can be excreted; trouble begins once glutathione stores run out.

a.o: The handout says heavy drinkers and starving people may be at higher risk.
a.x: These people should be said to have lower risk.
a.w: Alcohol can induce the enzyme that makes NAPQI, and starvation lowers glutathione stores.

s:
Short-answer exam, antimicrobials, question 2: "How do penicillins work?" Student Youssef Kamal writes that penicillins are beta-lactam antibiotics and that they kill bacteria rather than just stopping their growth.

He writes that penicillins work by binding the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome, which stops the bacteria making their proteins. He adds that bacteria can resist penicillin by making beta-lactamase enzymes, which break the beta-lactam ring, and that clavulanic acid is added to amoxicillin to block these enzymes.

He ends by saying that penicillin allergy can cause anaphylaxis, and that MRSA is resistant because it has an altered penicillin-binding protein. He draws a small diagram of a bacterial cell wall beside his answer. The examiner gave 6 out of 10.
h: penicillins work by binding the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome

a.o: Youssef says penicillins bind the 30S ribosome subunit and block protein making.
a.x: Penicillins block cell wall building in bacteria.
a.w: Penicillins bind PBPs and stop cross-linking of peptidoglycan, so the wall weakens and bacteria burst. 30S binders are aminoglycosides.

a.o: Youssef says clavulanic acid is added to amoxicillin to block beta-lactamase.
a.x: Clavulanic acid should be said to break down amoxicillin.
a.w: Clavulanic acid binds beta-lactamases, protecting amoxicillin from being destroyed by resistant bacteria.

a.o: Youssef says MRSA resists penicillins with an altered penicillin-binding protein.
a.x: MRSA should resist by pumping the drug out only.
a.w: MRSA carries mecA, which makes PBP2a, a binding protein that beta-lactams barely bind.

a.o: Youssef says penicillins kill bacteria rather than just stop their growth.
a.x: Penicillins should be said to only stop growth.
a.w: By wrecking the cell wall while bacteria grow, penicillins are bactericidal.

s:
Draft page "Aminoglycosides", antimicrobial chapter. The page says aminoglycosides such as gentamicin bind the 30S ribosome subunit and are very good against Gram-negative bacteria, but are not absorbed by mouth and are given into a vein.

It explains that they need oxygen to enter bacteria, so they do not work against anaerobes. It then says that their main side effect is the grey baby syndrome, and that kidney and ear damage are not a concern with these drugs.

The page says blood levels are checked to keep the trough low, and that the drug is often given once a day, because its killing depends on a high peak level. It ends by saying they act together with penicillins, which open the cell wall and help them get in.
h: their main side effect is the grey baby syndrome, and that kidney and ear damage are not a concern

a.o: The page names grey baby syndrome as the main harm, not kidney or ear damage.
a.x: Their main harms are to the kidneys and to hearing.
a.w: Aminoglycosides are nephrotoxic and ototoxic, which is why levels are watched. Grey baby syndrome comes from chloramphenicol.

a.o: The page says aminoglycosides need oxygen to enter bacteria and fail against anaerobes.
a.x: They should be called the best drugs for anaerobes.
a.w: Uptake into bacteria needs oxygen-dependent transport, so anaerobic bacteria are resistant.

a.o: The page gives a once-a-day dose because killing depends on a high peak.
a.x: The drug should be given in tiny doses all day long.
a.w: Aminoglycoside killing rises with peak level and has a long after-effect, so one large daily dose works well.

a.o: The page says penicillins help aminoglycosides get into bacteria.
a.x: Penicillins should be said to block aminoglycosides.
a.w: Damaging the cell wall with a beta-lactam lets more aminoglycoside enter, a synergy used in endocarditis.

s:
Flashcards "Anticholinergic drugs", made by Salma for the autonomic pharmacology quiz. Card 1 says atropine blocks muscarinic receptors, so it opposes the parasympathetic system.

Card 2 lists the effects of atropine: a fast heart rate, a dry mouth, less sweating, hot red skin, constricted pupils and blurred near vision. Card 3 says atropine is given for a dangerously slow heart rate, and before some operations to dry up secretions.

Card 4 says atropine is part of the treatment of organophosphate poisoning. Card 5 gives the memory aid for anticholinergic overdose: "hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter".
h: constricted pupils and blurred near vision

a.o: Card 2 lists constricted pupils among the many effects of atropine.
a.x: Atropine should widen the pupils instead.
a.w: Blocking muscarinic receptors on the iris sphincter lets the pupil widen. "Blind as a bat" comes from big pupils and lost focus.

a.o: Card 3 says atropine is given for a dangerously slow heart rate.
a.x: Atropine should be given to slow a fast heart.
a.w: Atropine blocks vagal slowing of the SA node, so the heart rate rises in symptomatic bradycardia.

a.o: Card 4 says atropine is part of treating organophosphate poisoning.
a.x: Atropine should be said to worsen this poisoning.
a.w: Organophosphates flood muscarinic receptors with acetylcholine, and atropine blocks those effects.

a.o: Card 2 lists a dry mouth and less sweating among atropine's effects.
a.x: Atropine should be said to cause heavy sweating.
a.w: Salivary and sweat glands work through muscarinic receptors, so atropine dries them up.

s:
Clinical pharmacology tutorial report, poisoning case, student Ahmed Lotfy. A farm worker arrived after spraying crops, with small pupils, heavy sweating, drooling, slow heart rate, wheezing and muscle twitching.

Ahmed wrote that the picture fits organophosphate poisoning, which blocks acetylcholinesterase so acetylcholine builds up at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. In the treatment plan he wrote: remove the clothes and wash the skin, give oxygen, and give neostigmine to bring the acetylcholine level back down.

He adds that pralidoxime can reactivate the enzyme if given early, before "ageing" of the bond, and that the doctor should watch for weak breathing muscles. The tutor marked one step of the plan in red.
h: give neostigmine to bring the acetylcholine level back down

a.o: Ahmed plans neostigmine to bring acetylcholine back down.
a.x: Give atropine and pralidoxime instead of it.
a.w: Neostigmine also blocks acetylcholinesterase and would make things worse. Atropine treats drooling, wheeze and slow heart.

a.o: Ahmed says pralidoxime can reactivate the enzyme if given early.
a.x: Pralidoxime should be said to work only days later.
a.w: Pralidoxime pulls the organophosphate off the enzyme, but only before the bond "ages" and becomes permanent.

a.o: Ahmed starts with removing clothes and washing the skin.
a.x: Washing should be skipped to save time.
a.w: Organophosphates are absorbed through skin, so removing contaminated clothes stops further dosing and protects staff.

a.o: Ahmed warns about weak breathing muscles.
a.x: Breathing muscles should be said to stay strong.
a.w: Excess acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors first twitches and then paralyses muscles, including the diaphragm.

s:
Handout for "Diuretics", renal pharmacology, by Dr. Sameh. Part 1 says furosemide is a loop diuretic that blocks the Na-K-2Cl transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, making it the strongest type.

Part 2 says thiazides such as bendroflumethiazide act on the distal convoluted tubule and are used for high blood pressure. Both loop and thiazide diuretics can lower blood potassium. The handout then says spironolactone also causes low potassium, so potassium supplements are usually needed with it.

Part 3 says spironolactone blocks aldosterone and is used in heart failure and liver disease with fluid in the belly. It ends by saying furosemide in high doses can damage hearing.
h: spironolactone also causes low potassium, so potassium supplements are usually needed with it

a.o: The handout says spironolactone lowers potassium and needs potassium supplements.
a.x: Spironolactone keeps potassium; it can raise it.
a.w: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone, which normally pushes potassium out in the urine, so it can cause high potassium.

a.o: The handout says furosemide blocks the Na-K-2Cl transporter in the thick ascending limb.
a.x: Furosemide should act on the collecting duct.
a.w: Furosemide blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, where a large share of sodium is reabsorbed.

a.o: The handout says thiazides act on the distal convoluted tubule.
a.x: Thiazides should act on the proximal tubule.
a.w: Thiazides block the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule.

a.o: The handout says high-dose furosemide can damage hearing.
a.x: Furosemide should be said to improve hearing.
a.w: Loop diuretics affect a similar transporter in the inner ear, so high doses can cause ototoxicity.

s:
Flashcards "Diabetes drugs", made by Islam for the endocrine pharmacology quiz. Card 1 says metformin is usually the first drug for type 2 diabetes and works mainly by reducing glucose output from the liver.

Card 2 says the main side effects of metformin are low blood sugar and weight gain, so patients must always eat when they take it. Card 3 says sulfonylureas such as gliclazide make the pancreas release more insulin, so they can cause low blood sugar.

Card 4 says metformin is stopped before contrast scans and in severe kidney failure because of a rare risk of lactic acidosis. Card 5 says SGLT2 inhibitors make the kidney pass glucose in the urine.
h: the main side effects of metformin are low blood sugar and weight gain

a.o: Card 2 names low blood sugar and weight gain as metformin's main side effects.
a.x: It mainly upsets the gut and rarely causes any hypos.
a.w: Metformin does not raise insulin, so it rarely causes hypoglycaemia and is weight neutral. Nausea and diarrhoea are common.

a.o: Card 3 says sulfonylureas raise insulin release and can cause low blood sugar.
a.x: Sulfonylureas should be said to lower insulin release.
a.w: Sulfonylureas close K-ATP channels on beta cells, releasing insulin whatever the glucose level.

a.o: Card 4 says metformin is stopped in severe kidney failure because of lactic acidosis.
a.x: Metformin should be said to be safest in kidney failure.
a.w: Metformin is cleared by the kidney and can build up, raising the rare risk of lactic acidosis.

a.o: Card 5 says SGLT2 inhibitors make the kidney pass glucose in the urine.
a.x: SGLT2 inhibitors should make the kidney keep more glucose.
a.w: Blocking SGLT2 in the proximal tubule stops glucose reabsorption, so it is lost in the urine.

s:
Handout for "Drugs for heart failure and atrial fibrillation", by Dr. Ola. Part 1 says digoxin blocks the sodium-potassium pump in heart muscle, which raises calcium inside the cells and makes each beat stronger. It also slows conduction through the AV node, which helps control a fast heart rate in atrial fibrillation.
