In the discussion she says untreated chlamydia in women can cause pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility, and that doxycycline or azithromycin is used for treatment. The lab technician corrected one line of her notes.
h: chlamydia is grown in the lab on ordinary blood agar like most bacteria

a.o: Mona says chlamydia grows on ordinary blood agar like most bacteria.
a.x: Chlamydia lives only inside cells and cannot grow on agar.
a.w: Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular bacterium; it needs cell culture to grow. NAAT is now the routine test.

a.o: Mona says the usual test is a NAAT on urine or a swab.
a.x: The usual test should be a chest X-ray.
a.w: Nucleic acid tests are sensitive, specific and work on easily collected samples.

a.o: Mona links untreated chlamydia with pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility.
a.x: Chlamydia should be said to protect against infertility.
a.w: Ascending infection scars the fallopian tubes, raising the risk of infertility and ectopic pregnancy.

a.o: Mona says doxycycline or azithromycin is used for treatment.
a.x: Treatment should be with penicillin only.
a.w: Chlamydia has no peptidoglycan-rich wall to target, so drugs acting inside the cell such as doxycycline are used.

s:
Flashcards "Vaccines", made by Ziad for the immunology and microbiology block. Card 1 says live attenuated vaccines contain a weakened germ that can still multiply, such as MMR, BCG and the yellow fever vaccine.

Card 2 says inactivated vaccines contain killed germs or parts of them, such as the flu injection, and often need boosters. Card 3 says live vaccines are the best choice for people with a weak immune system, such as those on chemotherapy, because they give the strongest protection.

Card 4 says toxoid vaccines, such as tetanus, train the body against a toxin rather than the germ. Card 5 says herd immunity protects people who cannot be vaccinated when most of the population is immune.
h: live vaccines are the best choice for people with a weak immune system, such as those on chemotherapy

a.o: Card 3 calls live vaccines the best choice for people on chemotherapy.
a.x: Live vaccines are usually avoided in weak immunity.
a.w: A weakened germ can still multiply and cause disease if the immune system cannot control it, so inactivated vaccines are used instead.

a.o: Card 2 says inactivated vaccines often need boosters.
a.x: Inactivated vaccines should never need boosters.
a.w: Killed germs do not multiply, so the immune response is weaker and repeat doses are needed.

a.o: Card 4 says toxoid vaccines train the body against a toxin.
a.x: Toxoid vaccines should contain the live germ.
a.w: A toxoid is an inactivated toxin; antibodies to it neutralise the real toxin.

a.o: Card 5 says herd immunity protects people who cannot be vaccinated.
a.x: Herd immunity should be said to help only the vaccinated.
a.w: When most people are immune, the germ cannot spread easily, so the unprotected are shielded too.

s:
Short-answer exam, virology, question 4: "Describe herpes simplex virus infection." Student Yasmin Fathy writes that HSV-1 usually causes cold sores around the mouth and HSV-2 usually causes genital herpes, though both can infect either site.

She writes that after the first infection, the virus hides in a latent state in the skin cells at the site of the sore, and comes back when those skin cells are stressed by sun or fever. She adds that it is a double-stranded DNA virus.

She ends by saying that HSV can cause a dangerous brain infection (encephalitis) that mainly affects the temporal lobes, and that aciclovir is the treatment. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the virus hides in a latent state in the skin cells at the site of the sore

a.o: Yasmin says HSV stays latent in skin cells at the sore.
a.x: HSV stays latent in sensory nerve ganglia.
a.w: HSV travels up sensory nerves and hides in ganglia such as the trigeminal ganglion, then travels back down to cause new sores.

a.o: Yasmin says HSV is a double-stranded DNA virus.
a.x: HSV should be said to be an RNA virus.
a.w: Herpesviruses are large, enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses.

a.o: Yasmin says HSV encephalitis mainly affects the temporal lobes.
a.x: It should mainly affect the cerebellum.
a.w: HSV encephalitis typically damages the temporal lobes, causing confusion, fits and odd behaviour.

a.o: Yasmin gives aciclovir as the treatment.
a.x: HSV should be treated with antibiotics.
a.w: Aciclovir is activated by viral thymidine kinase and blocks viral DNA polymerase.

s:
Handout for "Varicella zoster virus", by Dr. Mai. Part 1 says the first infection with VZV causes chickenpox, an itchy rash of blisters in crops, mostly in children.

Part 2 says the virus then lies dormant in the dorsal root ganglia and can come back years later as shingles, a painful band of blisters along one dermatome. The handout then says that a child who touches the blisters of a person with shingles will catch shingles, not chickenpox.

Part 3 says shingles is more common in older people and those with weak immunity, and that pain can last for months afterwards (post-herpetic neuralgia). It ends by saying there are vaccines for both chickenpox and shingles.
h: a child who touches the blisters of a person with shingles will catch shingles, not chickenpox

a.o: The handout says a child who touches shingles blisters will catch shingles.
a.x: A non-immune child exposed to shingles catches chickenpox.
a.w: Shingles is a reactivation of the virus already in the body. Someone never infected gets a first infection: chickenpox.

a.o: The handout says VZV lies dormant in the dorsal root ganglia.
a.x: The virus should be said to lie dormant in the liver.
a.w: After chickenpox, VZV stays in sensory ganglia and can reactivate along that nerve's dermatome.

a.o: The handout says pain can last for months after shingles.
a.x: The pain should be said to always end with the rash.
a.w: Post-herpetic neuralgia is nerve pain that persists after the rash heals, more often in the elderly.

a.o: The handout says there are vaccines for both chickenpox and shingles.
a.x: A vaccine should exist only for chickenpox.
a.w: Varicella vaccine prevents chickenpox; a zoster vaccine lowers the risk of shingles in older adults.

s:
Clinical microbiology tutorial, sore throat case, student Mostafa Hany. An 18-year-old has a sore throat, fever, swollen neck glands and great tiredness. He has had these symptoms for ten days. The blood film shows many atypical lymphocytes and the Monospot test is positive.

Mostafa writes that this is infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever), caused by the Epstein-Barr virus. In his plan he suggests amoxicillin to treat the infection, saying it is the best choice and has no special risk here.

He adds that the patient should avoid contact sports for some weeks because the spleen may be enlarged and could rupture, and that EBV is spread through saliva. The tutor marked his plan with a question mark.
h: he suggests amoxicillin to treat the infection, saying it is the best choice and has no special risk here

a.o: Mostafa plans amoxicillin as the best choice, with no special risk.
a.x: EBV is viral; amoxicillin is avoided as it causes a rash.
a.w: Antibiotics do not treat EBV, and amoxicillin gives a widespread rash in most patients with glandular fever.

a.o: Mostafa says contact sports should be avoided because the spleen may rupture.
a.x: Contact sports should be said to be safe straight away.
a.w: The spleen often swells in glandular fever and can tear after a blow, so sport is stopped for weeks.

a.o: Mostafa says EBV is spread through saliva.
a.x: EBV should be said to spread through mosquito bites.
a.w: It is called the "kissing disease" because the virus passes in saliva.

a.o: Mostafa links atypical lymphocytes and a positive Monospot with EBV.
a.x: These should be linked with a bacterial throat infection.
a.w: Activated T cells respond to EBV-infected B cells, and heterophile antibodies make the Monospot positive.

s:
Microbiology lab notebook, student Hager Lotfy. Today we did a disc diffusion test to see which antibiotics work against an E. coli from a urine sample. We spread the bacteria evenly on Mueller-Hinton agar and placed six antibiotic discs on top.

After 18 hours at 37 degrees C we measured the clear zones around each disc. I wrote that a small zone means the bacteria are sensitive to that antibiotic, and a large zone means they are resistant, so the drug with the smallest zone is the best choice.

At the end I noted that the zone sizes are compared with standard tables, and that the test does not tell us the exact MIC. The tutor asked us to recheck our interpretation.
h: a small zone means the bacteria are sensitive to that antibiotic, and a large zone means they are resistant

a.o: Hager reads a small zone as sensitive, a large as resistant.
a.x: A large clear zone means sensitive, not resistant.
a.w: The antibiotic spreads from the disc and stops growth where it is strong enough. A wide clear ring means the bacteria are easily stopped.

a.o: Hager says zone sizes are compared with standard tables.
a.x: Zone sizes should be judged by eye with no tables.
a.w: Breakpoint tables (such as EUCAST) convert zone size into sensitive or resistant for each drug.

a.o: Hager notes the test does not give the exact MIC.
a.x: The test should be said to give the exact MIC.
a.w: Disc diffusion gives a category, while broth dilution or E-tests measure the MIC itself.

a.o: Hager spreads the bacteria evenly on Mueller-Hinton agar.
a.x: The bacteria should be dotted in one corner only.
a.w: An even lawn on standard agar makes zone sizes reliable and comparable.

s:
Microbiology lab notebook, student Karim Nabil. Today we did a broth dilution test on a Staphylococcus aureus from a wound swab. We set up a row of tubes with the antibiotic halved in each tube, added the same amount of bacteria to each, and incubated them overnight at 37 degrees C.

The next morning the tubes with the most drug were clear and the weaker tubes were cloudy. I wrote that the MIC is the highest concentration that still lets the bacteria grow, so a high MIC means the drug works very well against this strain.

At the end I noted that a tube with broth and bacteria but no drug was used as a growth control, and that the MIC is compared with breakpoints to call the strain sensitive or resistant. The tutor circled one sentence.
h: the MIC is the highest concentration that still lets the bacteria grow, so a high MIC means the drug works very well

a.o: Karim calls the MIC the highest dose that allows growth, high meaning better.
a.x: The MIC is the lowest dose that stops visible growth.
a.w: A low MIC means little drug is needed to stop the bacteria, so the strain is more sensitive. A high MIC points to resistance.

a.o: Karim uses a tube with no drug as a growth control.
a.x: The control tube should contain the strongest drug dose.
a.w: A drug-free tube shows the bacteria can grow, so clear tubes truly reflect the drug's effect.

a.o: Karim compares the MIC with breakpoints to call the strain sensitive or resistant.
a.x: Breakpoints should not be used for MIC results.
a.w: Breakpoints are agreed MIC cut-offs for each drug and organism.

a.o: Karim halves the antibiotic in each tube along the row.
a.x: Each tube should hold the same drug dose.
a.w: Doubling dilutions give a range of doses, so the cut-off where growth stops can be found.

s:
Handout for "Bacterial growth", by Dr. Rania. Part 1 says bacteria divide by binary fission, and that under good conditions E. coli can double about every 20 minutes. When bacteria are put into fresh broth, they pass through four phases that can be drawn as a growth curve.

Part 2 describes the phases in order. It says the lag phase comes first, when the cells adapt and make enzymes but hardly divide. Then comes the stationary phase, when the number of cells rises fastest, followed by the log phase, when nutrients run out and growth equals death. Last comes the death phase.

Part 3 says many antibiotics, such as penicillins, work best on cells that are actively dividing, and that spores tend to form when conditions turn harsh.
h: Then comes the stationary phase, when the number of cells rises fastest, followed by the log phase

a.o: The handout swaps the order of the stationary and log phases.
a.x: The log phase comes before the stationary phase.
a.w: In the log phase cells divide fastest. In the stationary phase nutrients run out and new cells equal dying ones.

a.o: The handout says cells adapt and make enzymes in the lag phase.
a.x: The lag phase should be the time of fastest growth.
a.w: After transfer, cells first make the enzymes and parts they need, so numbers barely rise.

a.o: The handout says penicillins work best on actively dividing cells.
a.x: Penicillins should work best on resting cells.
a.w: Penicillins block new cell wall building, which happens mainly while cells are growing.

a.o: The handout says E. coli can double about every 20 minutes.
a.x: E. coli should be said to double once a week.
a.w: In rich broth at body heat, fast-growing bacteria like E. coli divide in about 20 minutes.

s:
Draft page "How bacteria share genes", microbiology chapter. The page explains that bacteria can gain new genes, such as antibiotic resistance genes, without sexual reproduction, through three main routes.

It states that transformation is when a bacterium takes up free, naked DNA from its surroundings. It then says conjugation is when a virus that infects bacteria (a bacteriophage) carries DNA from one cell to another, and transduction is when two bacteria touch through a pilus and pass a plasmid.

The page adds that plasmids are small circles of DNA separate from the chromosome, and that they often carry resistance genes, which is why resistance can spread quickly between bacteria in hospitals. It ends with a diagram of each route.
h: conjugation is when a virus that infects bacteria (a bacteriophage) carries DNA from one cell to another, and transduction is when two bacteria touch through a pilus

a.o: The page gives phages to conjugation and the pilus to transduction.
a.x: Conjugation uses a pilus; transduction, a phage.
a.w: In conjugation a sex pilus links two cells and a plasmid passes across. In transduction a bacteriophage carries the DNA.

a.o: The page says transformation is uptake of free, naked DNA.
a.x: Transformation should need a virus to carry DNA.
a.w: Some bacteria, like S. pneumoniae, can take up DNA released from dead cells.

a.o: The page says plasmids are DNA circles separate from the chromosome.
a.x: Plasmids should be called part of the chromosome.
a.w: Plasmids copy themselves on their own and often carry extra genes such as resistance.

a.o: The page links plasmids with quick spread of resistance in hospitals.
a.x: Plasmids should be said to never carry resistance.
a.w: Resistance plasmids can pass between species, spreading genes like ESBLs fast.

s:
Flashcards "Prions", made by Nour for the infection block. Card 1 says prions are misfolded proteins with no DNA or RNA, which make normal prion proteins misfold too.

Card 2 says prions cause diseases such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), with fast dementia, jerky movements and death within about a year. Card 3 says prions are easily destroyed by a normal autoclave cycle and by standard disinfectants, so surgical instruments are always safe to reuse after routine cleaning.

Card 4 says the brain shows tiny holes under the microscope, called spongiform change. Card 5 says variant CJD was linked to eating beef from cattle with mad cow disease. Nour added that there is no cure.
h: prions are easily destroyed by a normal autoclave cycle and by standard disinfectants

a.o: Card 3 says a normal autoclave easily kills prions.
a.x: Prions resist normal autoclaving and bleach.
a.w: Prions have no nucleic acid and are very stable, so they need special, harsher methods, and some instruments are destroyed.

a.o: Card 2 says CJD causes fast dementia and jerky movements.
a.x: CJD should be said to progress over decades.
a.w: Rapid dementia with myoclonus and death within months is typical of sporadic CJD.

a.o: Card 4 says the brain shows spongiform change.
a.x: The brain should show pus-filled abscesses.
a.w: Neurons die and leave small holes, giving the tissue a sponge-like look.

a.o: Card 5 links variant CJD with beef from mad cow disease.
a.x: Variant CJD should be linked with mosquito bites.
a.w: Eating infected beef products passed BSE prions to humans as variant CJD.

s:
Short-answer exam, parasitology, question 3: "Describe Entamoeba histolytica." Student Omar Sherif writes that it is a protozoan parasite that causes amoebic dysentery, with bloody diarrhoea and belly pain.

He writes that it is spread by the bite of the sandfly, which injects the parasite into the skin. He adds that it can spread from the gut to the liver and form a liver abscess, which can cause fever and pain in the right upper abdomen.

He ends by saying that the stool shows trophozoites that have swallowed red blood cells, and that metronidazole is the treatment, followed by a drug to clear cysts from the gut. The examiner gave 8 out of 10.
h: it is spread by the bite of the sandfly, which injects the parasite into the skin

a.o: Omar says E. histolytica spreads by sandfly bites.
a.x: It spreads by swallowing cysts in dirty water.
a.w: The cysts survive outside the body and pass by the faecal-oral route. Sandflies spread Leishmania.

a.o: Omar says it can form a liver abscess with right upper pain.
a.x: Spread should be said to reach only the lungs.
a.w: Amoebae travel via the portal vein to the liver, where they form an abscess.

a.o: Omar says the trophozoites have swallowed red blood cells.
a.x: The trophozoites should never contain red cells.
a.w: Eating red cells is a key sign that separates E. histolytica from harmless amoebae.

a.o: Omar gives metronidazole, then a drug to clear gut cysts.
a.x: Treatment should be antibiotics for bacteria only.
a.w: Metronidazole kills tissue forms; a luminal agent like paromomycin clears cysts.

s:
Handout for "Tapeworms", by Dr. Sameh. Part 1 says Taenia solium is the pork tapeworm and Taenia saginata is the beef tapeworm. Eating undercooked meat with larval cysts leads to an adult worm living in the gut, often with few symptoms.

Part 2 is about cysticercosis. It says that cysts form in the brain only in people who eat undercooked pork with cysts, and never from swallowing tapeworm eggs. It adds that brain cysts (neurocysticercosis) are a common cause of fits in many countries.

Part 3 says segments of the worm can be seen in the stool, and that praziquantel or albendazole is used for treatment. It ends by saying good hygiene and well-cooked meat prevent infection.
h: cysts form in the brain only in people who eat undercooked pork with cysts, and never from swallowing tapeworm eggs

a.o: The handout says brain cysts come only from eating pork.
a.x: Cysticercosis comes from swallowed tapeworm eggs.
a.w: Eggs from a human carrier hatch in the gut and larvae spread to the brain. Eating cysts in pork gives only the adult gut worm.

a.o: The handout calls neurocysticercosis a common cause of fits.
a.x: Brain cysts should be said to cause no symptoms.
a.w: Neurocysticercosis is a leading cause of acquired epilepsy where pork tapeworm is common.

a.o: The handout says segments of the worm can be seen in the stool.
a.x: Segments should only be seen in the blood.
a.w: Gravid segments full of eggs pass out in the stool and can be seen by eye.

a.o: The handout gives praziquantel or albendazole as treatment.
a.x: Tapeworms should be treated with antiviral drugs.
a.w: These drugs kill tapeworms and their larvae, often with steroids for brain cysts.

s:
Flashcards "Childhood rashes", made by Salma for the virology block. Card 1 says measles is caused by a paramyxovirus and spreads very easily through the air, so one case can infect many people.

Card 2 says measles begins with fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes before the rash. Card 3 says Koplik spots are small white spots inside the cheek and are a sign of rubella, not measles.

Card 4 says the rash of measles starts behind the ears and spreads down the body. Card 5 says measles can lead to pneumonia and, rarely, a brain disease years later called SSPE, and that the MMR vaccine prevents it. Salma studied them on the bus home.
h: Koplik spots are small white spots inside the cheek and are a sign of rubella, not measles

a.o: Card 3 makes Koplik spots a sign of rubella, not measles.
a.x: Koplik spots are an early sign of measles.
a.w: These white spots on the inner cheek appear before the measles rash and are almost unique to it.

a.o: Card 2 lists fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes.
a.x: The rash should come before any fever or cough.
a.w: The prodrome of cough, coryza and conjunctivitis comes before the rash.

a.o: Card 4 says the rash starts behind the ears and spreads down.
a.x: The rash should start on the feet and spread up.
a.w: The measles rash typically begins at the hairline and behind the ears.

a.o: Card 5 names pneumonia and SSPE as complications.
a.x: Measles should be said to have no complications.
a.w: Pneumonia is the main cause of measles deaths; SSPE is a rare late brain disease.

s:
Practical report, clinical microbiology, student Nada Wael. The task was to learn how urine samples are collected and tested for urinary tract infection. Nada writes that the lab looks for white cells, nitrites and the number of bacteria growing on agar.

In her notes she writes that the best sample is the very first part of the urine stream, collected straight into the pot, because it contains the most bacteria from the bladder. She adds that samples should reach the lab quickly or be kept in the fridge.

In the discussion she says that E. coli is the most common cause of urinary infection, and that a growth of many colonies of a single type suggests true infection, while mixed growth suggests contamination.
h: the best sample is the very first part of the urine stream, collected straight into the pot

a.o: Nada says the best sample is the first part of the urine stream.
a.x: A midstream sample should be collected instead.
a.w: The first part of the stream washes out skin and urethral bacteria. Midstream urine better reflects the bladder.

a.o: Nada says samples should reach the lab quickly or be chilled.
a.x: Samples should be left warm for a day before testing.
a.w: At room heat bacteria keep multiplying in the pot, giving falsely high counts.

a.o: Nada names E. coli as the most common cause of urinary infection.
a.x: The most common cause should be fungi.
a.w: Gut bacteria such as E. coli climb the urethra and cause most urinary infections.

a.o: Nada says mixed growth suggests contamination.
a.x: Mixed growth should always mean true infection.
a.w: A single organism in large numbers points to infection; several types suggest skin or vaginal flora.

s:
Ward round notes, medical ward, student Hazem Ali. A 70-year-old woman has a fever of 39 degrees C, shaking chills and low blood pressure. A urine dip is positive. The team suspects sepsis from a kidney infection.

Hazem writes the plan: start IV antibiotics now, and take blood cultures two days later once the antibiotics have had time to work, so the result is easier to read. He adds that two sets of blood cultures from different sites are taken.

He also writes that fluids are given for the low blood pressure and lactate is measured. The registrar said one part of the timing was wrong but agreed antibiotics should not be delayed.
h: take blood cultures two days later once the antibiotics have had time to work, so the result is easier to read

a.o: Hazem plans blood cultures two days into antibiotics.
a.x: Cultures go in before the antibiotics.
a.w: Antibiotics quickly kill bacteria in the blood, so later cultures are often falsely negative. Draw them first, without delaying treatment.

a.o: Hazem takes two sets of blood cultures from different sites.
a.x: Only one bottle should ever be taken.
a.w: Two sets raise the chance of catching bacteria and help tell true growth from skin contamination.

a.o: Hazem gives fluids for low blood pressure.
a.x: Fluids should be withheld in sepsis.
a.w: Septic shock causes leaky, dilated vessels, so fluid is given to restore blood pressure.

a.o: Hazem measures lactate.
a.x: Lactate should not be checked in sepsis.
a.w: A high lactate shows poor tissue perfusion and helps judge how sick the patient is.

s:
Draft page "Atypical pneumonia", microbiology chapter. The page says Legionella pneumophila is a Gram-negative rod that lives in water, such as cooling towers, air conditioning systems and hot water tanks.

It states that Legionnaires' disease spreads mainly from person to person by coughing, so patients must be kept in strict isolation. It adds that patients may have high fever, confusion, diarrhoea and a low sodium level.

The page says the diagnosis is often made with a urine antigen test, and that it does not grow on ordinary agar but needs special buffered charcoal yeast extract agar. It ends by saying macrolides or quinolones are used, since beta-lactams do not work well.
h: Legionnaires' disease spreads mainly from person to person by coughing, so patients must be kept in strict isolation

a.o: The page says Legionnaires spreads person to person.
a.x: It comes from water aerosols, not people.
a.w: People inhale aerosols from contaminated water systems. Spread between people is extremely rare, so isolation is not needed.

a.o: The page names confusion, diarrhoea and low sodium as features.
a.x: These should be said to rule Legionella out.
a.w: Legionella often causes symptoms outside the lungs, including low sodium and gut upset.

a.o: The page says it grows on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar.
a.x: It should be said to grow well on blood agar.
a.w: Legionella needs iron and cysteine, supplied by BCYE agar.

a.o: The page says beta-lactams do not work well.
a.x: Penicillin should be the best treatment.
a.w: Legionella lives inside cells, where macrolides and quinolones reach it but beta-lactams do not.

s:
Handout for "Pseudomonas aeruginosa", by Dr. Hany. Part 1 says it is a Gram-negative rod that lives in water and soil, and is a common cause of hospital infections, especially in burns, ventilated patients and people with cystic fibrosis.

Part 2 says it is oxidase positive, may make a blue-green pigment and has a sweet, grape-like smell on agar. The handout then says Pseudomonas is a strict anaerobe that cannot grow in air, which is why it is found mostly in deep wounds.

Part 3 says Pseudomonas is naturally resistant to many antibiotics, and that drugs such as piperacillin-tazobactam, ceftazidime or ciprofloxacin may be used. It ends by saying hospital sinks and taps can be a source.
h: Pseudomonas is a strict anaerobe that cannot grow in air

a.o: The handout calls Pseudomonas a strict anaerobe, unable to use air.
a.x: Pseudomonas is an aerobe and grows well in air.
a.w: It is an obligate aerobe that uses oxygen, which fits its life in water, on wet surfaces and in lungs.

a.o: The handout says it is oxidase positive with a blue-green pigment.
a.x: It should be oxidase negative with no pigment.
a.w: Pyocyanin gives the blue-green colour, and a positive oxidase helps identify it.

a.o: The handout says it is naturally resistant to many antibiotics.
a.x: It should be said to respond to every antibiotic.
a.w: Its outer membrane lets few drugs in and its pumps push many out.

a.o: The handout names sinks and taps as a hospital source.
a.x: Hospital water should be called a sterile source.
a.w: Pseudomonas forms biofilms in wet places such as drains, sinks and taps.

s:
Flashcards "Normal flora", made by Rana for the microbiology quiz. Card 1 says normal flora are microbes that live on the body without causing disease and help keep harmful germs out.

Card 2 says the skin is mostly covered by Staphylococcus epidermidis. Card 3 says the healthy vagina is dominated by Lactobacillus, which keeps the pH high and alkaline, around 8, so harmful bacteria cannot grow.

Card 4 says the large bowel holds the most bacteria in the body, mostly anaerobes such as Bacteroides. Card 5 says antibiotics can upset normal flora and lead to thrush or C. difficile diarrhoea. Rana added a drawing of the gut beside card 4.
h: Lactobacillus, which keeps the pH high and alkaline, around 8

a.o: Card 3 says Lactobacillus keeps vaginal pH near 8.
a.x: Lactobacillus keeps vaginal pH acidic, under 4.5.
a.w: Lactobacilli make lactic acid from glycogen, and this acid stops many harmful microbes from growing.

a.o: Card 2 says the skin is mostly covered by S. epidermidis.
a.x: The skin should be covered mostly by E. coli.
a.w: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are the main bacteria on healthy skin.

a.o: Card 4 says the large bowel holds mostly anaerobes.
a.x: The bowel should hold mostly aerobic bacteria.
a.w: The colon has little oxygen, so anaerobes like Bacteroides far outnumber aerobes.

a.o: Card 5 says antibiotics can lead to thrush or C. difficile.
a.x: Antibiotics should be said to protect normal flora.
a.w: Killing normal flora lets Candida or C. difficile overgrow.

s:
Short-answer exam, virology, question 5: "Describe rabies." Student Ali Mahmoud writes that rabies is caused by a bullet-shaped RNA virus spread mostly by the bite of an infected dog.

He writes that the virus travels to the brain along nerves, and that once symptoms such as fear of water and confusion begin, the disease is almost always fatal. He adds that after a bite, nothing can be done until symptoms appear, because vaccines only work before exposure.

He ends by saying the wound should be washed well with soap and water, and that the incubation period can be weeks to months, longer for bites far from the head. The examiner gave 6 out of 10.
h: after a bite, nothing can be done until symptoms appear, because vaccines only work before exposure

a.o: Ali says nothing can be done until symptoms start.
a.x: Vaccine and immunoglobulin go in right away.
a.w: The long incubation gives time for post-exposure vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin to stop the virus before it reaches the brain.

a.o: Ali says the virus travels to the brain along nerves.
a.x: The virus should travel to the brain in the blood.
a.w: Rabies virus moves slowly up peripheral nerves towards the central nervous system.

a.o: Ali says the wound should be washed well with soap and water.
a.x: The wound should be left unwashed.
a.w: Thorough washing removes much of the virus and lowers the risk of infection.

a.o: Ali says incubation is longer for bites far from the head.
a.x: Bites on the foot should act fastest.
a.w: The virus has a longer nerve journey from distant bites, so symptoms appear later.

s:
Handout for "Schistosomiasis", by Dr. Waleed. Part 1 says Schistosoma are blood flukes. Schistosoma haematobium lives in veins around the bladder and causes blood in the urine, while Schistosoma mansoni affects the gut and liver.

Part 2 says people are infected when they eat raw fish that carries the larvae, and that freshwater snails play no part in the life cycle. It adds that the eggs, not the adult worms, cause most of the damage by triggering inflammation and scarring.

Part 3 says long-term S. haematobium infection is linked with squamous cell cancer of the bladder, and that praziquantel is the treatment. It notes the disease was once very common among farmers along the Nile.
h: people are infected when they eat raw fish that carries the larvae, and that freshwater snails play no part in the life cycle

a.o: The handout says raw fish, not snails, spread it.
a.x: Larvae from snails go through skin in fresh water.
a.w: Snails release cercariae into fresh water, which burrow through the skin of people wading or swimming in it.

a.o: The handout says the eggs cause most of the damage.
a.x: The adult worms should cause all the damage.
a.w: Eggs stuck in tissue trigger granulomas, fibrosis and scarring of the bladder or liver.

a.o: The handout links S. haematobium with bladder squamous cancer.
a.x: It should be linked with brain cancer.
a.w: Chronic inflammation in the bladder wall raises the risk of squamous cell carcinoma.

a.o: The handout gives praziquantel as the treatment.
a.x: Schistosomiasis should be treated with antibiotics.
a.w: Praziquantel kills adult worms and is used in mass treatment campaigns.

s:
Histology lab notes, lung slide, student Mariam Essam. Under low power the lung looks like lace, made of thin-walled air sacs (alveoli) with small blood vessels between them. Larger airways with cartilage and glands are seen near the edge of the slide.

Under high power I noted two types of cells lining the alveoli. I wrote that type I pneumocytes are the round cells that make surfactant, while type II pneumocytes are the flat cells that cover most of the surface for gas exchange.

I also saw alveolar macrophages, called dust cells, inside the air spaces, some with dark specks of carbon inside. At the end I noted that the barrier between air and blood is very thin, which helps oxygen pass quickly. The tutor put a mark beside one line.
h: type I pneumocytes are the round cells that make surfactant, while type II pneumocytes are the flat cells

a.o: Mariam swaps the jobs of type I and type II cells.
a.x: Type II cells, not type I, make surfactant.
a.w: Thin type I cells cover about 95% of the alveolar surface for gas exchange. Cube-shaped type II cells make surfactant and can replace type I cells.

a.o: Mariam calls the alveolar macrophages dust cells.
a.x: These cells should be called goblet cells.
a.w: Alveolar macrophages eat inhaled particles like carbon, so they are nicknamed dust cells.

a.o: Mariam says larger airways have cartilage and glands.
a.x: Cartilage should be found in the alveolar walls.
a.w: Cartilage and glands are found in the bronchi and fade out in the smaller airways.

a.o: Mariam notes the air-blood barrier is very thin.
a.x: The barrier should be described as thick.
a.w: A thin barrier keeps the distance for diffusion short, so gases cross quickly.

s:
Flashcards "Skin", made by Hossam for the histology block. Card 1 says skin has three layers: the epidermis on top, the dermis below it, and the fatty hypodermis at the bottom.

Card 2 says the epidermis is a simple columnar epithelium, one cell thick, with no keratin. Card 3 says the dermis is made of connective tissue with collagen, blood vessels, nerves, hair follicles and sweat glands.

Card 4 says the epidermis has no blood vessels and gets its food from the dermis below. Card 5 says the deepest layer of the epidermis, the stratum basale, is where new cells are made by dividing. Hossam coloured each layer on a drawing beside the cards.
h: the epidermis is a simple columnar epithelium, one cell thick, with no keratin

a.o: Card 2 calls the epidermis simple columnar, with no keratin.
a.x: The epidermis is keratinised stratified squamous.
a.w: Many layers of cells, with a tough keratin layer on top, protect the body from damage, germs and water loss.

a.o: Card 3 lists collagen, vessels, nerves and glands in the dermis.
a.x: The dermis should be made only of epithelium.
a.w: The dermis is connective tissue that holds the skin's vessels, nerves and glands.

a.o: Card 4 says the epidermis has no blood vessels.
a.x: The epidermis should have its own capillaries.
a.w: Epithelia are avascular and get nutrients by diffusion from the dermis.

a.o: Card 5 says new cells are made in the stratum basale.
a.x: New cells should be made in the top layer.
a.w: Basal stem cells divide and push daughter cells up towards the surface.

s:
Short-answer exam, histology, question 2: "Describe the wall of the urinary bladder." Student Youssef Adel writes that the bladder has a mucosa, a thick muscle layer called the detrusor, and an outer adventitia or serosa.

He writes that the bladder is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium, which allows it to stretch when full. He adds that the detrusor muscle is smooth muscle arranged in layers, and that it contracts to empty the bladder.

He ends by saying that the mucosa forms folds when the bladder is empty, which flatten out as it fills, and that the top cells, called umbrella cells, help stop urine leaking into the tissue. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the bladder is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium, which allows it to stretch when full

a.o: Youssef says simple cuboidal epithelium lines the bladder.
a.x: Transitional epithelium lines the bladder.
a.w: Urothelium has several layers whose cells change shape from round to flat as the bladder fills, so it can stretch.

a.o: Youssef calls the detrusor smooth muscle that empties the bladder.
a.x: The detrusor should be called skeletal muscle.
a.w: The detrusor is smooth muscle under autonomic control that contracts to void.

a.o: Youssef says the mucosa folds when the bladder is empty.
a.x: The mucosa should stay flat at all times.
a.w: Folds (rugae) let the wall expand, and they flatten out as urine fills it.

a.o: Youssef says umbrella cells stop urine leaking into tissue.
a.x: Umbrella cells should be said to absorb urine.
a.w: Thick plaques in umbrella cell membranes make a tight barrier against urine.

s:
Handout for "The airway", histology, by Dr. Nermeen. Part 1 says the trachea is held open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, with the open part at the back closed by the trachealis muscle.

Part 2 says the trachea is lined by stratified squamous epithelium, the same as the skin, with no cilia and no goblet cells. It adds that the airway lining traps dust and germs in a layer of mucus.

Part 3 says that smoking damages the airway lining and its defence system, and that the submucosa contains seromucous glands. It ends by saying the trachea divides into the two main bronchi at the level of the carina.
h: the trachea is lined by stratified squamous epithelium, the same as the skin, with no cilia and no goblet cells

a.o: The handout gives the trachea a skin-like lining.
a.x: It has a ciliated pseudostratified lining.
a.w: Goblet cells make mucus and the cilia beat it up towards the throat, the mucociliary escalator that clears trapped dust.

a.o: The handout says C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings hold it open.
a.x: The rings should be made of elastic cartilage.
a.w: Hyaline C-rings keep the trachea open while letting the oesophagus bulge at the back.

a.o: The handout says the submucosa has seromucous glands.
a.x: The trachea should have no glands in its wall.
a.w: Submucosal glands add mucus and watery fluid to the airway lining.

a.o: The handout says it divides into two bronchi at the carina.
a.x: It should divide high up in the neck.
a.w: The trachea splits into right and left main bronchi at the carina.

s:
Histology lab notes, gut slides, student Rawan Tarek. The first slide was the oesophagus. Its wall has four layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa and adventitia. The lumen looks folded when empty, and the slide was stained with H&E.

I wrote that the oesophagus is lined by keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, with a dead keratin layer on top like the skin. I also noted mucous glands in the submucosa, which help food slide down.

I noted that the muscle in the upper third is skeletal, the middle third is mixed and the lower third is smooth muscle. At the end I drew the change to simple columnar epithelium where the oesophagus meets the stomach.
h: the oesophagus is lined by keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, with a dead keratin layer on top

a.o: Rawan says the oesophagus has a keratinised lining like the skin.
a.x: Its squamous lining is non-keratinised.
a.w: The many layers resist rubbing by food, but the surface stays moist and alive, with no dead keratin layer.

a.o: Rawan notes mucous glands in the submucosa.
a.x: The submucosa should hold no glands.
a.w: Oesophageal glands make mucus that lubricates the passage of food.

a.o: Rawan says the upper third is skeletal and the lower third smooth.
a.x: All of it should be skeletal muscle.
a.w: Swallowing starts under voluntary control, then smooth muscle takes over lower down.

a.o: Rawan draws a change to simple columnar epithelium at the stomach.
a.x: The lining should stay squamous into the stomach.
a.w: The junction shows a sharp change from squamous to the columnar lining of the stomach.

s:
Draft page "Small intestine", histology chapter. The page says the small intestine has circular folds (plicae), finger-like villi and microvilli on the surface cells, which together give a huge area for absorption. A diagram shows each part of the wall.

It states that Brunner's glands in the submucosa are found mainly in the ileum, where they make acid to help digest food. It adds that the ileum has large clusters of lymph tissue called Peyer's patches.

The page says Paneth cells at the base of the crypts make antimicrobial proteins such as lysozyme and defensins. It ends by saying goblet cells are spread along the villi and increase in number towards the colon.
h: Brunner's glands in the submucosa are found mainly in the ileum, where they make acid

a.o: The page puts acid-making Brunner's glands in the ileum.
a.x: They lie in the duodenum and make alkaline mucus.
a.w: Their alkaline secretion neutralises acid entering from the stomach, protecting the duodenal lining. They help identify the duodenum on a slide.

a.o: The page says the ileum has Peyer's patches.
a.x: Peyer's patches should be in the oesophagus.
a.w: Peyer's patches are lymphoid follicles in the ileum that sample gut antigens.

a.o: The page says Paneth cells make lysozyme and defensins.
a.x: Paneth cells should be said to make bile.
a.w: Paneth cells guard the crypt stem cells with antimicrobial proteins.

a.o: The page says goblet cells increase towards the colon.
a.x: Goblet cells should vanish towards the colon.
a.w: More mucus is needed as the stool gets firmer, so goblet cells rise down the gut.

s:
Histology lab notebook, student Ahmed Samy. Today we compared the small intestine and the colon. The tutor told us to look for features that let us tell them apart on a slide.

I wrote that the colon has long villi like the small intestine, and that its crypts are shallow with very few goblet cells. I noted that the outer muscle layer of the colon is gathered into three bands called taeniae coli.

At the end I wrote that the colon's main job is to absorb water and salts, and that its lining is simple columnar epithelium. I added that the small intestine has Paneth cells at the bottom of its crypts.
h: the colon has long villi like the small intestine, and that its crypts are shallow with very few goblet cells

a.o: Ahmed gives the colon villi and few goblet cells.
a.x: The colon has no villi and many goblets.
a.w: The colon has straight, deep crypts full of goblet cells, which make mucus for passing firm stool. Villi are a small bowel feature.

a.o: Ahmed notes the outer muscle forms three taeniae coli.
a.x: The muscle should form one complete sheet.
a.w: The outer longitudinal muscle of the colon gathers into three bands.

a.o: Ahmed says the colon absorbs water and salts.
a.x: The colon should mainly absorb protein.
a.w: Most nutrients are taken up earlier; the colon mostly recovers water and electrolytes.

a.o: Ahmed says the small intestine has Paneth cells.
a.x: Paneth cells should be found in the stomach.
a.w: Paneth cells sit at the base of small bowel crypts.

s:
Handout for "The liver lobule", histology, by Dr. Ihab. Part 1 says the classic lobule is a hexagon with a central vein in the middle and portal triads at the corners. Each portal triad holds a branch of the portal vein, the hepatic artery and a bile duct.

Part 2 describes the zones of the acinus. It says blood flows from the portal triads to the central vein. It then states that zone 1, near the central vein, gets the least oxygen and is the first to die when blood flow drops, while zone 3 near the triads gets the most oxygen.

Part 3 says that Kupffer cells, the liver's macrophages, line the sinusoids, and that bile flows the opposite way to blood, towards the portal triads.
h: zone 1, near the central vein, gets the least oxygen and is the first to die when blood flow drops, while zone 3 near the triads

a.o: The handout puts zone 1 by the central vein and zone 3 by the triads.
a.x: Zone 3, not zone 1, lies by the central vein.
a.w: Blood enters at the triads, so zone 1 gets the most oxygen. Zone 3 around the central vein is hit first by low blood flow.

a.o: The handout says each triad has a portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct.
a.x: The triad should hold the central vein.
a.w: The triad brings in blood from the portal vein and hepatic artery and drains bile out.

a.o: The handout says Kupffer cells line the sinusoids.
a.x: Kupffer cells should be in the bile ducts.
a.w: Kupffer cells sit in the sinusoids and eat bacteria and old red cells.

a.o: The handout says bile flows opposite to blood.
a.x: Bile should flow towards the central vein.
a.w: Bile moves from hepatocytes towards the triads, against the flow of blood.

s:
Histology lab notes, kidney slide, student Malak Said. Under low power I saw the outer cortex with round glomeruli and the inner medulla with straight tubules. Each glomerulus is a tuft of capillaries inside Bowman's capsule.

I wrote that the inner layer of Bowman's capsule is made of podocytes, cells with foot processes that wrap the capillaries. I noted that the distal convoluted tubule has a tall brush border of microvilli and pink cytoplasm, while the proximal tubule has a clear lumen and no brush border.

At the end I noted the juxtaglomerular cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole, which release renin. The tutor asked me to look again at the tubules.
h: the distal convoluted tubule has a tall brush border of microvilli and pink cytoplasm, while the proximal tubule has a clear lumen

a.o: Malak gives the brush border to the distal tubule.
a.x: The proximal tubule has the brush border.
a.w: The PCT reabsorbs most filtered water and solutes, so it has many microvilli and mitochondria. The DCT has a clearer lumen.

a.o: Malak says podocytes line the inner layer of Bowman's capsule.
a.x: Podocytes should line the collecting ducts.
a.w: Podocyte foot processes form filtration slits around glomerular capillaries.

a.o: Malak says glomeruli lie in the cortex.
a.x: Glomeruli should be found in the medulla.
a.w: Renal corpuscles are in the cortex; the medulla holds loops and collecting ducts.

a.o: Malak says juxtaglomerular cells release renin.
a.x: These cells should release insulin.
a.w: JG cells in the afferent arteriole sense pressure and release renin.

s:
Short-answer exam, histology, question 4: "Compare the three types of muscle." Student Farah Hamed writes that skeletal muscle has long cells with many nuclei at the edge and clear striations.

She writes that cardiac muscle cells are branched, joined by intercalated discs, and have many nuclei pushed to the edge of the cell, just like skeletal muscle. She adds that smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped with one central nucleus and no striations.

She ends by saying that intercalated discs contain gap junctions, so the heart cells contract together, and that skeletal muscle is under voluntary control. She also drew a labelled sketch of each type. The examiner gave 8 out of 10.
h: cardiac muscle cells are branched, joined by intercalated discs, and have many nuclei pushed to the edge of the cell

a.o: Farah gives cardiac cells many edge nuclei.
a.x: Cardiac cells have central nuclei only.
a.w: Unlike skeletal fibres, each heart muscle cell is short and branched with a centrally placed nucleus.

a.o: Farah says smooth muscle has one central nucleus.
a.x: Smooth muscle should have many edge nuclei.
a.w: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped with a single central nucleus.

a.o: Farah says intercalated discs contain gap junctions.
a.x: The discs should block all contact.
a.w: Gap junctions let ions pass, so the heart beats as one unit.

a.o: Farah says skeletal muscle is under voluntary control.
a.x: Skeletal muscle should be involuntary.
a.w: Skeletal muscle is controlled by somatic motor nerves.

s:
Flashcards "Smooth muscle", made by Kareem for the tissues quiz. Card 1 says smooth muscle is found in the walls of hollow organs such as the gut, bladder, uterus and blood vessels.

Card 2 says smooth muscle shows clear cross striations like skeletal muscle, because its actin and myosin are lined up in sarcomeres. Card 3 says smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped with a single central nucleus.

Card 4 says smooth muscle contracts slowly and can stay contracted for a long time with little energy. Card 5 says it is controlled by the autonomic nervous system and hormones, not by will. Kareem drew a vessel wall on the back of card 1.
h: smooth muscle shows clear cross striations like skeletal muscle, because its actin and myosin are lined up in sarcomeres

a.o: Card 2 says smooth muscle has striations and sarcomeres.
a.x: Smooth muscle has no striations.
a.w: Its actin and myosin run in a criss-cross net anchored to dense bodies, so no bands are seen.

a.o: Card 3 says the cells are spindle-shaped with one nucleus.
a.x: The cells should be long with many nuclei.
a.w: Smooth muscle cells taper at both ends with a single central nucleus.

a.o: Card 4 says it can stay contracted with little energy.
a.x: It should tire within seconds.
a.w: The latch state lets smooth muscle hold tone for long periods cheaply.

a.o: Card 5 says it is controlled by autonomic nerves and hormones.
a.x: It should be under voluntary control.
a.w: Gut and vessel walls work without conscious control.

s:
Handout for "Nervous tissue", by Dr. Sherif. Part 1 says neurons carry signals, while glial cells support them. Glial cells cannot fire signals, outnumber neurons and include astrocytes, microglia and the cells that make myelin.

Part 2 says myelin is a fatty wrapping that speeds up nerve signals. The handout then states that Schwann cells make myelin in the brain and spinal cord, while oligodendrocytes make myelin in the peripheral nerves, each wrapping just one axon.

Part 3 says that the gaps in myelin are called nodes of Ranvier, where the signal jumps along. It adds that microglia are the brain's immune cells and that astrocytes help form the blood-brain barrier.
h: Schwann cells make myelin in the brain and spinal cord, while oligodendrocytes make myelin in the peripheral nerves

a.o: The handout swaps Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes.
a.x: Oligodendrocytes myelinate the CNS.
a.w: One oligodendrocyte myelinates many CNS axons. Each Schwann cell wraps one segment of one peripheral axon.

a.o: The handout says signals jump between nodes of Ranvier.
a.x: Signals should travel only under the myelin.
a.w: Saltatory conduction lets the impulse skip from node to node, which is faster.

a.o: The handout calls microglia the brain's immune cells.
a.x: Microglia should be said to make myelin.
a.w: Microglia come from the same line as macrophages and clear debris and germs.

a.o: The handout says astrocytes help form the blood-brain barrier.
a.x: Astrocytes should be said to carry signals.
a.w: Astrocyte end-feet surround brain capillaries and support tight junctions.

s:
Practical report, bone slide, student Aya Hossam. The aim was to identify the cells and structures of compact bone. Aya writes that compact bone is made of osteons, each with a central canal surrounded by rings of bone called lamellae.

She writes that osteoclasts are the cells that lay down new bone matrix, and osteoblasts are the large cells with many nuclei that break bone down. She adds that osteocytes sit in small spaces called lacunae and talk to each other through tiny channels.

In the discussion she says the bone matrix is made of type I collagen hardened with calcium phosphate crystals, and that bone is constantly being remodelled throughout life.
h: osteoclasts are the cells that lay down new bone matrix, and osteoblasts are the large cells with many nuclei that break bone down

a.o: Aya swaps the jobs of osteoclasts and osteoblasts.
a.x: Osteoblasts build bone; osteoclasts resorb.
a.w: Osteoblasts lay down new matrix. Osteoclasts are big cells with many nuclei, formed from monocytes, that dissolve bone.

a.o: Aya says osteocytes sit in lacunae.
a.x: Osteocytes should sit in the central canal.
a.w: Osteocytes are trapped osteoblasts in lacunae linked by canaliculi.

a.o: Aya says the matrix is type I collagen with calcium phosphate.
a.x: The matrix should be type II collagen alone.
a.w: Type I collagen gives strength to bend; hydroxyapatite crystals give hardness.

a.o: Aya says bone is remodelled throughout life.
a.x: Bone should stop changing after childhood.
a.w: Bone is broken down and rebuilt all the time in response to load and hormones.

s:
Histology lab notes, ground bone slide, student Bassel Amr. The ground section shows compact bone as many round units called osteons, packed tightly together, like the rings of many small tree trunks. Between them are older bits of lamellae called interstitial lamellae.

I wrote that each osteon has a Volkmann canal running down its centre, along the length of the bone, carrying blood vessels and nerves. I added that Haversian canals run across the bone at right angles and link the osteons with each other.

At the end I noted dark spaces called lacunae arranged in rings, with fine lines (canaliculi) joining them, and that the outer surface of the bone is covered by periosteum.
h: each osteon has a Volkmann canal running down its centre, along the length of the bone, carrying blood vessels and nerves

a.o: Bassel swaps the Volkmann and Haversian canals.
a.x: The central canal is the Haversian canal.
a.w: Haversian canals run lengthways in the middle of each osteon. Volkmann canals cross at right angles to join them.

a.o: Bassel notes interstitial lamellae between osteons.
a.x: These lamellae should be in the marrow.
a.w: Interstitial lamellae are leftovers of older osteons after remodelling.

a.o: Bassel sees canaliculi joining the lacunae.
a.x: The lacunae should have no links.
a.w: Canaliculi carry osteocyte processes and let nutrients pass between cells.

a.o: Bassel says periosteum covers the outer surface.
a.x: The outer surface should be covered by cartilage.
a.w: The periosteum is a tough sheet with bone-forming cells, except at joint surfaces.

s:
Flashcards "Cartilage", made by Lina for the tissues quiz. Card 1 says cartilage is a firm, smooth connective tissue made of cells called chondrocytes sitting in spaces (lacunae) inside a rubbery matrix.

Card 2 says hyaline cartilage is the most common type and covers the ends of bones at joints. Card 3 says the outer ear and the epiglottis are made of fibrocartilage, which is why they are very stiff and do not bend.

Card 4 says fibrocartilage is found in the intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis, where it resists strong pulling and pressure. Card 5 says cartilage is covered by perichondrium, except at joint surfaces. Lina used a different colour pen for each type of cartilage.
h: the outer ear and the epiglottis are made of fibrocartilage, which is why they are very stiff and do not bend

a.o: Card 3 makes the ear and epiglottis stiff fibrocartilage.
a.x: The ear and epiglottis are flexible elastic cartilage.
a.w: Elastic fibres let the outer ear and epiglottis bend and spring back into shape.

a.o: Card 2 says hyaline cartilage covers joint surfaces.
a.x: Joint surfaces should be covered by elastic cartilage.
a.w: Smooth hyaline cartilage lowers friction where bones move against each other.

a.o: Card 4 puts fibrocartilage in discs and the pubic symphysis.
a.x: Fibrocartilage should be found mainly in the outer ear.
a.w: Thick type I collagen bundles in fibrocartilage resist pulling and squeezing.

a.o: Card 5 says joint surfaces have no perichondrium.
a.x: Joint cartilage should be fully covered by perichondrium.
a.w: Articular cartilage faces the joint space with no perichondrium over it.

s:
Short-answer exam, histology, question 6: "Why does cartilage heal poorly?" Student Hadi Mostafa writes that cartilage is made of chondrocytes inside a matrix of collagen and proteoglycans, which hold a lot of water and make it resist pressure.

He writes that cartilage has a rich network of capillaries running through its matrix, so its poor healing must be due to the cells being old. He adds that mature chondrocytes divide very little.

He ends by saying that a damaged joint surface often heals with weaker fibrocartilage instead of hyaline cartilage, and that the matrix of hyaline cartilage is mostly type II collagen. He also drew the knee joint. The examiner gave 6 out of 10.
h: cartilage has a rich network of capillaries running through its matrix

a.o: Hadi says cartilage has a rich capillary network.
a.x: Cartilage has no blood vessels in its matrix.
a.w: Chondrocytes get food by slow diffusion from the perichondrium or joint fluid, which is a key reason cartilage heals poorly.

a.o: Hadi says mature chondrocytes divide very little.
a.x: Mature chondrocytes should divide very fast.
a.w: Adult chondrocytes are trapped in matrix and have little power to multiply.

a.o: Hadi says damaged joint surfaces heal with fibrocartilage.
a.x: They should heal with new hyaline cartilage.
a.w: Repair tissue is fibrous and weaker than the original hyaline cartilage.

a.o: Hadi says hyaline cartilage is mostly type II collagen.
a.x: Hyaline cartilage should be mostly type I collagen.
a.w: Type II collagen forms fine fibrils that hold proteoglycans in hyaline cartilage.

s:
Haematology lab notebook, student Nada Ehab. Today we looked at a blood film stained with Leishman stain and counted 100 white cells. Most were neutrophils, followed by lymphocytes and monocytes, which matched a normal adult film.

I wrote that neutrophils have a nucleus with 3 to 5 lobes and large bright red-orange granules, while eosinophils have pale, very fine granules and many lobes. I noted only a few eosinophils and one basophil.

I described lymphocytes as small round cells with a large dark nucleus and little cytoplasm, and monocytes as the largest white cells with a kidney-shaped nucleus. At the end I noted platelets as small purple fragments with no nucleus.
h: neutrophils have a nucleus with 3 to 5 lobes and large bright red-orange granules, while eosinophils have pale, very fine granules

a.o: Nada gives the red-orange granules to neutrophils.
a.x: Eosinophils have the red-orange granules.
a.w: Eosinophils have a two-lobed nucleus and large orange-red granules. Neutrophil granules are fine and pale.

a.o: Nada describes lymphocytes with a large dark nucleus.
a.x: Lymphocytes should have a many-lobed nucleus.
a.w: Small lymphocytes have a round dark nucleus with only a thin rim of cytoplasm.

a.o: Nada calls monocytes the largest white cells.
a.x: Monocytes should be called the smallest white cells.
a.w: Monocytes are the biggest white cells, with a folded, kidney-shaped nucleus.

a.o: Nada notes platelets as purple fragments with no nucleus.
a.x: Platelets should each contain a large nucleus.
a.w: Platelets are cell pieces broken off megakaryocytes, so they have no nucleus.

s:
Draft page "Red blood cells", histology chapter. The page says red cells are the most common cells in the blood and carry oxygen bound to haemoglobin. In a film they look like pink discs with a paler centre.

It states that mature human red cells have a large central nucleus, which can be seen as a dark spot in the pale middle of each cell. It adds that red cells are shaped like discs that are thinner in the middle, which helps gas exchange.

The page says that red cells live about 120 days and are removed by macrophages in the spleen. It ends by saying that young red cells called reticulocytes still contain some RNA and make up about 1% of red cells.
h: mature human red cells have a large central nucleus, which can be seen as a dark spot in the pale middle

a.o: The page gives mature red cells a central nucleus.
a.x: Mature human red cells have no nucleus at all.
a.w: Red cells lose their nucleus before entering the blood, which leaves more room for haemoglobin. The pale centre is just thinner cell.

a.o: The page says red cells live about 120 days.
a.x: Red cells should be said to live a few hours.
a.w: Red cells survive about four months before spleen macrophages remove them.

a.o: The page says the disc shape helps gas exchange.
a.x: The disc shape should be said to slow gas exchange.
a.w: A biconcave disc has a large surface for its volume and bends through capillaries.

a.o: The page says reticulocytes still contain some RNA.
a.x: Reticulocytes should be said to contain a nucleus.
a.w: Young red cells keep leftover RNA for a day or two, seen with special stains.

s:
Histology lab notes, lymph node slide, student Tamer Fouad. The node is bean-shaped with a thin capsule, and a dent called the hilum on one side. Under low power I could see the outer cortex, a deeper paracortex and a central medulla.

I wrote that the round follicles in the outer cortex are full of T cells, and that the paracortex is mainly B cells. I noted some follicles had pale germinal centres where cells were dividing.

I noted the medulla had cords of cells, including plasma cells, with sinuses between them. The slide was clear. At the end I wrote that lymph enters through afferent vessels on the convex surface and leaves through an efferent vessel at the hilum.
h: the round follicles in the outer cortex are full of T cells, and that the paracortex is mainly B cells

a.o: Tamer swaps the T cell and B cell zones of the node.
a.x: B cells fill follicles; T cells, the paracortex.
a.w: B cells gather in follicles and form germinal centres. T cells meet antigen-presenting cells in the paracortex.

a.o: Tamer notes pale germinal centres in some follicles.
a.x: Germinal centres should be dark and inactive.
a.w: Germinal centres are pale areas where activated B cells divide and mature.

a.o: Tamer finds plasma cells in the medullary cords.
a.x: Plasma cells should be found only in the capsule.
a.w: Antibody-making plasma cells collect in the medullary cords.

a.o: Tamer says lymph leaves through the efferent vessel at the hilum.
a.x: Lymph should leave through the afferent vessels.
a.w: Lymph enters at the convex side and drains out of the hilum.

s:
Handout for "The spleen", histology, by Dr. Samar. Part 1 says the spleen is the largest lymphoid organ and has a capsule with trabeculae running inward. Its tissue is divided into red pulp and white pulp.

Part 2 says the white pulp is made of blood-filled sinusoids and cords where old and damaged red cells are trapped and removed. It says the red pulp is lymphoid tissue around the central arterioles, with the T cell sheath (PALS) and B cell follicles.

Part 3 says that people without a spleen are at higher risk of infection with encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, so they are vaccinated. It ends by saying the spleen can store platelets.
h: the white pulp is made of blood-filled sinusoids and cords where old and damaged red cells are trapped and removed. It says the red pulp is lymphoid tissue

a.o: The handout swaps the roles of red and white pulp.
a.x: Red pulp, not white, filters old red cells.
a.w: Red pulp sinusoids and cords trap and remove old red cells. White pulp is lymphoid tissue around central arterioles.

a.o: The handout says people without a spleen risk encapsulated bacteria.
a.x: They should be at no extra risk of infection.
a.w: The spleen clears coated bacteria and makes antibodies to their capsules.

a.o: The handout says the spleen has a capsule with trabeculae.
a.x: The spleen should have no capsule at all.
a.w: A connective tissue capsule sends trabeculae inward that carry vessels.

a.o: The handout says the spleen can store platelets.
a.x: The spleen should be said to destroy all platelets.
a.w: About a third of the body's platelets are held in the spleen.

s:
Flashcards "Thymus", made by Omar for the immunology and histology quiz. Card 1 says the thymus sits in the upper chest behind the sternum and is largest in childhood, then slowly turns to fat.

Omar made the cards from the lecture slides. Card 2 says the thymus is where T cells mature and learn not to attack the body's own cells. Card 3 says each lobule has a dark outer cortex packed with young T cells and a paler inner medulla.

Card 4 says Hassall's corpuscles are found in the cortex and are the main feature that tells it apart from the medulla. Card 5 says that most young T cells die in the thymus during selection, so only a few leave. Omar put a star beside card 2.
h: Hassall's corpuscles are found in the cortex and are the main feature that tells it apart from the medulla

a.o: Card 4 puts Hassall's corpuscles in the cortex.
a.x: Hassall's corpuscles are in the medulla.
a.w: These rings of flattened epithelial cells are found in the pale medulla and are a key sign of thymus on a slide.

a.o: Card 2 says T cells mature in the thymus.
a.x: T cells should be said to mature in the liver.
a.w: Thymic selection keeps useful T cells and removes self-reacting ones.

a.o: Card 3 says the cortex is dark and packed with young T cells.
a.x: The cortex should be the pale part.
a.w: Densely packed young T cells make the cortex stain darker than the medulla.

a.o: Card 5 says most young T cells die during selection.
a.x: Almost all T cells should survive.
a.w: Most thymocytes fail selection and die by apoptosis.

s:
Short-answer exam, histology, question 7: "Describe the thyroid gland." Student Reem Gamal writes that the thyroid is made of many round follicles lined by cuboidal cells and filled with pink colloid.

She writes that the colloid stores thyroglobulin, from which thyroid hormones are made. She adds that the parafollicular C cells, found between the follicles, make most of the thyroxine (T4) in the body.

She notes the gland sits in front of the trachea, below the larynx, and has two lobes joined by an isthmus. She ends by saying the follicle cells become taller when the gland is very active, and that TSH from the pituitary drives the gland. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the parafollicular C cells, found between the follicles, make most of the thyroxine (T4) in the body

a.o: Reem says C cells make most of the body's thyroxine.
a.x: C cells make calcitonin, not thyroxine.
a.w: Follicle cells make T4 and T3 from thyroglobulin. Parafollicular C cells make calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium.

a.o: Reem says colloid stores thyroglobulin.
a.x: The colloid should store insulin.
a.w: Thyroglobulin in colloid holds the iodinated tyrosines used to make hormone.

a.o: Reem says follicle cells get taller when the gland is active.
a.x: Active follicle cells should become flat.
a.w: Busy follicle cells grow tall and colloid shrinks as hormone is released.

a.o: Reem says TSH from the pituitary drives the gland.
a.x: The gland should be driven by insulin.
a.w: TSH binds follicle cells and boosts hormone making and release.

s:
Draft page "Adrenal gland", histology chapter. The page says the adrenal has an outer cortex and an inner medulla. The cortex has three zones: zona glomerulosa on the outside, zona fasciculata in the middle and zona reticularis on the inside.

It states that the zona glomerulosa makes cortisol, the zona fasciculata makes aldosterone, and the zona reticularis makes sex hormones (androgens). It adds that the fasciculata cells are pale and foamy because they are full of lipid droplets.

The page says the medulla is made of chromaffin cells that release adrenaline and noradrenaline when sympathetic nerves fire. It ends by saying the cortex is driven mostly by ACTH, except for aldosterone.
h: the zona glomerulosa makes cortisol, the zona fasciculata makes aldosterone

a.o: The page swaps the glomerulosa and fasciculata roles.
a.x: The outer glomerulosa makes aldosterone.
a.w: The outer glomerulosa makes aldosterone under angiotensin II. The middle fasciculata makes cortisol under ACTH.

a.o: The page says fasciculata cells look pale and foamy.
a.x: These cells should look dark and solid.
a.w: Lipid droplets of cholesterol for steroid making wash out, leaving pale cells.

a.o: The page says chromaffin cells release adrenaline.
a.x: The medulla should release cortisol.
a.w: Medullary chromaffin cells are modified sympathetic neurons.

a.o: The page says aldosterone is not mainly driven by ACTH.
a.x: Aldosterone should depend mostly on ACTH.
a.w: Angiotensin II and potassium are the main drivers of aldosterone.

s:
Histology lab notes, pancreas slide, student Ziad Hesham. The slide was stained with H&E. Most of the pancreas is made of exocrine acini, which make digestive enzymes and stain dark purple at the base and pink at the top.

Scattered among the acini I saw pale round islands, the islets of Langerhans. I wrote that alpha cells are the most common islet cells and make insulin, while beta cells make glucagon. I also noted delta cells, which make somatostatin.

At the end I wrote that the islets are the endocrine part of the pancreas and release their hormones straight into the blood, while enzymes from the acini go into ducts that drain into the duodenum.
h: alpha cells are the most common islet cells and make insulin, while beta cells make glucagon

a.o: Ziad says alpha cells, not beta, make insulin.
a.x: Beta cells, not alpha cells, make insulin.
a.w: Beta cells are the most common islet cells and make insulin. Alpha cells make glucagon, which raises blood sugar.

a.o: Ziad says delta cells make somatostatin.
a.x: Delta cells should make digestive enzymes.
a.w: Somatostatin from delta cells dampens both insulin and glucagon release.

a.o: Ziad says islet hormones go straight into the blood.
a.x: Islet hormones should drain into the duodenum.
a.w: Islets are endocrine and have a rich network of capillaries.

a.o: Ziad says acinar enzymes drain into the duodenum.
a.x: Acinar enzymes should go into the blood.
a.w: Exocrine acini send enzymes through the pancreatic duct into the gut.

s:
Practical report, tissue staining, student Laila Sobhy. The aim was to stain a section of liver with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E), the most common stain in histology. Laila writes that the tissue was fixed in formalin, set in wax, cut into thin slices and placed on slides.

She writes that haematoxylin stains the cytoplasm pink, while eosin stains the nuclei dark blue-purple. She adds that structures that take up haematoxylin are called basophilic, because they are acidic, like DNA.

In the discussion she says that fat is dissolved away during processing, leaving empty spaces, and that collagen stains pink with eosin. She ends by saying that special stains are needed for some things H&E does not show well.
h: haematoxylin stains the cytoplasm pink, while eosin stains the nuclei dark blue-purple

a.o: Laila swaps the colours of the two H&E dyes.
a.x: Haematoxylin colours the nuclei.
a.w: Haematoxylin binds acidic DNA and RNA, colouring nuclei blue-purple. Eosin colours proteins in cytoplasm and collagen pink.

a.o: Laila says acidic structures like DNA are basophilic.
a.x: DNA should be called eosinophilic.
a.w: Basophilic parts are acidic and bind the basic dye haematoxylin.

a.o: Laila says fat is dissolved away, leaving empty spaces.
a.x: Fat should stain bright red with H&E.
a.w: Alcohol and xylene in processing remove lipid, so fat cells look empty.

a.o: Laila says collagen stains pink with eosin.
a.x: Collagen should stain dark blue.
a.w: Collagen is a protein, so it takes up eosin and looks pink.

s:
Handout for "Collagen in tissues", by Dr. Reda. Part 1 says collagen is the most common protein in the body and is made by fibroblasts and other cells. There are many types, each found in certain tissues.

Part 2 says type I collagen is found in bone, skin and tendons, and type II in hyaline cartilage. It then says that the basement membrane under epithelia is mainly made of type I collagen in thick bundles, like a tendon.

Part 3 says type III collagen forms fine reticular fibres in the liver, lymph nodes and early wounds. It ends by saying vitamin C is needed to make strong collagen, and that its lack causes scurvy with bleeding gums.
h: the basement membrane under epithelia is mainly made of type I collagen in thick bundles, like a tendon

a.o: The handout makes basement membrane type I collagen.
a.x: Basement membranes are made of type IV collagen.
a.w: Type IV collagen forms a flat mesh, not fibres. It is the target in Goodpasture and Alport disease.

a.o: The handout says type III collagen forms reticular fibres.
a.x: Type III collagen should be found mainly in bone.
a.w: Fine type III fibres make the support net of soft organs and early scars.

a.o: The handout says vitamin C is needed for strong collagen.
a.x: Vitamin C should be said to weaken collagen.
a.w: Vitamin C is needed to add hydroxyl groups that make collagen chains stable.

a.o: The handout puts type II collagen in hyaline cartilage.
a.x: Hyaline cartilage should be type IV collagen.
a.w: Type II collagen is the main fibre of hyaline cartilage.

s:
Flashcards "Epithelial cells", made by Sara for the histology quiz. Card 1 says goblet cells are found in the lining of the airways and the gut, scattered among the columnar cells of the surface.

Card 2 says goblet cells make digestive enzymes such as amylase and lipase, which they release into the gut. Card 3 says goblet cells look pale on H&E because their product washes out during processing, and they look like a wine glass.

Card 4 says goblet cells stain bright magenta with the PAS stain. Card 5 says smokers have more goblet cells in their airways. Sara put a small drawing of a wine glass next to card 3.
h: goblet cells make digestive enzymes such as amylase and lipase

a.o: Card 2 says goblet cells make amylase and lipase.
a.x: Goblet cells make mucus, not enzymes.
a.w: Goblet cells make mucins, which form a protective mucus layer. Pancreatic acini make digestive enzymes.

a.o: Card 3 says goblet cells look pale and wine-glass shaped.
a.x: Goblet cells should look dark and spindle-shaped.
a.w: Mucin is lost in processing, so the swollen top of the cell looks pale.

a.o: Card 4 says goblet cells stain magenta with PAS.
a.x: Goblet cells should be negative on PAS.
a.w: PAS stains sugars, and mucins are rich in carbohydrate.

a.o: Card 5 says smokers have more airway goblet cells.
a.x: Smoking should reduce airway goblet cells.
a.w: Irritants make the airway lining grow more goblet cells and mucus.

s:
Histology lab notes, testis slide, student Mahmoud Reda. Under low power the testis is packed with round and oval sections of seminiferous tubules, with small groups of cells in the spaces between them. The whole organ is wrapped in a thick capsule, the tunica albuginea.

I wrote that the tall Sertoli cells lie in the spaces between the tubules and make testosterone, while the Leydig cells sit inside the tubules and support the developing sperm. I noted many layers of germ cells, from spermatogonia at the edge to sperm near the lumen.

At the end I noted that tight junctions between the supporting cells in the tubule form a blood-testis barrier, which protects the developing sperm from the immune system. The tutor marked one line to check.
h: the tall Sertoli cells lie in the spaces between the tubules and make testosterone, while the Leydig cells sit inside the tubules

a.o: Mahmoud swaps where Sertoli and Leydig cells sit.
a.x: Leydig cells, between tubules, make testosterone.
a.w: Leydig cells in the spaces between tubules respond to LH. Sertoli cells inside the tubules nurse sperm and respond to FSH.

a.o: Mahmoud places spermatogonia at the tubule edge.
a.x: Spermatogonia should sit next to the lumen.
a.w: Stem cells rest on the basement membrane, and cells mature as they move inward.

a.o: Mahmoud describes a blood-testis barrier of tight junctions.
a.x: There should be no barrier inside the tubules.
a.w: Tight junctions between Sertoli cells hide later germ cells from the immune system.

a.o: Mahmoud names the tunica albuginea as the capsule.
a.x: The capsule should be called the periosteum.
a.w: The tunica albuginea is a tough fibrous coat around the testis.

s:
Handout for "The ovary", histology, by Dr. Hala. Part 1 says the ovary has an outer cortex full of follicles at different stages and an inner medulla with blood vessels. Each follicle holds one egg (oocyte) surrounded by support cells.

Part 2 describes how oestrogen is made. It says the granulosa cells, under LH, make androgens, and the theca cells, under FSH, turn those androgens into oestrogen using the enzyme aromatase. It adds that a mature follicle has a large fluid-filled space called the antrum.

Part 3 says that after ovulation the follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which makes progesterone. It ends by saying the zona pellucida is a glycoprotein coat around the egg that sperm must cross.
h: the granulosa cells, under LH, make androgens, and the theca cells, under FSH, turn those androgens into oestrogen

a.o: The handout swaps the roles of granulosa and theca cells.
a.x: Theca cells make androgens for granulosa.
a.w: Theca cells respond to LH and make androgens. Granulosa cells respond to FSH and use aromatase to turn them into oestrogen.

a.o: The handout says the corpus luteum makes progesterone.
a.x: The corpus luteum should make only FSH.
a.w: After ovulation, luteinised cells make progesterone to prepare the uterus.

a.o: The handout says a mature follicle has a fluid-filled antrum.
a.x: A mature follicle should have no fluid space.
a.w: The antrum forms as follicular fluid gathers in the growing follicle.

a.o: The handout calls the zona pellucida a coat sperm must cross.
a.x: The zona pellucida should be a layer of muscle.
a.w: Sperm bind the zona glycoproteins before reaching the egg membrane.

s:
Flashcards "Blood vessels", made by Ola for the histology quiz. Card 1 says arteries and veins have three layers: the tunica intima on the inside, the tunica media in the middle and the tunica adventitia outside.

Card 2 says the inside of blood vessels is lined by a thick stratified squamous epithelium, many cells deep, to protect against the force of the blood. Card 3 says arteries have a thicker media with more smooth muscle and elastic tissue than veins.

Card 4 says capillaries are only one cell thick so gases and nutrients can pass easily. Card 5 says many veins in the limbs have valves to stop blood flowing backwards. Ola used red for arteries and blue for veins on her drawing.
h: the inside of blood vessels is lined by a thick stratified squamous epithelium, many cells deep

a.o: Card 2 gives vessels a thick stratified squamous lining.
a.x: Vessels are lined by one layer of endothelium.
a.w: Endothelium is a single layer of flat cells. It gives a smooth surface that stops clots and lets substances cross.

a.o: Card 3 says arteries have a thicker media than veins.
a.x: Veins should have the thicker muscle layer.
a.w: Arteries carry blood at high pressure, so their muscular, elastic media is thicker.

a.o: Card 4 says capillaries are one cell thick.
a.x: Capillaries should be many cells thick.
a.w: A thin capillary wall keeps the diffusion distance very short.

a.o: Card 5 says limb veins have valves.
a.x: Valves should be found only in arteries.
a.w: Valves in limb veins stop blood falling back with gravity.

s:
