Short-answer exam, histology, question 8: "Name the cells of loose connective tissue." Student Abdallah Kamal writes that fibroblasts are the most common cells and make collagen and other fibres of the matrix.

He writes that plasma cells are full of granules of histamine and are the main cells that cause sudden allergy and itching. He adds that mast cells make antibodies and have a clock-face nucleus.

He also lists the white blood cells that pass through the tissue from the blood. He ends by saying macrophages eat germs and dead cells, and that fat cells store lipid in one large droplet that pushes the nucleus to the side. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: plasma cells are full of granules of histamine and are the main cells that cause sudden allergy and itching. He adds that mast cells make antibodies

a.o: Abdallah swaps plasma cells and mast cells.
a.x: Mast cells, not plasma cells, hold histamine.
a.w: Mast cells release histamine in allergy. Plasma cells come from B cells, make antibodies and have a clock-face nucleus.

a.o: Abdallah says fibroblasts make collagen.
a.x: Fibroblasts should be said to eat germs.
a.w: Fibroblasts make collagen, elastic fibres and ground substance.

a.o: Abdallah says macrophages eat germs and dead cells.
a.x: Macrophages should be said to store fat.
a.w: Macrophages engulf debris and microbes and present antigens.

a.o: Abdallah says fat cells have one large droplet.
a.x: Fat cells should have many tiny droplets.
a.w: White fat cells hold one big lipid droplet with a squashed nucleus.

s:
Draft page "Cells of the liver", histology chapter. The page says hepatocytes make up most of the liver. They are large cells in plates, one or two cells thick, with blood sinusoids on each side.

It states that Kupffer cells live in the space of Disse and store vitamin A, and that when the liver is damaged they turn into cells that lay down scar tissue. It adds that hepatic stellate (Ito) cells are the macrophages lining the sinusoids.

The page says bile is made by hepatocytes and flows in tiny canaliculi between them, and that the sinusoid lining has gaps so plasma can reach the hepatocytes. It ends with a drawing of a liver plate.
h: Kupffer cells live in the space of Disse and store vitamin A

a.o: The page swaps Kupffer cells and stellate cells.
a.x: Stellate cells store the vitamin A.
a.w: Stellate cells in the space of Disse store vitamin A and make scar in cirrhosis. Kupffer cells eat germs and old red cells.

a.o: The page says bile flows in canaliculi between hepatocytes.
a.x: Bile should flow inside the sinusoids.
a.w: Canaliculi are tiny channels between hepatocytes that drain into bile ducts.

a.o: The page says the sinusoid lining has gaps.
a.x: The lining should be fully sealed.
a.w: Gaps in the endothelium let plasma reach hepatocytes freely.

a.o: The page says hepatocyte plates are one or two cells thick.
a.x: The plates should be ten cells thick.
a.w: Thin plates give every hepatocyte contact with blood.

s:
Handout for "Adipose tissue", by Dr. Mona. Part 1 says the body has two types of fat. White fat is the most common, stores energy, and has cells with one large lipid droplet.

Part 2 says brown fat cells have many small lipid droplets and very few mitochondria, which is why they are pale. It adds that brown fat is found in newborns, around the neck and between the shoulder blades.

Part 3 says brown fat makes heat using a protein called thermogenin (UCP1), which lets protons leak back across the mitochondrial membrane without making ATP. It ends by saying newborns use brown fat to keep warm because they cannot shiver well.
h: brown fat cells have many small lipid droplets and very few mitochondria, which is why they are pale

a.o: The handout gives brown fat very few mitochondria.
a.x: Brown fat is packed with mitochondria.
a.w: Its many iron-rich mitochondria give the brown colour and burn fat to make heat.

a.o: The handout says brown fat makes heat with thermogenin.
a.x: Brown fat should make heat by making more ATP.
a.w: UCP1 lets protons leak back, so energy is lost as heat instead of ATP.

a.o: The handout says newborns have brown fat on the back.
a.x: Brown fat should be found only in old age.
a.w: Babies have brown fat around the neck and between the shoulder blades.

a.o: The handout says white fat cells have one large droplet.
a.x: White fat cells should have many tiny droplets.
a.w: A single big droplet pushes the nucleus to the cell edge.

s:
Histology lab notes, brain slides, student Basma Yehia. The first slide was the cerebellum, with many folds called folia. Under low power I saw the grey matter cortex outside and white matter inside.

I wrote that the cerebellar cortex has three layers: an outer molecular layer, a middle layer and an inner granular layer packed with small cells. I wrote that the middle layer contains the pyramidal cells, the largest neurons of the brain, with their big dendrite trees spreading out.

The second slide was the spinal cord, where I saw large motor neurons in the anterior horn of the grey matter. At the end I noted that the white matter of the cord is outside the grey matter, the opposite of the brain.
h: the middle layer contains the pyramidal cells, the largest neurons of the brain

a.o: Basma puts pyramidal cells in the middle cerebellar layer.
a.x: That middle layer holds Purkinje cells.
a.w: Big Purkinje cells form one row between the molecular and granular layers. Pyramidal cells are found in the cerebral cortex.

a.o: Basma says the granular layer is packed with small cells.
a.x: The granular layer should be nearly empty.
a.w: Tiny granule cells are the most common neurons in the brain.

a.o: Basma sees motor neurons in the anterior horn.
a.x: Motor neurons should sit in the posterior horn.
a.w: Large motor neurons in the anterior horn send axons to skeletal muscle.

a.o: Basma says the cord's white matter is outside its grey.
a.x: White matter should be inside the cord grey matter.
a.w: In the cord, white tracts surround a central H of grey matter.

s:
Handout for "Cell junctions", histology, by Dr. Adel. Part 1 says epithelial cells are joined to each other by junctions, which can be seen with the electron microscope.

Part 2 says desmosomes are the seals near the top of the cells that stop fluid and molecules leaking between them, while tight junctions are spot welds that anchor intermediate filaments and resist pulling. It adds that gap junctions are channels that let small ions pass from cell to cell.

Part 3 says hemidesmosomes attach cells to the basement membrane below. It ends by saying that in the skin disease pemphigus, antibodies attack desmosomes, so skin cells come apart and form blisters.
h: desmosomes are the seals near the top of the cells that stop fluid and molecules leaking between them, while tight junctions are spot welds

a.o: The handout swaps tight junctions and desmosomes.
a.x: Tight junctions seal; desmosomes are spot welds.
a.w: Tight junctions near the top of the cell seal the gaps between cells. Desmosomes link keratin filaments to hold cells together.

a.o: The handout says gap junctions let small ions pass.
a.x: Gap junctions should block all passage.
a.w: Gap junction channels join the cytoplasm of nearby cells.

a.o: The handout says hemidesmosomes attach to the basement membrane.
a.x: Hemidesmosomes should join two cells side by side.
a.w: Hemidesmosomes anchor basal cells to the basement membrane below.

a.o: The handout links pemphigus with antibodies to desmosomes.
a.x: Pemphigus should target gap junctions.
a.w: Losing desmosome grip lets epidermal cells separate into blisters.

s:
Short-answer exam, histology, question 9: "Compare microvilli and cilia." Student Nour Hassan writes that both are projections from the top surface of epithelial cells.

She writes that microvilli are short and have a core of microtubules in a 9+2 pattern, which lets them beat. She adds that cilia are longer and are found in the airways and fallopian tubes, where they move mucus or the egg.

She draws both under the electron microscope. She ends by saying microvilli greatly increase the surface area for absorption, as in the brush border of the gut, and that a defect in cilia can cause chest infections and infertility. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: microvilli are short and have a core of microtubules in a 9+2 pattern, which lets them beat

a.o: Nour gives microvilli a 9+2 microtubule core that beats.
a.x: Microvilli have an actin core, not 9+2.
a.w: Microvilli are held up by actin filaments and only add surface area. The 9+2 microtubule pattern belongs to motile cilia.

a.o: Nour says cilia move mucus in the airways.
a.x: Cilia should be found only in the gut.
a.w: Ciliary beating moves mucus up the airway and the egg along the tube.

a.o: Nour says microvilli raise the surface for absorption.
a.x: Microvilli should reduce the surface area.
a.w: The brush border of microvilli gives a huge absorbing surface.

a.o: Nour links cilia defects with chest infections and infertility.
a.x: Cilia defects should cause no problems.
a.w: In primary ciliary dyskinesia, mucus is not cleared and sperm cannot swim.

s:
Flashcards "Skin receptors", made by Kholoud for the histology and physiology quiz. Card 1 says skin has several sense receptors, each built to respond to a different kind of touch.

Card 2 says Pacinian corpuscles lie just under the epidermis in the fingertips and sense light, fine touch. Card 3 says Meissner corpuscles are large, onion-like structures deep in the dermis that sense vibration and deep pressure.

Card 4 says free nerve endings sense pain and temperature. Card 5 says Merkel discs sit at the base of the epidermis and sense steady pressure and texture. Kholoud drew each receptor at its depth in the skin on the back of card 1.
h: Pacinian corpuscles lie just under the epidermis in the fingertips and sense light, fine touch

a.o: Card 2 swaps the Pacinian and Meissner corpuscles.
a.x: Meissner corpuscles sense light touch.
a.w: Meissner corpuscles sit in the dermal papillae for fine touch. Onion-like Pacinian corpuscles lie deep and sense vibration.

a.o: Card 4 says free nerve endings sense pain and heat.
a.x: Free nerve endings should sense only vibration.
a.w: Free nerve endings respond to pain, heat and cold.

a.o: Card 5 says Merkel discs sense steady pressure.
a.x: Merkel discs should sense only pain.
a.w: Merkel discs are slow-adapting receptors for shape and texture.

a.o: Card 1 says each receptor suits a type of touch.
a.x: All receptors should be said to sense the same thing.
a.w: Different structures and adaptation rates let each receptor detect certain stimuli.

s:
Practical report, thick and thin skin slides, student Youssef Tamer. The aim was to name the layers of the epidermis. Youssef lists them from deep to surface: stratum basale, stratum spinosum, stratum granulosum, stratum lucidum (only in thick skin) and stratum corneum.

He writes that melanocytes are found in the stratum corneum, the dead outer layer, where they make melanin. He adds that melanin protects the nuclei of skin cells from ultraviolet light.

In the discussion he says that thick skin is found on the palms and soles and has no hair, and that Langerhans cells in the epidermis are immune cells that catch antigens. He ends by saying the stratum granulosum has dark granules of keratohyalin.
h: melanocytes are found in the stratum corneum, the dead outer layer, where they make melanin

a.o: Youssef puts melanocytes in the dead stratum corneum.
a.x: Melanocytes sit in the stratum basale.
a.w: Melanocytes lie among basal cells and pass melanin to keratinocytes. The stratum corneum is made of dead keratin-filled cells.

a.o: Youssef says melanin protects nuclei from UV light.
a.x: Melanin should be said to raise UV damage.
a.w: Melanin caps over nuclei absorb UV and protect DNA.

a.o: Youssef says thick skin on palms and soles has no hair.
a.x: Thick skin should be the hairiest skin.
a.w: Thick skin has a thick corneum and a lucidum but no hair follicles.

a.o: Youssef calls Langerhans cells immune cells.
a.x: Langerhans cells should be said to make insulin.
a.w: Skin Langerhans cells are dendritic cells that present antigens.

s:
Histology lab notebook, student Hana Mohsen. Today we looked at the stomach. The tutor asked us to compare the gastric lining with the oesophagus on the same slide, at the gastro-oesophageal junction.

I wrote that the stomach is lined by stratified squamous epithelium like the oesophagus, which protects it from acid. I noted that the lining has many small pits (gastric pits) leading down into long glands.

At the end I noted that the stomach has an extra inner oblique layer of smooth muscle, which helps it churn food, and that the surface cells make a thick layer of alkaline mucus. I also noted that the folds of the empty stomach are called rugae.
h: the stomach is lined by stratified squamous epithelium like the oesophagus, which protects it from acid

a.o: Hana gives the stomach a squamous lining.
a.x: The stomach has simple columnar epithelium.
a.w: Mucus-making simple columnar cells line the stomach. The lining changes sharply from squamous at the junction.

a.o: Hana notes gastric pits leading into glands.
a.x: The stomach lining should have no pits.
a.w: Gastric pits open onto the surface and receive secretions from the glands below.

a.o: Hana says the stomach has an extra oblique muscle layer.
a.x: The stomach should have only one muscle layer.
a.w: An inner oblique layer adds to churning and mixing of food.

a.o: Hana calls the folds of the empty stomach rugae.
a.x: These folds should be called villi.
a.w: Rugae flatten out as the stomach fills.

s:
Draft page "Bone marrow", histology chapter. The page says red bone marrow makes all blood cells from shared stem cells. In adults it is found mainly in flat bones such as the pelvis, sternum and vertebrae.

It states that megakaryocytes are small cells that make red blood cells, and that platelets come from reticulocytes breaking apart in the blood. It adds that a bone marrow biopsy is often taken from the iliac crest.

The page says that with age, more of the marrow turns into yellow fatty marrow, and that the marrow has wide sinusoids through which new cells enter the blood. It ends with a picture of a marrow smear.
h: megakaryocytes are small cells that make red blood cells, and that platelets come from reticulocytes breaking apart

a.o: The page says megakaryocytes make red cells, not platelets.
a.x: Huge megakaryocytes make the platelets.
a.w: These giant cells with many-lobed nuclei shed platelets into marrow sinusoids. Reticulocytes are young red cells.

a.o: The page says marrow biopsies come from the iliac crest.
a.x: Biopsies should be taken from the skull.
a.w: The iliac crest is easy to reach and full of red marrow.

a.o: The page says marrow turns yellow and fatty with age.
a.x: Marrow should turn red with age.
a.w: Red marrow is slowly replaced by fat, mostly in long bones.

a.o: The page says new cells enter the blood through sinusoids.
a.x: New cells should leave through lymph vessels.
a.w: Mature cells pass through the thin sinusoid walls into the circulation.

s:
Flashcards "Week 1 of development", made by Rahma for the embryology block. Card 1 says ovulation releases a secondary oocyte, which is swept into the uterine tube by the fimbriae.

Card 2 says fertilisation usually happens inside the cavity of the uterus, where sperm meet the egg a few days after ovulation. Card 3 says that after fertilisation the zygote divides as it travels, forming a ball of cells called a morula, and then a hollow blastocyst.

Card 4 says the blastocyst has an inner cell mass, which forms the embryo, and an outer trophoblast, which forms part of the placenta. Card 5 says the egg can be fertilised for only about a day after ovulation. Rahma drew the route of the egg on the back of card 1.
h: fertilisation usually happens inside the cavity of the uterus

a.o: Card 2 places fertilisation inside the uterine cavity.
a.x: Fertilisation usually happens in the ampulla.
a.w: Sperm meet the egg in the wide ampulla of the uterine tube. The embryo then reaches the uterus as a blastocyst days later.

a.o: Card 3 says the zygote becomes a morula, then a blastocyst.
a.x: The blastocyst should come before the morula.
a.w: Cleavage makes a solid morula, which then fills with fluid to form a blastocyst.

a.o: Card 4 says the inner cell mass forms the embryo.
a.x: The trophoblast should form the embryo itself.
a.w: The inner cell mass gives rise to the embryo; the trophoblast forms placenta.

a.o: Card 5 says the egg can be fertilised for about a day.
a.x: The egg should stay fertile for about a month.
a.w: A released oocyte survives only about 12 to 24 hours without fertilisation.

s:
Handout for "Implantation", embryology, by Dr. Wafaa. Part 1 says the blastocyst reaches the uterus and hatches from the zona pellucida before it can attach to the uterine lining.

Part 2 says implantation begins on the first day after fertilisation, while the embryo is still a single cell in the uterine tube. It adds that the trophoblast splits into an inner cytotrophoblast and an outer syncytiotrophoblast, which digs into the endometrium.

Part 3 says the usual site of implantation is the back wall of the upper uterus, and that implantation in the tube is called an ectopic pregnancy, which can rupture and bleed. It ends by saying the lining of the uterus at this time is called the decidua.
h: implantation begins on the first day after fertilisation, while the embryo is still a single cell in the uterine tube

a.o: The handout starts implantation on day 1, in the tube.
a.x: Implantation starts around day 6 to 7, in the uterus.
a.w: The embryo travels down the tube for days and implants as a blastocyst after hatching from the zona pellucida.

a.o: The handout says the syncytiotrophoblast digs into the endometrium.
a.x: The cytotrophoblast should be the outer invading layer.
a.w: The outer syncytiotrophoblast erodes into the lining and maternal vessels.

a.o: The handout calls implantation in the tube an ectopic pregnancy.
a.x: It should be called a normal pregnancy.
a.w: A tubal pregnancy cannot grow safely and can rupture with heavy bleeding.

a.o: The handout calls the uterine lining at this time the decidua.
a.x: The lining should be called the amnion.
a.w: After implantation the endometrium changes and is called the decidua.

s:
Short-answer exam, embryology, question 1: "Describe the second week of development." Student Karim Wagdy writes that week 2 is the "week of twos", because the trophoblast forms two layers and the inner cell mass forms a two-layer disc.

He writes that the disc has an upper epiblast and a lower hypoblast, and that the hypoblast is the layer that later gives rise to all three germ layers of the embryo during gastrulation. He adds that the amniotic cavity forms on the epiblast side.

He ends by saying that the yolk sac forms on the hypoblast side, and that the connecting stalk later becomes the umbilical cord. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the hypoblast is the layer that later gives rise to all three germ layers of the embryo

a.o: Karim says the hypoblast gives all three germ layers.
a.x: The epiblast forms all three germ layers.
a.w: In gastrulation epiblast cells move through the primitive streak to form endoderm, mesoderm and ectoderm. The hypoblast is pushed aside.

a.o: Karim says the amniotic cavity forms on the epiblast side.
a.x: The amnion should form on the hypoblast side.
a.w: The amniotic cavity appears above the epiblast.

a.o: Karim says the yolk sac forms on the hypoblast side.
a.x: The yolk sac should form above the epiblast.
a.w: Hypoblast cells line the primary yolk sac under the disc.

a.o: Karim says the connecting stalk becomes the umbilical cord.
a.x: The stalk should become the placenta's villi.
a.w: The connecting stalk carries vessels and forms the umbilical cord.

s:
Draft page "Gastrulation", embryology chapter. The page says gastrulation is the process that turns the two-layer disc into a three-layer disc, and that it is one of the most important events in development.

It states that gastrulation happens in the eighth week, after the main organs have already formed. It says it begins with the primitive streak, a groove on the surface of the epiblast, and cells move through it to form the new layers.

The page adds that the primitive streak also sets the head and tail ends and the left and right sides of the embryo. It ends by saying that a leftover part of the streak can form a tumour at the base of the spine called a sacrococcygeal teratoma.
h: gastrulation happens in the eighth week, after the main organs have already formed

a.o: The page places gastrulation in week 8, after organs form.
a.x: Gastrulation happens in week 3 of development.
a.w: The three germ layers form in week 3. Organs then develop from these layers during weeks 3 to 8.

a.o: The page says the primitive streak is a groove on the epiblast.
a.x: The streak should be on the yolk sac wall.
a.w: The primitive streak forms on the epiblast surface at the tail end.

a.o: The page says the streak sets head, tail, left and right.
a.x: The streak should be said to set no body axes.
a.w: The streak marks the body axes, and signals here start left-right patterning.

a.o: The page links streak remnants with sacrococcygeal teratoma.
a.x: Its remnants should be said to form brain tumours.
a.w: Leftover streak cells can grow into a teratoma at the base of the spine.

s:
Embryology tutorial notebook, student Mona Ezzat. Today we made a table of what each germ layer forms in the adult body. The tutor gave us a list of organs to sort into ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.

I wrote that ectoderm forms the brain, spinal cord and the epidermis of the skin. I put the heart and blood vessels under ectoderm too, because the heart is linked so closely to the nerves that control it.

For mesoderm I wrote bone, cartilage, skeletal muscle and the kidneys. For endoderm I wrote the lining of the gut, the liver and the lining of the lungs. At the end I noted that the tutor said one item was in the wrong column.
h: I put the heart and blood vessels under ectoderm too

a.o: Mona puts the heart and vessels under ectoderm.
a.x: The heart comes from mesoderm.
a.w: The heart forms from mesoderm cells of the cardiac crescent. Nerve supply does not decide which layer forms an organ.

a.o: Mona says ectoderm forms the brain and epidermis.
a.x: The brain should come from endoderm.
a.w: Surface ectoderm makes epidermis and neural ectoderm makes the nervous system.

a.o: Mona puts bone, muscle and kidneys under mesoderm.
a.x: The kidneys should come from ectoderm.
a.w: Paraxial and intermediate mesoderm form muscle, bone and kidneys.

a.o: Mona says endoderm lines the gut and lungs.
a.x: The gut lining should come from mesoderm.
a.w: Endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the gut and airways and the liver cells.

s:
Handout for "The notochord", embryology, by Dr. Tarek. Part 1 says the notochord is a rod of cells that forms along the midline of the embryo in week 3, under the future spinal cord.

Part 2 says the notochord sends signals, such as sonic hedgehog, that tell the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate. It then states that the notochord itself grows into the adult spinal cord, so there is no notochord left in the adult body.

Part 3 says that the vertebral bodies form around the notochord from sclerotome cells, and that a rare tumour from notochord remnants is called a chordoma. It ends by saying the notochord defines the main axis of the body.
h: the notochord itself grows into the adult spinal cord, so there is no notochord left in the adult body

a.o: The handout says the notochord grows into the spinal cord.
a.x: It remains as the nucleus pulposus.
a.w: The spinal cord forms from the neural tube. The notochord shrinks away, leaving the jelly centre of each disc.

a.o: The handout says the notochord signals with sonic hedgehog.
a.x: The notochord should send no signals.
a.w: Notochord signals make the overlying ectoderm thicken into neural plate.

a.o: The handout says vertebral bodies form from sclerotome.
a.x: Vertebrae should form from the yolk sac.
a.w: Sclerotome cells move around the notochord and neural tube to form vertebrae.

a.o: The handout links notochord remnants with chordoma.
a.x: Chordoma should come from muscle cells.
a.w: Chordomas arise from notochord remnants, often in the skull base or sacrum.

s:
Case-based tutorial, neural tube defects, student Ahmed Raouf. A 28-year-old woman plans to get pregnant. Ahmed writes that the neural tube closes by about the end of the fourth week after fertilisation, often before a woman knows she is pregnant.

He writes that folic acid lowers the risk of spina bifida and anencephaly, and advises that she should start folic acid at the end of the first trimester, once the pregnancy is confirmed on ultrasound.

He adds that women who had a baby with a neural tube defect, or who take some epilepsy drugs, need a higher dose. He ends by saying a raised alpha-fetoprotein in the mother's blood can suggest an open defect. The tutor wrote a note beside his advice.
h: she should start folic acid at the end of the first trimester, once the pregnancy is confirmed on ultrasound

a.o: Ahmed starts folic acid after the first trimester.
a.x: Folic acid starts before pregnancy.
a.w: The tube closes by week 4, so folic acid must be taken before pregnancy and through the first 12 weeks.

a.o: Ahmed says the neural tube closes by about week 4.
a.x: It should close at about week 20.
a.w: The neural tube closes in week 4, often before the period is missed.

a.o: Ahmed says some women need a higher folic acid dose.
a.x: All women should take the same low dose.
a.w: A past affected baby or some epilepsy drugs call for 5 mg a day.

a.o: Ahmed links raised maternal AFP with an open defect.
a.x: AFP should fall with an open defect.
a.w: AFP leaks from an open neural tube into the fluid and the mother's blood.

s:
Flashcards "Neural crest", made by Nada for the embryology quiz. Card 1 says neural crest cells come from the edges of the neural folds and leave as the tube closes, travelling all over the body.

Card 2 says neural crest cells form the spinal cord and the brain itself. Card 3 says they form melanocytes in the skin and the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.

Card 4 says they form the dorsal root ganglia, the autonomic ganglia and the Schwann cells. Card 5 says that failed migration of neural crest cells to the bowel causes Hirschsprung disease. Nada drew arrows showing where the cells travel on a body outline.
h: neural crest cells form the spinal cord and the brain itself

a.o: Card 2 says neural crest forms the brain and cord.
a.x: The brain and cord come from the neural tube.
a.w: The neural tube forms the brain and spinal cord. Crest cells leave the tube and form ganglia, melanocytes and more.

a.o: Card 3 lists melanocytes and adrenal chromaffin cells.
a.x: Melanocytes should come from the endoderm.
a.w: Crest cells migrate to the skin and adrenal medulla.

a.o: Card 4 lists the ganglia and Schwann cells.
a.x: Schwann cells should come from the notochord.
a.w: Sensory and autonomic ganglia and Schwann cells come from crest.

a.o: Card 5 links failed crest migration to Hirschsprung.
a.x: Hirschsprung should come from extra gut nerves.
a.w: Without crest-derived ganglion cells, a bowel segment cannot relax.

s:
Short-answer exam, embryology, question 3: "Describe early heart development." Student Mariam Adly writes that the heart is the first organ to work in the embryo, because the growing embryo soon needs more than diffusion to get food and oxygen.

She writes that two heart tubes fuse into one tube, which then folds into a loop. She adds that the heart does not start beating until about week 12, when all four chambers have fully formed.

She labels a drawing of the tube. She ends by saying the tube loops to the right and that the septum between the atria leaves an opening called the foramen ovale. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the heart does not start beating until about week 12, when all four chambers have fully formed

a.o: Mariam says the heart first beats at about week 12.
a.x: The heart starts beating in about week 4.
a.w: The heart tube begins to beat around day 22, long before the chambers and septa finish forming.

a.o: Mariam says two heart tubes fuse into one.
a.x: One tube should split into two hearts.
a.w: Paired endocardial tubes fuse in the midline to form one heart tube.

a.o: Mariam says the heart tube loops to the right.
a.x: The tube should never fold or loop.
a.w: Rightward looping brings the chambers into their adult positions.

a.o: Mariam says the atrial septum leaves a foramen ovale.
a.x: The opening should be between the ventricles.
a.w: The foramen ovale lets blood cross between the atria before birth.

s:
Handout for "Fetal circulation", embryology, by Dr. Hany. Part 1 says the fetus gets oxygen from the placenta, so the lungs are full of fluid and receive little blood. Three shunts help blood bypass the lungs and liver.

Part 2 says the foramen ovale lets blood pass from the left atrium to the right atrium, because pressure is higher on the left side before birth. It adds that oxygen-rich blood from the umbilical vein goes to the heart through the ductus venosus.

Part 3 says that at birth the lungs expand, pressure in the left atrium rises and the flap of the foramen ovale closes. It ends by saying that a foramen ovale that does not seal fully, called a patent foramen ovale, is common in adults.
h: the foramen ovale lets blood pass from the left atrium to the right atrium, because pressure is higher on the left side before birth

a.o: The handout sends fetal blood left to right across the foramen.
a.x: Fetal blood crosses right to left.
a.w: Before birth right atrial pressure is higher, so oxygenated blood from the IVC crosses to the left atrium and on to the brain.

a.o: The handout says the ductus venosus carries blood to the heart.
a.x: The ductus venosus should go to the lungs.
a.w: The ductus venosus lets umbilical vein blood bypass the liver.

a.o: The handout says the foramen closes as left pressure rises.
a.x: The foramen should open wider at birth.
a.w: Breathing lowers lung resistance and raises left atrial pressure.

a.o: The handout says a patent foramen ovale is common in adults.
a.x: A patent foramen should be called very rare.
a.w: About a quarter of adults have a probe-patent foramen ovale.

s:
Draft page "Changes at birth", embryology chapter. The page says the ductus arteriosus is a vessel in the fetus that joins the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, so blood bypasses the fluid-filled lungs.

It states that after birth the ductus arteriosus closes and becomes the ligamentum venosum, and the ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. It adds that the ductus arteriosus is kept open in the fetus by prostaglandins.

The page says that drugs like indomethacin can help close a patent ductus in premature babies, and that the umbilical vein becomes the round ligament of the liver. It ends by saying that a patent ductus can cause a machine-like murmur.
h: the ductus arteriosus closes and becomes the ligamentum venosum, and the ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum

a.o: The page swaps the adult remnants of the two ducts.
a.x: Ductus arteriosus leaves the ligamentum arteriosum.
a.w: The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum by the aorta. The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum in the liver.

a.o: The page says prostaglandins keep the ductus open.
a.x: Prostaglandins should close the ductus.
a.w: Prostaglandin E keeps the ductus open; levels fall after birth.

a.o: The page says indomethacin can help close a patent ductus.
a.x: Indomethacin should keep the ductus open.
a.w: Indomethacin blocks prostaglandin making, helping the ductus close.

a.o: The page says the umbilical vein becomes the round ligament.
a.x: The vein should become the median umbilical ligament.
a.w: The obliterated umbilical vein forms the ligamentum teres of the liver.

s:
Practical report, placenta and cord, student Hossam Eid. The aim was to examine a cut section of an umbilical cord. Hossam writes that the cord is covered by amnion and filled with a jelly called Wharton's jelly, which protects the vessels.

He writes that the cord has two umbilical veins and one umbilical artery, and that the two veins carry blood with little oxygen from the baby back to the placenta. He adds that the vessels are coiled, which helps protect them from being squashed.

In the discussion he says that a cord with only one artery can be linked with other birth defects, and that the cord is usually about 50 to 60 cm long at birth.
h: the cord has two umbilical veins and one umbilical artery, and that the two veins carry blood with little oxygen

a.o: Hossam gives the cord two veins and one artery.
a.x: The cord has two arteries and one vein.
a.w: The two arteries carry low-oxygen blood to the placenta. The single vein brings oxygen-rich blood back to the fetus.

a.o: Hossam says Wharton's jelly protects the vessels.
a.x: The jelly should be said to block blood flow.
a.w: Wharton's jelly cushions the cord vessels against squeezing and kinking.

a.o: Hossam links a single artery with other defects.
a.x: A single artery should always be called normal.
a.w: A single umbilical artery is linked with kidney and heart anomalies.

a.o: Hossam says the cord is about 50 to 60 cm at birth.
a.x: The cord should be about 5 cm long at birth.
a.w: The usual cord length at term is about 50 to 60 cm.

s:
Short-answer exam, embryology, question 4: "Name the shunts of the fetal circulation." Student Salma Fawzy writes that the fetus has three shunts that let blood avoid organs that do not yet do their adult job.

She writes that the ductus venosus carries blood from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, bypassing the lungs. She adds that the foramen ovale lets blood cross between the atria.

She ends by saying the ductus arteriosus carries blood away from the lungs into the aorta, and that all three shunts close within days or weeks after birth. She also notes that the fetal lungs are full of fluid. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the ductus venosus carries blood from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, bypassing the lungs

a.o: Salma says ductus venosus bypasses the lungs.
a.x: The ductus venosus bypasses the liver.
a.w: The ductus venosus carries umbilical vein blood past the liver to the IVC. The lung bypass is the ductus arteriosus.

a.o: Salma says the foramen ovale joins the two atria.
a.x: The foramen should join the two ventricles.
a.w: The foramen ovale is an opening in the atrial septum.

a.o: Salma says all three shunts close after birth.
a.x: The shunts should stay open for life.
a.w: The shunts close in the days and weeks after birth as pressures change.

a.o: Salma says fetal lungs are full of fluid.
a.x: Fetal lungs should be said to be full of air.
a.w: Lung fluid is cleared during and after birth as breathing begins.

s:
Handout for "Pharyngeal arches", embryology, by Dr. Ola. Part 1 says the pharyngeal arches are bars of tissue in the neck of the embryo, and each arch has its own cartilage, artery, muscles and nerve.

Part 2 says the first arch is supplied by the facial nerve (VII) and forms the muscles of facial expression, while the second arch is supplied by the trigeminal nerve (V) and forms the muscles of chewing. It adds that the first arch cartilage forms parts of the jaw and two ear bones.

Part 3 says the third arch is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve and forms the stylopharyngeus muscle. It ends by saying the fourth and sixth arches are supplied by branches of the vagus nerve and form the muscles of the larynx and pharynx.
h: the first arch is supplied by the facial nerve (VII) and forms the muscles of facial expression, while the second arch is supplied by the trigeminal nerve (V)

a.o: The handout swaps the nerves of arches 1 and 2.
a.x: Arch 1 is trigeminal; arch 2 is facial.
a.w: The first arch is supplied by the trigeminal nerve and forms the chewing muscles. The second arch is facial and forms the muscles of expression.

a.o: The handout says arch 1 cartilage forms jaw and ear bones.
a.x: Arch 1 cartilage should form the hyoid.
a.w: Meckel's cartilage helps form the mandible, malleus and incus.

a.o: The handout says arch 3 forms stylopharyngeus.
a.x: Arch 3 should form the chewing muscles.
a.w: Stylopharyngeus is the only muscle of the third arch, supplied by IX.

a.o: The handout says arches 4 and 6 are supplied by the vagus.
a.x: Arches 4 and 6 should be supplied by VII.
a.w: Vagal branches supply the laryngeal and pharyngeal muscles from these arches.

s:
Flashcards "Pharyngeal pouches", made by Sherif for the head and neck embryology quiz. Card 1 says the pouches are pockets of endoderm on the inside of the pharynx, between the arches.

Card 2 says the first pouch forms the middle ear cavity and the auditory tube. Card 3 says the thymus comes from the first pouch, together with the middle ear. Card 4 says the third pouch forms the inferior parathyroid glands.

Card 5 says the fourth pouch forms the superior parathyroid glands and cells that become the thyroid C cells. Sherif added a note that the parathyroids from the third pouch end up lower than those from the fourth, because they travel down with the thymus.
h: the thymus comes from the first pouch, together with the middle ear

a.o: Card 3 gives the thymus to the first pharyngeal pouch.
a.x: The thymus comes from the third pouch instead.
a.w: The third pouch forms the thymus and the inferior parathyroids, which travel down together into the chest and neck.

a.o: Card 2 says the first pouch forms the middle ear cavity.
a.x: The first pouch should form the thyroid.
a.w: The first pouch forms the tympanic cavity and auditory tube.

a.o: Card 5 says the fourth pouch forms the superior parathyroids.
a.x: The fourth pouch should form the thymus.
a.w: Fourth-pouch parathyroids stay higher in the neck.

a.o: Sherif says third-pouch parathyroids end up lower.
a.x: They should end up above the fourth-pouch glands.
a.w: The inferior parathyroids are pulled down by the descending thymus.

s:
Handout for "Development of the thyroid", by Dr. Amira. Part 1 says the thyroid is the first endocrine gland to develop, starting in week 4 of development as a thickening of endoderm.

Part 2 says the thyroid begins in the upper chest and moves up into the neck, leaving a track behind called the thyroglossal duct. It adds that the duct usually disappears, but a leftover part can form a cyst in the midline of the neck.

Part 3 says that a thyroglossal cyst moves up when the patient sticks out the tongue, and that the foramen caecum on the tongue marks a key point of thyroid development. It ends by saying that thyroid tissue may sometimes be found at the back of the tongue.
h: the thyroid begins in the upper chest and moves up into the neck

a.o: The handout starts the thyroid in the chest and moves it up.
a.x: The thyroid starts at the tongue, moving down.
a.w: It begins at the foramen caecum in the floor of the mouth and descends in front of the hyoid into the neck.

a.o: The handout says a duct remnant can form a midline cyst.
a.x: Thyroglossal cysts should lie far to the side.
a.w: Leftover duct cells form a cyst in the midline of the neck.

a.o: The handout says the cyst moves when the tongue sticks out.
a.x: The cyst should never move with the tongue.
a.w: The duct track is tied to the tongue, so the cyst rises when it protrudes.

a.o: The handout says thyroid tissue can sit at the back of the tongue.
a.x: Thyroid tissue should never be found there.
a.w: If descent fails, a lingual thyroid stays at the base of the tongue.

s:
Short-answer exam, embryology, question 6: "Explain cleft lip and cleft palate." Student Rana Saber writes that the face forms from processes around the mouth during weeks 4 to 10.

She writes that cleft lip is caused by failure of the two palatine shelves to fuse in the midline. She adds that cleft palate is caused by failure of the maxillary process to fuse with the medial nasal process on one side.

She ends by saying the two can occur alone or together, that feeding is a main early problem, and that surgery can repair both. She notes that maternal smoking and some drugs raise the risk. The examiner gave 6 out of 10.
h: cleft lip is caused by failure of the two palatine shelves to fuse in the midline. She adds that cleft palate is caused by failure of the maxillary process

a.o: Rana swaps the cause of each kind of cleft.
a.x: Cleft lip is a lip process fusion failure.
a.w: Cleft lip comes from failed fusion of the maxillary and medial nasal processes. Cleft palate comes from failed fusion of the palatine shelves.

a.o: Rana says feeding is a main early problem.
a.x: Feeding should be said to be unaffected.
a.w: A gap in the lip or palate makes sucking and swallowing hard.

a.o: Rana says the face forms during weeks 4 to 10.
a.x: The face should form after birth.
a.w: The facial processes appear in week 4 and fuse over the next weeks.

a.o: Rana says maternal smoking raises the risk.
a.x: Smoking should be said to protect against clefts.
a.w: Smoking, some anti-epileptic drugs and genes raise cleft risk.

s:
Draft page "Development of the gut", embryology chapter. The page says the gut tube is divided into foregut, midgut and hindgut, each with its own artery: the coeliac trunk, the superior mesenteric artery and the inferior mesenteric artery.

It states that in week 6 the midgut grows so fast that it herniates into the umbilical cord. It then says that this herniation is always a serious birth defect, so any gut seen in the cord on a scan at 8 weeks needs surgery.

The page adds that the gut rotates 270 degrees anticlockwise around the superior mesenteric artery and returns to the abdomen by about week 10. It ends by saying that faulty rotation can lead to volvulus, where the gut twists and loses its blood supply.
h: this herniation is always a serious birth defect, so any gut seen in the cord on a scan at 8 weeks needs surgery

a.o: The page calls week 6 gut herniation a defect.
a.x: The herniation is normal and returns by week 10.
a.w: Physiological herniation is a normal stage. Only gut that stays outside after about week 12 points to omphalocele or gastroschisis.

a.o: The page gives the midgut the superior mesenteric artery.
a.x: The midgut should be supplied by the coeliac trunk.
a.w: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the whole midgut.

a.o: The page says the gut rotates 270 degrees anticlockwise.
a.x: The gut should rotate only 90 degrees clockwise.
a.w: The midgut turns a total of 270 degrees anticlockwise around the SMA.

a.o: The page links faulty rotation with volvulus.
a.x: Faulty rotation should be said to cause no problems.
a.w: Malrotation leaves a narrow base that can twist and cut off blood.

s:
Flashcards "Meckel's diverticulum", made by Hamza for the gut embryology quiz. Card 1 says Meckel's diverticulum is the most common birth defect of the gut, found in about 2% of people.

Card 2 says it is a remnant of the urachus, the tube that joined the bladder to the umbilicus. Card 3 says it is found in the ileum, about 2 feet (60 cm) from the ileocaecal valve, and is about 2 inches long.

Card 4 says it can contain stomach or pancreatic tissue, and that acid from stomach tissue can cause painless bleeding in a child. Card 5 says it can also cause inflammation that looks like appendicitis. Hamza wrote "rule of twos" in big letters at the top.
h: it is a remnant of the urachus, the tube that joined the bladder to the umbilicus

a.o: Card 2 calls Meckel's a remnant of the urachus.
a.x: It is a remnant of the vitelline duct.
a.w: The vitelline duct links the midgut to the yolk sac. If part stays, it forms a pouch on the ileum.

a.o: Card 3 places it in the ileum near the ileocaecal valve.
a.x: It should be placed in the duodenum.
a.w: Meckel's is on the ileum about 60 cm from the ileocaecal valve.

a.o: Card 4 says stomach tissue in it can cause bleeding.
a.x: Stomach tissue should be said to stop any bleeding.
a.w: Acid from ectopic gastric tissue can ulcerate nearby ileum and bleed.

a.o: Card 5 says it can mimic appendicitis.
a.x: It should never cause belly pain.
a.w: Inflamed Meckel's gives right lower pain much like appendicitis.

s:
Handout for "Development of the kidney", by Dr. Hossam. Part 1 says three kidney systems form in order: the pronephros, the mesonephros and the metanephros. The metanephros becomes the adult kidney.

Part 2 says the metanephric blastema forms the ureter, renal pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts, while the ureteric bud forms the glomeruli and the tubules of the nephron. It adds that the two parts send signals to each other, and without this the kidney does not form.

Part 3 says the kidneys start low in the pelvis and rise to the lumbar region. It ends by saying that if the lower poles fuse, a horseshoe kidney forms and gets caught under the inferior mesenteric artery.
h: the metanephric blastema forms the ureter, renal pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts, while the ureteric bud forms the glomeruli

a.o: The handout swaps the jobs of the blastema and bud.
a.x: The ureteric bud forms the ureter and ducts.
a.w: The ureteric bud branches into the ureter, pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts. The blastema forms the nephrons.

a.o: The handout says the metanephros becomes the adult kidney.
a.x: The pronephros should become the adult kidney.
a.w: The pronephros and most of the mesonephros disappear; the metanephros stays.

a.o: The handout says the kidneys rise from the pelvis.
a.x: The kidneys should move down from the chest.
a.w: The kidneys rise as the body grows, getting new arteries on the way.

a.o: The handout says a horseshoe kidney catches under the IMA.
a.x: It should catch under the coeliac trunk.
a.w: The fused lower poles rise until stopped by the inferior mesenteric artery.

s:
Short-answer exam, embryology, question 7: "How is male sex decided?" Student Youssef Magdy writes that until week 7 the gonads look the same in both sexes and are called indifferent gonads.

He notes the embryo's genetic sex is set at fertilisation by the sperm. He writes that the SRY gene on the X chromosome makes the gonad become a testis, which is why people with XX are male. He adds that the testis then makes testosterone and anti-Mullerian hormone.

He ends by saying that testosterone keeps the Wolffian ducts, which form the vas deferens and epididymis, and that dihydrotestosterone forms the external genitalia and prostate. The examiner gave 6 out of 10.
h: the SRY gene on the X chromosome makes the gonad become a testis, which is why people with XX are male

a.o: Youssef places the SRY gene on the X chromosome.
a.x: The SRY gene sits on the Y chromosome.
a.w: The SRY gene on the short arm of Y starts testis formation. Without it, an XX gonad normally becomes an ovary.

a.o: Youssef says gonads look the same until week 7.
a.x: The gonads should differ from the first week.
a.w: Before about week 7 the gonads cannot be told apart.

a.o: Youssef says testosterone keeps the Wolffian ducts.
a.x: Testosterone should remove the Wolffian ducts.
a.w: Testosterone keeps the Wolffian ducts, which form the epididymis and vas.

a.o: Youssef says DHT forms the external genitalia and prostate.
a.x: DHT should form the uterus and tubes.
a.w: 5-alpha-reductase makes DHT, which shapes the outer genitalia and prostate.

s:
Handout for "Genital ducts", embryology, by Dr. Nermeen. Part 1 says both sexes start with two pairs of ducts: the Mullerian (paramesonephric) ducts and the Wolffian (mesonephric) ducts.

Part 2 says that in females the Mullerian ducts form the uterine tubes, the uterus and the upper vagina. It then states that in males the Mullerian ducts are removed by testosterone made by the Sertoli cells, and anti-Mullerian hormone from the Leydig cells keeps the Wolffian ducts.

Part 3 says that if the Mullerian ducts do not fuse properly, a double uterus or a uterus with a dividing wall can form. It ends by saying that in females the Wolffian ducts mostly disappear without testosterone.
h: the Mullerian ducts are removed by testosterone made by the Sertoli cells, and anti-Mullerian hormone from the Leydig cells keeps the Wolffian ducts

a.o: The handout swaps the duct hormones and their cells.
a.x: Sertoli AMH removes Mullerian ducts.
a.w: Sertoli cells make anti-Mullerian hormone, which removes the Mullerian ducts. Leydig cells make testosterone, which keeps the Wolffian ducts.

a.o: The handout says Mullerian ducts form the uterus and tubes.
a.x: Mullerian ducts should form the vas deferens.
a.w: In females the Mullerian ducts form the tubes, uterus and upper vagina.

a.o: The handout links poor fusion with a double uterus.
a.x: Poor fusion should cause no change.
a.w: Failed fusion of the two ducts leaves a double or septate uterus.

a.o: The handout says female Wolffian ducts mostly disappear.
a.x: They should form the female uterus.
a.w: Without testosterone, the Wolffian ducts regress in females.

s:
Clinical embryology tutorial, newborn check, student Mostafa Sayed. A term baby boy has one testis that cannot be felt in the scrotum. Mostafa writes that the testes form high on the back wall of the abdomen, near the kidneys.

He writes that the testes normally descend into the scrotum only after puberty, so an empty scrotum at birth is expected and needs no follow-up. He adds that a cord called the gubernaculum guides the testis down.

He also writes that the processus vaginalis goes ahead of the testis, and if it stays open it can lead to an inguinal hernia. He ends by saying an undescended testis has a higher risk of cancer and poor fertility. The tutor wrote a comment beside his plan.
h: the testes normally descend into the scrotum only after puberty, so an empty scrotum at birth is expected

a.o: Mostafa says testes come down only after puberty.
a.x: Testes usually reach the scrotum before birth.
a.w: Most testes are in the scrotum by birth. One still missing needs follow-up and surgery in the first year or so if it does not come down.

a.o: Mostafa says the gubernaculum guides the testis down.
a.x: The testis should be pulled down by the ureter.
a.w: The gubernaculum anchors the testis and guides it into the scrotum.

a.o: Mostafa links an open processus vaginalis with hernia.
a.x: An open processus should block any hernia.
a.w: A patent processus vaginalis lets bowel or fluid enter the inguinal canal.

a.o: Mostafa says undescended testes raise cancer risk.
a.x: Undescended testes should carry no extra risk.
a.w: An undescended testis has a higher risk of cancer and low fertility.

s:
Draft page "The diaphragm", embryology chapter. The page says the diaphragm forms from four parts: the septum transversum, the pleuroperitoneal membranes, the dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus and muscle from the body wall.

It states that congenital diaphragmatic hernia happens most often on the right side, because the liver is weaker than the other organs and pushes through. It adds that gut in the chest presses on the lung and stops it from growing, which is the main danger.

The page says the diaphragm forms in the neck, at the level of C3 to C5, which is why the phrenic nerve comes from these roots. It ends by saying the diaphragm moves down as the body grows.
h: congenital diaphragmatic hernia happens most often on the right side, because the liver is weaker than the other organs

a.o: The page puts most of these hernias on the right.
a.x: Most diaphragmatic hernias are on the left.
a.w: The left pleuroperitoneal opening closes later, and the liver guards the right side, so most hernias are left posterolateral.

a.o: The page says gut in the chest stops the lung growing.
a.x: The gut should be said to help the lung grow.
a.w: Pulmonary hypoplasia from compression is the main cause of death.

a.o: The page links C3 to C5 with the phrenic nerve.
a.x: The phrenic nerve should come from T12.
a.w: The diaphragm forms in the neck, so its nerve comes from C3 to C5.

a.o: The page names the septum transversum as one part.
a.x: The septum should form the kidneys instead.
a.w: The septum transversum forms the central tendon of the diaphragm.

s:
Handout for "Lung development", embryology, by Dr. Walid. Part 1 says the lungs start as a bud from the foregut in week 4, and that the bud branches again and again to make the airways.

Part 2 says type II pneumocytes begin to make surfactant by week 8, so a baby born at 22 weeks has plenty of surfactant and breathes easily. It adds that steroids given to the mother before an early birth speed up lung growth.

Part 3 says that a hole between the trachea and the oesophagus can form if they do not separate properly, and that alveoli keep forming for years after birth. It ends by saying fetal breathing movements help the lungs grow.
h: type II pneumocytes begin to make surfactant by week 8, so a baby born at 22 weeks has plenty of surfactant

a.o: The handout says surfactant is made early, by week 8.
a.x: Surfactant starts at about 24 weeks.
a.w: Surfactant is made from about 24 weeks and rises near term. Very preterm babies lack it and get respiratory distress.

a.o: The handout says the lung bud comes from the foregut.
a.x: The lung bud should come from the hindgut.
a.w: The respiratory bud grows out of the ventral foregut in week 4.

a.o: The handout says steroids before birth speed up lungs.
a.x: Steroids should slow lung growth.
a.w: Antenatal steroids boost surfactant and lower breathing problems.

a.o: The handout says alveoli keep forming after birth.
a.x: Alveoli should all form before birth.
a.w: Most alveoli form after birth, through early childhood.

s:
Short-answer exam, embryology, question 8: "Describe limb development." Student Malak Hamdy writes that limb buds appear in week 4, with the arm buds a little before the leg buds.

She writes that the zone of polarising activity (ZPA) at the tip of the bud controls growth from shoulder to fingertip, while the apical ectodermal ridge (AER) on the back edge makes sonic hedgehog and sets the thumb and little finger sides.

She draws a limb bud. She ends by saying the upper limb rotates outward and the lower limb rotates inward, which is why the knee faces forward. She adds that thalidomide caused short limbs in babies. The examiner gave 6 out of 10.
h: the zone of polarising activity (ZPA) at the tip of the bud controls growth from shoulder to fingertip, while the apical ectodermal ridge (AER)

a.o: Malak swaps the roles of the AER and ZPA.
a.x: The AER, at the tip, drives growth.
a.w: The AER at the tip drives growth from shoulder to fingertip. The ZPA makes sonic hedgehog and sets thumb and little finger sides.

a.o: Malak says limb buds appear in week 4.
a.x: Limb buds should appear in week 12.
a.w: Upper limb buds appear around day 26, lower ones a few days later.

a.o: Malak says the lower limb rotates inward.
a.x: The leg should rotate outward like the arm.
a.w: Inward rotation of the leg brings the knee to face forward.

a.o: Malak says thalidomide caused short limbs.
a.x: Thalidomide should be called safe for limbs.
a.w: Thalidomide in weeks 4 to 7 caused severe limb shortening.

s:
Practical report, chick embryo limbs, student Ali Fathy. The aim was to watch how the digits form in a chick leg bud. Ali writes that the end of the limb first forms a flat paddle shape, called the hand or foot plate.

He writes that the fingers separate because the tissue between them grows faster than the digits and pushes them apart. He adds that ducks keep their webbing because this process is blocked between their toes.

In the discussion he says that if separation fails in humans, the fingers stay joined, which is called syndactyly. He ends by saying the digit rays are first formed of cartilage, which later turns to bone.
h: the fingers separate because the tissue between them grows faster than the digits and pushes them apart

a.o: Ali says growth between digits splits them.
a.x: Cells between digits die by apoptosis.
a.w: Programmed cell death removes the tissue between the rays and frees the digits. Ducks keep webs because this death is blocked.

a.o: Ali calls failed separation syndactyly.
a.x: Failed separation should be called polydactyly.
a.w: Syndactyly means joined digits; polydactyly means extra digits.

a.o: Ali says digit rays form first in cartilage.
a.x: The rays should form first in muscle.
a.w: Limb bones form by endochondral ossification of a cartilage model.

a.o: Ali says the limb end first forms a flat paddle.
a.x: The limb should start with separate fingers.
a.w: The hand and foot plates are paddle-shaped before the rays appear.

s:
Handout for "Teratogens", embryology, by Dr. Shaimaa. Part 1 says a teratogen is anything that can cause a birth defect, such as some drugs, infections, alcohol and radiation.

Part 2 says the embryo is least sensitive during weeks 3 to 8, and that the risk of major structural defects is highest in the third trimester, when the baby is growing fastest. It adds that in the first two weeks, damage tends to be all or nothing: the embryo either dies or recovers fully.

Part 3 lists examples: rubella can cause deafness, cataracts and heart defects, and isotretinoin for acne is strongly teratogenic, so women need reliable contraception while taking it. It ends by saying each organ has its own critical period.
h: the embryo is least sensitive during weeks 3 to 8, and that the risk of major structural defects is highest in the third trimester

a.o: The handout puts the peak defect risk in the third trimester.
a.x: Weeks 3 to 8 carry the highest risk of major defects.
a.w: The organs form in weeks 3 to 8, so this embryonic period is the most sensitive. Later exposure tends to affect growth and function.

a.o: The handout calls weeks 1 to 2 all or nothing.
a.x: Weeks 1 to 2 should be the most sensitive to defects.
a.w: Early damage either kills the embryo or is repaired by the remaining cells.

a.o: The handout links rubella with deafness, cataracts and heart defects.
a.x: Rubella should be said to cause no defects.
a.w: First-trimester rubella can give the classic triad of congenital rubella.

a.o: The handout says isotretinoin needs reliable contraception.
a.x: Isotretinoin should be called safe in pregnancy.
a.w: Isotretinoin is a vitamin A drug that causes severe facial, heart and brain defects.

s:
Short-answer exam, embryology, question 9: "Describe the placenta." Student Nourhan Atef writes that the placenta has a fetal part, from the chorion, and a maternal part, from the decidua.

She writes that the mother's blood and the baby's blood mix freely inside the placenta, which is how oxygen and food reach the baby. She adds that chorionic villi with fetal capillaries sit in spaces filled with the mother's blood.

She ends by saying the placenta makes hormones such as hCG and progesterone, and that IgG antibodies cross from the mother to protect the baby after birth. She also mentions it is delivered after the baby. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the mother's blood and the baby's blood mix freely inside the placenta

a.o: Nourhan says maternal and fetal blood mix freely.
a.x: Maternal and fetal blood stay separate.
a.w: Fetal blood stays inside villous capillaries, bathed by maternal blood. Gases and nutrients cross a thin barrier.

a.o: Nourhan says IgG crosses from the mother to the baby.
a.x: IgM should be the main antibody that crosses.
a.w: IgG is actively carried across the placenta to give newborn immunity.

a.o: Nourhan says the placenta makes hCG and progesterone.
a.x: The placenta should make no hormones.
a.w: The syncytiotrophoblast makes hCG, progesterone and other hormones.

a.o: Nourhan says the fetal part comes from the chorion.
a.x: The fetal part should come from the decidua.
a.w: The chorion forms the fetal side; the decidua forms the maternal side.

s:
Draft page "Amniotic fluid", embryology chapter. The page says that from the second half of pregnancy most amniotic fluid is made by the fetal kidneys as urine, and the fetus swallows the fluid.

It states that when both kidneys fail to form (bilateral renal agenesis), the uterus fills with too much amniotic fluid, called polyhydramnios. It adds that without enough fluid the lungs cannot grow properly, which is the main cause of death in these babies.

The page says that a blockage in swallowing, such as oesophageal atresia, leads to too much fluid, and that the fluid also cushions the baby. It ends with a picture of Potter facies, with flat nose and low-set ears.
h: the uterus fills with too much amniotic fluid, called polyhydramnios

a.o: The page says absent kidneys cause excess fluid.
a.x: No kidneys means too little amniotic fluid.
a.w: Without fetal urine, little fluid is made. The squashed fetus gets Potter facies, limb defects and small lungs.

a.o: The page says oesophageal atresia causes too much fluid.
a.x: Oesophageal atresia should cause too little fluid.
a.w: If the fetus cannot swallow, fluid builds up in the uterus.

a.o: The page says small lungs are the main cause of death.
a.x: The heart should be the main cause of death.
a.w: Pulmonary hypoplasia makes breathing impossible after birth.

a.o: The page says amniotic fluid cushions the baby.
a.x: Amniotic fluid should give no protection.
a.w: The fluid protects the fetus from knocks and lets it move.

s:
Flashcards "Tracheo-oesophageal fistula", made by Hesham for the embryology quiz. Card 1 says the trachea and oesophagus start as one tube that is split by a wall called the tracheo-oesophageal septum.

Card 2 says the most common type is a blind upper oesophagus with the lower oesophagus joined to the trachea. Card 3 says the newborn has drooling, chokes and coughs with the first feed, and may turn blue.

Card 4 says during pregnancy there is usually too little amniotic fluid, because the baby swallows more than normal. Card 5 says a tube passed into the mouth curls up in the blind pouch on X-ray. Hesham drew all the types on the back of the card.
h: there is usually too little amniotic fluid, because the baby swallows more than normal

a.o: Card 4 gives oesophageal atresia too little amniotic fluid.
a.x: It causes polyhydramnios, too much fluid.
a.w: The fetus cannot swallow fluid down to the gut to be absorbed, so it builds up in the uterus.

a.o: Card 2 names a blind upper pouch with a lower fistula as most common.
a.x: The most common type should have no fistula.
a.w: About 85% have upper atresia with a lower tracheal fistula.

a.o: Card 3 lists drooling and choking with feeds.
a.x: Babies should feed normally at first.
a.w: Saliva and milk cannot pass the blind pouch and spill into the airway.

a.o: Card 5 says a tube curls in the pouch on X-ray.
a.x: The tube should pass easily to the stomach.
a.w: A tube that coils in the chest on X-ray confirms the blind pouch.

s:
Handout for "Twins", embryology, by Dr. Lobna. Part 1 says twins occur in about 1 in 60 to 80 births, and can be identical or non-identical, and that the type depends on how many eggs and sperm were involved.

Part 2 says identical (monozygotic) twins come from two eggs fertilised by two sperm, while non-identical (dizygotic) twins come from one egg that splits. It adds that non-identical twins can be different sexes.

Part 3 says that in identical twins, the time of splitting decides whether they share a placenta and amniotic sac, and that very late splitting can lead to conjoined twins. It ends by saying non-identical twins are more common in older mothers and run in families.
h: identical (monozygotic) twins come from two eggs fertilised by two sperm, while non-identical (dizygotic) twins come from one egg that splits

a.o: The handout swaps how the two twin types form.
a.x: Identical twins come from one split egg.
a.w: One fertilised egg splitting gives identical twins with the same genes. Two eggs and two sperm give non-identical twins.

a.o: The handout says non-identical twins can be different sexes.
a.x: They should always be the same sex.
a.w: Dizygotic twins are no more alike than ordinary brothers and sisters.

a.o: The handout links late splitting with conjoined twins.
a.x: Late splitting should give separate placentas.
a.w: Splitting after about day 13 can leave twins joined.

a.o: The handout says non-identical twins run in families.
a.x: These twins should never run in families.
a.w: Double ovulation tends to run in families and rises with maternal age.

s:
Newborn check tutorial, student Amr Nabil. A baby boy's urethral opening is not at the tip of the penis. Amr writes that the urethra forms when the urethral folds fuse along the underside of the penis.

He writes that hypospadias is an opening on the upper (dorsal) side of the penis, and that it is caused by a problem with the genital tubercle. He adds that the baby should not be circumcised before repair, because the foreskin may be used in surgery.

He ends by saying hypospadias is one of the most common birth defects in boys, and that it can occur with undescended testes. He also notes that surgery is usually done in the first year or two. The tutor wrote a note beside his definition.
h: hypospadias is an opening on the upper (dorsal) side of the penis, and that it is caused by a problem with the genital tubercle

a.o: Amr puts the opening on the upper side.
a.x: Hypospadias opens on the underside.
a.w: The urethral folds fail to fuse fully, so the opening is on the ventral side. A dorsal opening is epispadias.

a.o: Amr says circumcision should wait until repair.
a.x: Circumcision should be done at once.
a.w: The foreskin is often used to rebuild the urethra in surgery.

a.o: Amr says hypospadias is common in boys.
a.x: Hypospadias should be called very rare.
a.w: It affects about 1 in 250 boys, making it one of the most common defects.

a.o: Amr links hypospadias with undescended testes.
a.x: The two should never occur together.
a.w: Low androgen effect can disturb both urethra and testis descent.

s:
Short-answer exam, embryology, question 10: "Describe eye development." Student Hagar Saad writes that the eyes begin to form in week 4. She writes that the eye starts as an outgrowth of the forebrain called the optic vesicle, which touches the surface ectoderm.

She writes that the optic vesicle folds to form the optic cup, and that the retina forms from the mesoderm that surrounds the cup. She adds that the lens forms from surface ectoderm that sinks in to make the lens vesicle.

She ends by saying that a gap in the optic cup that fails to close leaves a coloboma, a keyhole-shaped iris, and that rubella can cause cataracts. She notes the cornea forms in front of the lens. The examiner gave 7 out of 10.
h: the retina forms from the mesoderm that surrounds the cup

a.o: Hagar says the retina forms from mesoderm.
a.x: The retina comes from the optic cup.
a.w: The two layers of the optic cup form the neural retina and the pigment layer. The retina is an outgrowth of the brain.

a.o: Hagar says the lens forms from surface ectoderm.
a.x: The lens should form from endoderm.
a.w: The optic vesicle makes surface ectoderm thicken into the lens.

a.o: Hagar links a failed closure with coloboma.
a.x: Coloboma should be caused by a lens defect.
a.w: If the choroid fissure does not close, a keyhole defect remains.

a.o: Hagar says rubella can cause cataracts.
a.x: Rubella should be said to spare the eye.
a.w: Rubella in early pregnancy can damage the lens and cause cataracts.

s:
Handout for "Pituitary development", by Dr. Ramy. Part 1 says the pituitary sits in the sella turcica and is made of two parts that come from two different places and join together.

Part 2 says the anterior pituitary comes from a downgrowth of the brain (the infundibulum), and the posterior pituitary comes from Rathke's pouch, an upgrowth from the roof of the mouth. It adds that the posterior pituitary stores hormones made in the hypothalamus.

Part 3 says that leftover cells of Rathke's pouch can form a tumour called a craniopharyngioma, which may press on the optic chiasm. It ends by saying the anterior pituitary makes hormones such as growth hormone, TSH and ACTH.
h: the anterior pituitary comes from a downgrowth of the brain (the infundibulum), and the posterior pituitary comes from Rathke's pouch

a.o: The handout swaps the origins of the two pituitary lobes.
a.x: The anterior lobe is from Rathke's pouch.
a.w: The anterior lobe grows up from the roof of the mouth as Rathke's pouch. The posterior lobe grows down from the brain.

a.o: The handout says the posterior lobe stores hypothalamic hormones.
a.x: The posterior lobe should make TSH.
a.w: ADH and oxytocin are made in the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior lobe.

a.o: The handout links Rathke remnants with craniopharyngioma.
a.x: Rathke remnants should form a chordoma.
a.w: Craniopharyngioma grows from Rathke's pouch remnants above the sella.

a.o: The handout says the anterior lobe makes GH, TSH and ACTH.
a.x: The anterior lobe should make oxytocin.
a.w: The anterior pituitary makes GH, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH and prolactin.

s:
Flashcards "Chromosome problems", made by Rowan for the embryology and genetics quiz. Card 1 says Down syndrome is caused by an extra chromosome 21, called trisomy 21.

Card 2 says most cases come from nondisjunction, when chromosomes fail to separate. Rowan copied this card from a website. Card 3 says the main risk factor is older paternal age, and that the mother's age has little effect on the risk.

Card 4 says babies with Down syndrome often have heart defects such as atrioventricular septal defect. Card 5 says they have a higher risk of leukaemia and early Alzheimer's disease. Rowan put the risk factor card at the front of the pile.
h: the main risk factor is older paternal age, and that the mother's age has little effect on the risk

a.o: Card 3 makes older fathers the main risk.
a.x: Older maternal age is the main risk factor.
a.w: Most extra chromosomes come from the egg, and nondisjunction rises sharply as the mother gets older.

a.o: Card 2 says most cases come from nondisjunction.
a.x: Most cases should come from a single gene.
a.w: Failure of chromosome 21 to separate in meiosis causes most cases.

a.o: Card 4 names atrioventricular septal defects.
a.x: Heart defects should be called rare.
a.w: About half have heart defects, often AVSD.

a.o: Card 5 links Down syndrome with early Alzheimer's.
a.x: Alzheimer's risk should be lower than normal.
a.w: The APP gene on chromosome 21 leads to early amyloid build-up.

s:
Draft page "Spina bifida", embryology chapter. The page says spina bifida happens when the neural tube or the vertebral arches do not close properly, most often in the lower back, and it can range from mild to severe.

It describes spina bifida occulta as the most severe form, with the cord and nerves pushing out in an open sac, and myelomeningocele as the mildest form, where only a bony gap is present, often with a tuft of hair over it.

The page says that open defects raise alpha-fetoprotein in the amniotic fluid and the mother's blood, and that hydrocephalus often occurs with myelomeningocele. It ends by saying folic acid before pregnancy lowers the risk.
h: spina bifida occulta as the most severe form, with the cord and nerves pushing out in an open sac, and myelomeningocele as the mildest form

a.o: The page swaps occulta and myelomeningocele.
a.x: Occulta is the mild, hidden form.
a.w: Occulta is a hidden bony gap, often with a hair tuft. In myelomeningocele the cord and nerves bulge out in an open sac.

a.o: The page says open defects raise AFP.
a.x: Open defects should lower AFP.
a.w: AFP leaks from the open neural tube into the amniotic fluid.

a.o: The page links hydrocephalus with myelomeningocele.
a.x: Hydrocephalus should not occur with it.
a.w: A Chiari II malformation often blocks CSF flow and causes hydrocephalus.

a.o: The page says folic acid before pregnancy lowers risk.
a.x: Folic acid should raise the risk.
a.w: Folic acid before and in early pregnancy cuts neural tube defects.

s:
Handout for "Hirschsprung disease", embryology, by Dr. Sameh. Part 1 says the nerve cells of the gut wall come from neural crest cells that travel down the gut from the top to the bottom.

Part 2 says that in Hirschsprung disease the nerve cells are missing from the upper colon, while the rectum is always normal. It adds that the segment without nerve cells cannot relax, so stool cannot pass and the bowel above it swells.

Part 3 says babies may not pass meconium in the first 48 hours, and that diagnosis is made by a rectal biopsy showing no ganglion cells. It ends by saying it is more common in boys and in babies with Down syndrome.
h: the nerve cells are missing from the upper colon, while the rectum is always normal

a.o: The handout says the rectum is always spared here.
a.x: The rectum is always involved.
a.w: Crest cells travel top to bottom, so the last part reached, the rectum, is always involved, with spread up from there.

a.o: The handout says the aganglionic segment cannot relax.
a.x: The segment should be widely dilated.
a.w: Without nerve cells the segment stays tight, and the bowel above it dilates.

a.o: The handout says diagnosis is by rectal biopsy.
a.x: Diagnosis should rely on a blood test.
a.w: A suction rectal biopsy shows no ganglion cells.

a.o: The handout says it is more common with Down syndrome.
a.x: Down syndrome should lower the risk.
a.w: Hirschsprung is linked with trisomy 21 and is more common in boys.

s:
Case-based tutorial, fetal alcohol, student Dina Gamal. A 4-year-old is seen for poor growth and learning problems. His mother drank alcohol through pregnancy. Dina writes that alcohol crosses the placenta easily.

She writes that fetal alcohol syndrome only happens if the mother drinks in the last week before delivery, so drinking earlier in pregnancy is safe. She adds that the face shows a smooth philtrum, a thin upper lip and small eye openings.

She ends by saying the child may have small head size, poor growth and problems with learning and behaviour, and that no amount of alcohol in pregnancy is known to be safe. The tutor underlined one sentence in red.
h: fetal alcohol syndrome only happens if the mother drinks in the last week before delivery, so drinking earlier in pregnancy is safe

a.o: Dina says only drinking in the last week matters.
a.x: Early drinking harms the fetus too.
a.w: The facial and brain changes come from alcohol in the first trimester. No time in pregnancy is known to be safe.

a.o: Dina lists a smooth philtrum and thin upper lip.
a.x: The upper lip should be thick and full.
a.w: A smooth philtrum, thin lip and short eye openings are key signs.

a.o: Dina says alcohol crosses the placenta easily.
a.x: Alcohol should be stopped by the placenta.
a.w: Small fat-soluble alcohol molecules pass freely to the fetus.

a.o: Dina lists a small head and learning problems.
a.x: The head should be larger than normal.
a.w: Alcohol damages the growing brain, causing microcephaly and learning problems.

s:
Flashcards "Umbilical remnants", made by Mazen for the embryology quiz. Card 1 says the allantois is a small tube from the hindgut into the connecting stalk, and its inner part becomes the urachus.

Card 2 says the urachus joins the top of the bladder to the umbilicus and normally closes to become the medial umbilical ligament. Card 3 says the obliterated umbilical arteries form the median umbilical ligament.

Card 4 says that if the urachus stays open, urine can leak from the belly button. Card 5 says a urachal cyst can become infected and form a painful lump below the umbilicus. Mazen drew the bladder and its ligaments on the back.
h: the urachus joins the top of the bladder to the umbilicus and normally closes to become the medial umbilical ligament

a.o: Card 2 says the urachus becomes the medial ligament.
a.x: The urachus forms the median ligament.
a.w: The single urachus makes the median ligament. The paired umbilical arteries leave the two medial ligaments.

a.o: Card 4 says an open urachus leaks urine at the navel.
a.x: An open urachus should leak stool.
a.w: A patent urachus joins the bladder to the umbilicus, so urine escapes.

a.o: Card 5 says a urachal cyst can get infected.
a.x: A urachal cyst should never become infected.
a.w: Trapped fluid in a urachal cyst can become infected and painful.

a.o: Card 1 says the allantois leads to the urachus.
a.x: The urachus should come from the yolk sac.
a.w: The inner part of the allantois becomes the urachus.
